DAR ES SALAAM, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan on Saturday inaugurated the 2,115-megawatt Julius Nyerere Hydropower Plant, a landmark project expected to strengthen electricity supply and accelerate industrial and economic development.
Hassan inaugurated the plant in Rufiji District in Coast Region, saying the new generation capacity should produce measurable gains in manufacturing, trade, mining, modern agriculture, public services, investment and employment.
The nine-unit facility now accounts for nearly half of electricity dispatched to Tanzania's national grid, significantly improving reliability and security of supply, she said.
"This project has demonstrated Tanzania's capabilities. We must now harness that capacity to advance other strategic projects and build a strong, self-reliant nation," Hassan said.

Tan Jin, the project manager with Dongfang Electric, noted that they supplied all nine hydro-turbine generator units, main inlet valves and other complete sets of electromechanical equipment, and carried out their installation, commissioning and trial operation.
During construction, the China-involved construction work created about 14,000 jobs for local residents. Thousands of Tanzanians received professional skills training from Chinese engineers in areas such as welding, steel fixing, carpentry, heavy machinery operation and surveying, helping build a stronger local workforce, according to the two managers.
The project is also expected to improve electricity supply for households and public services, strengthen Tanzania's role in the regional energy market in East Africa, and provide reliable energy support for regional connectivity and socioeconomic development, said Humphrey Moshi, an economics professor at the University of Dar es Salaam in Tanzania. ■

OTTAWA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Saturday delivered a nationally televised address to outline Canada's position following the breakdown of trade talks with the United States, announcing that Ottawa's "dollar-for-dollar" retaliatory tariffs against 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of American goods would take effect on Sept. 8.
The prime minister said the counter-tariffs will cover a wide range of sectors, including dairy, steel, appliances, pulp and paper, and electronics.
The United States and Canada failed to reach a trade deal on Friday, and the United States imposed a 50-percent tariff on 20 billion U.S. dollars' worth of Canadian goods on Saturday which took effect just after midnight (0400 GMT).
Explaining why negotiations broke down at the last minute, Carney said that while both sides were close to a mutually beneficial agreement earlier this week, the U.S. side introduced last-minute changes that were "unfair, uneconomic and called into question the reliability of any deal."
The U.S. side's repeated disregard for existing free trade agreements such as the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement (CUSMA) sends a bad signal to international businesses and is "certainly not good news" for renewing the agreement in the future, Carney warned.
The rift comes as the United States, Mexico and Canada are trying to renew the CUSMA, a trade agreement that Trump negotiated in his first term and once praised as a triumph.
The United States has begun formal talks with Mexico to revamp the agreement, but talks with Canada have not yet begun.
The CUSMA is a trilateral trade pact that replaced the North American Free Trade Agreement when it took effect on July 1, 2020. On July 1, 2026, the United States officially declined to renew the agreement for another 16-year term, triggering an annual review process until the pact expires in 2036.
When asked why Canada was entering a trade dispute, the prime minister stated flatly: "Because we were attacked."
Carney reiterated his confidence in Canada's economic resilience, pointing out that Canada is creating jobs at four times the rate of the United States, with foreign direct investment reaching a 20-year high.
"Canada is becoming stronger and less dependent on America," he said. ■

Sadales tikls said the damage to the electricity network was extensive and complex, meaning repairs would take longer than usual. Some customers could remain without power for more than 24 hours.
Latvia's State Fire and Rescue Service (VUGD) said the number of weather-related emergency calls rose rapidly during the evening, with most involving trees brought down by strong winds and blocking roads.
According to local media reports, strong winds tore the roof off a building in Daugavpils, while a falling tree damaged a residential building. In Jekabpils, several vehicles were crushed by fallen trees.
LEGMC issued red, orange and yellow warnings for heavy rain and strong winds in Riga and across the country on Friday. A number of outdoor events around Latvia were subsequently canceled. On Saturday, local authorities repeatedly warned residents of heavy rain and strong winds through cell broadcast alerts. ■

Avinor said the escalation could have serious consequences for tens of thousands of passengers.
Passengers have been advised to monitor information from their airlines and report to airports as usual unless notified otherwise. Avinor said the situation could change at short notice. ■

====================================================================================================

I’d heard ringing in my ears before. This time, it didn’t stop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
20:00:14 UTC
05:00:14 KST

One night two years ago I was lying in bed when I began to hear a high-pitched, electronic hum. The scene that followed would be comical if it wasn’t so traumatic. I roamed around the house in my PJs, frantically pressing my ears against various electrical appliances. It took half an hour to realise the sound was coming from inside my own head.
I’d heard ringing in my ears before, rising then falling, like a one-note crescendo of an orchestra. As a kid I used to believe the myth it was the sound of dying ear cells, playing a swan song for a frequency I’d never hear again. This was different. This time, it didn’t stop.
Tinnitus is common, with a global burden similar to migraines. Fourteen per cent of adults experience tinnitus with 2% experiencing a severe form. It’s often triggered by age-related or noise-induced hearing loss, but I was only 36 and a trip to the audiologist revealed my hearing was perfect – the Kings Cross nightclubbing of my youth hadn’t come back to haunt me. Another trigger is stress.
The first few days after the ringing began felt increasingly claustrophobic. The alarm-like sound that no one else could hear followed me everywhere: to my writing desk, to coffee with a friend, into the shower and, worst of all, back into bed.
Tinnitus can be torturous for anyone, but for someone who worships the first birdcall breaking through a soundless dawn, who owns two dog-eared and underlined copies of Sara Maitland’s A Book of Silence – an exquisite manifesto of solitude and quiet – it felt especially cruel.
My GP thought I might have an ear infection. I cried in her office, tears of relief. “I’ve never been so happy to have an infection,” I told her. She gave me drops, a thick mucousy liquid that blocked both ears and made the ringing significantly louder. My days were a constant battle against steadily rising panic. Meditation was useless, for obvious reasons.
I drove to the ocean and sat there for hours. The dull roar of whitewater drowned out the sound and, there, I could breathe. I took the sea back to bed with me, a 10-hour playlist of deep-blue bliss. I dreamed about waves, but also about a bright light piercing the fog of sleep.
The drops dried up. If there was an infection it was gone. Weeks passed, but the ringing remained. I fell down the research rabbit hole.
Like all chronic conditions, you could spend a lot of money on trying to find a fix: supplements, acupuncture, hypnosis, antidepressants (not as a cure but a way to cope). But the most common advice is to just try to ignore it. To learn to live with it.
Because here’s the most disconcerting thing about tinnitus: the sound doesn’t exist outside your perception of it. It’s a type of false alarm, created by your nervous systems and brain rather than an actual wave of sound in the air, and – like the way we aren’t bothered by our clothes brushing our skin all day long – the less you pay attention to it the less you hear it.
Trust me when I say this does not feel helpful, or at all believable, when a semi-trailer’s brakes have been squealing in your ears for two months. I raged, I cried, I begged the universe. I didn’t want to live with this. I couldn’t live with this. There had to be something physical happening to me that a professional could fix.
It took seven excruciating weeks to get into an ENT. He performed test after test in his office before turning to me with a stern but sympathetic look. “There’s nothing wrong with you,” he said. And there was something in his voice. It felt like a magic spell, or some kind of blessing. Stop fighting this, it told me, you’re already free.
Over the following months, slowly but surely, my tinnitus began to soften around the edges. Through both natural habituation and intentionally training my attention, my nervous system learned to focus on more important, beautiful and interesting things. Sometimes, while watching the sun rise or reading a book, I didn’t hear it at all.
These days, although tinnitus is still my near-constant companion, I’ve stopped wishing things were different. Because when you remove hope and fear, some suffering transforms into a kind of melancholic but peaceful surrender.
I didn’t think I could learn to live with tinnitus, but every day is more proof that I can.
Now when stress causes the ringing to spike, or if I listen too hard for a silence that isn’t there, I refocus my attention on something I love and the sound soon stops bothering me. My new version of tranquility returns.

====================================================================================================

Could the macadamias hidden in Queensland’s rainforests be the key to saving ‘the world’s finest nut’?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
20:00:13 UTC
05:00:13 KST

We are bouncing over a rough, steep gravel road on the hunt for macadamia trees in the wild. Here in the tangled rainforest at Mary’s Creek in Queensland is the macadamia’s main ancestral home.
Ian McConachie has always been partial to a macadamia nut. As a boy in Brisbane in the 1940s he used to climb fences to steal them from people’s backyards. “We’d put them in a little hole in the concrete under the house and hit them with a hammer.”
Now 90, he has spent much of his life devoted to the nut, including developing a tree that has raised $2m in royalties for the Macadamia Conservation Trust, which seeks to preserve this scrappy rainforest plant.
Today macadamias are a $2bn global industry, grown in industrial quantities in subtropical climates in Hawaii, the Americas, Africa and Asia. But there was a time when Aboriginal people traded them for rum and tobacco with the white settlers here on this country.
“It is the world’s finest nut,” McConachie says. “It is an Australian icon and our only native plant that has become a commercial food.”
A couple of kilometres from here lives Macadamia integrifolia, which genetic testing has shown is the genesis tree of 70% of macadamia trees grown commercially around the world.
There are three other species: M. tetraphylla is also grown commercially, while M. ternifolia and M. jansenii are almost inedible, wild and rare.
Macadamias have been cultivated commercially since the 1920s, starting in Hawaii. Australia didn’t start commercial production until the 1960s. Only two to three generations out of the wild is “terribly young in the world of horticulture”, McConachie says. “So we simply don’t know what the potential of the wild macadamia tree is.”
After graduating from industrial chemistry and business management with a focus on food, McConachie spent 35 years in businesses involving macadamia nuts. Later, he developed 20 macadamia orchards in Gympie and Bundaberg for investor-owners. Australia was behind Hawaii in growing commercial crops, with the first domestic processing plant only opening in 1954.
Growers were given a tax deduction to help establish a local industry, McConachie says. This also attracted organised crime, seeking to launder money. “I’ve got wonderful stories which can never be printed. A guy working for us was charged with murder.”
All four macadamia species are native to a tiny patch of Australian subtropical rainforest in south-east Queensland and northern NSW. “Which is pretty much where everyone wants to live,” says Denise Bond, executive director of Wild Macadamia Conservation. “They [the trees] like expensive real estate, which makes them incredibly endangered because we’ve got so little rainforest left.”
Wild trees may hold the key to the next generation of climate- and disease-resilient nuts. McConachie says for commercial macadamia farming, “one of the very few things Australia has got going for it is the wild trees and their genetic potential”.
But more than 80% of the habitat that these trees evolved in over 120m years is reduced to remnant now.
One of the macadamia species, M. jansenii, is seriously endangered, so rare “a bushfire could totally wipe them out”, McConachie says. Their locations are kept secret to protect them. While the nuts are too bitter to eat, “it could be a major tool in terms of climate change because it is so hardy”. The other three species are listed as threatened or vulnerable.
McConachie has spent decades walking the remnant rainforests not far from where he lives, to find and document wild macadamias in situ. In August, he and fellow macadamia conservationist Russell Bennet take me on one of their hunts.
Bennet, a Kabi Kabi man, custodian and elder, who is driving, is known for his ability to spot them. “It’s some genetic ability handed down through the ancestors, I reckon,” he says.
First Nations Australians, though, have received vanishingly little financial benefit from the nut’s global popularity.
When he finds a new undocumented tree, Bennet says, “it’s almost like finding gold. You can go through a lot of rainforest and not see one.” Except in September, when they flower and put on a show. The rest of the year, their dark leaves retreat into the rainforest, easily overlooked.
“They’re quite cryptic,” says Bond, with a couple of trees scattered here and there.
Their modesty, says Bennet, “is their problem – they get dozed over”.
McConachie is “shocked” by the degradation of the trees we find. An invasive creeper called cat’s claw has been smothering them; some have been smashed by storms.
We come to a sudden halt at a “Keep Out” sign. Behind it is logging machinery. The hills are denuded, the small macadamia trees struggling in the dust. “The rainforest is tired,” McConachie says. “Whether the remaining trees are still there is unknown.”
Cultivated trees have significantly less genetic diversity than their wild counterparts, making those that remain “a genetic bank,” says Bond. “If anything were to happen, like a root rot fungus go through the commercial population, or any sort of pest or disease that commercial nuts can’t survive, if all the wild trees are gone you can’t go back and say, lets breed some resistance into the crop.”
They should be safe in the state forests of Mary’s Creek, Amamoor and Imbil, the largest continuous area of habitat – “but they’re not,” says McConachie.
“We can conserve DNA, but we can’t regenerate it. So one of the goals in the future will be to find out if we can store the genetics of the wild macadamias, so that they’re available for breeding for conservation.”
In 1981, McConachie and his wife, Jan, bought a rundown dairy farm near Wolvi. He flirted with other trees, mangoes, lychees, stone fruit, but quickly came back to his great love. After an extensive selection trial, he found a particularly hardy and accommodating tree, named it MCTI and secured planter breeding rights. “It has sold about a million and a half trees,” he says, “and raised about $2m in royalties.” All of that has been gifted to Wild Macadamia Conservation.
“We’re probably all a bit eccentric,” he says of the group, “but we’re passionate about the need to conserve the wild genetics.”

The moment I knew: Days after September 11, we flew through turbulence – all I could say was ‘I love you’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
20:00:12 UTC
05:00:12 KST

I noticed Justine before she noticed me. We were at a literary award ceremony and she was wearing a dress, upcycled from a black Velvet Elvis painting, talking to a man three times her age.
I asked my friend, Carol, who knew everyone, why I’d never seen her before. Carol explained that she was an Australian academic, researching the history of publishing, and led me across the room.
“Justine,” Carol said. “You’re researching science fiction in New York. This is Scott, he’s a science fiction writer in New York.”
Justine turned from the older man, glanced at me, then shook her head. “Not my period.”
I was too young. She was studying science fiction’s golden age, a time before either of us was born. No one under 80 was relevant, or worth remembering.
A week later, we ran into each other at a reading. This time we talked. We discovered we’re both fans of Samuel R Delany, Octavia Butler, Ursula K Le Guin, eggs with hot sauce, bushwalking, and exploring new cities.
We were seeing other people at the time, but continued to run into each other at science fiction gatherings. Then came Justine’s last week in the city before returning to Australia. At a big farewell dinner, we were sitting directly across from each other, with lively conversations on either side, and we made eye contact, momentarily alone together.
“I just broke up with my girlfriend,” I told her.
“Me too,” she said.
We spent her last weekend in NYC together.
Then Justine was back in Sydney, and we spent months talking on the phone and emailing. This was our romantic jet lag era, 10 time zones apart. She was waking up when I was going to sleep, and vice versa.
In early September 2001, I flew to Sydney to see Justine’s city, her family, her friends. It was spring and everything was in bloom. The harbour was sparkling, and the big local news was a host of flying foxes invading the Royal Botanic Gardens. I was utterly charmed.
Until bigger news happened. Justine and I were at one of Sydney’s finest restaurants, Tetsuya’s, eating an extraordinary degustation, discussing each and every dish and drinking too much. When we left at midnight, (10am in New York), the staff seemed oddly sombre. The taxi driver didn’t speak much English. We didn’t learn what had happened until the next morning when Justine ran into her addled flatmate on her way to the bathroom. “She says the Statute of Liberty exploded?”
We turned the radio on and lay in bed holding hands, listening to what had happened to the city we both loved. We tried to call friends, but reached only overloaded circuits.
We had a flight booked to Melbourne the next day, to meet more of Justine’s friends. We’d heard from our New York people by then. All of them safe, but shaken.
It felt like tempting fate, boarding an aircraft on 13 September 2001. Even the cabin crew wasn’t pretending it was a normal flight. Justine and I huddled in our row of two, staring out the window, holding hands again.
Halfway to Melbourne, we hit a stretch of turbulence. And it struck me: passenger jets were now weapons of war. International travel as we knew it might be over. What if I went back to the US, and couldn’t see Justine again for years?
I opened my mouth to say all this, but instead said: “I love you.”
My voice was calm and level. Here, with her, I felt certain, despite the tumult outside.
“Me too,” she said.
Australia felt very far from Ground Zero. Normal life was still under way, except when people asked where I was from, and I became the focus of a sweet, unnerving kindness, treated gently, given free drinks. Once, an actual fruit basket.
The fruit basket became a running joke, one of many we had that week. Part of navigating a crisis with a partner is knowing how to change emotional gears. Justine and I would talk about the coming war one moment, and about sulphur-crested cockatoos the next. We were skinless, our feelings always close to the surface.
With the world reorganising itself, we had to let each other feel the weight of history, but also remind each other to taste the wine in front of us.
There was a deeper question, one that many New Yorkers asked themselves in the days after 9/11: Who do you want to spend the apocalypse with? Who can you trust to make the right silly joke when the world is demanding to be taken so seriously?
Turned out, I’d found that person just in time.
Jets kept crossing the oceans, of course, and Justine returned to New York much sooner than expected: in November, to meet my parents. We were already married by then, eloped upstate without telling our friends, and have been together ever since.
- 
  The Mortons by Justine Larbalestier and Scott Westerfeld is available now through Penguin ($AU34.99).

A US Army unit in Georgia is offering active duty service members a four-day pass to play the highly anticipated Grand Theft Auto VI video game in exchange for at least two more years of service, CBS News reported Wednesday.
The report cited a memo that first appeared on US Army WTF! Moments, which says any soldier who signs a reenlistment contract between Aug. 1 and Nov. 14 will be authorized for a special four-day pass designated to coincide with "the highly anticipated release of the video game Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6)."
In exchange for the four-day playing pass, active duty soldiers would reenlist for a minimum of two years and up to six years.
Task & Purpose and Military.com were the first to authenticate the memo, the report said.
The offer was proposed exclusively for one battalion in Georgia, but the program could be expanded across the military.
Twenty soldiers at Fort Stewart in Georgia in the Army's 9th Brigade Engineering Battalion, part of the 3rd Infantry Division, have already agreed to the incentive, and approximately 130 soldiers are currently eligible for the offer.
US Army offers various incentives for enlistment
Over the years, the army has used various enlistment bonuses and incentives, including college tuition assistance, choice of duty station assignments, and access to special training programs where soldiers learn to jump from airplanes, to encourage soldiers to enlist or re-enlist.
The idea behind this reported offer is to connect with soldiers' unique interests.
"The idea was to have a unique incentives program that connects to what Soldiers are interested in," Lt.-Col. Angel Tomko, a spokesperson for the 3rd Infantry Division, said in a statement. "The command team, in conjunction with the career counselor, wanted to get soldiers excited to reenlist."
It has been over a decade since the last version of the game, GTA V, was published in 2013 by Rockstar Games, and the announcement of the the new publication has created intense anticipation for the gamers.
Again set in a fictional version of Miami and featuring its first female lead, the game is set for release on November 19th.
Notably, this isn't the first time the army has crafted a reenlistment incentive aimed at the gaming community.
After the army missed its recruitment goals in 2018 for the first time in more than a decade, recruiters were exploring alternative ways to sign new recruits.
Recruiters began attending gaming conventions, and the army launched an esports team focused on the popular video game franchise Call of Duty, along with other multiplayer games like Fortnite and League of Legends, to find potential recruits.

2 bodies recovered and about 12 missing after migrant boat capsized off Tunisian coast
TUNIS, Tunisia (AP) — A boat carrying migrants capsized off the coast of southern Tunisia, killing at least two people and leaving 12 missing, Tunisia’s national guard said Saturday. One survivor was rescued.
Guard spokesperson Houssem Eddine Jebabli told state news agency TAP that authorities recovered two bodies and transferred them to a hospital on the nearby island of Djerba. He told national radio Mosaique FM that about 15 people were believed to be aboard the boat when it took off between the cities of Zarzis and Ben Guerdane.
The boat had set off early Thursday, and a commercial ship found the sole survivor Saturday in a life jacket, Mosaique reported, citing testimony from the survivor.
A helicopter and coast guard boats were then dispatched to the area in search of more survivors, according to an Associated Press photojournalist at the scene. The migrants were believed to be headed toward Italy.
Zarzis has long been a departure point for Tunisians and others from around Africa or beyond attempting to cross the Mediterranean toward Europe.
The city witnessed a similar tragedy in 2022, when a boat carrying 18 people went missing. The incident sparked weeks of protests as families accused authorities of failing to properly search for their relatives and burying some recovered bodies without identifying them or informing their families.
Migrant departures from Tunisia have fallen sharply since the European Union and Tunisia signed a sweeping agreement in 2023. It included EU funding and technical support for Tunisian border control and coast guard training to help Tunisia curb irregular migration and deter human traffickers in the Mediterranean basin. The EU allocated 105 million euros ($121 million) in migration-related support to Tunisia in 2023 alone.
The decline in migration has not ended dangerous crossings from Tunisia’s southern coast, where families in the south, particularly in Zarzis, have for years searched for relatives who disappeared at sea.
Rights groups have raised concerns about the treatment of migrants and asylum seekers in Tunisia since the EU agreement, including reports of collective expulsions, racial violence, arbitrary detention and abuses against Black migrants.
In July, Amnesty International said EU support for border control in Tunisia continued to fuel serious rights violations. It said refugees and asylum seekers were being “deliberately trapped in a system that offers neither protection nor a safe way out.”

Israel’s election is approaching, but candidates are offering slogans instead of policies - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:52:56 UTC
04:52:56 KST

As Israel enters the final stretch of the election campaign, voters deserve something more than slogans, branding, and political attacks. With roughly two months left until election day, it is time for the candidates who want to lead Israel to tell us what they actually intend to do.
We have already heard plenty of rhetoric.
Can Gadi Eisenkot offer voters something more substantial than declaring Likud to be the “party of October 7”?
October 7 was a failure of leadership and preparedness, and we must examine responsibility honestly. But Eisenkot himself served as IDF chief of staff during the years preceding the attack. If we are going to have a serious discussion about responsibility, it cannot be reduced to a campaign slogan aimed at one political party.
And can Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu offer voters something more than the warning that if Likud is not in power, “the Left” will return Israel to the Oslo path? He claims to want to unify the country, but how exactly will he do that? Another partnership with the haredim (ultra-Orthodox) and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir?
Israel faces challenges far more complicated than these familiar political boogeymen. Israelis deserve to know what the candidates will actually do with the power they are asking us to give them.
Of course, there are challenges also facing the emerging Center-Right parties. Will they be able to put aside personal ambitions, egos, and competing political brands and unite behind a single viable alternative to Likud? Or will precious votes once again be divided among parties that may struggle to have a meaningful impact?
Does Avigdor Lieberman have a vision for Israel beyond positioning himself as potential kingmaker and, ultimately, the prime minister? Lieberman has made no secret of his ambition to become prime minister. But if Yisrael Beytenu emerges with enough seats to determine who forms the next government, voters deserve to know what Lieberman intends to demand in return.
What are his economic priorities? What is his plan for housing? How does he propose to resolve the haredi draft crisis? What does he believe Israel’s security and diplomatic strategy should be? Being the kingmaker is a political role. Being prime minister requires a governing vision.
Lieberman needs to show voters that he has a real one and not just empty, half-baked slogans.
And what about Yair Golan? Can he move beyond inflammatory rhetoric about settlers and religious Israelis and present a serious political program? Israelis need to hear what he proposes to do besides the failed, unrealistic policies of Oslo.
There is, however, one candidate who deserves credit for beginning to change the conversation: Naftali Bennett.
Bennett has increasingly been talking about economic policy and the practical challenges facing the country rather than simply attacking his political opponents. That is a welcome development.
Questions for Israel's future
Whatever one's political views, an election campaign should ultimately be about competing visions for Israel’s future.
And there is no shortage of issues requiring those visions.
How will the next government make housing genuinely affordable? Home ownership remains beyond the reach of so many young Israelis.
How will Israel resolve the haredi draft crisis? This cannot continue to be treated merely as a coalition-management problem. It is a fundamental question about shared responsibility, the IDF, and the social contract between different parts of Israeli society. Voters deserve to hear detailed proposals that are practical, principled, and politically achievable.
How will we reform education? Israel needs a revamped education system that prepares children for a rapidly changing economy while strengthening their connection to Jewish identity, civic responsibility, and the State of Israel. We need creativity and a slow move away from the antiquated bagrut (matriculation) system.
And these are only three of the enormous challenges facing the next government.
We also need serious plans for the economy – to lower taxes, reduce the cost of living, and improve national security. We need to finally tackle the relationship between religion and state, judicial reform, the healthcare system, public transportation, infrastructure, and Israel’s international standing.
The election campaign should not be a contest over who can produce the most effective insult or the most frightening prediction about what will happen if the other side wins.
The election campaign must be a genuine contest of ideas; a marketplace where competing visions for Israel’s future are put to the test. The best ideas should rise to the top; not the loudest slogans, the sharpest attacks, or the slickest political branding.
Israelis deserve a campaign that challenges candidates to present concrete solutions, defend their positions, and explain how they will lead the country forward. Let the ideas compete, let the voters judge, and let the strongest vision for Israel win.
The candidates who want to become prime minister, ministers, and members of the next Knesset have two months to tell us what they will actually do. Tell us their priorities. Tell us the timetable for implementing change. Tell us how much it will cost. Tell us what difficult choices will have to be made.
And, most importantly, they have to tell us how they intend to bring a divided country together sufficiently to get it done.
Israel has been through enough internal and external crises, especially since 2022. We do not need another election campaign built around empty rhetoric and recycled slogans.
There are two months left. Now is the time for real plans.
The writer is the Managing Partner of Dekel Capital Management, a resident of Beit Shemesh, a proud oleh who made aliyah 27 years ago and prides himself on always feeling like a new oleh. He is an avid Zionist who cares deeply about the future of the State of Israel and the Jewish people.

After the elections, Israel must repair the damage Netanyahu did to its US alliance - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:52:50 UTC
04:52:50 KST

As Israel heads towards pivotal elections this October, the country finds its international standing and brand at a nadir in most of the developed world, including the United States.
After decades of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at the helm, a new government must immediately begin the process of repairing the damage caused by a surfeit of tactical success coupled with a deficit of strategic common sense.
Failure to do so will result in deep and lasting impact diplomatically, commercially, and even militarily.
Israel continues to destroy Hamas as a fighting force and has secured multiple tactical victories since October 7, including against Hezbollah in Lebanon, and to a lesser extent, the implacably hostile regime in Iran.
Syria, an erstwhile enemy, underwent a revolution and is both defanged as a military adversary and seemingly interested in some kind of normalization of relations.
Lebanon – essentially a forward base for the IRGC over recent decades – has, for the first time in many years, a government interested in normalizing relations with Israel and, possibly, clipping Hezbollah’s wings by initiating a process of disarming it.
None of these successes would have been possible without the combination of two critical factors: intrepid Israeli ingenuity and military skill as well as steadfast American support spanning multiple administrations.
It is also abundantly clear that over the course of the conflict during the past three years, American popular support for Israel – and with it the historical bipartisan view of Israel as a critical ally which is worthy of American support in both the military and diplomatic spheres – has substantially eroded.
Israel is far from blameless in its loss of support among a wide swathe of Americans.
Despite the range of tactical successes achieved by the IDF and Israel’s security services, the Netanyahu government failed to appreciate the dictum of Carl von Clausewitz that “war is the continuation of politics by other means,” with the result that Israel has not translated its battlefield successes into creative statecraft.
It is reported that Netanyahu could have sealed a deal to release all the live hostages earlier than was the case; instead, he was ultimately forced to accept a deal by US President Donald Trump and the American negotiators at the cost of at least several hostages’ lives.
Netanyahu could have been responsive to the Lebanese government’s attempts to initiate talks for mutual recognition and potentially disarming Hezbollah after the November 2024 ceasefire. Instead, he hesitated.
Netanyahu could have agreed to allow a government of Palestinian technocrats to enter and begin to take control of the civil infrastructure in Gaza following the ceasefire.
Instead, he demurred, because to do so would have meant bringing upon him the wrath of his Jewish supremacist coalition partners.
Today Israel finds itself with reduced agency and degrees of freedom, its policies and posture increasingly limited by American dictat.
For decades, Netanyahu has overseen the gradual transformation of Israel from the object of bipartisan and full-throated American support into a country which many Americans – wrongly, unnecessarily, and with damaging results – perceive as morally suspect as well as arrogant in its assumptions about unfettered access to American support.
Henry Kissinger famously said that “Israel has no foreign policy, only domestic politics.” That dictum has been taken to an extreme by Netanyahu, who has seemingly prioritized his personal political survival over Israel’s national interests.
In the realm of US-Israeli relations, this myopic viewpoint has led to Israel’s increasing estrangement from the Democratic Party, from many American Jews, and recently even from significant parts of the Republican Party.
One has only to look at the mayhem and violence being perpetrated in Judea and Samaria by what American Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee has called Jewish terrorists to see the latest evidence of the damage such misguided priorities have wrought.
Meddling and moving forward
Netanyahu has – for good reason – been obsessed with the need to deny Iran access to nuclear weapons.
He has, however, been seemingly oblivious about the importance of maintaining bipartisan American support for Israel as an essential element in advancing that goal.
Netanyahu has repeatedly attempted to interfere – sometimes in a subtle manner, and other times blatantly – in American domestic politics.
He saw fit to testify in front of the American Congress as far back as 2002 while out of office and advocate for the removal of former Iraqi president Saddam Hussein. We know how that ended.
He openly supported the Republican presidential candidate, Mitt Romney (a highly capable and very pro-Israel politician for sure), in his race against former US president Barack Obama in 2008.
Netanyahu engineered the idea of addressing a joint session of Congress in 2010 on Iran – despite Obama’s vigorous opposition – in an attempt to block the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) agreement.
If any means justify the ends, then we should not be surprised that along the way, many American legislators and citizens have become wary of Israel and its government.
When one finds oneself in a hole, the first rule is to stop digging.
The next Israeli government will face a herculean task in beginning the long road towards rehabilitating Israel’s brand. It must resist any temptation to in any way appear to be interfering in domestic American political affairs.
Israel should similarly expect that no American government of either party will wish to interfere in Israel’s domestic politics.
And Israel should always seek to both inform and seek the collaboration with and acquiescence of its American partners in any major military or diplomatic initiative, all the while preserving Israel’s national independence and associated degrees of freedom.
A good place to start would be for a new Israeli government to voluntarily and immediately notify the US that it intends to forego American military aid.
Israel is a wealthy country with a higher GDP per capita than France and the UK. It can pay for its own defense, and doing so would both serve to dampen criticism (in Congress and in American public opinion) and create a more level playing field.
Israel and the US face a common need to rapidly increase the production of a new generation of weapons – AI-based, inexpensive, and capable of neutralizing asymmetric warfare threats.
Working together to address this challenge would meaningfully “shift and lift” the discourse about Israel.
Israel has no better friend than the United States. It depends on American support and on the (still) special relationship it has had with the world’s only superpower.
Moreover, Americans have a long history of supporting Israel based on shared values as well as realpolitik considerations. It will take a major effort and considerable time, but the task of rehabilitating Israel’s brand is both possible and essential.
Rebuilding Israel as a liberal democracy with equal rights and obligations for all citizens, as articulated in the country’s Declaration of Independence, and a high-functioning government is the best guarantee to ensure that Americans will once again look at Israel as an ally and worthy military and diplomatic partner.
The writer is a venture capitalist and the founder of the Shlomo Argov Fellows program at Reichman University.

Kazakhstan votes in first election for new unicameral parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:41:52 UTC
04:41:52 KST

Kazakhstan holds first elections on Sunday for its new 145-seat unicameral legislature, the Kurultai, with 545 candidates from seven political parties competing for five-year terms.
The election marks the first vote under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system, which replaced the former bicameral parliament with the Kurultai. The new Constitution took effect on July 1, ending the powers of both the Senate and the Mazhilis.
The name "Kurultai" for the new parliament was not chosen by chance — it is a reference to the historical traditions of nomadic steppe democracy. Kazakhstan is geographically located in the steppe zone, which was the cradle of nomadic civilizations, and one of them was predecessor of the current state.
The word "kurultai" has Turkic roots and translates as "assembly." In the past, this was the name given to important congresses among Turkic and Mongolian peoples, where key state matters were decided, rulers were elected, war was declared, peace was concluded, nomad territories and trade routes were distributed, and laws were adopted.
In the Kazakh Khanate, a historical nomadic state in Central Asia, the kurultai was the supreme body of power, representatives of clans, tribes, and zhuzes (a large association of Kazakh clans and tribes) gathered there to discuss and approve the most important decisions.
The return of the term kurultai to the modern constitutional practice of Kazakhstan symbolizes a connection with historical traditions, emphasizes the continuity of national statehood, and reflects a desire to combine contemporary democratic mechanisms with the traditions of steppe democracy.
It reinforces the principle of popular representation and embodies a new model of governance in which the representative body plays a more significant role in making key state decisions.
Under the new electoral system, all 145 Kurultai deputies will be elected by proportional representation from party lists in a single nationwide constituency. In other words, voters will not vote for specific people, but for parties and candidates nominated by them.
If a party gets 30% of the votes, it gets 30% of the seats in parliament. At the same time, the higher the candidate's place on the list, the more likely he is to get into parliament.
Voters will therefore choose a political party rather than an individual candidate.
The seven parties participating in the election are Adilet, the Nationwide Social Democratic Party, the Kazakhstan Green Party Baitaq, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Auyl, Ak Zhol and Respublica.
They will appear on the ballot in that order following a Central Election Commission drawing of lots.
The newly formed Adilet has the largest candidate list, with 186 nominees, followed by Respublica with 76, the People’s Party 72, Auyl 69, Ak Zhol 63, Baitaq 47 and the Nationwide Social Democratic Party 33.
Earlier this year, longtime ruling party Amanat voted to dissolve itself into Adilet, making it a central participant in the inaugural vote.
The parties have focused their campaigns on different priorities.
Adilet has emphasized state reform, economic development, digitalization, education, regional development and social protection.
Ak Zhol has campaigned on support for private business, competition and parliamentary accountability, while Auyl has focused on rural development, agriculture and food security.
Respublica, meanwhile, has highlighted entrepreneurship, digital government, infrastructure and economic competitiveness.
The People’s Party has stressed social protection, wages, healthcare, education and support for families and pensioners.
Baitaq has made environmental protection and the transition to a green economy central to its platform, while the Nationwide Social Democratic Party has focused on social justice, reducing inequality and strengthening political competition.
All seven parties complied with statutory requirements concerning the representation of women, young people and people with disabilities.
Across the registered lists, these categories account for 43.9% of all candidates, including 172 women, 74 candidates under 35 and 19 people with disabilities.
The election is also attracting considerable international attention.
The Central Election Commission has accredited international observers from foreign states and international organizations, including representatives of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) and Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) observation structures.
The CEC has described the level of international interest as "high."
Kazakhstan has also introduced measures aimed at making voting more accessible. Election authorities have prepared special facilities for voters with disabilities, including audio versions of ballots and Braille templates.
The authorities have registered 12,605,788 (12.61 million) voters nationwide and are producing 12,731,847 ballots (12.73 million), including a statutory 1% reserve.
The new parliamentary model is one of the central elements of Kazakhstan’s broader constitutional reform.
The new Constitution defines the Kurultai as the country’s highest representative body exercising legislative power and sets the term of its deputies at five years.
President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev described the transition to the new system as "a major stage in Kazakhstan’s political development," and said the forthcoming election would provide an opportunity to demonstrate "open, honest and competitive politics."
The first session of the newly elected Kurultai is to be convened by the president no later than 30 days after publication of the election results.

Hamas sent children to fly kites into Israel, IDF says, reviving Gaza border fears

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:25:23 UTC
04:25:23 KST

Four kites discovered near Gaza border communities since Friday have shaken residents and revived painful memories of October 7, but initial IDF assessments indicate they were launched by children and teenagers acting on instructions from Hamas commanders, with no explosives or incendiary devices attached.
The kites, believed to have been sent from northern Gaza, carried messages in Arabic. One bore the phrase “We will never calm down,” apparently intended as a psychological message.
The IDF Southern Command is closely monitoring the phenomenon and says it understands the effect on residents’ sense of security. At the same time, security officials are stressing that the launches should not be confused with a concrete military threat. Initial examinations found no explosives, charges or sabotage devices attached to the kites.
Officials said children and teenagers appear to have been launching them under Hamas direction. The Southern Command is also monitoring the possibility that Hamas could adopt fiber-optic drone tactics used by Hezbollah in Lebanon, though no evidence of such activity has so far been found in Gaza.
Fiber-optic drones are considered particularly difficult to counter because they are guided through a physical cable rather than a radio link. The IDF has been studying the threat from the northern front in recent weeks in preparation for the possibility that Hamas might copy the method.
Security officials say the operational reality in Gaza is now fundamentally different from the situation before October 7. According to the IDF, Israeli forces currently maintain broad operational control over roughly 63% to 64% of the Gaza Strip and enjoy extensive freedom of action.
Following several relatively quiet days in the sector, the Southern Command has also stepped up targeted strikes. The IDF says 13 terrorists were killed in precision air and ground strikes over the past week, including a company commander.
The military says the “yellow line” remains a firm operational boundary and that anyone crossing the perimeter is either fired upon immediately or detained.
At least four kites were found near Kibbutz Nahal Oz over the past two days. Another carrying Arabic writing was discovered nearby on Tuesday, while one was found in Moshav Shuva a week earlier. At least seven kites have been found in Gaza border communities since October 7.
Residents are not dismissing the phenomenon as harmless. Similar tactics were used in the past, when kites without incendiary material were initially sent across the border to gauge where they would land before later versions carried flammable materials that caused fires.
For communities along the Gaza border, even an apparently harmless kite crossing from Gaza into Israeli airspace is enough to bring back memories of a threat that once evolved into something much more dangerous.

'We're all gonna make it': What gymbros are getting wrong about Zyzz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:06:07 UTC
04:06:07 KST

What the Zyzz documentary tells us about the manosphere, looksmaxxing and peptides
For a certain generation of Australian men, the path to the gym began with a photograph of a shirtless young man from Sydney.
His videos were brash, his poses were deliberately ridiculous, and at times he said deliberately provocative and offensive things to garner attention.
His catchphrases spread through bodybuilding forums, YouTube and social media, and some are now resurfacing as a new documentary hits our screens about one of Australia's earliest social media celebrities.
Aziz Shavershian had the muscles, the tan, the hair, the confidence, and he's the subject of Stan's new movie, Poster Boy: Becoming Zyzz.
But for all this renewed attention, Aziz won't hear or see it, having died in Thailand at just 22 years of age in 2011.
Fifteen years after his death, Aziz, known by his online moniker Zyzz, has become part of a new wave of online content celebrating an earlier era of gym and rave culture.
But it also comes at a time when a new generation is encouraged to pursue physical perfection through so-called looksmaxxing by a slightly amorphous online world of male influencers pushing misogyny broadly referred to as the manosphere.
It is a strange moment to watch for his older brother, Said Shavershian, also known as ChestBrah.
He says the culture around young men's bodies and masculinity now looks very different to the one he and Aziz helped create.
"What me and Aziz always preached was we're all going to make it," he said.
"It's a message of just that, 'Hey man, if I made it, so can you.' And that was what we're always about, just uplifting the little guy and uplifting anyone to be the master of their destiny."
Before Tate, there was Zyzz
Andrew and Tristan Tate are now among the world's most recognisable figures in the online manosphere, building enormous audiences around a highly performative version of masculinity, wealth and status.
The brothers are currently in custody in the United States as the British government tries to extradite them to face charges of rape, assault and facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation.
In Poster Boy, it is put to the audience that the blueprint for the modern male influencer was being tested years earlier in Sydney, with Zyzz at the head of an "aesthetics movement".
But Said does not see the Tates as inheritors of his brother's message or goof representations of masculinity.
For him, masculinity is something far less flashy than fast cars and fancy watches.
"Being someone that's vulnerable, that's kind, that's loving," he says.
"Young men out there, young boys don't really have many positive role models to look up to in society and ones they can kind of feel relatable to."
From Sydney gyms to the looksmaxxing era
Together, the brothers helped turn bodybuilding into something less about standing on a competition stage and more about being part of a lifestyle.
"Shredding for Stereosonic" became a cultural in-joke, and Aziz became its poster boy.
But the pursuit has become much more extreme online since the height of Zyzz, with communities obsessing over facial structure, perceived attractiveness and where an individual sits in a hierarchy of male beauty in what is known as looksmaxxing.
Said sees the connection and the merits in taking pride in your appearance, but says "deep, deep down, it's quite toxic".
He points to practices, including "face pulling" and "bone smashing" as examples of where the pursuit of physical perfection can go, with men ultimately ranking themselves against others.
"With the digital age and social media, there's more information out there," he says.
"Anyone could just post anything, rage bait, any kind of content to kind of reel an audience in."
And once the algorithm finds an audience, it can keep serving them the same message, particularly targeting boys and young men at impressionable ages.
Documentary asks pertinent questions of peptides
Beyond its examination of modern masculinity, the film examines Zyzz's death and his use of steroids and peptides.
For years, the story repeated online was simple: the impossibly fit 22-year-old had suffered a heart attack in a Thai sauna.
The film reveals that Zyzz died from acute respiratory failure after taking a combination of morphine, cocaine and benzodiazepines.
He also had an enlarged heart, although the cause of that enlargement remains unclear.
There is no direct attribution to his use of steroids and other performance-enhancing substances.
Said, who is not a medical expert and uses some performance-enhancing drugs, has defended their use in controlled and managed settings.
"I think they definitely have their place in competitive sports, in bodybuilding, and in recovery," he said.
The ABC has reported not only on the booming unregulated trade of peptides, but also the severe health complications they can pose.
There are also medical concerns about the illicit trade of peptides and separately the side-effects of prescribed peptides.
It is a particularly pertinent question for the legacy of a man whose image has become synonymous with the pursuit of the perfect physique, and a confronting detail in a story that has otherwise been relentlessly mythologised, because Zyzz became something larger than the person his brother remembers.
"To me, I always would see him as my younger, goofy, dorky, highly intellectual brother," says Said.
He understands why people still idolise Zyzz, but is less comfortable with the comparisons that have turned his brother into a larger-than-life figure.
"Az was just as much human as you and I," he says.
Reflecting on Zyzz's life, Said said his flaws are what make him relatable.
"Why does a role model always have to be completely virtuous?" Said asks.
Aziz, he argues, was "imperfectly perfect".
A young man with faults, ambitions and insecurities who happened to become extraordinarily good at making people watch him.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has said that, starting September 8, Canada would impose tariffs on imports from the United States across a raft of sectors in retaliation for President Donald Trump’s new 50 percent tariffs, which came into effect at midnight.
"Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Carney said at a news conference on Saturday.
These retaliatory tariffs will hit sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics and will also include products currently subject to the unjustified Section 232 and 338 tariffs, Carney said in a spirited speech from the Parliament building in Ottawa.
"We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked," Carney said.
After days of intense negotiations, the two countries failed to reach a trade deal late on Friday, worsening an already delicate relationship between the two long-term trade partners and allies and complicating the future of a highly successful continental free trade pact called the US-Mexico-Canada agreement.
Trump's new tariffs hit a slew of sectors including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods, hockey equipment and cover some $20 billion of Canadian exports south of the border.
These duties do not give exemption to Canadian products under the USMCA, which have shielded most of Canadian exports to the US in the last 18 months.

Togo says it has 'serious' evidence against detained French filmmakers
Togo’s government said Saturday it had “serious and corroborative evidence” against two French documentary filmmakers arrested last month alongside their Togolese fixer. The three men deny charges of making “false declarations”.
Togo's government commented Saturday for the first time on the case of the two French film-makers and their Togolese colleague, who were arrested at the end of July in the west African country and have been in custody ever since.
The three men – Gaël Mocaër, Sebastian Perez Pezzani and Fred Vedomey – are being held on charges of making “false declarations”. Their lawyer said they deny the charges.
The media watchdog Reporters Without Borders (RSF) called again for their immediate release.
Togo's justice and security ministries said in a joint statement Saturday that the documentary team, arrested July 27, had used a drone in areas authorities regard as sensitive because of the threat of jihadist attacks in them.
The statement said that the authorisation to film had been signed only by the fixer, Vedomey, and not by the Frenchmen, and was "strictly limited" to specific, stated areas.
It also claimed "several irregularities" in the way the assignment was carried out, without elaborating.

The statement said the three men appeared before prosecutors on August 17, with their lawyer.
Their lawyer, Martial Akakpo, told AFP that his clients denied the charges against them.
Mocaer and Pezzani, with their fixer Vedomey, were making a documentary for France Televisions.
RSF said Pezzani suffers from serious health problems, requiring urgent treatment.
A Togolese doctor had warned he was at risk of developing sepsis, according to Patrice Lucchini, head of their company Tony Comiti Productions.

Romania is taking new measures to raise the water level in the Danube to cool the nuclear power plant
Kyiv • UNN
Due to the historically low level of the Danube, Romania will urgently deepen the riverbed and divert water to the nuclear power plant. Releases from reservoirs will also be increased.
Romania’s National Committee for Emergency Situations approved new measures to raise the water level in the Danube River and ensure cooling for the Cernavoda Nuclear Power Plant, the country’s government reported on Saturday, UNN writes, citing Reuters.
Details
The plant remains shut down due to historically low water levels in the Danube, and the country declared a state of emergency throughout August because of reduced electricity generation.
Emergency dredging of the Danube riverbed near the plant is planned.
A groyne will be built along the Old Danube riverbed to divert water toward the water-intake area for the plant’s cooling systems.
The hydropower plant operator Hidroelectrica will begin releasing water from reservoirs on the Olt River on Saturday for five days to supplement the Danube’s flow and generate additional electricity.
Powerful pumps will be mobilized to maintain, if necessary, the water level required for the plant’s operation.

6 EU countries renew push for excess profit tax on oil companies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:00:26 UTC
04:00:26 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Finance ministers from six EU countries have renewed calls for an EU-wide excess profit tax on oil companies amid high fuel prices, German broadcaster NTV reported.
Finance ministers from Germany, Portugal, Spain, Austria, Italy and Poland called for a common approach to taxing oil companies’ increased profits amid the sharp rise in energy prices.
“We are experiencing one of the biggest supply shocks in decades, and around the world, discontent is growing over the rising cost of living,” the ministers said in a letter addressed to Ireland’s finance minister, whose country currently holds the rotating EU Council presidency.
The letter said measures taken by governments so far had not been sufficient to permanently lower or stabilize energy prices for households and businesses.
“Therefore, we need a common approach that ensures those who profit from the crisis contribute their share to reducing the burden on the general population,” they said.
The ministers called for “an EU-wide framework to tax excess profits,” saying the experience of a similar measure introduced in 2022 should be taken into account.
They said lessons from the earlier measure could help determine how profits earned abroad by multinational oil companies can be more effectively included in an excess profit tax.
The ministers also called for the results of a European study into refinery margins to be released as soon as possible, saying they could provide a basis for measures to ensure refineries do not exploit the current energy situation.
The initiative was reportedly launched by German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, with the six ministers ideally seeking to put the issue on the agenda of an EU meeting of economic and finance ministers in Dublin scheduled for Sept. 18-19.
The renewed push comes as high fuel prices have increased pressure on European governments to intervene to ease the impact on households and businesses.
An excess profit tax was temporarily introduced in 2022 as an emergency response to soaring energy prices following Russia’s war in Ukraine, with energy companies taxed on exceptional profits.
Several major oil companies reported their quarterly financial results in July.
According to Oxfam, the combined profits of BP, Chevron, Eni, ExxonMobil, Shell and TotalEnergies reached nearly €40 billion ($46.6 billion) between April and June.
Oxfam estimates that the six companies could post combined profits of €147 billion ($171.2 billion) for the full year and has called for a permanent excess profit tax of at least 50% on profits exceeding a 10% return on investment.
Portugal presented a draft excess profit tax at the end of July, with the government saying revenues would support families and economic sectors affected by rising fuel prices.

Carney: Canada will enact retaliatory US tariffs starting September 8
The prime minister spoke hours after the US imposed 50 percent tariffs on nearly $20bn worth of Canadian goods.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has promised to issue retaliatory, “dollar-for-dollar” tariffs after the United States enacted steep new duties on the country.
Carney addressed Canadians on Saturday, just hours after the US imposed 50 percent tariffs on nearly $20bn worth of the country’s goods.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3US, Canada negotiators race to ink a deal as Trump’s tariff deadline looms
- list 2 of 3US imposes 50 percent tariffs on $20bn in Canadian goods after talks fail
- list 3 of 3How will Trump’s tariffs affect Canada’s economy?
The prime minister promised a “focused response”, beginning September 8, that would level tariffs on US imports like steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, paper and electronics.
“We pursued every opportunity to reach an agreement that protects Canadian workers and their families, that strengthens our economy and that respects Canadian sovereignty,” Carney said. “We take this step reluctantly.”
Carney’s remarks come after weeks of uncertainty over whether the tariffs would take effect. The newest import taxes were first announced in July, as part of an ongoing back-and-forth over trade between the two countries.
Since the start of his second term, Trump has sought to ratchet up pressure on Canada, as part of a push to increase US influence over the Western Hemisphere and advance US priorities.
In announcing the 50 percent tariffs on July 20, Trump accused Canada of “discriminatory treatment” in its trade policies. The two neighbours are longtime allies and have been among each other’s largest trading partners for decades.
Negotiators on both sides, however, have sought to stop Trump’s latest round of tariffs from taking effect, achieving a postponement from a previous deadline on Wednesday.
But despite marathon talks in the three days since, they failed to finalise a trade deal. The revised tariff deadline expired at midnight Eastern US time (04:00 GMT).
Carney, who said Canada had been “pragmatic, patient and persistent”, explained on Saturday that his country walked away from the discussions because the US “asked too much and they offered too little”.
He also accused the US of introducing last-minute demands that scuttled the negotiations.
“In recent days, the United States proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits for Canada and called into question the reliability of any deal,” Carney said.
When reporters pressed him for specifics, Carney referred to 11th-hour changes regarding car imports, as well as restrictions on Canada’s ability to forge new trade alliances.
“The US introduced in the last hours efforts to restrict our ability to have other trade deals,” Carney alleged.
“We’re the partner of choice in many respects for countries around the world, and the Americans wanted to restrict that. They had language that wanted to restrict that. Unacceptable.”
Carney also criticised the US’s shifting rationale for imposing the cross-border tariffs, pointing to remarks Trump has made citing drug-trafficking, television advertisements and wildfire smoke as reasons for increasing import duties on Canadian products.
Since taking office in 2025, Carney has been at loggerheads with Trump, who returned to the White House for a second term that same year.
Trump has repeatedly used far-reaching tariffs as leverage to secure more beneficial deals from US trading partners. Experts say his aggressive foreign policy has also alienated some of the country’s longstanding allies.
In the face of such tensions, Carney has advocated for the world’s “middle powers” to join forces as a counterbalance to superpowers like the US and China. He acknowledged Trump’s disruptive influence in global politics in Saturday’s speech.
“Our government understood before many that America would transform all of its commercial relationships, that it would put a series of tariffs on its closest allies and use economic integration as a weapon,” Carney said.
He also suggested that the US, under Trump, is prone to abruptly changing course. “We recognise that, sometimes, its signature was written in pencil.”
“The gap between partnership and competitor has, unfortunately, remained too wide in recent days,” he added.
The Trump administration, however, has sought to paint Canada’s demands as the impediment in this week’s tariff negotiations.
As late as Friday afternoon, a breakthrough between Ottawa and Washington seemed possible, with Trump telling reporters, “The deal with Canada is moving along.”
Reports emerged that the US had offered to lower tariffs on aluminium, cars and steel if Canada gave US businesses more access to its dairy and lumber markets.
But on Saturday, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News there are no future talks planned with Canada. Greer also revealed the US would be “moving forward with measures” to respond to its northern neighbour’s retaliatory tariffs.
“They’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that,” Greer said.
Carney, meanwhile, indicated that Canada would continue to strengthen its trade relations with other countries.
“We can’t control the storm that blows in from Washington,” Carney said. “We can, however, chart a new course by building Canada strong and diversifying our trading relationships abroad.”
One reporter asked Carney about his sombre tone, “Why does it feel like, today, Mark Carney is going to war? Trade war?”
Carney responded bluntly, “You’re at war when you get attacked. We got attacked.”

Why can't clinicians override inaccurate algorithm decisions?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:00:00 UTC
04:00:00 KST

analysis
While government reviews aged care algorithm, waitlists are growing and people are dying
"The idea of an Independent Assessment Tool didn't drop from the sky, we didn't come up with it."
"It was a very important recommendation of the Royal Commission into Aged Care."
That's what the Minister for Health, Mark Butler, said at a press conference last Tuesday, when asked about the aged care algorithm, featured in our Four Corners investigation the night before.
For clarity, the "Independent Assessment Tool", or IAT, that the minister refers to, is not the algorithm. It's the questionnaire completed by a clinician when assessing someone for aged care services. It was recommended by the royal commission.
On the other hand, the computer algorithm is a secretive formula devised by the government which scores people on the amount of aged care funding they should receive. It was never recommended by the royal commission.
Conflating the two — the questionnaire and the algorithm — has been a common tactic of the government and the Department of Health.
The reality is that these are two very different things, and their development and testing processes stand in stark contrast.
Loading...
Not a job for public servants
The questionnaire or IAT was tested on 22,000 people; there were three working groups involved in its development which included some clinicians; and there's a detailed report on its development and trial which is publicly available.
The algorithm underwent no live trial before it was launched; the Department of Health has been unable to give the name of any clinicians who signed off on it; and there's no detailed report explaining how it was developed and tested.
In fact, despite senators making a formal Order for the Production of Documents, the government has refused to release anything beyond publicly available Department of Health material.
The algorithm's design, evaluation and implementation are all details that have only been gleaned through some rigorous questions from the Coalition, the Greens and Senator David Pocock at Senate estimates.
Through those responses, it's been revealed there was a prototype of an algorithm — believed to have been designed by a consultancy — which was taken in-house by bureaucrats, modified and validated by them, and launched on November 1 last year.
Public servants have given evidence that they used data from 200,000 assessments to test and verify the algorithm at the back end, but there was no live trial.
Professor Kathy Eagar, honorary professor at UNSW, has a strong opinion on that: "[Public servants] should never have been asked to do a job that is so technically sophisticated."
Eagar should know. She designed a classification algorithm used to allocate funding to people in residential care. She led a team of researchers and experts in the field and her report was published in the Medical Journal of Australia. It contrasts starkly with what's happened with the algorithm at the centre of this controversy.
For our Four Corners, Eagar reverse-engineered the Support at Home algorithm and explained its flaws — that there's more than 500 questions in the IAT but the vast majority do not feed into the algorithm; that the detailed notes recorded by the clinician in more than 100 text boxes cannot be read by it; and that issues such as frailty, cognitive problems, mental health and carer fatigue come into the equation far too late to have any impact on someone's funding, and therefore the amount of care they receive.
Regarding other problems, she revealed that a one-point difference at a particular juncture in the algorithm equates to almost $40,000 a year lost or gained in funding.
Questions linger for government
There's little doubt that the government is aware of the problems.
The Senate has now voted for it to be ditched; the Ombudsman is investigating it after 800 complaints; and the government itself has committed $18 million to reviewing both the IAT and the algorithm.
Independent MPs are comparing it to Robodebt — something the Coalition has avoided doing for obvious reasons — and backbenchers report being inundated with calls from their constituents.
When summing up the issue on Tuesday, Butler acknowledged the problems, saying the government was "doing everything we can to monitor the rollout of this scheme" and "where we think we need to modify it, we've indicated a commitment to do that."
The question is, why doesn't it allow clinicians to override the algorithm's decisions when they think it's wrong — at least while it is being reviewed and refined?
It could compare funding decisions made by clinicians and the algorithm, as would have occurred in a real live trial.
Instead, the government voted down a Senate amendment to allow human override.
It says it will legislate a new pathway, allowing assessment agencies to ask for reviews of decisions when necessary.
That's not much different to what's in place now, except it's the older person or their family who has to lodge an appeal.
Loading
'People are giving up'
In its first five months, more than 1,000 people asked to have the algorithm's decision reviewed — that's six times the number from the entire financial year before its implementation.
The government says that's still less than 1 per cent of all assessments, indicating that it's not a real problem.
Eagar disagrees. "The reason that it's a very small percentage is because it's too hard and complex to appeal and also people are giving up," she told Four Corners.
"They know that if they appeal, the appeal is being considered by the very department that developed the system."
If the government wants a true indication of the level of feeling in the community, perhaps it should read the thousands of comments on Facebook where discussions about the algorithm, long waitlists, and people dying are growing by the day.
