On Thursday, leaders of more than a dozen countries, including Germany, France, and the UK, as well as the European Commission, issued a joint statement condemning the project as illegal and “unacceptable.”
Rising violence in the Palestinian territory has also drawn a warning from the US. Israeli settlers who take West Bank property belonging to Palestinian-Americans could face sanctions, US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee told Reuters.
Israel has occupied the West Bank since the 1967 Six-Day War. Around three million Palestinians live there along with more than 600,000 Israeli settlers. Under the internationally backed two-state solution, the West Bank would form part of a future Palestinian state together with East Jerusalem and Gaza.
Moscow has long stressed the conflict can only be resolved through the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.

====================================================================================================

ICE arrested the ‘worst of the worst.’ Washington made sure he walked free
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:48:49 UTC
03:48:49 KST

ICE arrested the ‘worst of the worst.’ Washington made sure he walked free
Imagine you are a Chilean who’s lived in America – the so-called “Land of the Free” – for decades in peace and tranquility. Suddenly, one humid day in late October 2025, in your adopted home of Fort Myers, Florida, you are snatched in broad daylight then imprisoned by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents.
Your capture remains completely unknown to the outside world until January the next year, when the US Department of Homeland Security names you among the “worst of worst criminal aliens” arrested by ICE to date. You are accused of committing “homicide” almost 50 years ago. Your incarceration makes international headlines, and comes as a personal shock. But not because you’re innocent.
You are no ordinary Chilean. You are Armando Fernandez Larios, a 76-year-old fascist intelligence veteran who in September 1976 helped assassinate former Chilean Defense Minister Orlando Letelier using a car bomb. An outspoken opponent of dictator Augusto Pinochet, Letelier fled Santiago a year after the September 1973 CIA coup that installed Pinochet in power.
What role precisely Fernandez Larios played in Letelier’s murder, which also took the life of his colleague Ronni Karpen Moffitt, is still not fully clear. He has told a variety of stories about what he knew, when he knew it, and what he did and did not do regarding the event. But Fernandez Larios was a key operative.
It seemed in 2025 ICE had gotten their man, in a huge win for immigration enforcement and international justice. But this March, Fernandez Larios was released from jail. Court documents obtained by the National Security Archive show he launched a legal action, accusing the US government of “breach of contract” by violating a plea deal he cut in 1987.
That agreement saw Fernandez Larios provide information to US prosecutors on Letelier’s assassination, in return for an extremely light prison sentence and promise the government “would neither seek to deport [him] to Chile nor to cooperate in his extradition to Chile.” Rather than let Fernandez Larios’ action go to court, ICE freed him. Presumably, he’s sunning himself in Fort Myers right now.
The CIA connection
A huge archive of declassified documents related to Letelier’s assassination analyzed by RT Investigates, including secret statements made to US officials by Fernandez Larios, sheds shocking light on the case. They show that in mid-1976, Fernandez Larios was tasked by Pinochet’s regime with obtaining fake passports and US visas to fly to Washington DC.
Fernandez Larios was joined by Michael Townley, Pinochet’s US-born lead hitman and CIA double agent. They secured visas from Chile’s US embassy, after claiming to be on a secret mission to meet with CIA deputy director Vernon Walters at Langley headquarters in Virginia. Fernandez Larios traveled to Washington first, to conduct surveillance on Letelier’s movements in advance of his assassination.
On September 9, 1976, 12 days before Letelier’s murder, Fernandez Larios met Townley in the lavatory of New York’s John F. Kennedy airport to provide him with a surveillance map, notes on Letelier’s home and office addresses, as well as cash for the operation. Townley then recruited members of the Cuban National Movement, to assist him in building, placing, and detonating the car bomb.
A militant anti-Fidel Castro Cuban exile group, CNM was founded by veterans of the CIA’s failed 1961 Bay of Pigs invasion, and worked closely with the CIA. Experts at explosives, the bomb was planted without detection then detonated as Letelier, Moffitt and her husband Michael were driving to work in downtown DC. Michael was sole survivor of the bombing.
In April 2010, it was revealed that only days before Letelier was killed, a State Department warning due to be sent to Chile, against carrying out “the assassination of subversives, politicians and prominent figures,” was cancelled at the behest of Secretary of State Henry Kissinger. His department had been extremely worried about Pinochet carrying out killings outside Chile.
“We are trying to head off a series of international murders that could do serious damage to the international status and reputation of the countries involved,” Kissinger had been informed by aides, but he was unmoved. A close confidante of Pinochet who’d personally assisted his bloodstained rise to power, did Kissinger know Letelier was due to be killed?
The coverup and polygraph test
In the aftermath of the assassination, Fernandez Larios participated in an extensive cover-up orchestrated by Chilean officials, including Pinochet himself. After being identified by the US media along with Townley as a lead suspect in Letelier’s murder, he deceived military investigators, gave false testimony to the Chilean Supreme Court, and lied to FBI and Justice Department investigators.
By 1985 though, Fernandez Larios was open to talking, having back-channel discussions with the US about testifying on Letelier’s assassination. In return for defecting and providing what he knew – or claimed to know – about the killing, and Pinochet’s intelligence operations generally, Fernandez Larios would receive extreme leniency, then be allowed to stay in the US, safe from extradition.
Fernandez Larios was debriefed by US officials in Santiago in mid-January 1987, then subjected to polygraph tests in Brazil. He consistently denied knowing his 1976 mission to Washington DC was an assassination plot. The lie detector results showed “consistent signs of deception in Fernandez’ disclaimers.” Under further debriefing, he finally admitted “his surveillance contributed to the death of Letelier and Moffitt.”
A late January 1987 State Department cable on what to do with Fernandez Larios however disregarded the polygraph tests, shockingly stating he was “not a murderer or party to a conspiracy to murder.” The memo judged his information on the Letelier-Moffitt case to be of “limited value”, but stated “foreign policy benefits” to providing him a generous plea deal were “substantial.”
In February 1987, Fernandez Larios pleaded guilty to being an “accessory after the fact” to Letelier’s assassination. Within just five months, a State Department legal advisor wrote to the US Parole Commission, praising Fernandez Larios’ “character” and “his willingness to come forward and pay his debt” over his role in the crime. He was paroled in autumn 1987.
The “Caravan of Death”
In keeping with “consistent signs of deception” when discussing his foreknowledge of Letelier’s assassination, Fernandez Larios also did not tell US officials about many violent atrocities he personally committed as a member of Pinochet’s elite military unit, the “Caravan of Death.”
Following Pinochet’s seizure of power this deadly Caravan flew around Chile kidnapping local officials who remained loyal to Salvador Allende, who died in contested circumstances during the coup. Approximately 72 dissidents were executed or “disappeared.” Fernandez Larios was identified by multiple witnesses as one of the most ruthless members of the military death squad.
After Pinochet’s fall in 1990, investigations into his regime’s many atrocities were opened in Chile. In several cases, substantial evidence against Fernandez Larios as a personal perpetrator of appalling crimes was found, leading to Santiago launching legal proceedings. In accordance with his plea deal though, Fernandez Larios remained at liberty in Florida.
It took until March 1999 for a civil suit to be launched against him in the US. The family of Winston Cabello, a 28-year-old Allenda-era regional planning director executed alongside 12 other political prisoners by the Caravan of Death in October 1973, accused Fernandez Larios of “extrajudicial killing, torture, crimes against humanity and cruel and inhuman treatment.”
Numerous Chileans identified Fernandez Larios as a participant in the torture and executions of prisoners in multiple municipalities. One witnessed him personally slashing Cabello to death with a knife. The three-week trial ended in October 2003, Fernandez Larios found liable for extrajudicial killings, torture and crimes against humanity. Cabello’s family was awarded $4 million in damages.
That sum remains uncollected, and Fernandez Larios is once again a free man after his recent spell in prison, despite him truly being the “worst of the worst” captured by ICE. A strong case for his deportation to a country other than Chile remains. He has not been granted a special “snitch” visa protecting foreign informants from deportation.

Following Russia's attack on a shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, which claimed the lives of 16 people, criminal proceedings have been opened over official negligence. As part of the proceedings, the actions of officials of the company that owns the Kryvyi Rih shopping mall and the tenants in the complex will also be examined. The director of one of the supermarkets has already been served with a notice of suspicion, Interior Minister Ivan Vygivskyi said on social media on Saturday, UNN reports.
Details
"At a time when Russia is deliberately striking shopping malls and hypermarkets, a responsible attitude toward people's safety must come first," the minister emphasized.
Police investigators in the Dnipropetrovsk region, under the procedural guidance of the Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor's Office, have launched criminal proceedings over official negligence. As part of the proceedings, they will examine, among other things, the actions of officials of the company that owns the shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, as well as the companies that rented premises in the complex. The police investigators and prosecutors have just served the director of one of the supermarkets with a notice of suspicion
According to the Interior Minister, "despite warnings from local authorities to suspend operations during air raids, the facility continued to operate. A significant number of the people killed were found there."
"As a result of this targeted Russian strike, 16 people were killed and around 130 more were injured. Approximately 20 minutes passed between the announcement of the air raid in the city and the first drone impact," he said.
According to the minister, "during the investigation, the police will establish, among other things, whether visitors and employees were properly informed, whether instructions to evacuate the building were issued in a timely manner, and will also examine information circulating online about blocked shelter doors."
"The actions of all responsible persons and the approved response algorithms will be comprehensively examined—whether they were adapted to the actual threats in the frontline region," Vygivskyi said.
The Interior Minister urged "managers at all levels to treat threats responsibly and take timely measures for the sake of people's safety." "This especially applies to all regions bordering the frontline and Russia. During an air raid, it is important to respond promptly—to prevent crowds from forming and to protect lives," the minister emphasized.

====================================================================================================

Salt-N-Pepa say they weren't always respected in hip-hop
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:43:52 UTC
03:43:52 KST

Hip-hop fans love a feud.
Decades before Kendrick Lamar took on Drake, even well before Biggie and Tupac's storied rivalry, the first hip-hop diss track came from a teenage girl from Queens, New York.
In 1985, Roxanne Shante released Roxanne's Revenge, a searing response to rap group UTFO's 1984 hit Roxanne, Roxanne, the 14-year-old clapping back with a devastating mix of confidence and sass.
Noticing the attention it received, two fellow young New York women, Cheryl James and Sandra Denton, tried a similar tack.
As Super Nature, they recorded The Show Stoppa, in response to Doug E Fresh and Slick Rick's song The Show.
"That was how women kind of got their recognition back then," James, aka Salt, tells Double J's Hau Latukefu.
"We ain't have no beef with [Doug E Fresh and Slick Rick] for real, but we saw Roxanne Shante do it, so we was like, 'Oh, we could do that. They're gonna pay attention if we do that.' It caused a lot of controversy."
It also opened a lot of doors. Not just for James and Denton, but for a string of women who would come after them.
Super Nature soon became Salt-N-Pepa, who alongside DJ Spinderella would become one of the first all-female rap groups to achieve mainstream success and prove women belonged at the centre of hip-hop.
The moment it became real
The group would go on to make some of the most enduring hip-hop of the 80s and 90s, with hits like Push It, Shoop, Let's Talk About Sex and Whatta Man still staples of the genre today.
But that first track started it all. After countless accolades, its success still means the world.
"We just wanted to hear our song on the radio," James, aka Salt, says.
Their producer, Hurby Luv Bug, sent the Salt-N-Pepa recording to DJ Marley Marl, the only man who could get the song out to the hip-hop-loving public.
"You could only hear hip-hop for 2 hours on the weekend, so everybody was tuned in," Salt recalls. "You just wanted to hear this new music."
The women jumped in Denton, aka Pepa's, car, a beat-up yellow Datsun with a hole in its floor, and cruised the streets with Marley Marl's show blaring through the radio.
"Then the record comes on and we go crazy," Salt says.
"Pep puts it in park in the middle of the boulevard. She jumps out the car. She's going, 'They're playing my song on the radio!'
"I swear, with all the accolades, all the awards, the Grammys — Salt-N-Pepa got them all at this point — that moment for me still remains the most exhilarating moment. Because that's when we knew this was really going to be something."
It became something enormous. Tens of millions of records sold, countless world tours, a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award and their 2025 induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.
"The reason that you even know Missy Elliott's name is because of Salt, Pepa, and Spinderella," Missy Elliott said when inducting the group.
"They are the bricklayers, the foundation that hip-hop stands on."
There's an endurance to their success too, which on one hand speaks to the timeless nature of the music and its subject matter.
But Salt reckons the quality of their material is only one part of the secret to their long-term success.
"I be taking breaks sometimes," she says frankly. "Every time I take a break, it ups the ante.
"You can't saturate the market. You gotta step away sometimes. You can't just be out there!
"But every time I do take a break and come back, it's like the floodgates just fly open. All of a sudden, we're back in the 90s and we're doing all the things.
"We're trying to keep up at this point. But it feels amazing: it's the people, it's really the fans. It's real love for Salt-N-Pepa out there."
Built to last
Salt-N-Pepa shaped the musical tastes of many, and they did it as underdogs.
It's hard to imagine now, but in the 80s and 90s, Salt-N-Pepa weren't just focused on whether a female hip-hop group would have staying power. They were wondering whether hip-hop could survive as an art form.
"That era [was] a challenging the time for hip-hop. [We were] wondering if it would last," Pepa says. "We were celebrating 10 years, 20 years …"
While they were flying the flag for the music that spoke to them, Salt-N-Pepa weren't always offered the reciprocal respect such a pivotal force in the popularisation of the genre deserved.
"We were getting flak back in the day," Pepa says.
"They used to call us pop. We were sellouts when we was getting hit records. Now everybody wants to be popular, right?"
No matter what naysayers might have said, the truth was in the material and the way audiences responded. In Australia alone they released over a dozen charting singles, four of them reaching the top five on the ARIA charts.
And while Salt-N-Pepa's songs are undeniably of their time, they have aged well.
Supplanting the machismo from sexualised hip-hop, the women rapped about female desire through a lens of safety and body positivity.
"It's so memorable for us when [people] tell us we were the soundtrack to their lives. It means a lot," Pepa says.
It turned out to be exactly what people were looking for.
More than 40 years on from their formation, and with over 15 million album sales, James and Denton keep the Salt-N-Pepa legacy alive.
This November they return to Australia for the first time in eight years, playing shows with fellow era-appropriate superstars Boyz II Men and Bell Biv DeVoe.
Demand has been rampant, with most shows sold out, and comment sections are packed with fans excited to reconnect with such a formative musical presence in their lives.
"It makes us feel like we're such a part of people's history," Salt says. "It helps us to understand the impact."
Salt-N-Pepa start their Australian tour in Perth on November 26, before shows in Sydney, Geelong, Hunter Valley and Brisbane.
Join Hau Latukefu for a massive hip-hop-fuelled party on The Block Party, Friday evenings from 7pm on Double J, or any time on ABC listen.

====================================================================================================

Their job is to influence politicians. An MP warns they can be powerful enemies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:43:52 UTC
03:43:52 KST

Inside Parliament House, powerful lobbyists can outnumber politicians
A senior officer in Canberra's Parliament House has received an urgent message.
An interloper is in one of the break rooms.
These rooms, with their kitchenette, dining table, and comfortable couches, are where Senate staffers can relax, have a cup of tea or eat their lunch in peace.
But today, a gatecrasher is sitting on a couch in one of the break rooms, holding a video meeting on his laptop.
Independent ACT senator David Pocock has seen this before.
"He's forever setting up shop in the break rooms, which are meant to be for staff to actually go and have a lunch break and use a microwave," he says.
"He's in there doing Zoom calls."
Staffers from the senator's office have emailed the Senate's senior administrative officer, known as the Usher of the Black Rod, to report the incursion.
But by the time a member of the Black Rod's office arrives, the man has left.
His identity is known to all in Senator Pocock's office.
"The guy is head of Responsible Wagering Australia," Senator Pocock says.
"He camps out in Parliament House … [and] has a lot of access."
His name is Kai Cantwell.
If Mr Cantwell feels at home inside Parliament House, it's because he's worked there before, as a senior ministerial adviser during the Morrison government.
Now he's a lobbyist for the sports betting industry.
The revolving door from government to lobbying
Mr Cantwell is a product of what's known around Canberra as "the revolving door" — the custom of outgoing ministers, senior advisers and public servants becoming lobbyists or corporate consultants.
Leveraging their connections and experience, they try to influence public policy, win government contracts and secure project approvals.
They represent a range of interest groups, including gas companies, alcohol retailers, religious organisations, weapons manufacturers and AI companies.
During Mr Cantwell's time in government, he served as chief of staff to then-Social Services minister Anne Ruston while she was responsible for managing gambling harm.
He is now the chief executive of Responsible Wagering Australia (RWA), the peak body representing some of Australia's most powerful sports betting companies, including Sportsbet and bet365.
"He's helped frame laws to reduce gambling harm … and then he's jumped the fence and he's working for the gambling industry," independent MP Monique Ryan says.
"You have to wonder, at what point did he start to have conversations with the gambling industry about taking up that role?"
The regulations granting inside access
Ordinary Australians are unable to see the true scale of lobbying in Australia, even if they search the public lobbyists register.
Mr Cantwell's name does not appear on the list.
That is because federal lobbying regulations only apply to "third-party" professional lobbyists who are engaged by external clients, and ignore the industry associations and hundreds of "in-house" lobbyists employed by companies and corporations.
Responsible Wagering Australia is considered an "industry association" under Commonwealth rules and therefore does not have to be registered.
It means RWA and its representatives are not subject to the Commonwealth Lobbying Code of Conduct and its sanctions.
Among a crowd of suits, briefcases and blazers moving through the building, the defining feature of a lobbyist is their orange pass.
Recent changes mean some of them will begin wearing a light blue pass instead.
By swiping a pass at security checkpoints, lobbyists can access restricted areas that are banned to the public, such as the labyrinth of corridors that lead to the offices of MPs and senators.
Ms Ryan says politicians are outnumbered by them.
"We are surrounded," she says.
Under changes introduced by the Albanese government, anyone wanting a pass now needs two parliamentarians to sponsor them instead of one.
Fear of making powerful enemies
During parliamentary sitting weeks, the RWA boss is everywhere.
If Mr Cantwell isn't conducting business in a break room, he can often be spotted walking the corridors or meeting people at Aussies, a café inside Parliament House where politicians, journalists, staffers and lobbyists swap information and gossip.
Here, media-related filming, recording and photography are strictly prohibited.
Alliance for Gambling Reform chief advocate Tim Costello knows the café well.
"Kai Cantwell effectively lives at Aussies," Reverend Costello says.
"He's set up permanent camp there, so he's very effective."
Labor MP and Parliamentary Friends of Gambling Harm Minimisation co-chair Mike Freelander is under no illusion about just how much influence the gambling lobby wields.
"The prime minister is very worried about making enemies of very powerful groups," he says.
"I think we saw that years ago when we tried to reign in the clubs and pubs around poker machines and things."
The gambling industry's access extends to almost every aspect of federal parliament.
During sitting weeks, MPs and staffers often gather at a field in the shadow of Parliament House to play soccer or touch football.
These hit-outs are organised by the Australian Parliament Sports Club.
As a former captain of the Wallabies rugby union team, Senator Pocock is arguably the club's most credentialed member in history.
But last year, the senator was stunned to discover the Parliament Sports Club was taking funding from the gambling industry.
"They were essentially being sponsored by a whole bunch of companies, industry groups, including the gambling lobby," Senator Pocock says.
"The gambling lobby were paying for access to events."
Dr Freelander says powerful lobby groups rarely donate money without getting some benefit.
"You should always follow the money, because the money always wins," he says.
Four Corners has analysed political donations from 93 federally-registered lobbying firms between 1998 and 2025.
All up, they disclosed about $13.5 million in donations.
For the top 10 firms, the combined total to Labor and the Coalition was about $4.8 million.
Of that, more than $3 million went to Labor, with lobbying firm Hawker Britton accounting for about $1.16 million alone.
Pyne & Partners donated about $68,000 to Labor, and $35,000 to the Coalition.
And those are just political donations from publicly registered firms.
Not all lobbyists are equal
On the other side of the lobbying fence to Mr Cantwell is Kate Seselja.
A mother of six who nearly lost everything to poker machines, Ms Seselja also sports an orange pass.
She is the co-chair of Gambling Harm Lived Experience Experts, a not-for-profit group formed to reduce the damage caused by gambling, and she is sponsored by Senator Pocock.
"Just because we both have an orange pass doesn't equal the same access," Ms Seselja says.
"It's incredibly hard to get meetings in Parliament House."
She says she recently found herself sitting near Mr Cantwell at Aussies when she received a phone call from a distressed father.
"He had just discovered his son was $150,000 in debt from sports betting," Ms Seselja says.
"I wanted to hand [Kai] the phone and go, 'Kai, you deal with this.'"
A bipartisan push for greater transparency
There is some bipartisan support in the parliament for industry groups, such as RWA, to be bound by the lobbyist register and the code of conduct.
"It's an organisation which seeks to change the behaviour of government by meeting with politicians and changing the way that we behave or the decisions that we make," Ms Ryan says.
"It's clearly a lobbying group."
Liberal MP and co-chair of the Parliamentary Friends of Gambling Harm Minimisation, Simon Kennedy, also backs tightening the rules.
"We should have as much transparency in this area as possible," he says.
"I don't want to see them treated any differently from any other group that comes to Parliament House to actively try and advance their interests."
Dr Freelander agrees RWA should be registered.
"When they are seeing individual parliamentarians, they need to show those credentials," he says.
"That's who they're lobbying for."
Mr Cantwell declined an interview request from Four Corners.
In a statement, RWA says it complies with all applicable laws, disclosure requirements and parliamentary protocols.
It says it rejects any suggestion its conduct has been improper, something Four Corners is not suggesting.
Labor's gambling reforms pass parliament
Last week the Albanese government passed a series of gambling law changes after landing a deal with the Coalition.
Instead of introducing a total ban on online gambling advertising, as recommended by a landmark review led by the late Labor MP Peta Murphy, the government will establish an online register for Australians to "opt out" of ads across platforms.
Betting companies will be responsible for identifying their own problem gamblers and cutting off inducements — a measure criticised by one Liberal MP as "putting Dracula in charge of a blood bank".
VIP account managers will be banned from earning a commission from customers' gambling spending.
Senator Pocock says the gambling lobby has had a massive win by stopping serious reform.
"This is a PM that is captured by the gambling lobby," he says.
"They've won this one because they got to the prime minister."

Sydney Swans fans grapple with scandal ahead of double header
In short:
Sydney Swans fans are reckoning with their support for their team as the club is engulfed in scandal ahead of a historic double header.
The GWS Giants have put rivalries aside and encouraged their fans to support the AFLW Swans match.
What's next?
The women are set to take on Essendon in the AFLW's round 2 before the men's side finishes its regular season with a clash against North Melbourne.
Sydney Swans fans are grappling with an emotional week of developments ahead of a historic double header, as a scandal continues to engulf the team.
Five players — Isaac Heeney, Nick Blakey, Chad Warner, Riley Bice and James Jordon — have been stood down by the Swans for breaching the club's standards on drinking and staying out late following last Sunday's win over Essendon in Melbourne.
Police from Victoria's sexual crimes squad are separately investigating a report of sexual assault, which the ABC understands centres on a player allegedly touching one of the women without her consent.
Police have not made any arrests or laid charges.
The lawyer representing two of the women present on the evening says his clients will be claiming damages for "pain and suffering", while the lawyer representing a third woman involved says a potential civil lawsuit is being looked at.
On Sunday, the women's side is set to take on Essendon in the AFLW's round 2 before the men's side finishes its regular season with a clash against North Melbourne.
The scandal has rocked the AFL and the wider community, with Swans fans left to reckon with their support ahead of the double billing.
Support swells for women's side
Lulu Clarke has been a Sydney Swans fan for as long as she can remember, and says this week has made her feel "pretty awful".
"I'm like, so incredibly disappointed … just to be a Sydney Swans fan," she told ABC News.
Before the scandal erupted, the 24-year-old says she had initially purchased tickets to the men's game this Sunday.
"I actually had no idea that the women were playing, I didn't see it publicised at all," she said.
"And then the news broke on Monday and I thought, 'Oh, I'm not going to that AFL game anymore.'
"There's no way I can go and support the men's AFL team, even if those five players aren't on the field; it's not something I can do."
Ms Clarke says she "flipped" her plans after learning how significant the double header was for the women's side.
"I decided that I'm just going to go to the women's instead of the men's, and do whatever I can to support them because they don't deserve to be overshadowed."
The GWS Giants have also put rivalries aside and encouraged their fans to turn out for the Sydney Swans women.
The Giants had their own double-fixture last weekend, and have urged members to support their "cross-town compatriots, be it wearing orange or red".
"This Sunday, the Swans AFLW will play in their own historic double header at the SCG, in what should be a celebration for their own team and support base," a statement read.
"As we will be playing the Demons away from home in Melbourne, we would like to encourage our Sydney-based and non-travelling fans to continue supporting the spectacle of women's football in Sydney by attending the match, before watching us play Melbourne.
"This is a moment to put rivalries aside and bolster the women's game in NSW by showing up and supporting the league and women in football".
On Friday, Sydney AFLW captain Lucy McEvoy and coach Colin O'Riordan said the women's program supported the sanctions imposed on the five male players, and said their actions did not reflect the Swans as a club.
McEvoy said the women's team has received a groundswell of support through social media in the wake of the allegations, which she described as "really special".
"The best way that we can support us in this moment is to get to the game on Sunday and hopefully break a record crowd that we once set a few years ago,"
Fans standing by club 'through the good times and the bad times'
Other Sydney Swans fans are opting to attend both matches.
"Everyone is entitled to do what they feel is best for them," says Liz, a Sydney Swans fan who wanted to be referred to by her first name only.
"Personally, I will be there to support the club, the girls and our boys, and support them as I always have," she told ABC News.
"Nothing for me for the club has changed. I can't comment on anyone else, I can only comment on how I'm feeling.
"I will be there for the boys and the girls and I will be cheering them on, because that's what I should be doing because we look after our club through the good times and the bad times."
Madison Clarke is the co-host of the unofficial Swans fan podcast, True Blood, and believes the notion of a "walkout" before the men's game is "coming from parts of the community that aren't necessarily Swans".
"I think there's a mainstream sentiment that is suggesting there may be a walkout," he said.
"We think all feelings on this matter, because it's a complex matter, we feel that all feelings are valid, broadly.
"But the overarching theme should be that while there are five guys that have seemingly dropped their standards and done the wrong thing, there's going to be 23 guys and the AFLW team, running out on the SCG on Sunday, that haven't done anything wrong, that need our support broadly."
Mr Clarke added this week had no doubt been difficult for many fans, and that coming together could be beneficial to navigating the news.
"It's felt for a lot of people to be quite isolating over this week," he said.
"I think what we've found therapeutic and comforting is actually having a dialogue with other Swan supporters.
"So there's nothing better to do, if you're able, than to get to the SCG and be around like-minded people who know how the week's been and know how you're feeling and it can be a really galvanising moment.
"So I think it's very important that we get there.
"Getting around the girls is absolutely paramount at this time as well.
"Getting around the girls and getting around the guys who haven't done anything wrong because I don't think we should be abandoning either the AFLW team or the AFL men's team."

‘We have no interest in escalation’: Israel says strike blocked Turkish military buildup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:43:35 UTC
03:43:35 KST

Israeli security officials said Saturday that this week’s strike on al-Duhur airbase deep inside Syria was intended as a warning after intelligence indicated that Turkey was preparing to establish a military presence there, including radar systems, air defenses and a Turkish commando force to operate them.
The officials said Israel believes Ankara could try to advance a similar move again in the future. According to the Israeli account, intelligence indicated that Turkey was preparing first to deploy radar at the base, followed later by air-defense systems and Turkish commandos tasked with operating them.
Israel presented the intelligence to U.S. officials, arguing that such a deployment could alter the regional balance of power and restrict Israel’s freedom of aerial action.
Israeli officials also warned that the deployment could complicate any future Israeli strike on Iran. The al-Duhur base is located in Idlib province, roughly 70 kilometers from the Syrian-Turkish border. Officials said Israel did not identify a precise timetable for the Turkish deployment but viewed the airbase as a potential site for a deeper Turkish military foothold in Syria.
Israel said the intelligence was shared both with Washington and with Syrian officials in an effort to stop the move diplomatically. Defense Minister Israel Katz made a similar claim in an unusual statement issued during Shabbat, saying the IDF had repeatedly recommended striking the base because of what he described as clear intelligence regarding Turkish intentions.
According to an Israeli official, when diplomatic messages failed to produce a change, Israel decided to send a military signal. The strike targeted, among other things, the airbase’s runways in an effort to prevent equipment or personnel from arriving by air and, above all, to warn the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu described the operation in similar terms. “We will not tolerate a Turkish military buildup moving southward, because it threatens us,” Netanyahu said. “We saw an intention by Turkey to establish itself at an airfield south of its line, near Aleppo, and we sent a message: Don’t.”
Public reports said the August 18 strike damaged runways and other facilities at the base. No casualties were reported. “Because the diplomatic message did not get through, Israel conveyed the message through a pinpoint strike, a warning strike,” an Israeli security official said.
“We have no interest in escalation, neither with Syria nor with Turkey,” the official added, also rejecting claims that the strike was politically motivated.
The same official said Mossad chief Roman Gofman strongly urged Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shibani not to allow Turkey to establish such a presence. “Gofman really implored the Syrian foreign minister not to let Turkey do this, but the Syrians did not internalize the message,” the official said.
Syria rejects Israel’s claim that a permanent Turkish military presence was planned at the site. Al-Shibani said Damascus had made clear to Israel that there was no intention to establish a Turkish base or permanent Turkish military presence there, and that rehabilitation work at the airfield was intended to restore it for use by the Syrian Air Force.
Turkey has also denied that Turkish forces were present at the base or that it planned to establish a military base there. Ankara says its military cooperation with Syria is focused on training and professional assistance.
The new details come after U.S. envoy Tom Barrack suggested the strike may also have been influenced by domestic Israeli politics, a claim Israeli officials have strongly rejected. For Israel, however, the concern extends beyond the immediate confrontation.
Officials fear that any Turkish radar and air-defense network established deeper inside Syria could eventually constrain Israeli air operations not only in Syria, but also along routes that could be relevant in a future confrontation with Iran.

Israel, Turkiye and the new regional reordering
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:35:48 UTC
03:35:48 KST

Israel, Turkiye and the new regional reordering
In Syria, Israel is not only at odds with Turkiye but also with the regional and international consensus.
On Tuesday, Israeli fighter jets attacked Abu al-Duhur airbase in northwestern Syria, drawing condemnations from the United States, the United Kingdom, the United Nations, as well as regional countries. The Israeli government claimed that it had intelligence of Turkish military movement to the site.
In a subsequent interview, US Ambassador to Turkiye and Special Envoy for Syria Tom Barrack said the US had received this intelligence from the Israelis six days before the attack. However, US intelligence conducted its own due diligence and found no basis for the claim.
The incident not only reflects a shift in the dynamics between Turkiye and Israel, but also signals a regional reordering that the latter is no longer at the centre of.
The Turkish response
Seeing the Israeli attack on the Syrian base as a provocation, Ankara refrained from escalating and instead provided an off-ramp out of the crisis. It framed the issue not in bilateral terms but as one between Israel and the US, and between Israel and the regional and international consensus.
Normally, there is a deconfliction mechanism between Turkiye and Israel. However, as Barrack indicated in the interview, Israel did not warn Turkiye about the attack, which could have triggered a military response.
The US envoy called for a deconfliction mechanism, but such an initiative can be effective only if the sides involved want it to be. In this case, there is no evidence that Israel sought de-escalation. In fact, it appears escalation was the intended outcome, as Israel notified neither Turkiye nor the US about the attack and acted on a pretext that the US intelligence found no basis for – a ploy to boost Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s electoral campaign.
After the US-imposed lull on the Iran front, Netanyahu is likely seeking escalation on other fronts, be it Syria, Lebanon or Gaza, in the run-up to the Israeli election. The challenge for Turkiye would be to avoid taking Netanyahu’s bait while also preventing the normalisation of such aggression.
That would require direct intervention by US President Donald Trump to rein in Netanyahu. Indeed, a trilateral deconfliction mechanism can work and be credible only if the US throws real weight behind it.
But even if a mechanism is in place, it would not change the fact that Syria has altered the lens through which Turkiye and Israel view each other. For a long time, the core of Turkiye’s discontent with Israel was the Palestinian issue. Hence, it was more humanitarian-, identity- and solidarity-based in nature.
Today, Ankara views Israeli attempts to undermine the Syrian transition as having direct repercussions for its national security. Therefore, Turkiye is no longer seeing Israel solely through the prism of the Palestinian question. Rather, it increasingly sees it as a national security challenge, with Israeli regional revisionism threatening its interests.
The international consensus on Syria
From the Eastern Mediterranean to the Horn of Africa and the wider Middle East, Turkiye and Israel have conflicting policies, priorities and threat perceptions. Despite this, Syria serves as a microcosm of Turkiye and Israel’s visions of the regional order.
Ankara wants its southern neighbour to be centralised, stable and capable militarily. In contrast, Israel wants a Syria that is weak, fragmented and bereft of serious military might.
Yet this is not merely a conflict between Turkish and Israeli visions. Israel is at odds with the regional and international consensus on Syria. The US, the UK, Europe and regional states have all supported a centralised and stable government in Damascus. In an ironic way, the only other regional state that probably wants a weak or failed Syria is Iran.
Like any other sovereign state, Syria will have an army. If Israel believes that the only way to ensure its own security is by keeping its neighbouring or regional states weak, fragmented and bereft of military capability, this is a recipe for perpetual wars and for regional and international isolation.
The undermining of the Syrian state and the failure of its transition would pave the way for non-state actors and radicalism, which would bode ill for the entire region, including Israel. Indeed, neighbouring Lebanon should serve as a cautionary tale. The Israeli occupation and the weakness of the Lebanese state gave birth to and empowered Hezbollah.
Post-Abrahamic Middle East
Israel and Turkiye’s ideas of regional order are also at odds. The recent Mecca Pact, which brought together Turkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, is not inherently anti-Israel. However, it represents a regional shift that signals the failure of the order envisioned by the Abraham Accords, or similar initiatives such as India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor (IMEC) or the strategic partnership between India, Israel, the United Arab Emirates, and the US known as I2U2.
The Abrahamic vision of the regional order was premised on Arab-Israeli normalisation and cooperation under the US security umbrella. Hard containment of Iran, soft containment of Turkiye, and de-emphasising the Palestinian issue were also part of the same vision.
Inherently, this Abrahamic vision had more to do with Israel and its regional normalisation than the Arab states and their needs and priorities.
However, with its aggressive and revisionist policies, Israel has deepened the prospect of its regional isolation, increased the cost of any normalisation, and doomed this Abrahamic – or Israeli-centric – vision of regional order.
Israeli revisionism is not only driving a wedge between Israel and other major regional states, but it is also revealing the gap between Israel and the US on the question of regional reordering.
While Israel opposes the Mecca Pact, Trump has hailed it, likely seeing it as aligned with his strategy of burden-sharing and burden-shifting with regional allies, and as enjoying more regional legitimacy and acceptance. The US position might also reflect a recalibration of Washington’s regional vision.
Over the last decade, the US invested heavily in creating a regional order premised on Israel and the Arab-Gulf states. But this was essentially an Israeli-centric project for the regional order.
This vision is no longer tenable, and no one is more responsible for its demise than Israel itself.

In Sweden, police probe online networks after a girl was killed in a sword attack at a school
Kyiv • UNN
The 18-year-old attacker killed a female student and seriously wounded two teenagers. Police are examining his links to online communities that promote violence.
Swedish police are investigating whether the 18-year-old man who attacked high school students with a sword on Friday, killing one, was involved in online communities that promote violence in schools, a police source told Reuters, UNN writes.
Details
The attacker stormed a school in the central Swedish town of Fagersta, also seriously injuring two teenagers before being arrested by police. The parents of the 17-year-old girl told the local newspaper Fagersta-Posten that their daughter had died as a result of the attack.
Police are investigating whether a TikTok account that posted a photograph of a sword 20 minutes before the attack belonged to the suspect, a Reuters source said. According to the newspaper Dagens Nyheter, the image was likely taken in a school toilet.
Before it was deleted on Friday, the month-old account contained videos mentioning two incidents of mass violence in Sweden and Norwegian far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, the newspaper writes. One of the videos mentioned the 2015 attack in which a masked man killed a teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhättan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by police.
"Investigators are looking into various online communities that may have incited the suspect to carry out the attack," a police source said.
Several party leaders canceled planned appearances on Saturday, suspending their campaign ahead of the September 13 election. Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson traveled to Fagersta to offer condolences to the families of those killed and visit the injured.
"What should never have happened has happened again," Kristersson told reporters in Fagersta. "Our thoughts are first and foremost with the families who have been incredibly severely affected by this," he said.
Sweden's worst mass shooting took place in February 2025 at a school in the south-central city of Örebro, when an armed man killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself.
On Saturday, police clarified that the suspect in the Fagersta attack had not been injured, contrary to what they had said on Friday.
"A service weapon was used, but the perpetrator was not injured in connection with the arrest and did not require medical attention," a police spokesperson told the daily newspaper Aftonbladet.
Prosecutors ordered the man's detention on suspicion of murder and several counts of attempted murder.
"The investigation is at an intensive stage. We are conducting interviews and gathering information, but I cannot go into details," prosecutor Ann-Sofie Trossing told Reuters.

In comedy clubs, Chinese women are having the last laugh
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

From Beijing comedy clubs to New York stages, China's female comedians are using stand-up to tell new stories about modern China.
On a Wednesday night not long ago, a crowd of Beijingers packed into Tribute Bar on Lucky Street. Beer glasses clinked, conversations faded, and the crowd of Chinese and expats turned towards a tiny stage for the night's open mic.
A young Chinese woman with long straight hair stepped into the spotlight. She wore black-framed glasses, a fitted black dress and high heels — a combination of nerdy and sassy. The room erupted into applause.
With a poker face, she started her set.
"I'm Alex Shi. Last name and pronoun," she paused, the audience cheered. "Alex isn't my real name. It's what people know me as on stage. Off stage, my real name is none of your business."
She adjusted her microphone.
"In a few days it'll be… what?"
The audience shouted answers.
"Yeah… the anniversary of my break-up. This room is a very good representation of my 2025… full of unavailable men."
More laughter.
The jokes came quickly, drawing on dating, situationships, awkward realities of modern relationships and cultural misunderstandings. Some stories resonated with Chinese audience members, whose lives are in a cross-cultural world, while others landed with the foreigners in the room.
Shi's entire performance was in English. She learnt the language in China and, despite building a career in Beijing's comedy scene, when we spoke a few weeks after the show Shi told me she has never performed stand-up in Chinese.
"It's like I've never dated Timothy Chalamet. Not because I don't want to — I just never tried," she laughed.
Shi imagines she would be "a very different person" if she ever stepped onto a Chinese-language stage.
It was at open mic nights in Beijing's multicultural Chaoyang district, filled with bars and restaurants popular with expats, that Shi first discovered she could make strangers laugh. Those early laughs gave her the confidence to keep returning.
"I started doing live storytelling first," she said told me later, "The end goal wasn't to be funny, but I got scattered laughs."
Open mics were democratic, she realised.
"Anyone could have a go".
So, she did.
From the Irish pub Paddy O'Shea's, to Lazy Bar and now Tribute Bar, Shi has gradually built a stage persona in English. She only lands a headline show every few months, and could arguably have a better chance of making a full-time career in China's much larger Mandarin stand-up market, she has stayed with the English-language scene. Today, Shi still balances comedy with documentary filmmaking to pay the bills, although she hopes one day stand-up will become her full-time career.
Like many comedians, Shi writes from her own life, but she insists comedy isn't therapy or activism.
"It's given me a community that turns out to be more understanding of my mental health than any other community I have," she says.
Her philosophy is simple: "Be funny first."
And Shi is not alone. Dawn Wong, a Chinese comedian based in Shanghai, went viral after turning her wedding speech into a stand-up routine in English and has an online following of more than 100,000.
Wong built her reputation on sharp observations about modern life, shifting effortlessly between relationships, Chinese family dynamics and cross-cultural misunderstandings. In English, she jokes about Donald Trump and American politics as comfortably as she pokes fun at Chinese perspectives on the United States, inviting audiences to laugh at the absurdities on both sides.
During COVID lockdown, Wong became widely known for her satirical daily videos chronicling life under restrictions, blurring the line between comedy and social commentary. There were problems, but more on that, later.
For these women, the microphone, the stage and a foreign language have become a form of liberation.
Wong once told the audience during a Beijing comedy show in 2025 that performing in English made her feel freer to express herself.
English liberates comedians like Wong and Shi from the cultural judgement they fear in Chinese. On stage, these funny women are able to tell their own stories on their own terms because what English really offers is distance. It allows female comedians to step outside their identity as Chinese women and the expectations of who they are supposed to be. It allows them to observe their own society from another perspective, and to say things that feel impossible to say in Chinese.
As one comedian, who wanted to remain anonymous, put it: censorship constrains political observations and traditional views can do the same when it comes to women's role.
"Some words you can say out loud in English, but not in Chinese," she said.
Stories that matter
The same microphone, it turns out, can mean very different things.
Thousands of kilometres away in New York, Maizi Li took to the stage to tell her stories in Chinese for a very different reason. For Li, the microphone was never just about making people laugh.
Born in Beijing's mountainous Yanqing district, Li has spent much of her life moving — first from the north to the south of China, then Britain and finally New York. Every move brought another chance to start again.
"I've spent my whole life becoming an outsider," she says. "But every time I moved, I wasn't running away. I was searching for a freer life."
As she becomes more comfortable in American society, Li hopes to perform in English one day. But for now, Chinese remains the language through which she tells her stories.
The former feminist activist now lives in Brooklyn, where she works with low-income Chinese migrant families, supporting children with autism, while also running what she describes as America's first independent Asian LGBTQ choir.
Long before Li performed stand-up in the US, she was already one of the most recognisable faces of China's young feminist movement. She helped pioneer a new generation of street activism that used performance, humour and spectacle to challenge gender inequality.
Wearing a blood-splattered wedding dress, Li joined the now-famous "Bloody Brides" campaign to protest domestic violence. She also helped organise the "Occupy Men's Toilets" movement in the southern city of Guangzhou, where women symbolically took over men's public toilets to highlight the chronic shortage of facilities for women. Following one of her advocacy campaigns, the Guangzhou municipal government increased the number of public toilets for women.
In March 2015, Li was detained for 37 days along with four other activists — known internationally as the "Feminist Five" — for planning to distribute anti-sexual harassment stickers on public transport ahead of International Women's Day. Their detention triggered an international campaign demanding their release including from then-US presidential candidate Hillary Clinton.
Unlike Alex Shi, who stumbled into comedy through Beijing's English-language open mics, Li first stepped onto a comedy stage using Chinese language after leaving China for New York with her partner three years ago.
Her first performance — at Women's Initiative, a platform that showcases women's stories and hosts annual Pride Month events — was deeply personal.
Rather than inventing fictional characters or telling observational jokes, Li drew directly from her life — her journey as a feminist activist, her same-sex marriage, and the experience of police disrupting her wedding celebration in China.
"The personal is political," she told me. "I've always tried to live by that."
For her second performance, Li chose a very different subject and continued to perform in Chinese to New York's large Chinese-speaking community. Instead of activism, she spoke about her grandmother.
Li's grandmother belonged to a generation of women whose lives were often overlooked. Yet Li credits her grandmother's quiet love with shaping the person she has become.
The audience cried.
Unlike the sharp, self-deprecating humour that filled Beijing's comedy clubs, Li's performance felt closer to a personal confession. Laughter came, but so did tears.
"It was the first time I'd publicly talked about my grandmother," Li says. "To realise that people connected with that story was incredibly moving."
Like Wong and Shi, Li believes that, in today's China, stand-up has become one of the cultural spaces where discussions about women's lives have flourished.
"Women's rights advocacy has become increasingly visible because it doesn't directly challenge political power or government policy," she says. "Female stand-up empowers women. Stand-up encourages women to step onto the stage."
Mixed messages
For decades, Chinese women have grown up with Mao Zedong's famous slogan that "women hold up half the sky". During the Mao era, women were encouraged to enter the workforce and participate in building the new socialist China. It represented an enormous shift from the traditional idea that women's primary place was inside the home.
The legacy of that change is still visible in everyday Chinese life. Most Chinese women, for example, keep their own surnames after marriage rather than adopting their husband's name. Some families even choose to give a child the mother's surname.
A consequence of China's Family (one-child) policy, for which I am personally grateful, is that as an only daughter my family's limited resources went into my education and eventually helped support master's degree. My father once told me that if I'd had a brother, I might have had to leave school early and work to help pay for his university education.
But government policy could not erase generations of son preference or traditional expectations about women's roles.
This is the contradiction facing many modern Chinese women. Society encourages them to become educated, financially independent and professionally successful. Yet older expectations can still demand that they marry at the "right" age, have children, care for their own parents and take responsibility for their husband's family.
Women face intense scrutiny over age and appearance and a woman who is highly successful or outspoken can still be described as "too strong".
The gap between the rhetoric of equality and political power is also striking: very few women make it into the senior ranks of Chinese politics.
Within these contradictions, female stand-up has found so much material.
Dating, marriage, divorce, children, beauty standards, mothers-in-law and disappointing boyfriends become punchlines because they are also familiar pressures in women's everyday lives. Female comedians can take expectations that have traditionally been directed at women and turn the gaze around.
That helps explain why one of Yang Li's most famous jokes — asking how men could be "so average, yet so confident" — struck such a nerve.
The rise of 'pǔxìn nán'
Before the American-style stand-up comedy arrived in China, audiences were already familiar with xiangsheng, or crosstalk, a traditional comic performance dating back to the Qing dynasty in the mid-19th century.
Typically performed by two comedians who exchange rapid-fire dialogue, wordplay, and satire, xiangsheng has long been one of China's best-known performing arts. And for most of its history, the stage was overwhelmingly dominated by men.
But in a reversal of long-standing stereotypes, the new generation of female comedians in China are turning the spotlight back on men.
Yang Li became one of China's most recognisable comedians after joking that some men could "look so average, but can be so confident"—a line that quickly gave rise to the now-famous phrase, 普信男, pǔxìn nán.
It was more than a joke. Reminiscent of Sarah Hagi's English language gag: "God give me the confidence of a mediocre white dude" — Yang's line flipped a familiar script.
Yang turned scrutiny of women's appearance, age, career choices and marital status back on men, poking fun not at their looks alone, but at what many women saw as unquestioned confidence and entitlement.
The related Weibo social media hashtag attracted more than 210 million views and 84,000 discussions. Yang herself amassed more than 2 million followers on the platform.
Alex Shi believes comedy has become another way women are reshaping public conversations, alongside women rejecting the male gaze in cinema, challenging misogynistic double standards in news coverage and campaigning to break menstrual taboos, Growing visibility of women in comedy reflects broader social change and a much broader cultural shift, she believes.
Maizi Li agrees: "When women take the stage," she says, "they take ownership of the microphone."
Comedy star Jiaoying Summers, who moved to the US at 18, performs primarily in English and is the first Chinese comedian to headline New York's Apollo Theater, says stand-up has given Chinese women more opportunities for their voices to be heard.
"I think women's points of view have historically been overlooked, dismissed, or even ridiculed in many parts of society," Summers told me. "Audiences are realising that the female perspective isn't a niche perspective, it's half the world."
The cost of being funny
The growing visibility of China's female comedians has also brought growing scrutiny. For some, the consequences have come from authorities.
In 2022, comedian Dawn Wong said police took her away after a satirical performance about COVID-19 lockdowns attracted official attention. She later returned to the stage, but the incident served as a reminder that, in China, comedy can carry political consequences.
For others, the backlash has come from audiences.
Yang Li's popularity also came at a price. Despite becoming one of China's best-known stand-up comics, she faced fierce criticism from some male internet users who accused her of promoting sexism and "man-hating". In 2021, JD.com dropped her from an advertising campaign following an online backlash, illustrating the commercial risks that can accompany gender-related comedy in China.
Yang has consistently refused to apologise for her comedy, arguing many critics had only seen short clips of her routines rather than the full performances. She also rejects the label of feminist icon.
"I hope people won't make me an opinion leader or a pioneer for women," she told Chinese media. "I'm just an ordinary stand-up comedian writing jokes. I don't have a theory, nor can I carry such a big label."
That caution was something I encountered repeatedly while reporting this story.
Several female comedians declined interview requests. One industry insider suggested that speaking to Western media carried greater perceived risks because, unlike Chinese media, there is no domestic editorial review — what Western-style journalism might label "censorship" — before publication.
Ironically, the experience echoed the contradiction at the heart of this story. On stage, women joke about dating, marriage, family expectations and gender roles. Off stage, some become reluctant to discuss those same subjects in an interview.
Jiaoying Summers said that earlier in her career she worried about adjusting her material for different audiences, particularly when performing in more conservative parts of the United States. Eventually, she stopped trying to please everyone.
Today, Summers says, whether performing for Chinese, American or even Australian audiences (she will perform in Sydney in October), she concentrates on her own life.
"I talk about family, marriage, gender, culture, motherhood, all the things that affect me personally. I realised that I'm not onstage to make friends," she says. "My job is to be funny. People can love me or hate me, as long as I make them laugh, I've done my job."
Shi puts it even more simply: "Young Chinese women have things to say. And the funny ones make them into jokes."

“The person killed in this incident is a young 17-year-old female. Her family has been informed,” police said on Saturday, declining to release further details.

MOSCOW, August 22. /TASS/. Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukrainian enterprises in response to Ukraine’s attacks on civilian targets in Russia, so it was the Kiev regime that opened a ‘Pandora’s box,’ Russian President Vladimir Putin told Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin in an interview.
In his words, Russian retaliatory strikes are more devastating than Ukraine’s strikes on Russia and produce a most positive effect on the battlefield situation.
He also said that the enemy is trying to intimidate Russians and disrupt the upcoming parliamentary elections, due in September, but these attempts will fail.
Below are the head of the state’s key remarks.
Kiev’s strikes
Ukraine’s attempt to defeat Russia in 40 days by carrying out massive drone and missile attacks is a risky and provocative move: "If we speak about what is happening now, then it is, of course, a result of a yet another provocative and risky move by the Kiev regime and its Western curators, who aimed to deal another strategic defeat to Russia," he said. "This time, as it is known, they wanted to achieve this in 40 days, and with the help of massive missile and drone attacks on our civilian sites and logistical routes."
The goal of Ukraine’s strikes on Russia was to make it collapse by destroying whole economic sectors and undermining the unity of its people: "In short, the goal was to bring Russia to collapse - something they have long dreamed of and something they constantly talk about."
The Kiev regime got an opposite result when it started to deliver drone and missile strikes on Russia: "Of course, no turning point in the confrontation with Russia could have occurred, nor has it occurred. The Kiev regime and its masters cannot gain any advantage; they have not gained it and they never will."
Russia’s response
Russia will always respond to strikes on its territory, including on the logistical infrastructure: "Do you want to disrupt our logistics? Well, our retaliatory measures will not be long in coming."
By deciding to launch strikes on civilian sites in Russia, the Kiev regime has opened a Pandora’s box and got retaliatory attacks on its most sensitive areas in return: "The Kiev regime has set the goal of harming our economy. What did it do? It was the one to open this Pandora’s box. Well, here’s what you get in response - strikes on the most sensitive areas of your economy, which, frankly speaking, are already struggling."
Russia has intensified its attacks on Ukrainian enterprises in response to Ukraine’s attacks on civilian targets in Russia: "We started to respond to the enemy’s actions regarding our civilian production sites and logistical network."
"At the same time, measures taken by the Russian armed forces are way more painful and way more devastating."
Wheat is among the main items of Ukrainian exports, but logistical problems caused by Russia’s retaliatory strikes, will not lead to a shortage on global markets: "As far as global problems are concerned, hardly anything will change, because, first of all, we have great export potential. Our agriculture minister [Oksana Lut] reported just yesterday that [the export potential] is no less than 60 million metric tons. This is a very good cushion. Yes, we do face certain difficulties related to the export of our goods, but we are resolving them, which means that there will be no deficit on the global market."
Situation in the special op zone
Russia’s strikes on targets in Ukraine have a direct positive effect on the battlefield: "Certanly, this has the most direct and the most positive effect on the battlefield from the point of view of achieving military goals."
"Of course these strikes are effective. They are timely. And, undoubtedly, they help our fighters, our heroes to resolve their combat missions. Why? Because they disrupt [the enemy’s] ability to deliver equipment and ammunition, to rotate personnel on the line of combat. They disrupt the capacity of defense enterprises to improve their products, which is exactly what they do with the direct involvement and support of their Western sponsors."
Russian troops have accelerated their offensive operations and continue to successfully attain the goals of the special military operation: "The adversary’s actions have had no effect on the situation on the battlefield. Moreover, not only our troops continue to advance in all directions, they have also accelerated the pace of their offensive operations."
In his words, the Russian armed forces keep successfully coping with their tasks until the goals of the special military operation are achieved.
Kiev’s unacceptable and exotic proposals
Russia’s response to Ukraine’s provocative actions are painful for Kiev, and so the enemy is trying to prevent possible catastrophic developments through mediators: "Russia’s response to a yet another provocative act by the Kiev regime is apparently quite painful, leading to serious consequences and bringing the situation in certain crucial areas to critical levels. That is why now the Kiev government is trying to find a way out from the situation that they themselves provoked, by seeking help from mediators, whose opinions we undoubtedly value."
According to the president, the Kiev regime is trying to prevent the current situation from escalating into catastrophic scenarios, and, apparently "they are already realizing the possibility of such a scenario."
Putin described the latest proposals received by Russia from Kiev as "exotic" and unacceptable: "We are always ready for dialogue, but only based on realities on the ground."
The Kiev regime "is probing various directions of possible agreements."
"It would be premature to get ahead of ourselves and speculate on what possible agreements could be based on."
Russia will not be intimidated
Kiev’s strikes on de-facto unprotected civilians and civilian infrastructure: "The loss of a human life is always a tragedy - for the family, for friends and for the whole country."
Russia needs to improve its air defense network, enhance coordination between its security agencies and civilian authorities, engage state enterprises and private companies into the effort, which is "of particular importance in the run-up to elections to the State Duma."
"The enemy is trying to intimidate us and to disrupt the vote. We will not let them do this. I’m sure that this attempt to exert psychological pressure and psychologically impact the Russian society is doomed to fail. We will certainly continue to strengthen the Russian statehood and the legitimacy of its authorities.".

A moderate earthquake of magnitude 5.9 shakes eastern Japan. No tsunami alert is issued

Unknown Publisher

A moderate, magnitude 5.9 earthquake shakes eastern Japan. No tsunami alert is issued
TOKYO (AP) — A moderate earthquake with a preliminary magnitude of 5.9 rattled eastern Japan, including the Tokyo area, early on Sunday, but there was no danger of a tsunami, the country’s meteorological agency said.
According to the Japan Meteorological Agency, the quake occurred in the southern Ibaraki prefecture, at a depth of 70 kilometers (42 miles).
The United States Geological Survey recorded a preliminary magnitude of 5.8.
There were no immediate reports of injuries or damage. The government set up a task force to assess the extent of possible damage, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said on X.
The temblor also set off emergency quake alerts on mobile phones and shook the Tokyo area, but NHK public television showed traffic on roads in nearby cities, including Mito and Saitama, seemingly normal.
An underground water pipe ruptured in Tokyo’s eastern ward of Koto, with water pouring out onto the road, NHK footage showed. About 460 homes in Tokyo had power outages, according to TEPCO Power Grid.
There were no reports of anything out of the ordinary from about a dozen nuclear power plants and other facilities that handle nuclear materials, the Nuclear Regulation Authority said.
Last month, a magnitude 7.1 quake struck the Kumamoto area on Japan’s southernmost island of Kyushu, killing 38 people and injuring 364. It also destroyed more than 1,500 buildings and damaged nearly 20,000 others.

Scores of people kidnapped from a mosque as armed groups attacked multiple villages in Nigeria
A number of people were kidnapped from a mosque in a spree of abductions at several villages in Nigeria ‘s north-central Niger state, police said Saturday.
The assailants attacked a mosque in Kpenya village after attacks in a string of villages in the remote Borgu Local Government Area of Niger state Friday, police spokesperson Wasiu Abiodun said.
Such attacks are common in Nigeria, where multiple armed groups operate, killing and kidnapping people for ransom. The groups sometimes clash in competition with each other. No group has claimed responsibility for the Friday attacks.
Abiodun did not provide figures but said no lives were lost in the Friday attacks, and said the military was deployed to the area. Residents said scores of people were abducted, with some estimating between 60 and 80 people were kidnapped. A search for survivors was underway Saturday.
Borgu area council chairman Abdullahi Mohammed Nasir said at least 60 people were kidnapped and an unspecified number of people sustained gunshot injuries while trying to escape the gunmen.
“People were abducted while praying at a Juma’at mosque on Friday,” Nasir said. “That was when the bad people came and surrounded the mosque and took them away.”
Zubairu Umar Talba, a youth leader in the Dekara area in Borgu, told The Associated Press that his 85-year-old father was among those who were taken. “Nobody can tell you the exact number of people abducted because, so far, about 80 of our people have been abducted and many have fled the area,” he said.

Latvia hit by most destructive storm since 2005 – more than 100,000 households without electricity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

03:21:24 KST

On Saturday evening, 22 August, Latvia was hit by its most destructive storm since January 2005, according to meteorological data.
According to electricity distribution operator Sadales tīkls, more than 100,000 households are currently without electricity.
So far, the storm has hit Zemgale, Sēlija and Latgale the hardest, as well as parts of Kurzeme. Moving in from the south, the storm has now reached Vidzeme.
The strongest wind gusts recorded in Latvia by 8 p.m. reached 26 metres per second in Bauska, Saldus and Ventspils and 27 metres per second in Rēzekne, according to data from the Latvian Environment, Geology and Meteorology Centre.
In Kurzeme, southwesterly winds are beginning to ease, while parts of Vidzeme are expected to experience the strongest winds only during the night.
As previously reported, wind gusts are expected to reach 25–30 metres per second across much of Latvia, with an even more powerful storm possible along the Vidzeme coast. Winds are expected to be less severe in southwestern Kurzeme and around Rūjiena.
The storm is expected to snap and uproot large numbers of trees, potentially blocking roads and railway lines and damaging power lines. Further widespread damage is also expected.

Seventeen-year-old girl killed in sword attack at school in Sweden

A 17-year-old girl has been killed after a teenager brandishing a sword attacked students at a school in Sweden, police have confirmed.
Three other people were wounded in the incident during classes in the central town of Fagersta on Friday afternoon, including two boys aged 12 and 17 who sustained minor injuries.
The third person, who was also under 18, was also left with minor injuries and has been discharged from hospital, Swedish news agency TT reported.
The parents of the 17-year-old girl told local newspaper Fagersta-Posten their daughter was killed in the attack.
An 18-year-old man has been arrested over the incident at Brinell high school.
Swedish police are investigating whether the suspect was involved in online communities promoting school violence, a police source said.
Detectives are investigating whether a TikTok account that posted a picture of a sword 20 minutes before the attack belonged to the person responsible, the source told Reuters.
The image appeared to have been taken in a restroom at the school, according to the Dagens Nyheter newspaper.
Before the image was taken down on Friday, the month-old account contained videos that referred to two episodes of mass violence in Sweden and to the far-right mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik, who killed 77 people in Norway in 2011.
One of the videos referenced a 2015 attack in which a masked swordsman killed a teaching assistant and two boys at a school in Trollhättan, western Sweden, before being shot dead by police.
“The investigators are looking into various online communities that may have egged on the suspect to carry out the attack,” the police source said.
Several party leaders cancelled planned speeches on Saturday, pausing campaigning ahead of Sweden’s 13 September general election.
The prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, and opposition leader Magdalena Andersson travelled to Fagersta to offer condolences to the bereaved family and visit the injured.
Kristersson told reporters: “What should never happen has happened again. Our thoughts go first and foremost to the families who have been incredibly hard hit by this.”
Sweden’s worst mass shooting occurred in February 2025 at a school in the south-central city of Örebro, when a gunman killed 10 people before turning the weapon on himself.
On Saturday, the police clarified that the suspect in the Fagersta attack had not been shot, contrary to what they had said on Friday.
“Service weapons were used but the perpetrator has not been injured in connection with the arrest, and has not been in need of medical attention,” a police spokesperson told the Aftonbladet daily.
Prosecutors ordered the man’s detention on suspicion of murder and several counts of attempted murder.
