Too old for aliyah? This centenarian Jewish couple proved age is no barrier to moving to Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:04:54 UTC
03:04:54 KST

At first glance, the basic story of Sandy and Rosalie Goldstein’s aliyah seems unremarkable and not much different than the typical aliyah experience. The retired couple made aliyah from Englewood, New Jersey, in March 2023 and settled in Netanya, near their daughter, where they enjoy spending time with their family in Israel.
However, upon closer examination, the tale becomes far more compelling. That’s because Sandy will be celebrating his 105th birthday next week, and 100-year-old Rosalie will be blowing out 101 candles in January. One more impressive statistic: The couple will be observing their 79th wedding anniversary next month.
Sitting in their apartment on a sweltering summer afternoon, bowed by old age but not broken, Sandy and Rosalie tell the story of their lives, their aliyah, their thoughts about Israel, and their wishes for the future.
Though it’s nearly 35 degrees Celsius outside, their apartment is quite cool, and they both wear warm clothes to ward off the air-conditioning chill. Sandy wears a white textured crew-neck sweater, and Rosalie wears a cream-colored jacket with red embroidered trim over a red-and-black patterned blouse. Her nails are painted red to match her blouse, and she wears several rings, a bracelet, and a watch.
Sandy sits at the head of the table, Rosalie is to his left, and I sit close to his right because he has hearing issues. I speak slowly and clearly.
Born in 1921 in Fall River, Massachusetts, Sandy’s parents moved to the Borough Park neighborhood of Brooklyn when he was a child. His parents operated a dry cleaning and tailoring store. Sandy’s mother was a talented seamstress, and his father ran the cleaning operation.
As an enterprising 12-year-old, Sandy sold copies of the Saturday Evening Post to commuters leaving the subway station for 10 cents, making two cents profit on each copy. Later, he worked in his parents’ business, riding his bicycle to deliver clothes to clients and collect payment.
Sandy attended City College in New York and studied accounting. On a lark, he took a civil service exam to qualify to work in the federal government. On December 7, 1941, the Empire of Japan attacked the US Pacific Fleet that was stationed at Pearl Harbor in Oahu, Hawaii, bringing the US into World War II.
“All of a sudden after Pearl Harbor,” he recalls, “I would get telegrams every day saying that I was needed in Washington.”
Evidently, Sandy had scored high enough on the civil service exam to qualify for government work. He came to Washington and worked for the War Department for a year, handling accounting and vouchers. After the first year, the department was decentralized, and he returned to New York, working for the War Department there until the Japanese surrendered on August 15, 1945.
Sandy returned to City College, graduating with a degree in accounting, and becoming a CPA.
On Thanksgiving of 1947, Rosalie Aron, a Brooklyn native, was invited by her girlfriend to dinner, then went with her to a dance at the local synagogue. “I said to my girlfriend, ‘I’m looking for the tallest man here, because they were all shrimps.’ Sandy came with his friends, and he said that he was looking for the tallest girl there.”
The lanky Sandy invited Rosalie – the taller of the two friends – to go on a date with him. “We hit it off. Everything was smooth and likable,” recalls Sandy. Says Rosalie, “I could tell in a minute that he was flipping out over me.”
After their wedding in 1948, Rosalie worked briefly as a typist before becoming a stay-at-home mom. Looking at their wedding photos, Rosalie says with a smile, “I didn’t have a gray hair on my head.” The couple had three children – two girls and a boy – and were not fully Jewishly observant at the time.
Throughout his life, Sandy dedicated himself to community and Jewish causes, including many years of activism on behalf of Soviet Jewry, working for the freedom and emigration of Jews behind the Iron Curtain.
When their youngest child, Risa, became interested in Torah observance and joined NCSY, the National Conference of Synagogue Youth, the Jewish youth group sponsored by the Orthodox Union, Sandy and Rosalie followed suit and became more involved in religious practice.
After graduating high school, Risa spent a year in Israel studying at Neve Yerushalayim seminary, and her parents visited. Though it wasn’t their first trip to the country, this visit made a deep impression on them.
‘If not now, when?’
Some 10 years earlier, when the couple was in their 40s, they had actually considered aliyah and met with aliyah officials. “They were looking for CPAs to move to Israel, and we said that this was our opportunity. They interviewed us, and they asked him how old he was. He said he was 40, and they said that he was too old for aliyah,” Rosalie says, with a trace of irony in her voice.
Risa moved to Israel in 1995 and then returned to the US, making aliyah a second time in 2008.
Sandy and Rosalie lived in Englewood, NJ, near their older daughter. They both became ill with COVID-19 and were treated in a rehabilitation center. When they were released, the family decided it was time for them to move to Israel. As Risa says, “If not now, when?”
Rosalie adds, “There was always something that stopped us earlier. But when we thought the time was now, we retook it.”
Risa returned to the US in February 2023, helped her parents pack, and brought them to Israel on March 1 of that year. Rosalie was 97, and Sandy was 102. Risa had just relocated to Netanya, and her parents moved in with her until she remarried a year ago and settled nearby with her husband, Raymond Chazan.
Word had spread in Netanya that the elderly couple had made aliyah, and neighbors held an impromptu celebration in front of their building. “They had a big party, with singing and dancing, and I didn’t even know these people, and they didn’t know me. I was really overwhelmed with the reception,” says Rosalie.
In their family’s embrace
Since moving to Israel, Rosalie and Sandy have visitors on an almost daily basis – whether it is people from the neighborhood or one of their five grandchildren or 13 great-grandchildren. Sandy, an avid chess player for most of his 105 years, enjoys playing the game with his grandchildren and great-grandchildren.
“Moving at 97 and 102 was a massive leap,” Rosalie admits. “In truth, staying in our comfort zone made us procrastinate aliyah for a long time, but necessity pushed us to make the best decision of our lives. If we hadn’t taken that step, we would have missed the incredible joy of being surrounded by our extended family, including 13 great-grandchildren.”
Since their aliyah, Sandy and Rosalie have participated in numerous family events, including their daughter Risa’s remarriage last year, the brit milah (circumcision) of a great-grandson, at which Sandy was the sandak (godfather), and bar and bat mitzvahs.
“It’s amazing,” says Rosalie. “I didn’t know most of my great-grandchildren. And now they come, they kiss me, and they hug me, and they say, ‘I missed you.’” Fortunately, she adds, they all speak English.
Sandy is not much of a Hebrew speaker but has read the Bible many times in English.
“I recommend that everyone read it carefully,” he shares. He is particularly emphatic about God’s promise to the Jewish people that he would give them the Land of Israel. “In the first part of the Bible, God tells Abraham to go to Israel, and all of it will be yours. That’s the important point: all. Not 82%, not part here, part there, but all of it. And He said the same message to Isaac and Jacob.”
Longevity, life
On August 28, Sandy will celebrate his 105th birthday with a helping of his favorite flavor of ice cream – chocolate. He attributes his longevity to steady consumption of blueberries and yogurt, maintaining a balanced diet, and following his doctor’s instructions.
Rosalie, no slouch herself at age 100, when asked for the secret of her long life, looks at her husband and says, “I hang with him.”
What is the secret of their long and successful marriage? “I gave in to you all the time,” Rosalie says to Sandy, with a gentle smile. Sandy adds, “The secret is to talk about everything, and to compromise.”
Recalling his years of advocacy for Soviet Jews, Sandy comments, “I could have spent time as an accountant picking up clients and making money, but I chose not to. I chose to help Jews.”
Having lived through the Depression, World War II, the establishment of the State of Israel – “I heard it on the radio,” says Rosalie – and Oct. 7, the Goldsteins are happy to be home in Israel.
“It can be frightening at times,” she admits, “but it’s better than the alternative. The alternative was to stay. In America, there is more antisemitism growing every day. Here, we have fighters fighting for us on our behalf.”
Sandy is a bit more feisty and insists that Israel must eliminate Hamas and the PLO. “It’s about time and total victory. This is what we need.” At the age of 105, Sandy remains engaged and optimistic, and says, “You can’t pray and hope you’ll keep alive. You’ve got to fight first, and then pray.”
Rosalie also remains optimistic but is a bit more placid, saying, “Thank God, I feel pretty good. Not perfect, but pretty good. Over a century, you face many changes and challenges. Learning about tradition, running a kosher home, and welcoming friends into our home as a homemaker helped me grow, believe in myself, and pass those values to my children.”
As our hour-long visit comes to a close, I ask Rosalie and Sandy what message they most want to pass on to their descendants. “Never give up,” says Sandy. “Set a high goal and work for it. If you need tutors, get tutors. If you need help, get help. Persist.
“I have always said, ‘The best helping hand is at the end of your own arm.’ Throughout my life – from working hard as a CPA to advocating for Soviet Jewry – I learned that real accomplishment requires personal initiative and hard work. Goals are worth pursuing no matter how long they take. If something matters to you, keep striving for it – even if it takes a lifetime.”
To the Jewish community around the world, he adds, “Jews are one. Reform, Conservative, or Orthodox. We should all strive to help one another, and it’s time to come home to Israel.”
And what would they say to an older person who thinks that it’s too late to make a change in life and make aliyah? Reflects Rosalie, “If you’re well enough to get on a plane, come.”■
Aliyah after 65: Resources for retirees
Not everyone needs to wait until they become centenarians to make aliyah.
Retirees aged 65 and up are a significant minority of new immigrants to Israel. In 2025, 548 retirees made aliyah from North America with Nefesh B’Nefesh – more than 13% of the year’s 4,150 olim and substantially more than the 332 retirees who arrived during the pandemic year of 2020.
Miriam Naiman, senior liaison and special needs guidance manager, Post Aliyah & Advocacy Division for Nefesh B’Nefesh, says that the organization is seeing significant growth in the senior olim population, as more parents choose to make aliyah and reunite with their children and grandchildren in Israel.
Many older people are making aliyah while they are still independent, active, and able to make important decisions about how and where they want to build their lives in Israel. Senior olim choose a variety of living arrangements, from their own apartments to independent and assisted-living communities.
Making aliyah at this stage of life brings a distinct set of challenges, says Naiman, particularly around healthcare, community integration, and navigating Israel’s increasingly digital systems.
Naiman points out that leaving behind a familiar medical system, where individuals know their doctors, understand their coverage, and have established ways of managing their health, and entering an entirely new system can be daunting and overwhelming.
Nefesh B’Nefesh can help senior olim understand Israel’s healthcare landscape, learn how to advocate for themselves, and develop the knowledge and tools they need to navigate the system with greater confidence and independence.
Another growing area of support is digital literacy. Many essential aspects of everyday life in Israel, from healthcare and transportation to banking, government services, and translation, require the use of websites and mobile applications.
Every quarter, Nefesh B’Nefesh offers “Tech Made Simple,” a gathering where senior olim can become more familiar with these tools and receive individualized assistance navigating the apps and online services they need in daily life.
Readers interested in more information about services that Nefesh B’Nefesh offers retirees should visit nbn.org.il or call (02) 659-5800.

WATCH: Malki Roth’s family fought to bring her Sbarro killer to justice - but leaders failed to act
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:04:45 UTC
03:04:45 KST

Before we proceed to ambassadors and American Jewish leaders, an addendum.
I heard that a wise person once said, “Don’t say six million Jews were killed in the Holocaust. Say six million and one.” It’s easier to identify with one person than with six million.
Malki Roth was not the only victim of terror. The Jewish Virtual Library has collated statistics from a number of sources, including the Foreign Ministry, and it states that more than 4,800 Israeli and foreign civilians have been killed in Arab and Palestinian terrorist attacks since 1948 (including all of 1948, before the state was established in May). This does not include the pre-1948 acts of terror, such as those in Hebron and elsewhere in 1929, and many others. There have always been those who did not want us here.
Malki Roth was also not the only American, but her heartbreaking story has brought numerous issues to the forefront.
In a column published in the Israel Nation News on July 31, 2013, as Israel was about to release 104 terrorists, supposedly as a goodwill gesture to restart peace talks, Sherri Mandell – whose 13-year-old son Koby was murdered by Arab terrorists in May 2001, and who demonstrated along with others against the release – was quoted as saying (which she confirmed to the Magazine), “I’m happy that they were never found, because I don’t want to have to be horrified that Koby’s killers had been released by the State of Israel.”
Like his parents, Koby was an American citizen.
In Koby’s memory, Sherri and Seth Mandell created the Koby Mandell Foundation, which helps bereaved mothers, fathers, widows, orphans, and siblings to rebuild their lives and create meaning out of suffering.
Thinking back to the Taylor Force Act I described in Part II, I remembered another act. After Koby’s murder, the Koby Mandell Act was introduced into Congress on June 7, 2001. In short, it directs the US Attorney-General to establish within the Department of Justice (DOJ) an office to monitor acts of Palestinian terrorism, to offer rewards for information about terrorists, and – most important – to implement methods to “apprehend, indict, prosecute, and convict individuals who commit such acts.”
Sounds impressive. But it didn’t pass immediately, in that form.
Sarah Stern, founder and president of the Endowment for Middle East Truth, told the Magazine that the Koby Mandell Act was also introduced into the Senate on March 21, 2003, and was passed in December 2004 when it was “included as a title within the massive year-end federal omnibus spending bill signed by president George W. Bush.” According to the Congress.gov website, it was included in the Department of Justice’s Office for Victims of Overseas Terrorism (OVT). That office, as stated on its website, is “to support US victims of overseas terrorism by helping them navigate foreign criminal justice systems....”
Stern told the Magazine she worked on the bill for three years. Regarding the new OVT, Stern said, “They publish websites, pamphlets, and flow charts. Unfortunately, they have never prosecuted a single perpetrator who has committed acts of terrorism. What we envisioned for this office, and what it ended up doing, was a profound disappointment.”
The Magazine wrote to the OVT to ask if it has ever prosecuted terrorists. Its response was: “Refer to US District Court of DC.”
MALKI ROTH, 15, was one of three American citizens murdered in Sbarro. After the release of Ahlam Tamimi, who had masterminded the attack, there was no reaching out to the Roths on the part of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or any other senior Israeli figure.
Tamimi has lived the life of a celebrity in Jordan since the moment she returned there, after being freed in the Schalit deal.
In an interview filmed with her while she was still a prisoner in Israel, she was proud and joyful about the deaths she had orchestrated. She continues to promote the cause of terrorism and jihad through the media and in speeches throughout the Arab world.
Tamimi should have been extradited to the US, in compliance with a treaty signed by King Hussein, the father of today’s ruler of Jordan, and US president Bill Clinton in 1995. But that hasn’t happened, in spite of charges against Tamimi by the Department of Justice in 2013 and the FBI’s putting her on the Most Wanted Terrorists list in 2017.
US ambassadors to Israel
In pursuing US justice, the Roths sought out meetings with ambassadors to Israel, starting when Tamimi was released.
The first such meeting was with Dan Shapiro, who served in Israel, under president Barack Obama, from August 3, 2011, to January 20, 2017.
Arnold Roth said, “He and I met twice – once when I came to the US Embassy in Tel Aviv as part of a group of three grieving fathers whose children had been murdered by terrorists. Then privately, after his term as ambassador ended. He provided no meaningful support for our efforts to get justice, but was polite and empathetic; in our circumstances, that’s nothing to sneeze at.
“One outstanding issue relating to his term as ambassador has gotten little coverage.
“Years after it happened, he told me that when the 2011 Schalit deal was about to take place and the 1,027 terrorists were to walk free, the US Embassy, he said, had asked Israel not to free Tamimi, on the grounds that her bombing attack on Sbarro took US lives.
“He said the approach was rebuffed by Israel, and I know it was not at all reported at the time. I asked him who specifically was approached in the government of Israel. He said he could not tell me.”
Shapiro impressed him, said Roth, with his concern and empathy.
But Roth said that despite Shapiro being well-wired into the inner workings of Washington and in particular the State Department, and despite giving Roth assurances he would investigate in Washington and get back with what he could, no information ever came back.
“At some point, you wake to the realization that Washington insiders who convey – without saying it explicitly – that they don’t care that much about justice, Jordan, and the Tamimi case, actually have neither more nor less insight than the better guys from Washington. It’s a depressing situation – especially when it goes on and on for years.”
The Magazine asked Ambassador Shapiro to respond. He wrote, “The Roth family’s grief and anger is justified, and nothing can relieve it. The US relationship with Jordan is complex, and includes important strategic aspects. That said, I believe more US pressure should be exerted on Jordan to extradite Ahlam Tamimi, and have advocated for it.”
Following Shapiro’s response, Roth shared with the Magazine more details about the US request not to free Tamimi, citing an exchange he had with a journalist in February 2020.
“The journalist said, ‘Someone told me the US administration asked Israel before the Schalit deal not to release anyone with American blood on their hands. Do you know about this? Do you have a link to it reported somewhere?’
“I told him, ‘The US indeed said what you quoted. But in my opinion, there was no evidence at the time of the Schalit deal that any US official asked Israel to hold back those terrorists with American blood on their hands (like Tamimi). The relevant State Department press briefing at the time makes no mention.’
“The alleged intervention by the US on the eve of Tamimi being freed in the Schalit deal came up again in two ways,” he continued.
“The first is when I testified in the US Congress to its House Oversight Committee on National Security on February 2, 2016. I was seated beside Justice Department official, deputy assistant attorney-general Brad Wiegmann of the DOJ’s National Security Division. He’s caught on the video record of the session saying: ‘We certainly understand the concern about Israel’s recent release of prisoners that harmed Americans, a step the US urged Israel not to take.’”
Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah) was chairman of the US Congressional Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. In that 2016 hearing of the Subcommittee on National Security, “Seeking Justice for Victims of Palestinian Terrorism in Israel,” whose transcript is 60 pages long, Sherri Mandell submitted testimony, and Arnold Roth testified in person.
Ron DeSantis (R-Florida), the subcommittee chairman, concluded, “We face, as Americans, a global jihad, and Israel is ground zero for that fight. And when we have Americans visiting, studying, living in Israel, and they’re killed, they’re wounded by terrorists, we’re not going to forget that. We can’t forget that. And we will get justice. And we’ll be patient if we need to be, but we are not going to let justice be denied.”
“Secondly,” said Roth, “a letter dated January 30, 2012, came to Frimet and me from then-US attorney-general Eric Holder.” Extract: “The US Embassy in Tel Aviv, together with the Department of Justice and the Department of State, urged the Government of Israel prior to both releases in question not to release prisoners responsible for murdering or injuring US citizens before serving their full sentences.”
David M. Friedman served as US ambassador from May 15, 2017, until January 20, 2021.
Roth said, “I made efforts to engage with Friedman, starting right after he was nominated in the first Trump administration, before he was confirmed, and continuing over and over again until most of the way through his term of office.
“At some point, many months into this effort, I realized I had been defeated again and stopped trying.
“But this had an epilogue. Friedman and I did eventually meet and talk about the Tamimi case. That happened days after his term in Jerusalem ended. A helpful third party intervened. The meeting that resulted was the opportunity for me to clarify face-to-face with the diplomat how astonished I was by how he and his office cold-shouldered us throughout his entire service in Israel.
“It’s instructive to know that for someone as unabashedly supportive of Israel and of Jewish peoplehood issues, he allowed this to go on throughout his term. America’s most senior diplomatic representative to Israel just looked away the whole time.
“Was that galling? Of course. But it’s sadly consistent with the way the State Department in Washington, through several layers of its senior management, has dealt with us, leaving aside minor and mostly inconsequential exceptions, from the time of my meeting in Washington with the DOJ in 2012, which eventually led to charges being issued against Tamimi, right up until today.”
The Magazine reached out to Amb. Friedman for a response, and he replied, “The Roths have undergone unimaginable suffering and deserve that Ahlam Tamimi be brought to justice. I wish there was more I could have done for them.”
Thomas R. Nides served from December 5, 2021, to July 21, 2023, under president Joe Biden. The Roths met personally with Nides, but they said that nothing helpful came from the meeting, and what the ambassador did say was, at his request, off the record.
The Magazine reached out to Nides for a response, but he had not replied at press time.
Jack Lew was the ambassador, still under Biden, from November 5, 2023, to January 20, 2025.
Arnold Roth said, “I understood he’s an observant Jew like my wife and me. Given that reality and the utter lack of any progress with every relevant part of the Biden administration, asking for a meeting with Lew was an unbearable thought, one step too far. We didn’t ask for a meeting.
“And there’s this. Notwithstanding the seriousness of the Jordan/Tamimi case and the years of neglect and thwarting of US justice it represents, it’s worth noting that Lew had no contact with us either. No email, no phone call. I can understand that. The State Department’s position on Jordan/Tamimi clearly makes at least some of its people uncomfortable.”
The Magazine reached out to Amb. Lew, but he had not responded at press time.
US AMBASSADOR Mike Huckabee began on April 21, 2025, under the second Trump administration, and is still serving. (Some of this was reported in Part II.)
Roth said, “He responded positively to our request for a private meeting, which took place in the Jerusalem embassy in May 2025. His approach was frank, supportive, informed, and encouraging – as different as things get by comparison with all the previous interactions with ambassadors.
“He said something I haven’t heard till now from any other American official: ‘I don’t understand how this can happen. I need to find out.’ The connection goes on, and he assures us that he has not forgotten the issues. There have been some follow-on calls. We trust him.”
The Magazine reached out to Ambassador Huckabee about his interaction with the Roths, and this is what he replied:
“My visit with the Roth family touched me in a profound way and personal way. They gave me a photo of Malki and I have kept it framed in my office since that day, so there is not a day that goes by [that] I fail to think of the injustice to her and her precious family. One of my goals as ambassador is seeing justice done. Malki would be 40 years old this year.”
Since then, Huckabee has even more assertively called for the extradition of Tamimi. On August 9 this year, Huckabee posted on X: “Twenty-five years ago today, a Hamas suicide bomber murdered 16 people and injured more than 120 at the Sbarro pizzeria in Jerusalem. Among the victims were Americans Judith Greenbaum, Chana Nachenberg, and 15-year-old Malka Roth. May their memories be a blessing. We stand with @Israel against terrorism in all its forms and remain committed to bringing every last fugitive of this heinous act to justice.”
He also cited the State Department’s Rewards for Justice page, which states: “Rewards for Justice is offering a reward of up to $5 million for information on Ahlam Ahmad al-Tamimi... as part of its 1993 Violence in Opposition to the Middle East Peace Negotiations reward offer.”
Also on August 9 this year, Ambassador Rabbi Yehuda Kaploun, special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism at the State Department, posted on X:
“Today, we mark 25 years since the Hamas terrorist attack at the Sbarro pizzeria in Jerusalem. We remember the 16 victims murdered – including Americans Judith Greenbaum, Chana Nachenberg, and Malki Roth – and the more than 120 others injured. The United States will never forget and remains committed to bringing the perpetrators, including Ahlam Ahmad al-Tamini, to justice.”
He also quoted the Rewards for Justice page.
American Jewish leadership
Throughout this saga, where were our brethren?
Roth said, “Many of the executives who manage major American Jewish organizations exposed themselves to me in 2020. I wrote letters to most of the constituent groups that make up the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations and one or two others [not under the conference’s umbrella], asking them to sign on to a declaration calling on ‘our government’ (the US) to press for the extradition of Tamimi.”
The letters went out in mid-June 2020 and several weeks after that.
The letter summarized what happened in the Sbarro terror attack, referred to the US citizens murdered, and added:
“WHEREAS, the unrepentant plotter of the bombing, Ahlam Tamimi, now lives in Jordan; and… the Government of Jordan, an American ally and the world’s fourth-largest recipient of US financial aid, refuses to extradite Tamimi to the United States, in direct contravention of its treaty... we, the undersigned EXPRESS our collective outrage over the Kingdom of Jordan’s refusal to extradite the murderer of American citizens. STAND in solidarity with the families of the victims and their quest for justice. CALL upon our government to hold the Kingdom of Jordan accountable to its commitments... including... recent government legislation significantly impacting US financial aid to Jordan [and] PLEDGE to join forces with the families of the victims until their demand to see justice meted out to the murderer of American citizens is realized.”
Roth prepared a meticulous chart indicating who signed (23), who declined (10), and those who ignored the letter (15), according to him.
Since there is no way to determine whether those who did not respond at all did so intentionally or whether the letter went into spam or a bureaucratic black hole, I’ll cite only a few examples of those who signed and those who wrote back that they declined.
Regarding rabbinical or religious organizations, signers included the Rabbinical Assembly, which describes itself as the “international association of Conservative/Masorti rabbis”; Agudath Israel of America, identified with the haredi population; and the Union of Orthodox Jewish Congregations of America (OU) and National Council of Young Israel – which indicates the response at least partly crossed the denominational lines. Those who actively declined included Reconstructing Judaism and Women of Reform Judaism.
Non-rabbinical/religious organizations that signed included AIPAC; B’nai B’rith International; Coalition for Jewish Values; Conference of Presidents (signed on behalf of the conference, though some of those under its umbrella did not); Religious Zionists of America-Mizrachi; Hadassah; Jewish Federations of North America; World Jewish Congress North America; the Coalition for Jewish Values; and the Zionist Organization of America.
Roth said, “Under William Daroff, the Conference of Presidents continues to actively stand with us in our battle.”
This August 9, Daroff publicly posted a short summary of a letter the conference sent to Secretary of State Marco Rubio on August 4. (The full letter can be found on the conference’s website and Facebook page.)
The summary reads: “Today marks the 25th anniversary of the August 9, 2001, Sbarro restaurant bombing in Jerusalem. The Conference of Presidents urges the United States to demand that Jordan immediately extradite Ahlam Aref Ahmad Al-Tamimi. The US Department of Justice charged Al-Tamimi for her role in the attack, which murdered 16 people, including three Americans. She remains on the FBI’s Most Wanted Terrorists list. Twenty-five years later, the victims and their families still await justice. Jordan must fulfill its extradition treaty obligations and send Al-Tamimi to the United States to face trial.”
Roth shared with the Magazine some of the correspondence he had with those who explicitly declined to sign.
They included the Jewish Council for Public Affairs, which wrote, “[It is] beyond our organization’s mandate”; and the Jewish Institute for National Security of America, which told Roth, he said, after four unsuccessful tries: “What an awful, awful tragedy. No parent should have to experience what you have. However, JINSA doesn’t sign statements put out by others and rarely issues even its own statements. We’re more a think tank, not an advocacy organization. I still commend you for rallying support for this statement from Jewish organizations.”
T’ruah: The Rabbinic Call for Human Rights, wrote, “We are so sorry for your loss. We at T’ruah unconditionally condemn this and all other acts of terrorism. We are not going to participate in this particular policy initiative, which may have negative implications for Israel and for US foreign policy.”
The decliners of the above examples all expressed some form of sympathy even though they didn’t sign.
The exception was Americans for Peace Now, whose responder wrote only, “I consulted with my colleagues regarding the statement. We thank you for reaching out to us. As an organization, APN will pass on this statement.”
The American Jewish Committee also declined to sign. However, Roth said, he received the following letter on June 9, 2020. The letter said:
“Dear Mr. Roth, Thank you for reaching out to AJC in pursuit of justice for Malki, HY”D . Please know that we share your conviction that morality and the rule of law demand nothing less than the harshest punishment for those who planned and carried out your daughter’s savage murder, including Ahlam Tamimi. AJC has engaged and will continue aggressively to engage senior officials of our government, as well as Jordanian and Israeli authorities, to facilitate any and all means to assure the administration of justice too long denied.”
The chief policy and political affairs officer said he looked forward to being in touch.
Hillel: The Foundation for Jewish Campus Life also did not sign. Roth told the Magazine, “Their CEO, in his letter to me of July 2, 2020, wrote: ‘As you know, our mission at Hillel is an educational one, to help students build connections with Jewish life, learning, and Israel. In that vein, while Hillel does not itself advocate on political or policy issues, we work with numerous Jewish organizations that do so....’”
Some of those who didn’t sign raised an ironic eyebrow, on my part. For example, T’ruah. What is more relevant to human rights than extraditing a terrorist who joyously said she would do it again? And what were the human rights of Malki and the other victims?
And regarding Hillel, its non-signing in 2020, which preceded the havoc and Jew-hatred on college campuses since Oct. 7, 2023, is even more troubling in retrospect.
And what about those who signed and then did nothing further?
Roth said, “A journalist, Benjamin Weinthal, was intrigued by that very question and asked some questions a year ago for a follow-up analysis published by i24News. He based himself on publicly available data. My understanding is that most of the groups he approached did not respond to his follow-up questions.
“Some, however, did, and made terrifically positive claims to him about being with us all the way in this battle for justice. I told Weinthal that it actually felt, and still feels, very different to [wife] Frimet and me. So different, in fact, that in most cases we had never received any indication – not even a clue – of the urging and the pushing and the advocating they have been supposedly doing all along so that the Sbarro savage is... delivered to Washington to face trial.
“To his great credit, one of the organization leaders I phoned told me, almost as soon as he heard who was on the phone, that he’s deeply sorry. He had been less than frank with Weinthal and regretted it. So much so that he said he was going to take some corrective steps the next day. And indeed, he did. It didn’t amount to much, but knowing that there are still some American Jewish leaders with the backbone to say ‘We should have done more’ is encouraging.”
‘Eminent personages’
Roth also sent invitations to what he terms “eminent personages,” and 69 signed. It reads like a who’s who of scholars, leaders, and writers from diverse religions and countries.
A partial list includes Irwin Cotler, former justice minister and attorney-general of Canada, and chairman of the Raoul Wallenberg Centre for Human Rights; Bari Weiss, esteemed journalist and CBS News editor-in-chief; Bassem Eid, Palestinian Arab social worker and human rights advocate; Stephen M. Flatow, father of terror victim Alisa Flatow; American scholar Prof. Susannah Heschel; Marvin Kalb, award-winning journalist-author; Col. Richard Kemp, former commander of British forces in Afghanistan, who led the international terrorism team at Britain’s Joint Intelligence Committee; Beate and Serge Klarsfeld, anti-Nazi and pro-Israel advocates; Sen. Joseph I. Lieberman, first Jewish candidate on a major presidential ticket in the 2000 race; American novelist Cynthia Ozick; and Dr. Judea Pearl, distinguished academic and father of murdered journalist Daniel Pearl.
Signed on also are Daniel Pipes, president of Middle East Forum; Dr. Asaf Romirowsky, executive director of Scholars for Peace in the Middle East; Rabbi David Rosen, president of Religions for Peace; noted historian and author Prof. Ruth Wisse; Zuhdi Jasser, founder-president of American Islamic Forum for Democracy and co-founder of Muslim Reform Movement; and Prof. Gerald Steinberg, president, Institute for NGO Research; among many other distinguished personages.
Roth said, “Tamimi’s high-profile freedom all these years amounts to an act of betrayal by people and groups who should be standing beside us, amplifying our voices. Instead, they decline to help or say they are helping while, in my view, doing nothing.
“Some represent America’s Jews in Congress. Some are major American Jewish organizations. Some are Jewish religious leaders. Some have served as special envoy to monitor and combat antisemitism.
“And a special mention goes to the Republican Jewish Coalition and the Jewish Democratic Council of America. They are among a long list of our brethren in positions of power who could have done more.
“Living through this battle has sensitized me to the painful gulf between our aspirations as a Jewish community and our achievements. I prefer not to be more explicit than that. There is huge scope for improving ourselves.”
Roth family struck again by Hamas
Before we concluded our long interview, Frimet spoke about their son-in-law, Naftali Yonah Gordon, married to the Roths’ daughter, Pesi; they have two little children.
On Oct. 7, 2023, while they were all observing Simchat Torah, Gordon immediately went into action to join his reserve unit. He died after his tank took a direct hit in northern Gaza on December 7.
“Naftali was a highly regarded physiotherapist, a beloved individual,” Arnold Roth told i24 TV at the time, and added now, “We adored him.”
Frimet said, “In recent times, since we lost Naftali, I haven’t really been as involved in this [bringing Tamimi to justice] as Arnold has. I’m not at all involved in drumming up interest in it. If there is some kind of meeting with an official that’s been arranged, then I try to go, not always. And that is because of Naftali.
“The grief over Naftali is just so raw. It kind of consumes me, and helping our daughter to deal with our grandchildren.
“I don’t write anything anymore, almost nothing. Maybe for every yahrzeit of Malki I’ll write something, but that’s about it.
“And they were both murdered by the very same group, the very same haters of us, Hamas. How about that? Twenty-three years later, they were just as vicious, and hateful, and powerful as they were then.
“Nothing changed, nothing.”
In conclusion
Arnold Roth does not live in a bubble. He had positive personal experiences with Jordan before Malki’s murder.
“I used to do business in Jordan. In the late 1990s I led a technology venture for one of Israel’s best-known hi-tech conglomerates and traveled twice to Jordan to discuss with Jordanian entrepreneurs the development of a joint venture there. I visited several times in the late 1990s to develop business ties – they have nice people, lots of unrealized potential in technology business, also lots of need.”
Since Israel released Tamimi and the Jordanian government is not cooperative, the Roths continue to bring pressure on US officials to extradite this terrorist, who continues to thrive and be emulated in the Arab world, while still hoping American Jewish leaders and organizations will help in this mission.
Arnold said, “When Frimet and I write or meet with people, it’s never about us seeking sympathy or balm for our wounds. We believe in American justice as a precious value, and we see it being trampled in front of our eyes. It’s a disgrace that it falls to us – bereaved parents of an American child – to be the ones left to press the politicians and the officials to assert US rights, to stand up for US justice, to make law enforcement happen.
“We have real lives, a solid marriage, lovely children and grandchildren to warm our lives. We live productively, and have created and now manage an effective charity in Malki’s name – the Malki Foundation – that does good every day. And we have made our home in Jerusalem with family living close by. We’re content.
“And yes, we are passionate about justice – just justice. And to be painfully clear about this, on our own, we can’t make it happen. It’s disappointing to acknowledge how hard getting help has been and still is.”
Frimet added, “Tamimi remains free. She has never seen the inside of a US courtroom.
“Our life’s mission is to make that happen.”
Arnold: “This is not about vengeance, but entirely about seeing justice done.”
Some final questions
Will the US government be “deaf to the voice of justice,” as it accused its “British brethren” in the Declaration of Independence? Or will it prove once and for all that it really does consider all its citizens equal?
Halevai – may it be so – that Malki Roth’s case will be the landmark case that changes the way the US Department of Justice operates in this realm.
Will organizational Jewish leaders worldwide – who view themselves as part of the “Am Yisrael hai” community – pick up the gauntlet?
The Sbarro terror attack happened on the watch of prime minister Ariel Sharon (Likud). The extreme increase in terrorism started after the signing of the Oslo Accords, under prime minister Yitzhak Rabin (Labor). Ahlam Tamimi was released to Jordan in the Schalit deal conducted by Prime Minister Binyamin Netanyahu (Likud). Terrorists with blood on their hands are heroes elsewhere throughout the Arab world.
There is enough responsibility for the major political parties to share.
Will Israel’s leaders rethink what they did or did not do in the past, and find a better way?
We are in the Hebrew month of Elul, a time of introspection and teshuva – repentance.
If not now, when?■

This specific type of positive emotion predicts life satisfaction better than the rest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:00:51 UTC
03:00:51 KST

An analysis of data from two longitudinal studies conducted in Germany and the Netherlands found that both energized and pleasant positive emotions are associated with life satisfaction, but that this association was much stronger with pleasant positive emotions. The paper was published in the Journal of Positive Psychology.
Subjective well-being is a person’s overall evaluation of how well their life is going. It is typically described as a combination of how satisfied people are with their lives and how frequently they experience positive and negative emotions. Yet researchers still disagree about exactly how these components fit together and whether they reflect a single underlying form of well-being.
One particularly important source of confusion concerns positive affect, which is often treated as if it were one simple psychological state. In reality, the term can refer to very different experiences, ranging from calm pleasure and happiness to excitement, enthusiasm, interest, and energetic engagement.
This means that two studies can both claim to measure positive affect while actually assessing rather different emotional experiences. The distinction matters because pleasant and energized positive emotions may play different roles in well-being. Pleasant feelings may be especially closely connected to satisfaction because they signal that things are going well or that important goals have been achieved. More energized states such as interest, engagement, and enthusiasm may instead be especially useful for motivating activity, exploration, and personal growth.
Study author Jinrui Liu and her colleagues conducted a study in which they explored whether positive emotions and life satisfaction are associated with each other over time. They also wanted to know whether energized and pleasant positive emotions have associations of similar strength with life satisfaction. Finally, they wanted to know whether personality traits that predict energized positive emotions are the same ones that predict pleasant positive emotions.
Study authors analyzed data from the Panel Analysis of Intimate Relationships and Family Dynamics from Germany (PAIRFAM) and the Longitudinal Internet Studies for the Social Sciences (LISS) from the Netherlands. PAIRFAM is a longitudinal study of more than 12,000 individuals from three different birth groups (those born between 1971 and 1973, between 1981 and 1983, and between 1991 and 1993). Study authors analyzed data collected between 2014 and 2021.
The LISS data used in this analysis was collected between 2013 and 2024. The LISS conducted monthly internet surveys of a sample of Dutch individuals aged 16 and older from 5,000 households in each data collection wave. They were recruited randomly from the Dutch population. The sample analyzed in this study included 17,532 participants. 53.3% of them were women.
The measure of pleasant positive emotions used in this analysis was derived from an assessment of depression in PAIRFAM, using items initially meant to capture a lack of depressive symptoms, which actually describe the presence of pleasant feelings (e.g., “I am happy”, “I feel good”).
The assessment of energized positive emotions came from the LISS dataset where the Positive and Negative Affect Scale was used. Both datasets contained a measure of life satisfaction. Additionally, both datasets contained assessments of participants’ personalities in line with the Big Five model (the BFI-20 in the PAIRFAM, and IPIP-50 in the LISS).
Results showed that both pleasant and energized positive emotions were associated with life satisfaction, but that the association with pleasant positive emotions was much stronger. The associations ran in both temporal directions, meaning that earlier life satisfaction was associated with later positive emotions and vice versa.
The associations of the two types of positive emotions with personality traits of extraversion and neuroticism also differed. Neuroticism showed a stronger negative association with pleasant positive emotions, while energized positive emotions were more strongly associated with extraversion.
“In sum, our results indicate that pleasant and energized PA [positive affect] are not interchangeable in longitudinal SWB [subjective well-being] dynamics. Both PA types showed bidirectional within-person associations with LS [life satisfaction] beyond their shared trait-like SWB factor, supporting the view that these SWB elements are further causally related beyond a common underlying construct. However, these associations were consistently stronger for pleasant PA with LS than energized PA,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the theoretical conceptualization of subjective well-being. However, it should be noted that the study authors’ measurements of energized and pleasant positive emotions were driven by the data that were available in the datasets they used. It is possible that different ways of measuring these two categories of positive emotions would yield different results.
The paper, “Jingle all the way? Pleasant and energized positive affect show differential longitudinal relationships with life satisfaction and personality,” was authored by Jinrui Liu, Joar Vittersø, Irene J. E. Teulings, Ragnhild Bang Nes, Lilian Mayerhofer, and Espen Røysamb.

Munitions jobs jump by half as Britain rebuilds stocks

18:56:41 BST
02:56:41 KST

Jobs supported by defence spending on weapons and ammunition manufacturing rose by 51 per cent across the United Kingdom in 2024/25, according to figures published by the Ministry of Defence on Friday.
The increase amounts to 2,000 additional posts, taking the total to 5,900 across the manufacture of weapons, ammunition and military fighting vehicles.
According to the department, the rise reflects a drive to rebuild what it calls a sovereign, always on pipeline of munitions supply, so that artillery and missiles can be produced at greater scale domestically. It describes that capability as central to warfighting readiness and deterrence while creating skilled manufacturing jobs.
Luke Pollard, Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “These figures show that a rising defence budget is creating more good jobs across the UK. Defence is an engine for growth and our investments are driving reindustrialisation. As we increase our military readiness and capabilities we are generating good well-paid jobs nationwide.”
The 51 per cent figure is the sharpest movement in the statistics, which otherwise record MOD expenditure with industry of £31.9 billion in 2024/25 supporting 274,000 jobs across the country.
Munitions production has been among the most exposed weaknesses in Western defence since 2022. Artillery consumption in Ukraine has run at rates no European producer was sized for, and states discovered that output could not be raised quickly because plants had been closed, tooling scrapped and specialist suppliers lost across three decades of low demand. Explosive fill and propellant, rather than shell bodies, proved the tightest constraint.
The Strategic Defence Review of 2025 identified magazine depth as a weakness across the British armed forces, and the government has committed to a series of new energetics and munitions facilities.

RUSI questions core principle of UK targeting project
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:55:24 BST
02:55:24 KST

A principle set out by the team building Britain’s Digital Targeting Web fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of safeguards, according to a new report from the Royal United Services Institute, which warns that legal and ethical checks cannot speed up a targeting cycle any more than friction can speed up a moving object.
The paper, Modern Targeting in European Militaries, is written by Robert Tollast, Noah Sylvia and Matthew Savill, and is the first in a series examining the Digital Targeting Web. It draws on interviews with British policymakers, practitioners and industry experts.
Announced in May 2025 and detailed in the Strategic Defence Review, the Digital Targeting Web is an attempt to pull successive British digital integration efforts under one initiative, connecting sensors and decision-makers to weapons and non-lethal effectors across the joint force. Its stated battlefield vision is the ability to “sense, understand, decide, act and assess faster than they can”.
‘Accelerate tempo, not constrain it’
The report singles out one of the project’s strategic principles, which its core team lists as: “assurance, legalities, ethics and security must accelerate tempo, not constrain it.”
The authors write: “On its face, the statement fundamentally misunderstands the purpose of safeguards, which by their nature slow down processes. Technical assurance processes, legal reviews and security protocols are extra steps added into targeting procedures, thereby increasing the steps and time needed for a cycle to complete. Even if partially or wholly automated, safeguards cannot be expected to increase the speed of a targeting cycle any more than friction can be expected to increase the speed of a moving object.”
They note that the view is not confined to the project team. A number of practitioners interviewed expressed doubts about the need for rigorous legal and ethical safeguards, the report says, “since the UK’s/NATO’s enemies do not feel bound by such rules, the slowing of one’s own operations by these safeguards presents an unacceptable risk on the battlefield.”
Ministers will have to let go
The report’s most direct implication for Whitehall concerns who authorises strikes. It argues that the habits of the counter-terrorism era, where commanders, civil servants and ministers were closely involved in individual operations planned over weeks, cannot survive a war involving hundreds of strikes a day.
The authors write: “In the event of large-scale operations, the decision-making authority for most strikes, especially for targets of opportunity, will have to be devolved to mid-level or even junior commanders in the field. Commanders will inevitably take action that, whether intentional or not, causes significant civilian harm and/or escalation in enemy response. MoD officials and ministers must grow accustomed to these realities of modern operations, where they will bear the political consequences for actions outside their control.”
They conclude that the issue is “less about process and more about habit and culture: senior officials and ministers will have to become more comfortable with delegation and risk, or at least be more precise in the parameters they set out for targeting.”
Working against that is public scrutiny. One MOD official is quoted saying: “BDA is instantaneous on social media, leading to demands of accountability from ministers.” The report judges this likely to reduce the risk ministers find tolerable at exactly the moment the battlefield demands more delegation.
Scale and speed
The report opens with the American and Israeli strike campaign against Iran, which began on 28 February 2026. It records that the American Operation Epic Fury ran at a tempo not seen since the invasion of Iraq in 2003, with some reports claiming nearly 900 strikes in the first twelve hours, followed by hundreds of daily strikes for five weeks.
That scale, the authors write, was possible only through collating decades of data points from a myriad of sources. They note that various countries including the UK have made targeting central to force modernisation, with one European general describing a desire to identify 3,000 targets per day.
On the civilian consequences, the report states that strikes on Iran hit thousands of sites and killed over 2,000 civilians, with damage in some cases intentional and in others, such as strikes on the Minab school that reportedly killed over 150 people, mainly children, attributed to human error.
It adds: “Advanced digitalised systems appear to enable the speed and scale of such actions, both intentional and accidental. It remains difficult to separate the civilian toll from the public decision by the US Department of War to cut civilian protection offices in the Pentagon in favour of prioritising ‘maximum lethality, not tepid legality’.”
The authors say this should concern the Ministry of Defence, which has recently highlighted vulnerabilities in its own civilian harm mitigation policies.
Allies out of step
On coalition operations, the report warns that gaps in interoperability could see allies categorise the same targets differently or strike them twice with limited, expensive weapons.
It says: “Targets which one force may identify as posing a collateral damage risk may be erroneously identified by an unconnected Allied targeting system as legitimate sites to strike.” British and French thinking is both moving towards striking the enemy at depth, which by definition involves targeting close to dual-use infrastructure.
The conclusion is that aligning targeting policy and procedure between allies is needed “now rather than later”, and that the training and doctrine implications “must be addressed before the onset of conflict.”
Does it change anything?
The report finds no consensus within British defence about how much the Digital Targeting Web actually changes. Many policymakers and some practitioners describe it as essentially implementing Network Enabled Capability concepts, with one senior policymaker saying modern targeting policy is “nothing fundamentally different” to that of recent decades, and targeting policy remaining grounded in traditional documents.
The authors end on the limits of the technology rather than its promise, arguing that prioritising quantifiable metrics such as a goal of a set number of targets in a set time “can enable greater lethality, but risks excising the human perceptions, judgements, reactions and ingenuity without which a war cannot be won.”
They note that the strike campaigns against Iran and in Gaza were historic in speed and scale, and that in neither case can the result yet be considered a strategic victory. The project was supported by Fujitsu, Leonardo, Systematic and Thales, with RUSI stating that it retains independence in its research outputs and that the views are the authors’ alone.

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA. Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
There have been small rallies and protests outside Indiana Fever games after the issue came to a head when Sophie Cunningham of the Fever said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. There are rallies planned before the Liberty face the Fever on Saturday night in Brooklyn.
“Knowing that rallies are happening on both sides shows the platform that the W has and the stunts for attention are just continuing to try and ride the wave that we have,” Stewart told a small group of reporters Saturday morning. “I want Liberty fans and even Indy fans that are going to come here tonight to be able to have this arena be a safe space.”
At least three fans were asked by WNBA security personnel to cover shirts that had messages about transgender women participating in women’s sports during last Sunday’s game at Atlanta between the Dream and the Fever. The league later said the fans should have been free to wear those shirts.
Stewart said Liberty fans specifically, but WNBA fans in general, come to games because “they can feel like they can be themselves in whatever capacity that is and we don’t want to lose sight of that.”
The Liberty forward said everyone is entitled to their own opinion and if that stops being allowed there are much bigger issues. However, she said, trying to divide teams and players shouldn’t be tolerated.
“If we don’t allow (free speech), we need to like really kind of go back and look at more things. I think the bigger thing is people are trying to divide us as teams, but also as teammates or as opponents,” she said. “This league is incredibly inclusive and what we continue to fight for and stand up against. So, we don’t want to take that platform away.”
Stewart has been an ally for the transgender community during her career. She faced some online backlash last year when one of her signature shoes had a Harry Potter theme to it. Stewart is a huge fan of the Harry Potter books and subsequent movies by author J.K. Rowlings, who has drawn criticism for her anti-trans stance.
Stewart has donated royalties from that shoe to The Trevor Project, a suicide prevention and crisis intervention nonprofit organization for LGBTQ+ youth.

Trump seeks to block the BBC’s attempt to subpoena Ivanka Trump, Trump Jr

United States President Donald Trump has called on a federal court to deny a motion by the BBC to subpoena members of his immediate family, as part of a $10bn lawsuit over a documentary the broadcaster aired.
On Friday, lawyers for Trump argued that the BBC had embarked on a “politically charged discovery campaign” by seeking to compel testimony from Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr, his first daughter Ivanka Trump and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.

list of 3 items

Trump’s team appealed to the court to reject the BBC’s motion, comparing it to a fishing expedition that goes beyond the scope of the case.
“This case concerns a narrow wrong — the BBC’s deliberate splicing together of two passages of President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech spoken nearly fifty-five minutes apart,” Friday’s court filing said.
“Rather than litigate that narrow claim, the BBC has attempted to pursue a sweeping investigation disguised as discovery.”
The case began in December, when Trump announced he would sue the BBC over an episode of the documentary series Panorama, which chronicled the Republican leader’s path to a second term as president.
Part of the documentary focuses on the events of January 6, 2021, the day the results of the 2020 election were to be certified. Trump had lost that election but falsely claimed his defeat was the result of fraud.
At a speech in front of the White House on that day, he repeated the unfounded accusation that the election had been “rigged” to a rally of his supporters, some of whom participated in an attack on the US Capitol in the hours afterwards.
The Panorama episode included snippets from Trump’s speech, and critics argued that two sentences from his address had been edited together to sound like one continuous quote.
The first line was: “After this, we’re going to walk down, and I’ll be there with you, we’re going to walk down.” The second came from later in the speech: “And we fight. We fight like hell.”
Though the BBC apologised for the editing and took the Panorama episode down from its platforms, Trump nevertheless filed a multibillion-dollar lawsuit accusing the broadcaster of defamation.
The BBC has denied that charge and pledged to fight the lawsuit in court. The case is currently being heard before the US district court in southern Florida.
As part of its defence, the BBC has sought testimony from figures close to Trump, to establish his thoughts and actions on the day of the January 6 attack.
It pointed out that both Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump were present at their father’s speech, and that they spoke to the president and his inner circle as the violence erupted at the Capitol.
Text messages released by the US Congress show Donald Trump Jr urged his father’s chief of staff to “condemn this sh**”, a fact cited in the BBC’s motion.
While Kushner was not present at the White House, the BBC maintains that his role as Trump’s adviser would also help establish the facts of that day.
Lawyers for the broadcaster say that, after speaking with congressional leaders, Kushner drafted “a proposed statement” for Trump to present, “which would have condemned the use of violence”.
The testimony of Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and Kushner can help illustrate the president’s “burden to prove that it would be materially false to imply that he incited violence on January 6”, according to the BBC’s motion.
But, the motion added, the BBC has been unable to serve the three family members with subpoenas due to the presence of their US Secret Service protection.
The BBC reportedly attempted to deliver subpoenas to Ivanka Trump and Kushner at their residence in May, only to face Secret Service agents who said they were not authorised to accept the documents.
Likewise, that same month, the BBC was unable to hand Trump Jr a subpoena at Trump Tower in New York. It has therefore asked the court for permission to use certified mail to deliver the documents instead.
But in Friday’s court filing, Trump’s lawyers accused the BBC of carrying out a “cynical” campaign that involved the “harassment of the President’s family, associates, staff, officials, and others”.
It also called the BBC’s efforts “a boundless re-investigation of the events that occurred on January 6, 2021”.
The filing suggests that any interactions involving Ivanka Trump and Kushner are “subject to the executive privilege” of the presidency, since the husband-wife duo served as adviser and senior adviser to Trump, respectively.
Trump has made sweeping claims to executive privilege throughout his two terms in office.
Just this month, the US Department of Justice issued a memo saying such privilege shielded communication even with private advisers who worked outside the executive branch, effectively declaring interactions with companies and private individuals off-limits for subpoenas.
Critics fear the memo will be a hurdle to government transparency under Trump — and may even prevent Congress from accessing investigative materials.
Senator Adam Schiff of California framed the memo as an insurance policy against congressional oversight, should the Republican Party lose its majorities in Congress during November’s midterm elections.
“This latest opinion should be seen as a partisan measure to insulate the president and his corrupt activities from Congressional subpoenas when the majority flips,” he wrote in a statement on August 11.
The federal court in southern Florida has yet to rule on the BBC’s subpoena requests.
The BBC, meanwhile, has sought to have the entire case tossed, on the basis that Trump is attempting to dampen free speech.

‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:47:02 UTC
02:47:02 KST

‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. But politicians say they were not consulted.
Monrovia, Liberia – Samwar Fallah began receiving calls this week from people in the United States seeking information about 20 relatives sent to Liberia, a country none of them is a citizen of.
The families asked the Monrovia-based lawyer to find out where their relatives were taken and what would happen to them. He could not tell them much.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4First group of US deportees, out of an expected 1,200, arrive in Liberia
- list 2 of 4Liberia to take 1,200 deportees from the US
- list 3 of 4Liberia’s kush crisis: The hidden trade behind a generation at risk
- list 4 of 4From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past
He knows the group landed at Roberts International Airport near capital Monrovia on Thursday and was driven away in a bus by Liberian officials. He does not know where they were taken, whether they are free to leave, or what legal status they now hold.
Fallah avoids calling them deportees because the government has not defined their status under Liberian law.
“You cannot relocate a citizen from one country to another without clear information as to why that person has been relocated,” Fallah told Al Jazeera. “Imagine you coming from maybe El Salvador and then you find out you are on a plane to Liberia.”
The group is the first transferred under an arrangement allowing Liberia to receive up to 1,200 people deported from the US over the next 12 months.
The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. Politicians say they were not consulted.
Fallah, assisting the families without charge alongside two US immigration lawyers, said they want to know whether their relatives may settle in Liberia, choose where they can go, or eventually return to the US.
He has no answers.
The arrangement involves third-country deportation: sending people to a country other than their country of citizenship. It has raised questions about executive power, sovereignty and the rights of those transferred.
‘Guests of the Republic’
The government said the deportees have not been detained and described the arrangement with the US as humanitarian.
Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said those transferred would be received as “guests of the Republic”. They are free to leave and may seek asylum, he added.
Piah linked the decision to Liberia’s history as a settlement for free and formerly enslaved Black people from the US and a country whose citizens sought protection abroad during 14 years of civil war.
“Liberia’s gesture is entirely humanitarian and in keeping with the country’s longstanding traditions,” he said.
Piah insisted Liberia would not bear the cost. Accommodation, food and eventual onward travel would be covered by the US government and an international partner organisation, he said.
However, the government has not provided further information about the people who arrived on Thursday. It has not disclosed their full nationalities, where they are being housed, the legal documents under which they entered Liberia, or the identity of the international organisation paying for and managing their stay.
The Reuters news agency on Friday reported that five of those people refused to leave the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea. Al Jazeera has not verified the report independently.
Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh said Liberia reviews each passenger list and may reject anyone. “Most of them are people who had immigration violations and offences,” he said.
But the government has not published its screening criteria or said whether any arrivals had US protection orders preventing their return to their countries.
Al Jazeera found out that most of those deported were nationals of Latin American countries, including Venezuela and Cuba.
But “guests” does not establish a legal status under Liberian law. It remains unclear whether those people entered on temporary permits, whether they can work, or whether they must apply for asylum or residency.
Although Piah said the group was free to leave, officials did not allow journalists to speak with them at the airport. They walked down the aircraft steps, boarded a bus and were driven away under official supervision.
Was legislative approval required?
Some of the strongest objections came from politicians who say the arrangement may require legislative approval.
Nimba County Senator Samuel Kogar cited Article 57 of Liberia’s constitution, which empowers the president to conduct foreign affairs and conclude treaties, conventions and similar agreements “with the concurrence of a majority of each House of the Legislature”.
“Was this arrangement brought before both Houses of the Legislature and approved by the required majority?” Kogar asked. “If not, then under what legal authority was this agreement made?”
The government said the arrangement rests on diplomatic notes exchanged on September 4 and September 10 last year.
Third Country Deportation Watch, a project operated by Refugees International and Human Rights First, said the text appeared on the US State Department’s website in March. Most Liberians heard about it only in August.
Representative Anthony F Williams, a member of House committees covering national security, human rights and foreign affairs, rejected the idea that the executive could act alone.
“No agreement that borders on the national security of this country, the sovereignty of the country, can just be entered into by the executive branch alone,” he told Al Jazeera.
The legislature is on a break until October. Williams said he would seek answers on housing, healthcare, screening and Liberia’s authority to detain or remove anyone.
His concerns, he said, were about state capacity, not the arrivals.
Liberia lacks the biometric systems and trained personnel to document as many as 1,200 people moving across counties or porous borders, he said, adding that those fleeing persecution could also be traced by the governments they escaped.
Eddie Jarwolo, executive director of NAYMOTE Partners for Democratic Development, said no published plan showed how Liberia would accommodate the arrivals without further straining public services.
Civil society groups were not consulted, he said. He called for independent monitoring of living conditions, spending and legal compliance.
Was there a diplomatic tradeoff?
The government insists Liberia received no payment or diplomatic reward for accepting the transfers. Critics have called for disclosure of the negotiations.
The arrangement emerged amid several US decisions affecting Liberia. On December 9, 2025, the countries signed a five-year, $124m health memorandum. Washington also extended B1/B2 visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months.
Al Jazeera previously reported that those measures followed Liberia’s agreement to accept Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose mistaken removal from the US to a Salvadoran prison became a political and legal flashpoint.
The US later sought court permission to send him to Liberia.
Meanwhile, migrant visas for Liberians were halted in January, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, and the US awarded Liberia $5m this year for migration management.
Neither government has publicly established a direct link between the deportation arrangement and the visa move. Jarwolo of NAYMOTE said the two nations should disclose whether visa extension was linked to accepting third-country deportees.
“If they were linked, it would raise serious concerns about Liberia’s negotiating position, national sovereignty and public safety,” he said. “Development assistance should not require Liberia to accept individuals whose backgrounds and legal status have not been transparently disclosed and properly assessed.”
University of Liberia Student Union president William Sando said he learned of the arrangement through Facebook before Piah confirmed it.
“They have not adequately informed the Liberian people,” he said, rejecting the minister’s argument as “disconnected from the current reality”.
Sando wanted the government to disclose where the arrivals will live and whether those who remain may work.
Kogar, the senator, said the questions went beyond an opposition to migration.
“This is not a small issue,” he said. “We are talking about our sovereignty, our laws, our national security, and the responsibility we have to the Liberian people. Where are we, the Liberians?”

Iranian artist showcases “Constitutional Revolution of Iran” at US exhibition

Iranian artist showcases “Constitutional Revolution of Iran” at US exhibition
TEHRAN- Iranian photographer and filmmaker Armin Amirian is participating in the 13th International FL3TCH3R Exhibition in the US with his artwork “Constitutional Revolution of Iran.”
The exhibition is being held from August 7 to September 27, at the Fishman Gallery in Johnson City, Tennessee, bringing together works by international artists selected by this year’s juror and curator, Jessica Burke.
“Constitutional Revolution of Iran” is part of Amirian’s “Until History Freezes” series, which he created in 2020 as a continuation of his narrative approach to art.
In the series, figures associated with Iran’s Constitutional Revolution emerge beneath a layer of ice, creating a visual interpretation of a pivotal chapter in the country’s modern history.
The Constitutional Revolution, which began in 1905 and culminated in the establishment of a constitutional system in Iran, marked a major turning point in the country’s political and social development. The movement sought to establish the rule of law and limit absolute royal authority through the creation of a parliament and a constitutional framework.
Amirian’s participation in the Fletcher exhibition marks another step in an international artistic career that includes more than 100 exhibitions and festivals around the world. He has previously received several honors, including the Distinguished Artist Award from the Fletcher Foundation.
Works from the “Until History Freezes” series have previously been presented in solo exhibitions in Iran, Italy and France, as well as in international exhibitions at venues including the Saatchi Gallery in London and exhibitions in the United States, Germany and Spain.
The Fletcher exhibitions were established in memory of Fletcher Dyer, with the aim of continuing his legacy of addressing social and political issues through art. The annual exhibition provides an international platform for artists whose works engage with contemporary social and political themes.
This year’s exhibition features works selected by Burke, who serves as the juror and curator of the 13th edition. The Fletcher Exhibition awards ceremony is scheduled to take place on September 4 at Fishman Gallery.

Duncan Macmillan’s “People, Places and Things” on stage at Art Palace
TEHRAN – The play “People, Places and Things” by the British playwright Duncan Macmillan is currently on stage at Art Palace in Tehran.
Masoumeh Beygi has translated and directed the 75-minute play. She also performs in the play along with Hamidreza Bodaghi, Sara Sajadi, Iman Sayad Borhani, Reza Karimi, Navid Askari, Shayan Mohammadi, and Pouria Nikkhah.
Duncan Macmillan’s intoxicating hit play is about Emma, a struggling actress whose life is spinning recklessly out of control.
Emma, a talented theatre actress, collapses during rehearsals for a staging of “The Seagull” by Chekhov, due to the abuse of alcohol and drugs; the company she works for dismisses her and requires her to detox in order to return to acting. Unwillingly, Emma checks in a rehabilitation clinic, initially determined to stay there only for the time necessary to be declared clean and return to work, but she ends up staying there for several months.
Emma was having the time of her life. Now she’s in rehab. Her first step is to admit that she has a problem. But the problem isn’t with Emma, it’s with everything else. She needs to tell the truth. But she’s smart enough to know that there’s no such thing. When intoxication feels like the only way to survive the modern world, how can she ever sober up?
The play is a harrowing look at drug and alcohol addiction and recovery. Its writing was prompted by Macmillan's desire to write a leading part for an actress: he has said he “wrote this play believing very strongly that there were a lot of brilliant actresses who just weren't getting parts that would push them and that they could excel in.”
“People, Places and Things” will remain on stage until October 7 at the Art Palace, located at No. 50, Zand-e-Vakil Alley, Razi St., Neauphle le chateau St., Hafez Ave.

Iranian movie, filmmaker participating in 39th Herceg Novi Film Festival
