A 2026 production, the 27-minute film, which is Ghanati’s debut film, depicts Sepehr, a village boy gifted with a beautiful voice and a great passion for singing, who attempts to apply for a talent show, facing numerous obstacles along the way.
The two-time Oscar winner, Iranian director and screenwriter Asghar Farhadi, is also a guest at the 39th Herceg Novi Film Festival. Farhadi will attend the screening of his latest film, “Parallel Tales,” which will take place on Sunday at Forte Mare Fortress.
Farhadi will also hold a special masterclass on Tuesday as part of the Montenegro Film Rendezvous industry program, organized by the Film Centre of Montenegro. The masterclass will take place at Park Hall, with Vuk Perović serving as moderator.
The film “Parallel Tales” was produced by the French production company Memento Production in 2026 and has a runtime of 139 minutes. The film was screened at this year’s Cannes Film Festival.
Asghar Farhadi, 54, began making films as a teenager, joining the Isfahan Young Cinema Society in 1986, where he made short films on 8mm and 16mm. He graduated in Dramatic Arts from the University of Tehran in 1998 and, several years later, earned a master’s degree in Theatre Direction, with a thesis devoted to Harold Pinter and the significance of silence and pauses in his dramatic writing.
He made his directorial debut with “Dancing in the Dust” (2002), and gained international recognition with “About Elly” (2009), for which he received the Silver Bear for Best Director at the Berlinale. This was followed by “A Separation” (2011), which received more than seventy awards, including the Academy Award and César Award for Best Foreign Language Film.
He shot “The Past” (2013) in France, with Bérénice Bejo winning the Best Actress award at Cannes for her performance. With “The Salesman” (2016), he won the awards for Best Screenplay and Best Actor at Cannes, as well as his second Academy Award, while “A Hero” (2021) received the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival.
The Herceg Novi Film Festival is the most significant film festival in Montenegro, running for over three decades. The festival has been accredited by the International Federation of Film Producers Associations (Fédération Internationale des Associations de Producteurs de Films – FIAPF), becoming part of the global network of the world most prestigious international film festivals.
The primary aim of the festival is to promote regional and world cinema, with a particular focus on creating space for female and male filmmakers and films that nurture an authentic artistic sensibility, a courageous approach to social reality, cinematic language and production, with an emphasis on presenting a cross-section of contemporary poetics and forms of expression.
As part of the festival, Montenegro Film Rendezvous is held, organized by the Film Centre of Montenegro — a film industry event dedicated to strengthening ties between the Montenegrin and European film industries, and to supporting the career development of Montenegrin filmmakers and film professionals.
Having launched on August 22, this year’s edition of the festival will run until August 28 in the coastal city of Herceg Novi.

The constants and variables in the political dynamics of West Asia
LONDON — The policy of the West Asia region is drawn based on political dynamics. These are either constants that are not subject to change or variables. This is especially with regard to the political situation in Lebanon and Syria, and the regional or international sponsorship of political directions.
The first constant is a primary hostility between Iran and the Israeli occupation entity, where it is not possible to reach a settlement between the two sides. The second constant is the Turkish-Israeli competition over influence in Syria, regulated so that it does not reach an armed conflict. The third constant is that the final decision on Syria’s future rests with Turkey. The fourth constant is the project of the New Middle East and "Greater Israel" that has ended with no return, because it failed on every front.
As for the variables, they are based firstly on the state of hostility between America and Iran, which can result in the administration of the Strait of Hormuz belonging to Iran. The second variable is that if this matter is accomplished, Iran and its allies will be recognized, and their presence will be considered legitimate. This includes the Lebanese resistance movement Hezbollah, Yemen’s Ansarullah, and likewise the balancing of the situation in Iraq.
The third variable is that the Turkish-Israeli conflict over Syria has not yet reached a final result. The fourth variable is between the Turkish-Syrian role and the Saudi role in Lebanon, with boundaries that have not yet become clear. The fifth variable is the scope of the Israeli-Turkish conflict over Syrian territory and Lebanon, which has yet to become clear, as the Trump administration has not yet reached a final decision on the matter.
As a result of these constants and variables, we can draw the first conclusion: the relationship between the Lebanese resistance movement and Syria’s Al-Sharaa is largely governed by the Iranian-Turkish relationship. Turkey considers its national security to begin in Beirut and views the Lebanese resistance movement’s existence as a factor that keeps the Israeli occupation entity preoccupied. It therefore sees the movement as a barrier to Israeli expansion and, on this basis, seeks to protect its own interests and national security. Accordingly, it can be concluded that there will be no Syrian military intervention in Lebanon against the Lebanese resistance.
Secondly, in the Israeli-Lebanese relationship, America will pass whatever is agreed upon by the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, through the framework agreement between the Israeli occupation entity and Lebanon. The small table joins the big table as the Islamabad Understanding is much bigger than the framework agreement.
It is now suspended, but when it is implemented, America will impose on the Israeli occupation entity withdrawal from all of Lebanon regardless of the course of the framework agreement. However, America will seek to pass it through the framework agreement. Therefore, the Israeli presence in Lebanon is heading toward contraction.
Thirdly, there will likely be Turkish-Saudi competition in Lebanese internal affairs. Generally, decision-making in Beirut is largely influenced by Saudi Arabia; in the north, particularly Tripoli and Akkar, it is shaped by Turkish-Syrian interests; and in the south, the Lebanese resistance movement holds the decisive influence.
Fourth, following a possible implementation of the Islamabad Agreement, the Lebanese resistance movement will play an important role in Lebanon’s internal affairs at the official level.
Fifth, the Israeli occupation entity will contract to the boundaries of historic Palestine of 1948, and America will force it to withdraw from Syria. Otherwise, a resistance movement is expected to form in Syria in the face of the Israeli occupation.
Sixth, Iran's control over the Strait of Hormuz will impose all these equations.
Seventh, the Iran will become an urgent necessity for the Persian Gulf states and for all countries whose economies are affected by the Strait of Hormuz.
Eighth, the coming phase is the phase of recognition of Iranian influence in the region, and it is an Iranian phase par excellence.

Iran on Saturday denounced US plans to announce new sanctions that could put further strain on the Islamic Republic's economy and have an impact on its most important trading partners including China.
After nearly six months of war since the US and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran on February 28, the sides are not firing at each other but also showing no sign of pursuing peace talks.
Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorized oil tankers that try to transit the vital waterway, and Iran's economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday after threatening "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran.
Bessent has also urged cooperation with Washington by China, which buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Beijing has urged diplomacy.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said on Saturday the imminent U.S. announcement of new economic sanctions was an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations."
"Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law," he said in a post on X.
The chief of staff of Iran's armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi, promised on Friday that Iran would respond to enemy threats militarily with "crushing, punishing and devastating responses.”
US President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides "any type of lifeline to Iran," said on Friday that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict.
"They would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion," Trump said of Iran.
HORMUZ TRAFFIC HALTED
While the US has effectively blockaded Iranian vessels in their ports, the Strait of Hormuz remained bottled up with thousands of seafarers stranded on hundreds of vessels.
Only four commodity ships sailed along the strait on Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, ship-tracking data showed.
However, Iran has granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday.
IRNA said obtaining special permission for Iraqi tankers was one of Baghdad’s main requests during a visit to Iraq by Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US military helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels a day of oil through the strait. That's down from more than 20 million per day before the war or about one of every five barrels consumed worldwide.
US attacks have severely diminished Iran's economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capability to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals.
Abdollahi, the armed forces chief of staff, sought to underline Iran's missile capabilities during a visit to an underground plant manufacturing ballistic missiles that was reported by state television on Saturday.
"This plant has been able, much better than in the past, to produce equipment superior both in capacities and quality and in quantity," he said.
Qalibaf, Iran's parliamentary speaker, said Tehran had received "numerous messages" from neighbouring countries about establishing new regional security arrangements and economic cooperation. Qalibaf, who did not say which countries he was referring to, accused the U.S. of endangering the security of its allies in the region for the sake of Israel, adding that an independent, "homegrown" regional order would deliver peace and security.
Trump, meanwhile, has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war such as dismantling Iran's nuclear programme - the state of which remains uncertain given that U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025 - and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
Thousands have been killed, mainly in Iran, where 168 Iranian school children were killed on the first day of the war. The U.S. has reported more than 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.
While Iran remains defiant, President Masoud Pezeshkian has also called for a diplomatic solution.
"It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals, and infrastructure and is hated in the world," the ISNA news agency quoted him as saying on Friday.

What follows Kushner’s meetings with al-Hayya and Netanyahu?
TEHRAN – Gaza remains caught between Israeli intransigence and electoral calculations, U.S. pressure, and Palestinian efforts to preserve the agreement. This is keeping the region in a state of neither war nor peace until the outcome of the upcoming elections becomes clear.
Jared Kushner, the U.S. presidential envoy and “Peace Council” member, met with the Palestinian delegation led by Khalil al-Hayya, head of Hamas’s political bureau, in Cairo. He also held a four-hour meeting with Netanyahu in Tel Aviv. The talks focused on advancing the roadmap for the Gaza agreement, a 15-point framework that the Palestinians had accepted, and the Israeli regime had rejected.
Kushner pledged to al-Hayya that he would pressure Netanyahu to give the agreement a chance to succeed, after the Palestinian leader reportedly told him: “Your turn has come. We have negotiated at length; now it is your time to act and pressure the occupying forces.”
Al-Hayya refused to even discuss reopening negotiations or revisiting the agreement’s provisions. Kushner came away with a positive impression of the Palestinian position, but he failed to make any breakthrough with Netanyahu. The reason is clear: the upcoming Israeli elections and the declining prospects of the regime’s coalition government winning, according to public opinion polls.
The agreement and Netanyahu’s electoral calculations
It is clear that Kushner’s visit did not produce a substantive breakthrough. However, it did demonstrate to the United States how difficult it will be to move forward with implementing the agreement at a time when the occupying regime’s commitment is required, while an election campaign is pushing Netanyahu toward greater rigidity and escalation on multiple fronts.
What Netanyahu has accomplished is showcasing his hardline stance that does not yield to American pressure, bolstering his standing among his extreme right-wing base.
The agreement, which was approved by all parties, including the United States, mediators, and guarantors, except Israel, explicitly stipulates that the gradual withdrawal of Israeli Occupation Forces (IOF) from the Gaza Strip should proceed in parallel with measures to contain and store heavy weapons.
The Israelis, however, insist that both light and heavy weapons held by Palestinian resistance forces must be dismantled before any IOF withdrawal or reconstruction of the Palestinian territory can begin.
The gap between the position of the mediators and Palestinians, on the one hand, and the regime’s position, on the other, appears to be widening. Despite recognizing how difficult it would be to achieve a breakthrough in the regime’s position at this stage, no one has an interest in declaring the agreement dead.
The Palestinian side has succeeded in backing Netanyahu into a corner, leaving him looking as though he is taking punches, even if they are soft ones, from one of his closest allies, the United States.
This is in addition to the explicit condemnations from the eight mediating and guarantor states. Those condemnations had largely faded before the last agreement was reached despite relentless IOF violations. Now, international censure of the regime has resumed, and Gaza has once again taken center stage on the global agenda.
Netanyahu, by contrast, is not concerned with the broader picture, including the regime’s growing isolation internationally and the reported decline in its relationship inside the United States, as well as the deteriorating relations between Netanyahu and Trump.
What Netanyahu wants is simple: to win the election, or, at the very least, to prevent the Israeli opposition from being able to form the next government and from reaching the 61 number of seats in the Knesset (Parliament). Either he wins, or he remains as head of a transitional government preparing for new elections, a scenario that appears increasingly likely in the upcoming Israeli political landscape.
The Palestinian position in the face of Israeli intransigence
The Palestinians understand that showing greater flexibility and agreeing to reopen the latest agreement for negotiations would allow Netanyahu to carry out every form of aggression against Gaza without restraint, criticism, or pressure, under the pretext that negotiations are still ongoing.
The Palestinians would then be portrayed as the ones refusing and obstructing progress, while pressure would once again be placed on them to show greater flexibility. For this reason, the Palestinian delegation is likely to remain committed to its position: there will be no renegotiation of what has already been agreed upon.
The Palestinians understand that the Israeli position on weapons and its refusal to begin reconstruction and withdrawal before disarmament means that the regime will neither withdraw from Gaza nor allow reconstruction to begin.
Gaza could therefore remain as it is for many years, with no one knowing when the situation will end. The Netanyahu regime will find sufficient pretexts to exploit the issue of weapons and evade its commitments.
Moreover, Israel’s rejection of the agreement is consistent with its post-October 7 policy, which rejects containment and deterrence strategies and refuses to return to the pre-war rules of engagement.
Instead, it seeks to impose a new reality across all fronts that grants it the right to continue its policies of assassinations, airstrikes, and aggression, as seen in the massacre that killed seven in Gaza port, the targeting of police commanders in Gaza following Kushner’s visit, recent strikes on Syria, and the aggression on Lebanon that resulted in casualties.
The message is clear: the regime will continue what it calls “eliminating threats” and maintaining “freedom of security” operations across the region, whether an agreement exists or not.
Despite the high costs, which the occupying regime is paying diplomatically and economically, the declining sense of security among settlers, the military’s near-permanent state of alert, and the ongoing uncertainty stemming from its failure to achieve absolute victory or any decisive military outcome, Israel believes its current policy is producing only tactical and temporary losses that can eventually be addressed and repaired.
However, various Israeli figures and institutions see the current path itself as a strategic loss, one for which Netanyahu’s government bears responsibility. They argue that the government has failed to translate military achievements into political results. In their view, the regime lost strategically.
Neither agreement nor war
The current situation in Gaza and across the region is unlikely to undergo any meaningful changes before the end of the Israeli elections. There will be neither a genuine de-escalation nor a full-scale war, nor an agreement, nor a formal withdrawal from the agreement.
Although it is difficult to bet on a significant change in the regime’s position even if Netanyahu loses the election, all parties and actors have little choice but to get through the next two months, even if that means maintaining a fragile calm without a final settlement.
Netanyahu, however, wants a fragile escalation, raising the ceiling of his negotiating positions through heightened aggression short of full-scale war.
The question remains: Did Kushner understand Netanyahu’s domestic position and give him the green light to raise the level of escalation ahead of the Israeli elections?
Given the pattern of American positions, they have consistently offered their staunchest ally in West Asia every opportunity, cover, and unlimited support.
However, Trump has his own domestic calculations as well. He is seeking a foreign policy achievement after his massive blunder in Iran, making him more eager to advance the negotiation track, de-escalate, and reach an agreement in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria.
The U.S. president has publicly called on Netanyahu to curb IOF attacks on Gaza, while his envoy Tom Barrack denounced the recent IOF assault on the Abu al-Duhur airbase in Syria.
This suggests that, at this stage, U.S. policy in the region is seeking to limit Israeli military escalation, particularly on the Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria fronts. After successfully keeping the regime out of the current confrontation with Iran, where Tehran’s response had been seriously misjudged in Washington.
Yet the escalation of IOF aggression on all three fronts indicates that the United States has failed to impose its policy on the regime there.
Netanyahu may have reached an understanding with Kushner that gives the regime greater room for calculated escalation in Gaza, Lebanon, and Syria in exchange for a commitment not to get engaged with Iran.
If so, the region will remain in a state of neither peace nor war, with controlled levels of escalation across all fronts, until the end of this year, when both the Israeli and American election results become clear.

America cannot turn a failed policy into a winning card

From broken promises to open war: The contradictions of Trump’s Iran policy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:39:21 UTC
02:39:21 KST

From broken promises to open war: The contradictions of Trump’s Iran policy
Islamabad — There is a rhythm to Donald Trump’s approach toward Iran. A warning is issued. Markets react. Military assets move into position. Diplomats search for an opening. Then, just as confrontation appears inevitable, Washington steps back.
That pattern defined Trump’s first presidency. It followed Iran’s downing of a US surveillance drone over the Strait of Hormuz in 2019 and resurfaced after Iran’s missile strike on Al Asad Air Base in 2020. Trump’s rhetoric repeatedly suggested war was imminent. His decisions usually stopped short of it.
 
 His return to the White House changed the pattern.
 
 Diplomatic deadlines increasingly ended in military operations. Direct American strikes on Iranian territory followed economic pressure. Negotiations gave way to demands for “unconditional surrender,” before diplomacy returned amid an unresolved conflict.
 
 Read across a decade, Trump’s speeches and official statements reveal more than confrontational rhetoric. They trace the changing purpose of American pressure—from leverage, to deterrence, to military coercion, and ultimately direct war.
 
 For Tehran, one question grew harder to ignore: if Washington’s demands kept expanding while pressure never eased, where was diplomacy supposed to lead?
Tearing up the deal
Iran stood at the center of Trump’s foreign-policy vision long before he entered the White House.
 
 Speaking at the AIPAC Policy Conference in March 2016, Trump called the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA) “disastrous” and pledged to dismantle it. He accused the Obama administration of empowering Tehran while failing to curb its missile program and regional influence.
 
 By September, the rhetoric had hardened further. Campaigning in Pensacola, Florida, he warned that Iranian vessels harassing US Navy ships “will be shot out of the water.”
 
 Once in office, he acted.
 
 On May 8, 2018, Trump withdrew the United States from the JCPOA and restored sanctions under the “maximum pressure” campaign. Washington argued that unprecedented economic pressure would force Tehran back to negotiations on American terms.
 
 Tehran reached the opposite conclusion.
 
 Iranian officials argued that Washington had abandoned an agreement negotiated over years, endorsed by the UN Security Council and repeatedly verified by the International Atomic Energy Agency. If one US administration could discard a signed agreement, they asked, why should another be trusted to honor a replacement?
 
 That question would shape every subsequent negotiation.
Pressure without war
By 2019, “maximum pressure” was colliding with events on the ground.
 
 Attacks on commercial shipping and a rocket strike near the US Embassy in Baghdad prompted Washington to deploy B-52 bombers, additional fighter aircraft and an aircraft carrier strike group. Trump warned that if Iran chose to “fight,” it would mean “the official end of Iran.”
 
 Weeks later, Iran shot down a US Global Hawk surveillance drone near the Strait of Hormuz.
 
 Trump approved retaliatory strikes, then cancelled them minutes before they were due to begin.
 
 He later explained that advisers had estimated roughly 150 Iranian casualties and that such a response would have been disproportionate to the loss of an unmanned aircraft.
 
 To many in Tehran, the episode exposed a recurring contradiction. Washington threatened force while insisting diplomacy remained its preferred option. Iranian officials argued that negotiations conducted under constant military pressure could never be negotiations between equals.
 
 The pattern resurfaced after attacks on Saudi Arabia’s Abqaiq and Khurais oil facilities. Trump declared the United States was “locked and loaded” but again chose reinforcement over retaliation.
 
 The major exception came in January 2020.
 
 Trump authorized the drone strike that martyred Lieutenant General Qassem Soleimani and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis near Baghdad International Airport. Washington described the operation as self-defense. Tehran condemned it as state terrorism.
 
 Five days later, Iran struck Al Asad Air Base with ballistic missiles.
 
 Trump again stepped back.
 
 Instead of escalating, he declared Iran “appears to be standing down” and said the United States was “ready to embrace peace with all who seek it.”
 
 Even in his final months in office, restraint remained visible. Reuters later reported that Trump examined military options against Iran’s Natanz enrichment facility before senior advisers argued against action.
 
 By January 2021, Washington had abandoned the nuclear agreement, imposed unprecedented sanctions, assassinated one of Iran’s most senior military commanders and repeatedly threatened military action.
 
 It had still stopped short of direct war.
From restraint to ‘hit the nuclear first’
After leaving office, Trump defended that record.
 
 He argued that his Iran policy had weakened Tehran while keeping America out of another Middle Eastern war. In the Bedminster recording later made public, he portrayed himself as the president who had restrained military advisers pressing for escalation.
 
 Three years later, campaigning for another term, he offered a different message.
 
 Asked whether Israel should strike Iran’s nuclear facilities, he replied:
 
 “Hit the nuclear first, and worry about the rest later.”
 
 For many in Tehran, the remark reinforced a growing belief that Washington’s objectives had moved beyond nuclear restrictions. Pressure itself had become the policy.
 
 The question would soon move from campaign rhetoric to presidential action.
Crossing the Rubicon
Trump’s second presidency began with diplomacy.
 
 In March 2025, he sent a letter to the Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei proposing negotiations while giving Tehran sixty days to respond. Indirect talks opened in Oman, even as Washington warned there would be “all hell to pay” if diplomacy failed.
 
 Iranian officials insisted that any agreement required guarantees Washington could no longer credibly provide after abandoning the JCPOA.
 
 The negotiations collapsed.
 
 Three days later, Israel launched large-scale strikes against Iranian nuclear and military facilities. Trump called the operation “excellent.”
 
 Soon afterwards came another phrase:“Unconditional surrender.”
 
 In Tehran, those words confirmed suspicions that Washington’s objectives had expanded beyond the nuclear file.
 
 Nine days later, American aircraft entered the war.
 
 Under Operation Midnight Hammer, B-2 bombers struck Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan. Trump declared Iran’s nuclear program had been “completely and totally obliterated.”
 
 For Tehran, the sequence mattered as much as the strikes.
 
 Washington had withdrawn from one agreement, imposed sweeping sanctions, reopened negotiations, coupled diplomacy with military ultimatums and then joined direct attacks after talks failed.
 
 The comparison with 2019 spoke for itself.
 
 Then, Trump cancelled strikes because casualties were judged disproportionate.
 
 Six years later, he authorized the largest direct American attack ever carried out against Iran’s nuclear infrastructure.
 
 Iran answered with missile strikes on Al Udeid Air Base in Qatar before a ceasefire ended the Twelve-Day War.
 
 The fighting paused.
 
 The policy did not.
 
 The New Objective
 
 The ceasefire created breathing space, not reconciliation.
 
 Regional governments resumed diplomatic efforts, but Washington’s language continued to evolve.
 
 During his first presidency, Trump insisted the United States was “not looking for regime change.” By late 2025, that distinction had blurred. American debate increasingly extended beyond Iran’s nuclear program to the future of the Islamic Republic.
 
 Inside Iran, the debate changed as well.
 
 Officials argued that Washington’s objectives now reached beyond limiting nuclear capabilities to reshaping Iran’s political order.
 
 When fighting resumed in early 2026, the United States and Israel launched a broader campaign. Trump increasingly framed the conflict in political terms, publicly questioning Iran’s leadership.
 
 Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei was martyred alongside senior military and security officials. The conflict widened across the region and disrupted traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.
 
 Even then, diplomacy returned.
 
 Negotiations resumed through regional intermediaries before fighting restarted. Tehran maintained that talks conducted under military coercion could not produce a lasting settlement.
 
 For Iranian policymakers, the pattern had become unmistakable. Each diplomatic initiative arrived under heavier sanctions, stronger military pressure and broader political demands than the one before.
When the rhythm changed
Donald Trump entered American politics promising to tear up a nuclear agreement.
 
 A decade later, he had presided over the first direct American strikes on Iran’s principal nuclear facilities.
 
 His own words trace the evolution.
 
 In 2016, the JCPOA was “disastrous.”
 
 In 2019, he warned of the “official end of Iran” before cancelling planned strikes.
 
 In 2020, he declared the United States was “ready to embrace peace.”
 
 By 2024, he argued that Israel should have “hit the nuclear first.”
 
 Months after returning to office, he demanded Iran’s “unconditional surrender.”
 
 There is a rhythm to Donald Trump’s approach toward Iran.
 
 For years, threats were followed by negotiations, negotiations by sanctions and military deployments, before Washington stepped back.
 
 The rhythm survived.
 
 What changed was the point at which Washington stopped stepping back.
 
 From Tehran’s perspective, the lesson was not simply that American policy became more forceful. It was that the space between diplomacy and coercion steadily disappeared. Every negotiation unfolded under greater sanctions, stronger military pressure and broader political demands than the last.
 
 That, more than any single speech or military operation, remains the defining contradiction of Trump’s Iran policy.

International Peoples’ Assembly: Solidarity with Iran means confronting the aggressor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:31:11 UTC
02:31:11 KST

International Peoples’ Assembly: Solidarity with Iran means confronting the aggressor
TEHRAN – An open letter published by The Guardian on August 20 has drawn criticism for placing Iran and the U.S. and Israel which launched a war against the Islamic Republic within what critics describe as a morally misleading framework.
The letter, addressed to Iranian political prisoners and signed by a number of prominent international academics and activists, portrays them as caught “between two blades of a scissors,” equating domestic repression with the external military and economic assault on Iran.
While the letter formally condemns U.S. and Israeli attacks as well as sanctions, its framing has been criticized for obscuring the fundamental distinction between aggressors waging war and a country defending its sovereignty.An open letter published by The Guardian on August 20 has drawn criticism for placing Iran and the U.S. and Israel which launched a war against the Islamic Republic within what critics describe as a morally misleading framework.
The letter, addressed to Iranian political prisoners and signed by a number of prominent international academics and activists, portrays them as caught “between two blades of a scissors,” equating domestic repression with the external military and economic assault on Iran. While the letter formally condemns U.S. and Israeli attacks as well as sanctions, its framing has been criticized for obscuring the fundamental distinction between aggressors waging war and a country defending its sovereignty.
An appeal circulated by the International Peoples' Assembly, written by Indian historian and commentator Vijay Prashad, takes the opposite position. It argues for a clearer stance of solidarity with Iran, saying that criticism of internal conditions cannot be pulled apart from the fact that the country is currently under sustained military attack.
Prashad opens by setting that context. For six months, he writes, Iranian civilian and military sites have come under fire, with hospitals, schools, energy facilities and residential neighborhoods among the targets hit. Iran did not begin this war, he states plainly, and he argues that fact has to shape how anyone writing about the country today thinks about their own political responsibility.
His sharpest objection is to the scissors image itself. The trouble isn't just that the two blades are unequal in strength, he says. It's that the metaphor puts the aggressor and the country being attacked on the same moral footing, stripping out the history and hierarchy between them.
"The error of the scissors," he writes, "is not merely that its blades are unequal. It is that the image makes the aggressor and the attacked appear as parallel sources of the same danger." From there he traces how U.S. power has imposed sanctions, backed Israel, and now brought direct war to Iranian territory, while Iran has spent decades absorbing invasion, sanctions, sabotage and assassinations.
He isn't arguing Iran should be off limits for criticism. He says outright that people can oppose the death penalty, demand due process, call for humane treatment of prisoners, and listen to workers, women, minorities and political activists. His point is narrower than that: such criticism can't be lifted out of the conditions under which it's being made.
He also raises a pointed question about the Guardian letter's signatories, many of them based in the United States, and why they chose to direct their appeal mainly at Iran rather than at their own governments. The letter does call on the U.S. and Israel to end their wars and sanctions, but that demand only shows up in the closing lines, after most of the letter's energy has already gone into building an equivalence between Iran's prison system and the war being waged against the country.
For Prashad and the International Peoples' Assembly, the priority right now is resisting any narrative that treats the aggression as ordinary, especially one that ends up weakening the country under attack at the exact moment it's defending itself. He argues that calling Iran's anti-imperialism "hollow" doesn't hold up while the country is under direct military pressure and fighting to hold onto its independence.
Drawing on the history of anti-colonial movements, he notes that societies living under constant threat of invasion, sabotage and regime change tend to develop real internal contradictions. But those contradictions, he insists, shouldn't be used to erase the line between the side attacking and the side being attacked.
He closes on a simple note. "At this hour," he writes, "solidarity begins with a clear demand: the United States and Israel must end their illegal war, and they must retreat."

====================================================================================================

Trump’s coalition fractures as midterm reckoning looms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:29:48 UTC
02:29:48 KST

Donald Trump’s name will not appear on the ballot when Americans vote on November 3, but the midterm elections are increasingly shaping up as a referendum on his presidency.
Less than two years after returning to the White House with a victory that dramatically expanded the Republican coalition, Trump now faces sharp erosion among independent voters, Hispanics and more moderate Republicans, even as his core MAGA base remains overwhelmingly loyal.
The stakes are enormous. Republicans currently hold narrow control of the House and a Senate majority. Losing either chamber would make it significantly harder for Trump to advance legislation, confirm nominees and avoid congressional investigations during the final two years of his term.
The central problem for Republicans is that Trump’s 2024 coalition extended well beyond traditional MAGA voters.
He made major gains among Hispanics, younger voters and working-class Americans, while also attracting people who did not consider themselves reliable Republicans. Pew analysis found that 48% of Hispanic voters backed Trump in 2024, up from 36% in 2020, with especially strong gains among Hispanic men and voters without college degrees. Now, parts of that coalition are moving away.
The reasons vary. For many Hispanic voters, the economy is central. Among independents, frustration reflects a combination of the cost of living, the war in Iran and broader dissatisfaction with the president. Inside the Republican Party, the divide between loyal MAGA supporters and more moderate Republicans is becoming increasingly visible.
For congressional candidates, however, the reason matters less than the result: some of the voters who helped Trump win in 2024 are no longer in the same place politically.
The nearly six-month war with Iran has added another major burden for Trump. He returned to office promising to tackle the cost of living and avoid prolonged wars. Instead, the conflict has disrupted oil trade through the Strait of Hormuz and contributed to higher fuel prices, turning a foreign-policy crisis into an immediate economic issue for American households.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll published this week put Trump’s approval rating at 33%, the lowest of his current term, while 64% said they disapproved of his performance. Eight in 10 Americans believe U.S. involvement in Iran will continue for a long time, including 71% of Republicans. Only one in five Americans said the war had been worth the cost.
An Economist/YouGov poll painted a similarly difficult picture. Fifty-seven percent said going to war was the wrong decision, while only 25% said it was the right one. Sixty-five percent want Washington to reach an agreement ending the conflict as quickly as possible, including 48% of Republicans. Among independent voters, 61% believe the war will last at least another year. For many voters, the debate over Iran ultimately comes down to what they pay at the gas station.
Why the midterms matter
Midterm elections are held halfway through a president’s four-year term. The presidency is not on the ballot, but all 435 seats in the House of Representatives are. Republicans currently hold a narrow House majority, meaning even a relatively small shift in competitive districts could hand control to Democrats.
If Democrats capture the House, they could block or delay White House legislation, control congressional committees, launch investigations and summon administration officials for testimony.
The Senate operates differently. Senators serve six-year terms, with roughly one-third of seats contested every two years. In November, 33 regularly scheduled seats will be up for election, along with additional special elections.
Republicans currently hold 53 Senate seats, while Democrats have 45. Two independents, Bernie Sanders and Angus King, caucus with Democrats, effectively giving the Democratic bloc 47 votes. That means Democrats would need four more seats to reach 51 and control the Senate outright. Losing the Senate would also make it harder for Trump to secure confirmation of senior administration officials and judges.
MAGA remains loyal. The problem is everyone else
Trump’s core support remains exceptionally strong. In an Economist/YouGov poll conducted August 14-17, 95% of Republicans who identified as MAGA supporters approved of his performance, while only 4% disapproved.
But among Republicans who do not identify with MAGA, approval dropped to 59%, with 40% disapproving. That divide is increasingly visible even on immigration, one of Trump’s signature issues.
A new POLITICO poll found that 50% of Americans believe the administration’s mass deportation campaign has become too aggressive. Nearly a quarter of voters who backed Trump in 2024 also said the policy had gone too far.
Reuters/Ipsos data show another warning sign: the Republican advantage over Democrats on which party is better equipped to handle immigration has collapsed from 26 percentage points at the start of 2025 to just two points today. Trump is not facing a revolt from his base. The danger is that the voters around that base are weakening in their support.
No group better illustrates that shift than Hispanic men. They were among Trump’s biggest electoral success stories in 2024, helping Republicans argue that the old assumption that minority voters would reliably support Democrats was beginning to break down.
CNN polling analyst Harry Enten presented data this week showing how dramatically that support has changed. Trump won Hispanic men by 10 percentage points in 2024. His current net approval among them stands at minus 41, a 51-point swing.
On the economy, the shift is even larger. Before the 2024 election, Hispanic men preferred Trump over Kamala Harris on economic issues by 11 points. His current net rating on the economy among that group is minus 49, a 60-point reversal.
The comparison is not exact, since election results and approval ratings measure different things. But CNN also presented data directly tied to the coming congressional vote. Republicans won Hispanic men by eight points in the 2024 congressional elections. Democrats now lead among them by 20 points, a 28-point shift.
Independents move sharply away
Independent voters may be even more important. According to Ipsos data cited by CNN, Trump’s net approval among independents now stands at minus 47. At the beginning of his second term, it was minus one.
Economist/YouGov found that only 21% of independents approve of his performance, while 74% disapprove. That does not mean all of those voters will support Democrats. Some may vote for local Republican candidates, choose independents or simply stay home. And that may be enough to hurt the GOP.
In close congressional districts, Republicans do not necessarily need Trump voters to defect to Democrats. They simply need too many of them to lose motivation and stay home.
Inside the party, signs of unease are already visible. Republican Sen. Jim Justice of West Virginia said this week that anyone failing to see how Americans are being hurt by food and fuel prices is “living in a cave,” arguing that Republicans need to pay more attention to economic pressure on voters.
Arizona Republican strategist Barrett Marson put the political danger even more starkly, telling CNN that there is one person who is not sufficiently worried about gas prices, and that “one person controls our fate”: Trump.
Congress has also seen defections over the Iran war. In July, four House Republicans joined Democrats in supporting a resolution calling for an end to U.S. military operations against Iran without congressional authorization.
The measure was largely symbolic, but it highlighted the extent to which the war has become a political problem even within the GOP.
‘Why should we vote if he isn’t doing what he promised?’
Behind the polling are voters who supported Trump in 2024 and are now reconsidering their political choices.
Reuters has been following a group of Trump voters throughout his second term. The group is not statistically representative, but their interviews offer a glimpse into the mood among parts of the coalition that returned him to office.
Juan Rivera, 26, from the San Diego area, said he still intends to vote for Republican candidates. But while canvassing Latino voters, he encountered disappointed Trump supporters who had lost enthusiasm. “Why should I vote when the president isn’t doing what he promised?” he said some voters asked him.
Steve Egan, a 65-year-old Florida business owner who voted for Trump, told Reuters that tariffs had increased his business costs while the war had pushed up fuel and other prices. His opinion of Trump had deteriorated so much, he said, that an endorsement from the president could now make him less likely to support a candidate.
Robert Billups of Washington state said he no longer feels committed to Republican candidates and will vote in November for whoever offers what he considers the best plan, regardless of party. These voters are not necessarily becoming Democrats. That is precisely the problem.
The coalition beyond MAGA
Trump still dominates the Republican Party, and loyalty among MAGA voters remains extraordinarily high. But he did not win in 2024 only because of voters who would support him under almost any circumstances.
He won by expanding the coalition, drawing in Hispanic men, working-class voters, independents and people who had not previously been reliable Republican voters. In November, Republicans need those voters again, but Trump himself will not be on the ballot to draw them out.
Democrats currently lead registered voters 46% to 39% in the Economist/YouGov generic congressional ballot. Among voters who say they are extremely enthusiastic about voting, the gap is much wider: 60% say they plan to vote Democratic, compared with 37% Republican.
Trump’s MAGA base remains intact. The question facing Republicans is whether the broader coalition that returned him to power still exists. For now, the numbers suggest it is beginning to fracture.

Status of the Unmanned Systems Forces’ "MoLoChKa" operation: blocking any movement of vessels of russia’s shadow fleet in the Sea of Azov and through the Kerch Strait, and restricting movement in the northern and northeastern parts of the Black Sea. During August, the Birds of the Unmanned Systems Forces struck 36 vessels of the shadow fleet (242 vessels from the beginning of the operation on July 6 through August 22, namely: 134 in the Sea of Azov and 108 in the Black Sea).

Canada to hit US back with tariffs after trade talks fail
August 22, 2026
In an ongoing trade dispute with the US, Canada said on Saturday that it would introduce tariffs on several US products starting September 8.
The announcement comes in retaliation to the US imposing 50% tariffs earlier on Saturday on a broad range of Canadian products after the two sides failed to reach a trade deal on Friday.
"Canada will match Washington's new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses," Prime Minister Mark Carney told reporters in Ottawa.
"In the coming days, we will release the details of these new tariff measures, which will come into force the Tuesday after Labor Day,” he said.
While the United States had blamed Canada for declining to finalize the trade pact with Washington on Friday, Carney defended Ottawa's position, explaining, "We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked."
He later on Saturday met virtually with provincial and territorial premiers to discuss the suspension of the trade talks with the US.
What products are affected by the tariffs?
The US tariffs will affect a broad range of products, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods, and hockey equipment, and cover some $20 billion (€17 billion) worth of Canadian exports to its southern neighbor.
Canada's retaliatory tariffs would, in turn, target steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, Carney said.
The US currently accounts for roughly 70% of Canadian exports, making Ottawa potentially more vulnerable in the standoff Carney explicitly described as a trade "war."
"You're at war when you get attacked. We got attacked," he said, adding that Canada had the reserves, resilience and plan to respond.
Friendly ties turned sour
The fresh tariffs are the culmination of long and tense trade negotiations between the two sides and mark a sharp reversal from just two days earlier, when officials from both sides appeared optimistic that a compromise was in the making.
According to the AP news agency, no further talks were planned to resolve the situation.
The US administration's approach to Canada is a major change from the friendly ties the two countries have traditionally had. US President Donald Trump has often said he wants tariffs on Canadian goods to encourage companies to move manufacturing back to the United States.
He has also made controversial comments about making Canada the 51st US state. Carney said Canada understood that "America has changed" and that the two countries would "not return to their old relationship."

World in churn, and India’s foreign policy needs to adapt to it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:26:08 UTC
02:26:08 KST

There is a growing sense that something is seriously amiss in India’s foreign policy. Yet, foreign policy debate is still tiptoeing around the big questions.
There were three foundational assumptions that underlay Indian choices at the turn of this century. First, no great power in history had acquired such preponderance over its rivals as the US had by 2000. US primacy also meant there was no way to avoid hitching a ride with the US.
Second, to make the arrangement mutually attractive, a common antagonist, China, was projected to help overcome decades of dissonance and suspicion that had divided Indians and Americans. The new discourse played on Indian ego and US greed. Washington would lift Delhi in the international pecking order, while India would generate business and arms sales for America. If everything unfolded as planned, India would become a prized Western sentinel in Asia, cementing US hegemony for the 21st century.
Third, although the world economy had broadened by the early 2000s, the US was firmly at the helm in connecting the Global South to the G-7. Interdependence was a euphemism for a US-led geoeconomic order that would dominate innovation, supply chains and international trade.
All three assumptions have been shattered in recent years. One, the US has not just lost its primacy, it has lost its ability to control major geopolitical events. Every roll of the dice in recent years to arrest its decline — the trade standoff with China, NATO’s confrontation with Russia, the clash against Iran — has produced a blowback that has further weakened it.
Historically, the balance of power has always been ultimately revealed through major war. The present phase is no exception. The Ukraine and Iran wars have not just depleted NATO arsenals, they have exposed the doctrinal fragility of Western military power.
Two, China has raced so far ahead that the rhetoric from two decades ago of an Indian ‘catch-up’ and ‘the 21st century rivalry’ appears absurd to any sober observer. The Chinese lead is not merely in aggregate economic terms but in the underlying policy institutions, human capital and technologies.
And, most crucially of all, the commanding heights of the world economy are inexorably shifting towards the east. From manufacturing and high technologies to energy and natural resources, consumer demand, and financial capital, the greater Eurasian continent and its periphery have all the core requirements of sustaining a dynamic geoeconomic order without dependence on the Atlantic West. At no point in recent centuries was such a Eurasian-centred globalisation possible.
But even as world events have upended the Indian foreign policy consensus, a network of gatekeepers is stubbornly impervious to change. The defenders of the failed policy erect a straw man to frighten policymakers from a thoughtful reassessment. China, they say, must remain the raison d’être of Indian policy planning even as US predatory actions seek to eviscerate the last vestiges of India’s strategic independence and authority in the subcontinent. Much has changed between 2005 — when the US pledged to help make India a “major power in the 21st century” — and 2026, when a US diplomat publicly warned that India would never be permitted to acquire the sinews of a great power. Pentagon official Elbridge Colby even had the cheek to imply that US strategic interests vis-à-vis China would not be held hostage to disputes within Asia.
Must India be the only rigid actor amidst all these churnings and machinations around it? The search for a workable modus vivendi with China must acquire a bipartisan policy priority, not as an afterthought to merely prevent conflict in the Himalayas but as a means to diversify a dangerous dependence on the West. India needs to permanently discard the proxy role that it assumed during the unipolar moment and recover its regional power identity that allows for differences as well as shared responsibilities with China. The world is becoming multipolar. And such a future demands responsible Eurasian powers to safeguard world order and stability. It is in India’s vital interests to play such a role.
India’s foreign policy debate can’t be stuck on an old framework, one that prides itself on managing the distance between Delhi and the great powers. There is no geopolitical room or surplus strength in any great power’s tent to underwrite India’s social, economic and security challenges. The Cold War is over. The post-Cold War era is over too. The transformation in world politics demands a new intellectual framework where sovereignty, regional interdependence, new geoeconomic networks of trade and investment, international public goods and order-building are placed at the front and centre of India’s foreign policy.
To change course, Indian leaders need to look at the day after tomorrow.

When the judge is punished: America, the veto and the unravelling of international law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
17:25:53 UTC
02:25:53 KST

When the judge is punished: America, the veto and the unravelling of international law
“When law becomes subordinate to power, justice becomes a privilege rather than a right”
GOA, India - There is something profoundly disturbing about the spectacle now unfolding before the world. The United States, which has for decades presented itself as the principal architect and defender of the rules-based international order, is increasingly behaving as though international rules are legitimate only when they serve American power.
When those rules inconvenience Washington or its closest allies, the language changes. Sovereignty is invoked. National security is invoked. American exceptionalism is invoked. And now, increasingly, sanctions are invoked against those who attempt to apply international law.
The latest assault is directed not merely at a foreign government but at the International Criminal Court itself. On August 18, 2026, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on ICC President Tomoko Akane and senior trial lawyer Abdoulaye Seye. The sanctions freeze assets within American jurisdiction and cut the targeted officials off from the US financial system.
The ICC has condemned the action as a flagrant attack on its independence. Japan, Akane's country, has described the sanctions as “very unfortunate”, while European governments have reaffirmed their support for the Court.
This is not an isolated act. It is the culmination of a long American hostility towards international institutions when they threaten to place American conduct or that of its allies under legal scrutiny. The United States signed the Rome Statute establishing the ICC in 2000 but never ratified it. In 2002, Washington formally notified the United Nations that it did not intend to become a party to the treaty. Under George W. Bush, the United States even sought guarantees protecting its nationals from ICC jurisdiction. Under Donald Trump in 2020, ICC personnel were subjected to sanctions.
President Biden subsequently revoked those sanctions, but his administration continued to oppose the Court's jurisdiction over the Palestinian situation. Trump returned to the offensive in February 2025 with an executive order authorising sanctions against ICC personnel.
What has changed now is the ferocity of the campaign. The United States is no longer merely refusing the jurisdiction of a court it never joined. It is attempting to intimidate the institution, punish its officials and encourage countries to abandon it.
Washington's hostility intensified after the ICC issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former “Defence” Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes connected with the Gaza war. The United States and Israel reject the Court's jurisdiction, but disagreement with a judicial decision is not a legitimate justification for attacking the judiciary itself.
This brings us to the deeper crisis: the gradual unhinging of the United Nations system itself.
The Security Council was born in 1945 out of a compromise among the victorious great powers. The veto was designed to ensure that the major powers would remain inside the system rather than walk away from it. But what may once have been a political compromise has become a structural instrument of impunity. Five countries retain the extraordinary ability to prevent the Council from taking substantive action, even when an overwhelming majority of the international community supports it.
The United States has not been alone in abusing this privilege. Russia has used it to protect its interests, China has employed it to shield allies and positions it considers vital, and Britain and France have historically exercised the veto in defence of their own geopolitical interests. The problem is therefore larger than American conduct. The problem is the architecture itself: a supposedly universal organisation in which five states remain constitutionally more equal than the other 188.
 
 But America's use of the veto, particularly in relation to Palestine, has made the contradiction impossible to ignore.
During the Gaza war, Washington repeatedly blocked Security Council initiatives calling for ceasefires. On February 20, 2024, it vetoed an immediate ceasefire resolution despite overwhelming international support. In April 2024, it vetoed a resolution that would have opened the way for the General Assembly to consider Palestine's application for full UN membership, despite 12 of the 15 Security Council members voting in favour. On June 4, 2025, Washington again vetoed a resolution demanding an immediate, unconditional and permanent ceasefire in Gaza.
The consequences of such vetoes are not abstract. A veto in a diplomatic chamber can become a bomb falling on a hospital, a family denied food, a displaced population denied protection or a humanitarian agency denied access. International law becomes meaningless when its implementation can be suspended by the geopolitical preference of one powerful state.
The founders of the UN could not have anticipated the extent to which the veto would become an instrument of political paralysis. But the world has been warning about the problem for decades. The UN's own historical records document repeated concern about the way vetoes diminished the role of non-permanent members and damaged the credibility of the Council.
The General Assembly has attempted to respond. In April 2022, it adopted Resolution 76/262, establishing what became known as the “veto initiative”. Whenever a permanent member casts a veto, the General Assembly is to meet and debate the veto within a specified period. It was an important step towards accountability, but it does not remove the underlying problem. A veto can still kill a resolution before the General Assembly gets the opportunity to discuss its consequences.
That is not enough.
If the Security Council is repeatedly paralysed by the very states entrusted with maintaining international peace and security, the international community must ask a fundamental question: what purpose does the Council serve if its permanent members can disable it whenever their own interests are at stake?
The answer cannot be to abolish the United Nations. The world needs the UN more than ever. It needs a universal institution capable of mediating conflicts, organising humanitarian assistance, establishing international norms and giving smaller nations a diplomatic voice. What must be challenged is the undemocratic concentration of power within the Security Council.
The first reform must therefore be the abolition, or at the very least radical restriction, of the veto.
There should be no veto where genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes or mass civilian atrocities are credibly alleged. A government should not be able to prevent the international community from responding to mass atrocities simply because it is one of five privileged members of an institution created 81 years ago.
If abolishing the veto altogether is politically impossible in the immediate future, states should establish a binding political convention that no permanent member will exercise it in cases involving mass atrocities. France and Mexico have already advocated restraint in the use of the veto in such circumstances. The proposal deserves to become an international norm rather than remain a diplomatic aspiration.
Second, the General Assembly must be given a much stronger role whenever the Security Council is paralysed. The historic “Uniting for Peace” mechanism, developed during the Korean War, offers a precedent. If the Council cannot act because of a veto, the Assembly should automatically assume a greater political responsibility. It should be empowered to recommend collective measures, establish investigative mechanisms and mobilise international humanitarian and diplomatic action.
Third, the composition of the Security Council must change. A Council designed in 1945 cannot claim democratic legitimacy in a world in which Africa has no permanent seat, India has no permanent seat and Latin America has no permanent seat. The distribution of political power must reflect the contemporary world rather than the geopolitical settlement at the end of the Second World War.
Fourth, international judicial institutions must be insulated from retaliation by powerful states.
The ICC is imperfect. It can be criticised. Its procedures can be debated. Its jurisdiction can be challenged through law. But a state that disagrees with a court does not acquire the right to sanction its judges. If Washington believes the ICC is exceeding its jurisdiction, it should make its case before the international community. If it believes the Rome Statute is defective, it should propose amendments. It should not attempt to destroy the institution because its investigations have become politically uncomfortable.
The danger is enormous. If the United States can punish ICC judges, another powerful state will inevitably claim the same right. Russia can punish investigators who examine Russian conduct. China can punish officials who investigate Chinese conduct. Israel can reject international judicial authority. Other governments will learn the same lesson: international law applies to the weak; power protects the strong.
That is the precise opposite of what the post-war international system was supposed to achieve.
There is also a profound irony here. Washington routinely invokes a “rules-based international order” when criticising Russia, China, Iran or other adversaries. Yet the legitimacy of rules cannot depend upon the identity of the accused. A rule that applies to one's adversary but not to oneself is not a rule. It is an instrument of power.
The ICC crisis therefore presents the world with a test far larger than the fate of two officials in The Hague. It asks whether international justice is going to remain genuinely international.
The answer should be unequivocal.
The countries that support the ICC must refuse to be intimidated. They should provide alternative banking and financial arrangements for sanctioned Court personnel, guarantee the independence of ICC operations, strengthen diplomatic support for the Court and reject American demands that they withdraw from the Rome Statute.
The European Union, Japan, Canada, Australia, African states and countries of Latin America should make clear that sanctions against judges cannot become an accepted instrument of international diplomacy.
The same principle must apply to the UN. The permanent members cannot be allowed to convert the veto from a safeguard of great-power participation into a licence for great-power impunity.
The world is approaching a dangerous crossroads. One path leads towards a genuinely multilateral system in which law is stronger than power. The other leads towards competing spheres of influence in which the powerful write the rules, interpret the rules and exempt themselves from the rules.
The United States is not destroying the international order alone. Russia, China and other powers have contributed to its erosion. But Washington occupies a special position because it has long claimed to be the guardian of that order. Its responsibility is therefore greater. When the self-proclaimed guardian begins attacking the institutions of international law, the damage is not merely national. It is systemic.
The United Nations cannot remain an organisation in which five governments possess a permanent political escape hatch. Nor can the ICC survive as a court that is expected to prosecute the crimes of the powerless while fearing retaliation from the powerful.
The international community must therefore reclaim the principle that sovereignty is not immunity and power is not innocence. The Security Council must be democratised, the veto must be radically curtailed, the General Assembly must be strengthened and international courts must be protected from political retaliation.
Otherwise, the world will have institutions that look international but function according to the hierarchy of power. And that would be the final humiliation of the UN: a world organisation reduced to asking permission from the powerful to enforce the law against them.
When the powerful can veto justice and then sanction the judges, the world does not have a rules-based order. It has a dictatorship of power wearing the robes of international law.

He was referring to the continuation of the United States’ maximum-pressure policy and economic sanctions against Iran, which Tehran has long described as a form of economic warfare.

According to Khatibzadeh, hundreds of international documents concerning 'new acts of terrorism' have been prepared by the Foreign Ministry over the past year and several months and submitted to international organizations.
He also accused the United States, Israel and some of their allies of seeking to prevent such cases from reaching international bodies. 'Tehran would continue efforts to pursue accountability through diplomatic channels,' added the diplomat.
'Terrorism has no good or bad side,' Khatibzadeh said, arguing that international relations should not be governed by 'the logic of force.'
He pledged that Iran’s diplomatic apparatus would continue pursuing those responsible for 'acts of terrorism and would not allow alleged perpetrators to remain without accountability.'
Khatibzadeh’s remarks came as Tehran continues to frame economic sanctions and maximum-pressure policies as part of a broader confrontation with Iran, while emphasizing domestic resilience, coordination among state institutions and diplomatic efforts to challenge the measures internationally.
Despite the pressure, he said, Iran had prevailed in previous confrontations and would do so again.

I experienced this at the Defence Ministry, I fought it, I dismantled those schemes there and I stopped them. A large number of law enforcement officers support them, and a large number of people are building these schemes.
This isn't about one project or one branch of government. It's about a new social contract. Let's find people who make effective decisions to stop the war, let's give them the opportunity to work, let's assess them through the subsequent democratic process. Because when there is no such process… We are no longer surprised by the latest NABU [National Anti-Corruption Bureau] recordings. Even if they appear every week, it seems now that the whole of society understands: 'Everyone steals.' But this is not normal."
Details: Asked why he did not name the corrupt individuals concerned, Fedorov said: "The time will come when all Ukrainians will learn their names. Some will learn them from recordings made by the law enforcement agencies, some from journalistic investigations, and some for other reasons. We are also doing our homework in this area. And eventually all the names... everyone in our country will find out everything; it has always been this way. That is our culture. And it will happen in this case as well."
Fedorov went on: "We are not talking about one or two people, or just some senior officials; we are talking about hundreds of people who over the years have become accustomed to making money from the state budget."
When the interviewer asked why these people have prevailed, given that Fedorov has not been reinstated as defence minister, he replied: "I think these people will lose, because that was a battle for the Defence Ministry, whereas this is a war for the development of the country, and they will definitely lose that war. I see a lot of evidence of this – both the activity of our citizens who took to the streets in protest and the work of the anti-corruption agencies."
Asked whether he is still in contact with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Fedorov said: "I think we haven't spoken for a few weeks, definitely."
Background: In a video address on 18 August, Fedorov said that Ukraine is facing a "systemic crisis of governance" and criticised the influence of private interests on the work of parliament, particularly with regard to defence, pharmaceuticals, gambling and taxation.

Tropical Storm Moke advances toward Hawaii as winds strengthen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22

Tropical Storm Moke advances toward Hawaii as winds strengthen
HONOLULU (AP) — Tropical Storm Moke advanced toward Hawaii Saturday, likely bringing more heavy rainfall and strong gusts to the Big Island, where residents are still dealing with the aftermath of heavy flooding and damaging winds from Hurricane Lala.
Moke, which formed Friday in the Pacific Ocean, was located about 470 miles (755 kilometers) southeast of Hilo, moving west-northwest at 12 mph (19 kph), as of 5 a.m. on Saturday in Hawaii. Maximum sustained winds were around 50 mph (85 kph), the National Hurricane Center said.
As with Hurricane Lala, the Big Island is expected to bear the brunt of Moke’s rain and heavy winds as it passes south of a direct hit late Saturday into early Sunday.
Moke will then continue its westward path near the islands through early Tuesday, said Casey Oswant, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Honolulu.
“There will still be impacts, especially to the windward and southeast sides of the Big Island, but it will probably be a little bit more limited than what we saw with Lala,” Oswant said.
Lala downed trees, swept buildings off their foundations, damaged roads and bridges and left roads covered in mud and rocks. One storm-related death was reported.
Rainfall predictions for this weekend for the southeast and windward sides of the Big Island were 5 to 10 inches (13 to 25 centimeters), with as much as 15 inches (38 centimeters) in isolated areas, Oswant said. Across the rest of the island chain, 1 to 2 inches (2 to 5 centimeters) of rain was expected, though parts of east Maui could see up to 4 inches (10 centimeters), she said.
There were no coastal watches or warnings in effect early Saturday morning, but people were urged to closely monitor the storm’s progress. The rainfall has the potential to cause dangerous rip currents, life-threatening flooding and mudslides, especially in steep areas and places where the ground remains saturated, the center said.
The northeast coast of the Big Island saw the heaviest total rainfall from Lala, at 43.54 inches (1.1 meters), according to the weather service. About 9,000 customers on the Big Island remained without power Saturday, according to poweroutage.us.
Hawaii Gov. Josh Green and other state officials held a news conference ahead of Moke, urging people to prepare by restocking food, medicine and other essentials.
“There’s definitely tension in the air” at the thought of more rain in communities that floodwaters turned into rivers, said Tiffany Edwards Hunt, a teacher living in Keaau, on the east side of the Big Island.
___
Associated Press writer Alexa St. John contributed from Detroit.

Canada to impose retaliatory tariffs across a raft of US sectors, PM Carney says
- Canada will impose retaliatory tariffs on US imports starting Sept 8 to match President Trump's new 50% tariffs on Canadian goods.
- The tariffs affect multiple sectors, threatening jobs and businesses, with Canada planning support measures for impacted industries.
- Negotiations failed due to last-minute US demands seen as unfair, and no new talks are currently planned between the two countries.
AI generated
OTTAWA - Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Aug 22 that Canada would impose tariffs starting Sept 8 on imports from the United States across a raft of sectors in retaliation for President Donald Trump’s new 50 per cent tariffs that took effect at midnight.
After days of intense negotiations, the two countries failed to reach a trade deal late on Aug 21, worsening a delicate relationship between the long-term trade partners and allies and complicating the future of the continental free trade pact called the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement.
Trump’s new tariffs hit a slew of sectors, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods and hockey equipment, and cover some US$20 billion (S$25 billion) of Canadian exports to the US. These duties do not exempt Canadian products under the USMCA, which has shielded most Canadian exports to the US in the last 18 months.
“Canada will match Washington’s new tariffs dollar for dollar in order to protect Canadian workers, farmers, families, and businesses,” Carney said at a news conference.
Canada’s tariffs will hit US sectors such as steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics, along with some sectors the US previously targeted in Canada, Carney said from Ottawa’s Parliament building. The government will release details over the next several days, Carney said.
“We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked,” Carney said.
Trump had expressed hope that a deal with Canada could happen on Aug 21.
But Carney said the US administration’s last-minute demands halted progress.
“In recent days, the US proposed new terms that were uneconomic, unfair, and undermined the net benefits to Canada, calling into question the reliability of any deal,” he said, adding these demands included curtailing Canada’s ability to forge new trade deals.
Carney said Canada would announce support measures next week for industries that are hit by the new US duties, alongside new tariffs on the US.
‘Bad deal’
The new US tariffs cover around 5 per cent of Canada’s exports to the US. They could expose some vulnerable industries such as softwood lumber and wine to severe damage and lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.
“We will be mobilising our network of businesses in all regions and all sectors to brace for impact and make the best of a bad situation,” said Candace Laing, chief executive officer of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford, one of the most vocal opponents of US tariffs, supported Carney’s decision to retaliate.
“I’m glad he didn’t sign that deal because it was a bad deal. It was a bad deal for Ontario. It was a bad deal for the auto sector, the steel sector, and manufacturing sector,” Ford told reporters on Aug 22.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told Fox News on Aug 22 that no new talks are planned with Canada.
“We’re moving forward with measures that respond to Canadian retaliation,” Greer said. “They’ve always had the best deal, and they still would have an even better deal, but they didn’t want that.” REUTERS
