Roundup: Polish experts see growing potential for AI cooperation with China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
23:43:14 CST
00:43:14 KST

WARSAW, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- As artificial intelligence (AI) moves rapidly from laboratories into factories, hospitals and classrooms, its expanding applications are creating new opportunities for scientific and technological cooperation between China and Poland.
Polish experts see growing potential for deeper China-Poland AI cooperation, citing the complementary strengths of China's mature industrial ecosystem and broad application market and Poland's expertise in mathematics, engineering and basic research.
Katarzyna Kaniewska, an official with the Foreign Cooperation Office of the Polish Chamber of Commerce, said China and Poland can deepen cooperation in healthcare, climate-related services and education.
Both China and Europe face population aging and declining birth rates. AI can help ease pressure on healthcare systems by handling some routine examinations, laboratory tests and administrative tasks, allowing medical professionals to devote more time to work requiring human judgment, Kaniewska said.
It can also support climate monitoring and early warning, while serving as an auxiliary tool for teachers and students, she added.
For companies, cooperation can help develop AI solutions tailored to local market demand. For researchers, it can expand existing personnel exchanges into joint work in basic research, said Roman Szewczyk, director of the Systems Research Institute of the Polish Academy of Sciences.
Cezary Blaszczyk, director of the Department of International Cooperation at the National Centre for Research and Development of Poland, said Chinese and Polish researchers have shown a strong willingness to work together and that the potential for AI cooperation is substantial.
According to Szewczyk, basic research should remain central to AI cooperation. His institute has trained doctoral students from China, and he hopes collaboration can expand beyond personnel exchanges to joint fundamental research.
Krzysztof Pyrc, president of the Foundation for Polish Science, said the potential of research cooperation with China remains underestimated by some scientists abroad.
Greater links among universities, research institutes, funding bodies and enterprises can help convert complementary strengths into concrete results, he said.
For China and Poland, robotics cooperation can bring together AI algorithms, sensors, control systems, mechatronics and manufacturing expertise, creating opportunities in areas ranging from industrial automation to medical and elderly-care services.
The benefits, however, will extend beyond robotics.
The same model -- joint research followed by local testing and adaptation -- can be applied in healthcare, climate services and education. It can also make AI tools more accessible to Polish small and medium-sized enterprises, helping them improve efficiency and develop new products and services.
Blaszczyk emphasized that companies generally approach cooperation in practical terms, focusing on technological strengths, product competitiveness and market demand.
Such an approach can help turn scientific collaboration into viable products and services with wider economic and social value.
"I hope the challenges brought by AI development can be addressed through bilateral cooperation, and that AI can benefit humanity and create more possibilities for future cooperation," said Blaszczyk. ■

ADDIS ABABA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Experts and policymakers on Friday called for building a resilient regional health economy in East Africa, through expanded domestic medical manufacturing, enhanced public-private partnerships, and accelerated cross-border integration.
They made the call during the 13th East African Health Federation Conference and International Exhibition, which opened Friday in Addis Ababa, the capital of Ethiopia, with the aim of building resilient health systems across the region and beyond.
The three-day high-level gathering, running until Sunday, has brought together more than 2,000 delegates from over 20 countries, including decision-makers, private sector leaders, medical supply manufacturers, experts, and digital health innovators, under the theme "Resilience: Building the East African Health Economy."
Addressing the conference, Workneh Gebeyehu, Executive Secretary of the Intergovernmental Authority on Development, an East African bloc, said that health sovereignty represents "the absolute bedrock of national sovereignty." He noted that historical vulnerabilities to global supply chain disruptions must be converted into enduring regional industrial strength and healthcare resilience.
"Healthcare is a strategic, high-growth economic driver. It creates skilled jobs, attracts global investment, accelerates industrial manufacturing, and safeguards our most precious asset: our human capital," said Gebeyehu.
Calling for the structural alignment of the public and private sectors to address regulatory and trade barriers, he emphasized the necessity of deploying long-term capital into pharmaceutical manufacturing, digital health networks, and cold-chain infrastructure to establish a unified East African health economy.
According to the organizers, deliberations at the three-day conference are strategically structured around four core pillars: excellence in health service delivery, local manufacturing, investment financing, and regional integration.
Ethiopia's Deputy Prime Minister Temesgen Tiruneh called for a fundamental shift in the region's health sector approach toward greater local production. He highlighted the East African country's ambition to become an African hub for specialized healthcare and medical tourism, mainly through expanded domestic production of essential pharmaceuticals, diagnostics, and medical equipment, while deepening critical public-private partnerships.
Experts and policymakers at the conference stressed that building robust regional health systems requires more than public financing, emphasizing the critical need to put in place a thriving, well-governed private sector that partners with governments to invest, manufacture supplies, and mobilize capital.
Echoing this sentiment, Ethiopia's Health Minister Mekdes Daba highlighted that public health challenges, including supply chain disruptions and climate change, extend beyond borders and demand collaborative solutions. She noted that strengthening local research and development as well as medical manufacturing remains essential to minimizing vulnerabilities to future global crises.
As East Africa's flagship healthcare event, the conference has also attracted more than 80 exhibitors from Africa and beyond to showcase medical products, services, technologies, and innovations, serving as a platform to connect solution providers with healthcare decision-makers, according to the organizers. ■

DR Congo Ebola cases top 5,300 as UN warns outbreak "growing exponentially"

23:42:49 CST
00:42:49 KST

KINSHASA, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) has surpassed 5,300 confirmed cases and 2,550 deaths, as a senior United Nations official warned that the country's deadliest-ever Ebola epidemic is "growing exponentially" and outpacing the response.
The DRC has recorded 5,375 confirmed cases and 2,557 deaths across six provinces as of Thursday, according to the latest figures released Saturday by the country's public health authorities. The overall case fatality rate stood at 47.6 percent.
A total of 1,167 patients have recovered.
Briefing reporters Friday from Bunia, capital of Ituri province, UN Senior Ebola Coordinator Julien Harneis warned that the outbreak was "growing exponentially," with half of all deaths recorded in just the previous 20 days.
"The epidemic is spreading to an area that is bigger than France," Harneis said, warning that the outbreak was "growing faster and wider than the Ebola response."
The epidemic, declared by the DRC government on May 15, has already become the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history and the second-largest on record globally, behind only the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic.
Harneis said responders were operating under "brutal" conditions, citing insecurity, poor roads, attacks on frontline workers and health facilities, as well as weak basic services and difficulties in moving funds into affected areas.
Three months into the outbreak, 160 healthcare workers have contracted Ebola and 43 have died, he said. Ambulances have been burned or stoned and healthcare facilities attacked in some affected communities.
Funding shortages have also emerged as a major concern. "We're only covered for the next weeks, and very soon funding will run out," Harneis said, calling for immediate international support.
"Every delay in funding and implementation makes this epidemic more deadly, more difficult to stop and more expensive," he warned.
Harneis said humanitarian organizations operating in the region had lost more than 30 percent of their capacity amid cuts to aid funding over the past two years, although UN agencies, the DRC authorities and humanitarian partners continue to scale up disease surveillance, treatment, safe burials and community engagement.
The latest warning comes as international partners move to reinforce the response. The World Health Organization said earlier this week that 70,000 doses of the Ervebo Ebola vaccine had been approved for immediate release to the DRC, including 20,000 doses for a Phase 3 clinical trial and 50,000 for frontline and health workers.
A first batch of 16,520 doses of the Ervebo vaccine arrived late Friday in the capital Kinshasa. ■

Details
In an interview with one of the Russian media outlets, Putin stated, in particular, that "we are always ready for dialogue, but only on the basis of the realities taking shape on the ground." Putin spoke of Ukraine’s proposals for peace as "exotic" and "unacceptable" to Moscow, but refused to clarify what he meant. Putin also commented on Ukrainian strikes against Russian infrastructure facilities, threatening that "you will get a response."
The Center for Strategic Communications’ response
"On August 22, the Kremlin dictator repeated familiar narratives about Ukraine’s "failure," Russia’s "response," and Kyiv’s alleged unwillingness to negotiate," the Center for Strategic Communications pointed out.
"Putin produced a new batch of fantasies: five claims that do not correspond to reality," the Center for Strategic Communications emphasized, dissecting the five main manipulations:
-  Fake No. 1: «Ukrainian strikes against Russia did not lead to any turning point.» 
"In fact, Ukrainian long-range strikes forced Russia to redeploy air defense systems, restore damaged logistics facilities, and acknowledge the damage to its own infrastructure. Just days ago, Putin himself admitted that Ukrainian attacks were causing damage to Russia, although he attempted to downplay their effect," the Center for Strategic Communications noted.
-  Fake No. 2: «Kyiv has not gained and will never gain any advantage.» 
"In fact, the aim of Ukrainian strikes is to weaken Russia’s military potential, logistics, and defense industry. The Ukrainian campaign has already forced Moscow to change its system for protecting strategic facilities and spend additional resources eliminating the consequences of the attacks," the Center for Strategic Communications pointed out.
-  Fake No. 3: «Ukraine provoked the situation itself and is now asking Russia for a way out of it.» 
"In fact, it was Russia that launched the full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022. Attempts to shift responsibility onto Kyiv are one of the basic narratives of Kremlin propaganda, intended to justify the aggression," the Center for Strategic Communications emphasized.
-  Fake No. 4: «The massive strikes against Ukraine are a response to Zelenskyy’s "40-day campaign."» 
"In fact, Russia has systematically attacked Ukrainian cities, energy infrastructure, and civilian infrastructure throughout the full-scale war. The latest massive strikes against Kyiv alone resulted in numerous civilian casualties and the destruction of residential buildings and social infrastructure facilities," the Center for Strategic Communications pointed out.
-  Fake No. 5: «Kyiv opened the "Pandora’s box" itself, and therefore is receiving strikes against its economy.» 
"In fact, the Kremlin is trying to present deliberate terror against civilian infrastructure as supposedly a "legitimate response." This is informational cover for attacks that Russia has been carrying out for more than four years, despite numerous violations of international humanitarian law," the Center for Strategic Communications noted.

Iran on Saturday denounced US plans to announce new sanctions that could put further strain on the Islamic Republic's economy and have an impact on its most important trading partners, including China.
After nearly six months of war since the US and Israel launched airstrikes against Iran on February 28, the sides are not firing at each other but also showing no sign of pursuing peace talks.
Oil shipments are at a virtual standstill in the Strait of Hormuz, with Tehran threatening to strike any unauthorized oil tankers that try to transit the vital waterway, and Iran's economy is already under immense pressure from sanctions.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to hold a press conference at 2 p.m. EDT (1800 GMT) on Monday after threatening "the toughest sanctions in history" on Iran.
Bessent has also urged cooperation with Washington by China, which buys more than 80% of Iran's shipped oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler. Beijing has urged diplomacy.
Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baghaei, said on Saturday the imminent US announcement of new economic sanctions was an "assertion of extraterritorial sovereignty over every independent member state of the United Nations."
"Such secondary sanctions find no foundation in international law," he said in a post on X.
The chief of staff of Iran's armed forces, Major General Ali Abdollahi, promised on Friday that Iran would respond to enemy threats militarily with "crushing, punishing and devastating responses.”
US President Donald Trump, who has warned of economic consequences against any country that provides "any type of lifeline to Iran," said on Friday that Washington was observing "what happens" in the conflict.
"They would love to make a deal, but they're not ready to make the right deal, in my opinion," Trump said of Iran.
Strait of Hormuz traffic bottled up
While the US has effectively blockaded Iranian vessels in their ports, the Strait of Hormuz remained bottled up with thousands of seafarers stranded on hundreds of vessels.
Only four commodity ships sailed along the strait on Thursday, none of them large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers, ship-tracking data showed.
However, Iran has granted permission for a number of Iraqi oil tankers to pass through the Strait following repeated requests from Baghdad, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported on Saturday.
IRNA said obtaining special permission for Iraqi tankers was one of Baghdad’s main requests during a visit to Iraq by Parliament speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said the US military helped move a seven-day average of 8 million barrels a day of oil through the strait. That's down from more than 20 million per day before the war or about one of every five barrels consumed worldwide.
US attacks have severely diminished Iran's economy and devastated its navy and air force, but Tehran maintains enough missile and drone capability to impede oil tanker traffic and attack regional rivals.
Abdollahi, the armed forces chief of staff, sought to underline Iran's missile capabilities during a visit to an underground plant manufacturing ballistic missiles that was reported by state television on Saturday.
"This plant has been able, much better than in the past, to produce equipment superior both in capacities and quality and in quantity," he said.
Iran exploring new security arrangements with neighbors
Qalibaf, Iran's parliamentary speaker, said Tehran had received "numerous messages" from neighboring countries about establishing new regional security arrangements and economic cooperation.
Qalibaf, who did not say which countries he was referring to, accused the US of endangering the security of its allies in the region for the sake of Israel, adding that an independent, "homegrown" regional order would deliver peace and security.
Trump, meanwhile, has yet to achieve objectives he set at the start of the war such as dismantling Iran's nuclear program - the state of which remains uncertain given that U.N. inspectors have been shut out since 2025 - and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow their clerical rulers.
Thousands have been killed, mainly in Iran, where 168 Iranian school children were killed on the first day of the war. The US has reported more than 750 military personnel wounded and 18 killed.
While Iran remains defiant, President Masoud Pezeshkian has also called for a diplomatic solution.
"It would be better to end the war today, when we are powerful and have dignity, and the whole world acknowledges our victory and emphasizes that America, contrary to all regulations, attacked our schools, hospitals, and infrastructure and is hated in the world," the ISNA news agency quoted him as saying on Friday.

Over 100 ex-diplomats urge France, UK to sanction Israel over Palestine

Over 100 ex-diplomats urge France, UK to sanction Israel over Palestine
An open letter demands a ban on arms transfers and a freeze on EU-Israel and UK-Israel trade agreements.
A coalition of 102 former French and British diplomats is calling on their countries to jointly sanction Israel, warning in an open letter that Israeli policy in occupied Palestinian territory threatens to permanently erase the possibility of a Palestinian state.
France and the United Kingdom “must act together to uphold international law in Palestine”, said the letter published on Saturday by French outlet Le Monde. It urged the two governments to push for “equal rights for Israelis and Palestinians”.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Why Israeli tenders for illegal E1 West Bank settlement prompted outrage
- list 2 of 3Palestinian victims of Israeli settler attacks face battle for justice
- list 3 of 3‘Shameful’: Western allies slam Israel ending probe on aid worker killings
The signatories include former British ambassadors to the United Nations, Jeremy Greenstock and Emyr Jones Parry, and former French Middle East directors, Yves Aubin de la Messuziere and Denis Bauchard, drawing on decades of diplomatic postings across the region.
“Palestinian house demolitions and rampant settler violence – with the connivance of the Israeli army and police – amount to ethnic cleansing,” said the letter. “The world no longer sees Israel as a genuine democracy,” it added.
Such language, said Nicholas Hopton, a former UK ambassador to Iran, Qatar and Yemen and one of the signatories, was not invented by the diplomats themselves.
“The words are not our own,” he told Al Jazeera. “They are taken from the international legal bodies, the UN, those who have been observing from a neutral position and with expertise.”
The letter arrives against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 72,000 Palestinians since October 2023. Despite a ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, Israeli attacks have continued, killing at least 1,285 Palestinians since, according to Gaza’s Ministry of Health.
‘Action, not words’
For Hopton, the more immediate trigger was Israel’s renewed push to expand settlements in the occupied West Bank.
“There is a move by the Israeli government to allow settlements to be created in the West Bank in a way that would almost realistically prevent a future Palestinian state being able to be created there,” he said.
Peter Millett, a former British ambassador to Libya and another signatory, told Al Jazeera the letter marks a shift from words to demands. “What we’re asking for is action, not words,” he said.
“Our ministers over the last few months and years have issued statements of criticism, of condemnation and so forth, but as the letter makes clear, this is the time now where we need to see action on trade, action on settlements, more support for aid to go into Gaza, and the ending of the arms trade.”
France and the UK recognised a Palestinian state in 2025, a step the letter argues now needs to be “made real by urgent action.” The signatories trace their countries’ responsibility back to the mandates the UK and France held over Palestine, Syria and Lebanon after World War I, which shaped the region’s modern borders.
“Our two nations believe that those responsible for war crimes and crimes against humanity must be held to account,” the letter states. “Only then can our governments rebut the accusation of double standards.”
The letter lays out specific measures for France and the UK to adopt jointly: suspending EU-Israel and UK-Israel trade agreements and halting arms transfers and military cooperation with Israel.
It also calls for a ban on trade with Israeli settlements, a ban on citizens purchasing property on occupied Palestinian land, and guaranteed humanitarian access to Gaza through UNRWA and other UN agencies, with protected access for journalists, diplomats and parliamentarians.
“These actions, imposing penalties for law-breaking, safeguard the rule of law and show that there is an alternative to violence,” the letter states.
‘We cannot stand by’
Millett said he wants his government to go further still, including openly backing the International Court of Justice (ICJ) and confronting Israeli settler violence directly.
“What they’re trying to do is force these Palestinians to cross the River Jordan into Jordan itself,” he said, describing Jordan as a longstanding Western ally.
“We cannot stand by and see this continually happen in Israel, which is explicitly saying it will never accept a two-state solution,” he said.
Asked whether he thinks Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu is listening, Millett was doubtful, but said pressure still matters: “Action on trade, if it affects the prosperity of Israel, then maybe that’s a step that would actually have some repercussions in Israel itself.”
The letter is not directed solely at Israel; it also calls on Palestinian leadership, which it describes as “unrepresentative and dysfunctional”, to ensure the internationally recognised state remains “democratic and law-abiding”, pointing to elections scheduled for November as an opportunity for renewal.
For Hopton, though, the real test lies with governments willing to act rather than simply condemn, and he singled out the United States as the most consequential actor.
“The United States … has the most influence over the actions of the Israeli government,” he told Al Jazeera, warning that continued inaction “will create a longer-term, irreconcilable problem and store up future violence and future tragedies”.

Comprehensive housing plan being drafted at Ministry of Transport, Urban Development
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:30:20 UTC
00:30:20 KST

Comprehensive housing plan being drafted at Ministry of Transport, Urban Development
TEHRAN- The financial and economic advisor to the Minister of Transport and Urban Development announced that a comprehensive housing plan is being drafted within the ministry, designed in two phases to serve as a roadmap that accounts for the sector's complexities—an initiative that had been neglected for years.
According to IRNA, Behrouz Maleki, speaking at the Future of the Construction Industry conference held on the sidelines of the Construction Industry Exhibition, highlighted the inherent complexities of housing. He noted that housing is a time-consuming, capital-intensive, and location-bound commodity—meaning that housing needs in one province cannot be met in another province or even another city.
Maleki stated that housing is a good with heterogeneous demand and depends on infrastructure and services, so not every residential building immediately becomes "housing." He also emphasized that identity is a unique issue in housing, and the commodity is long-lasting, with mistakes leaving lasting effects for years.
Maleki stressed that housing policy does not operate in a vacuum and inevitably intersects with all aspects of human life. He rejected the notion that the government's responsibility equals providing housing for everyone, adding that providing land is not the solution either—abundant land does not equal abundant housing, and land is not necessarily habitable. For land to be habitable, proper land use, accessibility, infrastructure, and services must be in place, and even soil quality matters. Sometimes land preparation costs rival construction costs, requiring careful discussion of land issues.
Referring to the experience of new towns, Maleki noted that significant investment has been made over the years, but actual settlement remains below 1.5 million people. He pointed to vast empty lands and vacant residential units as resource waste. Not only are many plots empty, but 30–40% of housing units in new towns remain unoccupied.
On construction patterns, he challenged the argument against building smaller homes for dignity reasons, stating that those making such claims have not experienced homelessness. With shrinking household sizes and rising one- or two-person households, old construction models no longer apply. He observed that a large volume of construction is dedicated to units over 150 square meters, which many households cannot afford—oversizing effectively prices housing out of reach.
Regarding the annual target of building one million units, Maleki asked where, for whom, and with what purchasing power these units should be built, and whether demographic changes have been factored in. He cited international experiences—Japan in the 1990s and China in recent years—as examples of mass construction ignoring real demand leading to large vacancy rates.
On informal settlements, he argued that as long as they are not officially recognized, their problems cannot be properly resolved. He also addressed tax and pricing policies, noting that using taxation to suppress prices or rate-setting to control markets is not new, and their effectiveness should be carefully reassessed.
Maleki identified other areas needing review, including rural housing, deteriorated urban fabrics, referral systems, national building regulations, and related policies. He concluded that housing complexities stem from two sources: inherent and unavoidable complexities arising from the sector's nature, and complexities resulting from incorrect assumptions and misguided policies—and that policymakers are now on a path requiring inevitable correction.

US court overturned Trump&apos;s ban on immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:28:14 EEST
00:28:14 KST

US court overturned Trump's ban on immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries
Kyiv • UNN
A federal judge ruled the ban on immigrant visas for citizens of 75 countries unlawful. The Trump administration may appeal the decision.
A federal judge in the United States on Friday overturned the Trump administration's ban on issuing immigrant visas to nationals of 75 countries, ruling that it "contradicts the law" and exceeds the authority of U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, UNN writes, citing CNN.
Details
In January, the U.S. State Department suspended the issuance of immigrant visas to citizens of nearly 40% of the world's countries, including Brazil, Colombia, Egypt, Haiti, Somalia, and russia, stating that this would prevent the entry of people who "will receive social and government assistance."
Judge Jeanette Vargas of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Manhattan disagreed with the State Department's justification for the policy, overturning any visa denial based solely on that ground — another blow to the Trump administration's immigration policy.
Under the law, an immigrant may be denied entry only as a potential "public charge" (a person who is expected to depend on government support) after a consular officer assesses that person's financial situation, age, health, skills, and family status.
Judge Vargas found that, in practice, U.S. consular officers had been instructed to deny visas to applicants, even those who could support themselves, solely on the basis of their country of origin.
The visa ban suspended the issuance of immigrant visas for permanent residence to people reuniting with family members or taking up employment in the United States, but did not apply to nonimmigrant visas, such as tourist or student visas.
Denials based on other legal grounds remain in effect, even when an official also cited the ban, leaving unclear how many decisions are expected to be overturned.
Most of the 75 countries are not European; they are located in the Caribbean, sub-Saharan Africa, the Balkans, the Middle East, Central Asia, and Southeast Asia, and the list includes several U.S. partners, including Jordan, Egypt, and Georgia. The State Department compiled its list based on data from the Council of Economic Advisers, selecting countries where more than 30 percent of immigrant families receive some form of government assistance.
The administration secured a victory on one narrower point: the judge agreed that the policy is not a formal rule that must be submitted for public comment before taking effect.
Vargas, who was appointed by former President Joe Biden, gave both sides until September 11 to propose a way to resolve the remaining part of the case. The administration may appeal the decision.

Trump urges court to reject BBC’s bid to secure records from his family in defamation case
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump has urged a federal judge to reject the BBC’s request for the court’s help in securing testimony and documents from three family members in response to his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster.
The BBC is trying to gain “politically-driven leverage” over Trump by serving subpoenas on daughter Ivanka Trump, son-in-law Jared Kushner and son Donald Trump Jr., personal lawyers for the Republican president argued in a court filing Friday.
U.S. District Judge Jeffrey Kuntz in Miami did not immediately rule on the dispute.

In May, a process server working for the BBC tried to serve subpoenas on Ivanka Trump and Kushner at their residence but encountered Secret Service agents who said they were not authorized to accept it, according to the president’s lawyers. They said the process server also visited Trump Tower in New York several days later in a failed attempt to serve Donald Trump Jr.
In a court filing last week, the broadcaster asked for the court’s permission to serve subpoenas on Trump’s family members by certified mail instead of in person.
Trump’s lawsuit, filed in December, accuses the BBC of deceptively editing portions of the speech that he delivered near the White House on Jan. 6, 2021, when a mob of his supporters attacked the Capitol to stop Congress from certifying Democrat Joe Biden’s victory over Trump. The suit claims the BBC spliced together separate parts of Trump’s speech to intentionally misrepresent what he said.
The lawsuit alleges the BBC aired its documentary a week before the 2024 presidential election in “a brazen attempt to interfere in and influence” the outcome to Trump’s detriment.
“The relief that the BBC’s Motion seeks cannot be segregated from the politically charged discovery campaign that it is based on, and which has already been ruled as improperly overbroad by this Court,” Trump’s lawyers wrote.
The BBC has apologized to Trump for the misleading edit, but it denies defaming him.

Federal judge vacates Trump policy that suspended processing of immigration visas from 75 countries
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:23:01 UTC
00:23:01 KST

Federal judge vacates Trump policy that suspended processing of immigration visas from 75 countries
A federal judge in New York has vacated a Trump administration policy that suspended the processing of visas from 75 countries, including Afghanistan, Iran, Russia and Somalia, whose nationals the Trump administration deemed likely to require public assistance in the United States.
U.S. District Judge Jeannette Vargas, an appointee of former President Joe Biden, set aside the policy Friday as “contrary to law and in excess of statutory authority.”
Secretary of State Marco Rubio exceeded his authority by issuing the policy, which “runs afoul” of the Immigration and Nationality Act by mandating “the refusal of visas to eligible applicants without any basis in law,” the judge ruled.
Judge says power lies with consular officers
Vargas said the policy also undermines the congressional requirement that puts consular officers at the forefront of any visa decision.
“Congress imbued these officers with exclusive authority and discretion to determine if an immigrant is eligible for a visa based upon review of specific and detailed criteria set forth in the statute,” she wrote. “The Policy, which categorically prohibits the issuance of immigrant visas based upon the nationality of the applicant, represents a direct abrogation of this statutory scheme.”
The policy was challenged by two nonprofit organizations along with 11 individuals, including six whose family members had been refused visas. The remaining five are outside the country and had filed “employment-based petitions” to come to the United States.
Advocates say keeping families apart is cruel
“We welcome this ruling because, at its heart, this case is about keeping families together,” said Anna Gallagher, the executive director of CLINIC, a national nonprofit that provides training, resources, and support to a network of immigration legal service providers and was one of the plaintiffs.
“Catholic social teaching calls us to uphold the dignity of every person and recognize the family as the foundation of society,” she said in a statement. “This decision affirms both those values and the rule of law, allowing families to once again move forward toward reunification.”
Another plaintiff is African Communities Together, a Harlem-based nonprofit. One of its leaders called the ruling “a tremendous victory for the rule of law.”
“This unlawful and racist ban caused immeasurable harm, cruelly keeping families and loved ones apart,” Diana Konate, deputy executive director for policy and advocacy, said in a statement. “Today, we are elated to tell our community members: this ban is no more.”
Trump expands his anti-immigration agenda
President Donald Trump has imposed a growing list of immigration and travel bans mostly for people from Africa, Asia and Latin America. The State Department said Saturday that the Trump administration is “protecting the American people by upholding the highest standards of screening and vetting of visa applicants,” and that it would not comment on pending litigation.
At the time the policy was issued, the State Department said it had instructed consular officers to halt immigrant visa applications from the 75 countries in accordance with a broader order in November that tightened rules around potential immigrants who might become “public charges.” Relying on Council of Economic Advisers data, the State Department said that more than 30 percent of households with immigrants from these countries received some form of public assistance.
A separate notice sent to all U.S. embassies and consulates said that non-immigrant visa applicants also should be “fully vetted and screened” for the possibility that they might seek public benefits in the United States.
The cable, a copy of which was obtained by The Associated Press, noted several times that the applicant must prove they won’t apply for public benefits while in the U.S., and that consular officers who suspect the applicant might apply should require them to fill out a form proving their financial bona fides.
The ruling is the latest example of the courts upending Trump’s immigration agenda. In June, a federal judge struck down a Trump administration policy that made it harder for immigrants from dozens of countries to enter and stay in America — affecting elements like asylum, work permits, green cards, and citizenship applications. That judge said the policy threw countless immigrants’ lives “into indeterminate legal limbo,” and accused the U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services of ignoring the law.

A trade war between Canada and the US deepens rupture in what had been a close and durable alliance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:23:01 UTC
00:23:01 KST

A trade war between Canada and the US further ruptures a once-close and durable alliance
TORONTO (AP) — For decades, Canada built much of its prosperity on privileged access to the United States. Now, after the collapse of trade talks, one of the world’s closest and most durable alliances has been fundamentally altered, with both countries facing the risk of a full-scale trade war.
Prime Minister Mark Carney acknowledged the break after last-ditch negotiations failed Friday, saying Canada had recognized that “America has changed” and that the countries would “not return to our old relationship.”
The United States imposed 50% tariffs on about $20 billion worth of Canadian goods early Saturday. Carney said Canada would retaliate dollar for dollar beginning Sept. 8, targeting sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics.
Carney foreshadowed the shift at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, declaring that the world was experiencing “a rupture, not a transition” and urging countries such as Canada to reduce their vulnerability to economic coercion by strengthening their economies at home and diversifying abroad.
He said in Ottawa on Saturday that warning had been borne out. He accused the U.S. of using “economic integration as a weapon” and said its “signature was written in pencil.”
“The collapse of the tariff talks points to the fact that the old Canada-U.S. relationship is over and, for many Canadians, it also confirms the perception that Canada can’t trust the Trump administration,” said Daniel Béland, a political science professor at McGill University in Montreal.
The pressure from Republican President Donald Trump has gone well beyond tariffs.
He has questioned Canada’s economic viability, repeatedly talked about making it the 51st U.S. state and used trade measures to encourage production to move from Canada to the United States. That has angered many Canadians and fueled a sense of betrayal in a country that had long regarded the U.S. as its closest ally.
Canadian travel to the U.S. remains sharply lower than before the dispute, with July return trips down nearly 29% by car and 27% by air from July 2024, Statistics Canada said.
The failed negotiations underscored how far the relationship had shifted. Canada had been prepared to accept some U.S. tariffs for market access and greater certainty — a break from decades of policy aimed at eliminating trade barriers.
For Canadians accustomed to preferential access under the 1989 Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, NAFTA and its successor, even reduced tariffs would mark a retreat from the old relationship.
The collapse also puts Carney’s approach to Trump to the test.
The prime minister’s “elbows up” posture — hockey shorthand for playing aggressively and refusing to be pushed around — has helped keep him popular at home. His decision to resist U.S. pressure could also resonate abroad with those impressed by his Davos call for countries to resist economic coercion and reduce dependence on great powers.
Provincial and conservative leaders broadly backed Carney. Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe said “the old status quo is not possible,” while Ontario Premier Doug Ford praised Carney for rejecting what he called a bad deal for the auto, steel and manufacturing sectors.
Ford said Trump “is not to be trusted whatsoever.”
Former Alberta Premier Jason Kenney said Canada was “not cravenly surrendering in the face of constant economic and political aggression.”
Lana Payne, national president of Unifor, Canada’s largest private-sector union, accused Trump of trying to weaken Canada’s industrial base.
“What we have seen from the U.S. administration, or Donald Trump, is this consistent attempt to try and destroy the industrial economy of Canada with tariffs that have been strategically designed to attack us,” Payne said.
The economic risks of fighting back and a s
hift seen as perhaps lasting beyond Trump
Nearly three-quarters of Canada’s goods exports go to the United States. The U.S. economy is roughly 10 times larger than Canada’s, limiting Ottawa’s ability to retaliate dollar for dollar without inflicting disproportionate damage at home.
Royal Bank of Canada economists estimate the tariffs directly affect about 0.4% of Canada’s GDP because they cover only about 5% of Canadian exports to the U.S. The damage could grow if retaliation broadens, more sectors are targeted or the dispute curbs investment and disrupts supply chains.
Carney himself acknowledged the cost of retaliation, saying the Canadian measures would “raise costs and reduce choice for Canadians.” He said his government would announce additional assistance for affected businesses and workers.
Béland said the countries were witnessing “the beginning of a full-scale trade war,” though he cautioned that the situation could change rapidly.
The dependence is not one-sided.
Carney said Canada supplies 99% of U.S. natural gas imports, 85% of its electricity imports and 60% of its crude oil imports. Trump has focused much of his pressure on autos, steel and aluminum, fueling resentment among Canadians who see the push as an effort to hollow out key industries.
Goldy Hyder, president and CEO of the Business Council of Canada, said businesses still view the U.S. as Canada’s most important trading partner but increasingly see the shift as lasting beyond Trump.
“There is a new trade and investment model, one that could well be kept in place by future U.S. administrations whether Democrat or Republican,” Hyder said.
Canada looks beyond the United States because ‘things will never be the same’
The breakdown adds urgency to Carney’s push to diversify beyond the United States. He has traveled abroad seeking investment and new trade ties, aiming to attract $1 trillion Canadian (US$730 billion) by 2030 and double non-U.S. investment over the next decade. Canada has signed more than 20 trade and security agreements across five continents in the past year.
That made Washington’s effort to restrict Canada’s ability to negotiate trade agreements with other countries particularly significant.
In July, Ottawa and Alberta advanced plans for a new Pacific Coast oil pipeline to give Canadian crude greater access to Asian markets and reduce reliance on U.S. buyers.
The immediate question is how long the latest tariff confrontation will last.
Béland said the deeper change probably will, partly because U.S. protectionism is likely to remain influential under future administrations.
“The idea that things will return to ‘normal’ once Donald Trump leaves the White House is probably just wishful thinking,” Béland said. “It doesn’t mean the relationship might not improve in the future but that things will never be the same.”

The kippah in his pocket: Don’t hide your Judaism, you never know who needs to see it - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:22:27 UTC
00:22:27 KST

Four loaves of challah, a Friday afternoon in Australia, and the long reach of one Jew who refused to be embarrassed.
I am currently in Perth, Australia, celebrating my granddaughter’s bat mitzvah. When I arrived, I was shown a photograph. It is not a picture of my family, or of Israel, or of anything a stranger would think worth saving.
It is a photograph of four loaves of challah, slightly lopsided, still steaming on a wire rack in a kitchen somewhere in Australia. It was sent by a young man I have never met, to my son, whom he had known for only three weeks.
Let me explain how it got there.
My son is a rabbi. Recently, he spent three weeks on an intensive residential course in Australia – long days outdoors, very little sleep, and a great deal of mud. The organizers made sure he had kosher food. This meant airline meals. Anyone who has eaten a long-life kosher airline meal will tell you it is less of a lunch than an act of faith.
So there he sat one afternoon in the dining hall, with his tray of foil-sealed devotion in front of him and his kippah on his head. Another participant sat down beside him. He mentioned, quietly, that he too was Jewish. Then he reached into his pocket and pulled out a kippah of his own.
He did not normally wear it. He had not felt comfortable wearing it there. But now that somebody else was wearing one, he said, he would wear his too. He wore it for the rest of the course.
I have thought about that pocket a great deal since. A young Jewish man, capable and committed, carrying his Judaism folded up where nobody could see it. Waiting. Not for permission, exactly. Waiting for company.
The program did not pause for Shabbat. There were activities on Saturday, as there had to be. My son kept Shabbat, of course, but in somewhat difficult circumstances, as Jews have done in every generation. And as the two of them walked, they sang “Lecha Dodi,” the song that welcomes the Shabbat. Two Jews walking through the Australian bush, welcoming the Shabbat bride in the only way available to them. I cannot think of a purer act of Jewish defiance in a long time.
My son told me that something else extraordinary also happened. The non-Jewish participants noticed. They watched this young rabbi stay committed to the strictures of Shabbat observance and, instead of mockery, they offered to assist him by, for instance, carrying the bags he was not permitted to carry.
During the rest of the week, my son did the same for them. Christians, Muslims, and people of no faith whatsoever quietly worked out between themselves how to make room for one man’s covenant.
The bond that formed between them was not built on anybody pretending to be less than they were. It was built on the opposite.
On the Friday after they came home, the young man baked challah. And he sent my son the photograph, with a message thanking him for giving him back his Jewish identity.
Nobody preached. Nobody argued. Nobody won a debate. One man simply ate his terrible airline schnitzel with his head covered, and the ripples reached a kitchen he will never stand in.
Same pocket, different setting
Now for the uncomfortable half of this article, because I am not writing a feel-good story. I am writing a warning wrapped in one.
We are living through the ugliest wave of open Jew-hatred most of us have known, and the Jewish response, in too many places, has been to get smaller.
The baseball cap over the kippah (I admit that I did just that on my Emirates flight this week). The Star of David tucked inside the shirt on the train. The mezuzah taken down from the door of the apartment. The Hebrew name shortened on the office directory. The hesitation before saying where you spent the summer.
I wrote recently about a statistic that stopped me cold: requests for kosher meals in some British hospitals have reportedly halved in two years. Not because British Jews stopped keeping kosher, but because, at the moment they were most frightened and most dependent, they hesitated to tick a box that said, “I am Jewish.”
That is the same pocket. It is simply a different setting.
I understand the instinct completely. It is not cowardice; it is arithmetic, done quickly, by frightened people: Why invite the risk? And in genuinely dangerous situations, discretion is no sin. Our tradition has never demanded martyrdom over a hat.
But we should be honest about the price. A kippah that goes into a pocket does not merely make one Jew invisible. It withdraws the permission that another Jew was waiting for.
That young man was not converted by an argument. He was released by an example. Had my son quietly accepted the standard meal and left his head bare – which might have been entirely understandable, even defensible – there would have been no conversation in that dining hall, no singing on that walk, no challah on that Friday.
The absence would have cost nothing anyone could measure, which is exactly what makes it so dangerous. We can never see the ripples we fail to make.
The late Rabbi Jonathan Sacks put it with characteristic bluntness: non-Jews respect Jews who respect Judaism, and they are embarrassed by Jews who are embarrassed by Judaism.
Forty years in medicine have taught me he was right about something deeper still. Patients, colleagues, and strangers all take their cue from your posture. Apologize for your existence, and you invite others to audit it. Stand comfortably inside your own skin and, in the overwhelming majority of cases, the world simply makes room. The people around my son did not respect him despite his Shabbat. They respected him because of it. Nobody is inspired by a person hiding.
Our oldest story says the same thing. The midrash teaches that our ancestors were redeemed from Egypt because they did not change their names, their language, or their dress. Not because they out-argued Pharaoh, but because in the middle of an empire built to erase them, they remained visibly, stubbornly, unmistakably themselves.
I am not asking anyone to be reckless. I am asking us to notice what is at stake when we shrink.
Wear it, or don’t – that is between you and your own courage on any given morning. But understand what you are carrying.
Somewhere in your office, your ward, your lecture auditorium, or your neighborhood, there is a Jew with something folded up in a pocket, waiting to find out whether it is safe to be who they are. You may never meet them. You may never know it happened.
But three weeks later, somebody bakes challah.
The writer is a rabbi and physician. He writes and teaches on Jewish ethics, leadership, and resilience. His work appears on rabbidrjonathanlieberman.substack.com and youtube.com. @rabbidrjonathanlieberman.

Zagreb to Opatija: Discovering Croatia’s northern Adriatic treasures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:22:22 UTC
00:22:22 KST

Surprisingly, 2026 has been a landmark year for direct flights to Croatia’s capital, making Zagreb more accessible than ever for Israeli travelers.
For many years, however, Zagreb and northern Croatia remained an underrated destination, often overshadowed by Croatia’s famous Adriatic destinations, with Dubrovnik in the south as the crown jewel.
For me, the city became something far more personal. While my daughter, Lihi, studied medicine at the University of Zagreb, it became a home away from home during my many visits. Those trips opened the door to discovering the hidden gems of northern Croatia, an enchanting region of elegant towns, breathtaking landscapes, and rich cultural heritage.
This summer marked a particularly meaningful journey. As Lihi graduated, adding another Israeli doctor of medicine to the healthcare system, I returned to Croatia to help her pack and to celebrate this special milestone.
Seaside town of Opatija
From there, I set my sights on the aristocratic seaside town of Opatija, where timeless elegance, grand Habsburg architecture, and the sparkling Adriatic create one of Croatia’s most captivating destinations.
Opatija is the closest Adriatic seaside destination to Zagreb, just a two-hour drive from the Croatian capital or an easy three-hour bus journey, with comfortable services starting from around €14. Its convenient location makes it the perfect escape, whether for a weekend getaway or as the gateway to exploring northern Croatia.
A coastal gem that has enchanted travelers for more than 180 years, Opatija is where historic elegance meets the shimmering Adriatic.
Often referred to as the riviera of northern Croatia, the town is renowned for its grand Austro-Hungarian villas, elegant seaside promenades, lush gardens, and refined atmosphere, which has attracted royalty, artists, and distinguished visitors since the 19th century.
Standing proudly on the shoreline is Opatija’s most recognizable symbol, the iconic Maiden with the Seagull. Gazing across Kvarner Bay, the graceful statue has become the town’s enduring emblem, embodying its maritime heritage and romantic spirit.
Visitors are drawn to Opatija by the calm, crystal-clear waters of Kvarner Bay, its Mediterranean climate, sophisticated coastal charm, and rich cultural heritage. The famous 12-kilometer Lungomare promenade reveals one breathtaking panorama after another.
One of Opatija’s greatest pleasures is the scenic walk to the neighboring village of Icici along the famous trail-promenade. Stretching beside the Adriatic, this leisurely rocky pedestrian route takes around an hour at an easy pace, with breathtaking views accompanying you every step of the way.
For my money, this is one of the most beautiful sceneries I have ever experienced. Not to be missed. The path winds past elegant Austro-Hungarian villas, grand historic hotels, charming cafés, and beautifully landscaped gardens, while the turquoise waters of Kvarner Bay remain constantly in view.
Along the way, countless swimming platforms and ladders invite you to pause for a refreshing dip before continuing your stroll.
One of Opatija’s most delightful features is how effortlessly the sea becomes part of everyday life. Nearly every stretch of the waterfront is equipped with these inviting ladders, allowing visitors to step directly into the refreshing Adriatic whenever temptation strikes.
Israelis, accustomed to sandy beaches, will be puzzled to see both locals and travelers spreading towels on hard concrete surfaces or endless rocks. I was intrigued as well. However, surprisingly, it was an interesting, pleasant experience, as the Kravner beaches here are similar to swimming pools – only wider, saltier and cleaner.
Postcard-worthy views
And then there is the scenery. Every turn reveals another postcard-worthy view. Elegant architecture framed by palm trees, sailboats gently gliding across the bay, the green slopes of Mount Ucka rising behind the town, and the endless blue horizon stretching toward the Adriatic.
At the heart of Opatija lies the magnificent Villa Angiolina Park, widely regarded as the birthplace of tourism in the town. It was here, in the mid-19th century, that Villa Angiolina welcomed European aristocracy, transforming Opatija into one of the continent’s first fashionable seaside resorts.
Today, the beautifully preserved botanical park remains a tranquil oasis, where centuries-old trees, exotic plants collected from around the world, elegant pathways, and seasonal blooms tell the story of the town’s remarkable heritage. Surrounded by impressive marinas, it continues to capture the refined character that has defined Opatija for generations.
As a backdrop to the iconic Slatina Fountain stands the newly opened Keight Opatija, a boutique-style luxury hotel and Croatia’s first international property. Perfectly positioned in the heart of Opatija, the hotel blends effortlessly into the town’s elegant streetscape while introducing a fresh, contemporary energy to this historic seaside resort.
Keight stands apart as Opatija’s first true lifestyle luxury hotel. Rather than recreating the grandeur of the Austro-Hungarian era, it embraces bold modern design, sophisticated interiors, and an intimate boutique atmosphere that appeals to today’s luxury traveler while respecting the town’s rich heritage.
Unlike the grand historic hotels that have defined Opatija for generations, Keight delivers beautifully appointed guest rooms, thoughtfully designed wellness facilities, and personalized hospitality.
Davor Kovcalija, cluster hotel manager of Curio Collection by Hilton, is especially proud of the hotel’s unique highlight – the rooftop bar.
“Here, guests sip handcrafted cocktails, unwind beside the infinity-style outdoor pool, and soak in sweeping views of Kvarner Bay as the sun slowly sets behind the surrounding islands and mountains,” he rightly says.
With Croatia's beaches ranked among the most beautiful in Europe, our journey continued northwest to the enchanting Istrian Peninsula, the largest peninsula in the Adriatic Sea.
Shared by Croatia, Slovenia, and Italy, Istria is a fascinating blend of cultures, cuisines, and architectural influences.
While all three countries lay claim to part of the peninsula, Croatia encompasses the largest and most diverse stretch, where medieval hilltop villages, Roman heritage, crystal-clear coves, vineyards, and olive groves come together in one unforgettable destination.
At Istria, within easy driving distance from Opatija (even a day trip would be rewarding), magical surprises await.
Rovinj, a feast for the senses
One of its undisputed jewels is Rovinj, a town that effortlessly captures the romance of the Adriatic. Rising from a small peninsula, its pastel-colored houses, winding cobblestone alleys, lively harbor, and charming squares create one of Croatia’s most photographed settings.
Beyond its beauty, Rovinj is a feast for the senses, with boutique galleries, waterfront cafés, artisan shops, and elegant restaurants. Don’t miss dishes with the local finest white and black truffles. Enjoying lunch in one of the narrow streets, while fishing boats gently sway in the picturesque marina, is an experience.
Heading south brought us to Pula, the largest city in Istria and one of the Adriatic’s greatest historical treasures.
Located at the peninsula’s southern tip, Pula combines a relaxed Mediterranean atmosphere with over 3,000 years of history.
Unlike many historic cities that feel like open-air museums, Pula remains a vibrant, lived-in destination where Roman monuments blend naturally into everyday life.
Its compact historic center is filled with reminders of the Roman Empire, highlighted by the city’s crowning glory – the magnificent Pula Arena, one of the world’s largest surviving Roman amphitheaters and among the best-preserved anywhere outside Rome. Once the stage for gladiator contests, it today hosts concerts, film festivals, and cultural events, creating a remarkable connection between ancient history and modern Croatia.
Indeed, Opatija is far more than an elegant seaside resort. It’s the perfect gateway to Croatia’s northern Adriatic.
Yet after every adventure, there’s something special about returning to Opatija as a base. Here, sunset strolls along the Lungomare, refined waterfront dining, and the timeless charm of Kvarner Bay guarantee evenings as memorable as the day itself.
The writer is the publisher of Travel Flash Tips.

Tracing roots: Why every Jew should reclaim family histories disrupted by the Holocaust - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:22:09 UTC
00:22:09 KST

This year is the 50th anniversary of the publication of Alex Haley’s widely acclaimed, best-selling book Roots – The Saga of an American Family.
Roots, which was also made into a miniseries, set off an ongoing global trend of tracing family origins.
Not all such searches are for positive reasons. Many German citizens want to know if their grandparents or great-grandparents were Nazis. Now, with access to the US National Archives catalog, they can find out.
In some cases, it’s merely curiosity about a long-held family secret and a desire to know the truth. In others, it’s fear that they may have inherited the evil DNA.
Among Jews, tracing ancestry is a voyage of discovery. Many Jews of European background grew up believing that all their relatives on both sides of their families had been murdered during the Holocaust.
Nonetheless, some such Jews join genealogical societies to seek pre-Holocaust information about their forebears.
Many have discovered through DNA tests and other means that some of their relatives survived the Holocaust and, together with their progeny, are living in another country or even close by.
In Israel, a long-overdue family reunion is taking place this month. Facilitated by MyHeritage, one of the myriad Jewish genealogical organizations, its key players are Adrianna Turk, 74, from Australia, and Raanan Gidron, 73, from Israel.
The two are second cousins. Her grandmother and his grandfather were siblings.
Turk and Gidron have more than 50 other relatives around the world. Turk, the daughter of a Jewish father, grew up in New Zealand believing that no one from her father’s family was left.
Gidron’s mother had miraculously survived Theresienstadt and Auschwitz.
After learning from her DNA test that she had relatives abroad, Turk reached out to some of them through social media. She met Gidron virtually several months ago and met him face-to-face in Israel earlier this month.
Countless similar reunions have taken place in Israel and around the world since the Holocaust.
In Israel, there was a special office dedicated to searching for relatives of Holocaust survivors. The searches were broadcast on the radio and often published in newspapers.
That was long before the founding of the International Association of Jewish Genealogical Societies (IAJGS) in 1988. There were Jewish genealogical societies before that, but they operated without an international roof body.
There are an abundance of stories about family reunions and the tracing of family histories.
One heart-warming Israeli story is about two elderly men who shared a bench in a shopping center. They began a conversation. It transpired that both were Holocaust survivors from Romania. Each thought that he was the sole survivor of his family.
As the conversation progressed, each spoke of the place in which he was born and raised. It happened to be the same village.
Both had adopted Hebrew surnames. Then each stated his original name.
They found out they were brothers who had lived around the corner from each other for years. Their appearances had radically changed with time, which is why they had not recognized each other.
But the most amazing story is that of Genie Milgrom, a Cuban-born American woman of Spanish ancestry, who was raised Catholic but did not feel comfortable as a Christian. Her family kept certain Jewish customs without knowing their background.
Curiosity drove Milgrom to begin exploring her ancestry.
She learned that she was descended from conversos. More important was the discovery that she was descended from a 22-generation maternal line of women that went back to pre-Inquisition Spain and Portugal.
Milgrom has spoken at many genealogical gatherings and has won awards for her research. To help other descendants of Jews from Spain and Portugal, Milgrom has written books with guidelines for the accessibility of birth, marriage, death, and Inquisition documents.
From the past to looking toward the future
The major obstacles for researchers are the different spellings, abbreviations, and translations of surnames.
For instance, Cohen can also be Cohn, Kohn, or Cowen. In my own family, my maternal grandmother’s maiden name, Joskowitz, had been abbreviated to Joske and Joss.
In Israel, someone whose last name is Shahor may have previously been called Schwartz or Black.
IAJGS has published extensive material on surnames.
The umbrella organization was founded with the help of Sallyann Sack, a veteran genealogist, clinical psychologist, and editor of Avotasynu, a journal on Jewish genealogy, and the late Rabbi Malcolm Stern, a long-time genealogist with the American Jewish Archives,
IAJGS collects, preserves, disseminates, and researches Jewish ancestry and promotes public access to records containing genealogical data relevant to Jews.
Some 90 societies now come together under the IAJGS banner.
Current IAJGS president Susan Weinberg of Minnesota is in the planning stages of the organization’s 46th annual conference, which will run from April 4-6, 2027. The planning committee is calling for new ideas and for people to present papers, tell stories, or run workshops.
The best-known Jewish genealogical societies are JewishGen, MyHeritage, IGRA, LitvakSIG, and JRI Poland. Most genealogical societies are non-profits.
One of the world’s largest, which does operate for profit, is Ancestry, which boasts more than 70 billion records, including those of Jews.
Genealogy dates back to ancient Jewish times.
The Bible is full of details of who begat whom, plus the names of all the important members of the 12 tribes, and before that – Adam and Eve and their children, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob and their wives and offspring, and later the family of Moses.
Interest waned in the post-biblical centuries. Families in which distinguished positions were passed on from generation to generation were among the rare exceptions, and some of their family trees can be found in Israel’s National Library in Jerusalem.
The Holocaust, with its enormity of family tragedies, rekindled interest in the desire to know about past generations from which individual Jews were spawned.
Young children nowadays know both their grandparents and their great-grandparents. Few Jews born between 1930 and 1950 knew their grandparents, and in many cases were not even aware of their great-grandparents’ names.
Longevity now enables in-the-flesh connections between young people and their great-grandparents. Young members of four-generation families not only know the names of their great-grandparents but also how they look and how they sound.
Yet for all that, and the significant number of professional and amateur genealogists, if one were to stop people at random, in the street or on public transport, and ask them to name all of their great-grandparents, it’s doubtful that anyone would be able to.
That is likely to change in the future.
According to the Central Bureau of Statistics, there are more than 3,300 people in Israel who are over the age of 100.
There are many more nonagenarians, so it stands to reason that many more future generations will have relationships with their great-grandparents at family gatherings.
Until recent years, IAJGS held its annual conferences in a different city every year. Most conferences were in the US, but have also been in Jerusalem, London, Warsaw, Paris, and Toronto.
Epidemics and travel restrictions prompted virtual conferences, allowing for many more participants.
Next year’s conference will also be virtual.
Detailed information is available from the Program Committee at Program@IAJGS.org

US imposes 50% tariffs on Canadian goods after deal fails, USTR Greer says no new talks planned
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:21:44 UTC
00:21:44 KST

The US imposed 50% tariffs on some Canadian goods on Saturday after the two longstanding allies failed to reach a trade deal, with each side accusing the other of derailing days of talks.
The tariffs that came into effect just after midnight (0400 GMT) on some $20 billion of Canadian goods - things like wooden ice hockey sticks that are rarely used anymore - are far from an economic game-changer for the largest US trading partner after Mexico. That represents just over 5% of Canada's exports to the US.
But the new tariffs mark an increase in tensions between President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney, and will likely make broader talks to renew the US-Mexico-Canada free trade agreement more difficult.
Carney said he had suspended trade negotiations and Canada would retaliate "dollar for dollar" on the new tariffs.
"I have decided to suspend trade negotiations with the US and have directed Canada’s negotiators to return to Ottawa," Carney said in a statement.
"They (negotiators) have worked hard, in good faith, to defend the interests of Canadians throughout these negotiations up until the very last minute," he said. "However, last-minute changes in the US proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal."
Polls show Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump
Carney, the only person to ever run the central banks of two major economies, was elected last year on promises to stand up to Trump, and remains broadly popular. Polls show most Canadians oppose making any concessions to Trump.
Hours earlier, the two sides had seemed close to an agreement that sources said would have lowered tariffs on steel, aluminum and autos and potentially brought American alcohol back to Canadian liquor stores.
"Tonight, Canada declined to finalize the trade deal under the terms agreed earlier this week," US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said during a White House briefing.
"This is a missed opportunity for Canada to partner with the United States, which is the fastest-growing economy in the G7," Greer said.
A senior Trump administration official said the US offer would have put Canada in the best tariff position of any major exporter to the US, but that Canada had sought additional concessions, especially on steel, aluminum, autos and softwood lumber.
No new US-Canada talks have been scheduled
No additional talks are scheduled as the US implements the new duties, the official said.
Trump last month threatened to impose a raft of duties on a range of Canadian imports, including wine, furniture, dairy products, cement, clothing, fishing rods, and hockey equipment.
The tariffs, which do not qualify for preferential treatment under the US-Mexico-Canada free-trade agreement, open up some already vulnerable sectors to potential severe damage that could lead to job losses and business closures, trade experts have said.
 
The decision by the US administration followed three days of talks in Washington between Canada's minister for trade with the US, Dominic LeBlanc, and Greer.
The new duties add to existing US tariffs on steel, lumber and autos, which have taken a major hit in the last 18 months, although the malaise has been largely contained within these sectors.

The meeting in July, hosted by Macron in Paris, launched a grouping of 10 European countries to develop an anti-ballistic missile system as a cheaper alternative to the Patriot.
At that time, Macron said France would advance the deployment of the new SAMP/T system to Ukraine and license Kyiv to manufacture the interceptor missiles, as well as the SCALP long-range cruise missile and other munitions.

What was most emphasized at this event was the necessity of transforming the actual capacities of the cooperative sector into a more effective role in production, distribution, trade, and border area development policies—a capacity that activists in this field believe, with greater attention and support, could become one of the key pillars of economic growth and public participation in the economy.

Discounts no longer work: how service and emotions are overcoming price-cutting in an oversaturated flower market
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:16:47 EEST
00:16:47 KST

Discounts no longer work: how service and emotions are overcoming price-cutting in an oversaturated flower market
Kyiv • UNN
Discounts no longer work: how service and emotions are overcoming price-cutting in an oversaturated flower market.
The modern floristry market in Ukraine is characterized by an exceptionally low barrier to entry. Every day, dozens of new local Instagram shops appear, trying to quickly capture an audience. Their main, and often only, weapon is drastically cutting prices. However, sharing their marketing experience, established industry players unequivocally state: competing solely on price in 2026 is a dead end. Dumping destroys business economics, since flowers are perishable goods with a high write-off rate. An attempt to sell more cheaply inevitably leads to savings on flower quality, the florist's qualifications, or delivery reliability.
After having a celebration ruined by a wilted bouquet from a no-name seller, consumers quickly return to established services. The experience of companies such as flori1.com, Flowers.ua, 7roses.com, pandafl.com.ua, kamelia-shop.com.ua, and flowers-city.com.ua shows that retaining customers sustainably amid fierce competition from Instagram shops is possible by focusing on Lifetime Value metrics, a well-designed loyalty program, and deep service personalization. The long-term profitability of a business is based not on a one-time transaction, but on building trust, so that customers choose one service for all important occasions over many years.
The economics of emotions works differently from the market for consumer goods. When a man orders a bouquet for his wedding anniversary, he is not buying 25 roses, but a guarantee of his wife's wonderful mood and his own peace of mind. If a delivery service guarantees that the bouquet will fully match the photograph on the website, that it will include a branded card with a personal message from the sender, and that the courier will be polite and punctual, the customer chooses reliability over questionable savings. That is why marketing budgets are now being reallocated from discount campaigns to improving the customer experience, developing convenient mobile interfaces, and providing systematic staff training.

Father leaves 7-year-old alone on Mount Fuji to keep climbing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
15:16:44 UTC
00:16:44 KST

A father in Japan was reprimanded by police after leaving his 7-year-old son alone on Mount Fuji in rain and fog so he could continue climbing toward the summit with his older child, Japanese media reported.
The incident happened Thursday morning on Japan’s highest mountain, where rapidly changing weather can make climbing conditions dangerous. The 48-year-old father, a tourist from Nagoya, had set out to climb the 3,776-meter mountain with his two sons, ages 7 and 12 or 13, according to Japan Today.
The three were climbing the Fujinomiya Trail, where many hikers begin near the fifth station at roughly 2,400 meters. Near the sixth station, at an altitude of about 2,490 meters, the younger boy reportedly became restless and complained that he was tired.
Instead of waiting for him to recover or abandoning the attempt to reach the summit, the father reportedly told him, “Wait here,” gave him snacks and a soft drink, and continued uphill with the older boy.
At around 7:30 a.m., a worker at one of the mountain stations found the child sitting alone on a bench as rain fell and fog began to build.
The worker brought him inside and contacted police. Officers then reached the father, who had already made it to the eighth station, at approximately 3,250 meters, and ordered him to return.
It is not clear exactly how long the child had been left unsupervised. Japan Today noted that the official Mount Fuji climbing website estimates it takes about three hours to climb from the sixth station to the eighth, meaning the boy may have been left alone at around 4:30 a.m.
Had the child not been found, he potentially could have remained alone for many more hours. The climb from the sixth station to the summit takes a little more than five hours, with another roughly two and a half hours needed for the descent.
Police reprimanded the father after he reunited with his son. “Leaving a child behind is unacceptable,” officers reportedly told him. No additional punishment or referral to welfare authorities was reported.
The father apologized, saying: “I made a reckless decision, and I deeply regret it.” Police later warned Mount Fuji climbers about the dangers of leaving members of their group behind and urged hikers to match their pace and ambitions to the stamina of everyone traveling with them.
Mount Fuji is known for highly unpredictable weather, with visibility and ground conditions capable of deteriorating quickly. More than 220,000 people climb the mountain during the July-to-September season, with many hiking overnight in hopes of watching the sunrise from the summit.
The mountain also holds deep cultural and religious significance in Japan and has been regarded as sacred for centuries. Authorities in recent years have introduced entrance fees and limits on visitor numbers in an effort to reduce overcrowding.
Mount Fuji remains an active volcano. It has erupted around 20 times in recorded Japanese history, most recently between December 1707 and January 1708.
The mountain has also seen several recent rescue incidents. Last month, a 99-year-old woman was rescued after falling and injuring her pelvis and back. Last year, a 27-year-old climber had to be rescued twice within four days after returning to the mountain to search for a phone he had lost.

Putin hints at ‘catastrophic scenario’ for Ukraine
Ukraine is facing a “catastrophic scenario” from Russian retaliatory strikes after it “opened Pandora’s box” with its attacks on economic and civilian infrastructure, President Vladimir Putin said on Saturday.
In spring, Kiev sharply escalated its long-range drone attacks on Russia’s oil and gas infrastructure, thereafter extending the strikes to e-commerce warehouses and civilian logistics facilities. Russia retaliated by targeting Black Sea shipping and key port facilities it said were handling Ukraine’s military-related imports, effectively severing the country’s main export route.
Kiev is now reaching out through intermediaries to try to “prevent this situation from developing into a catastrophic scenario,” Putin said in an interview with Russia 1. However, their trajectory is apparent, he added.
Ukraine initiated this with its “massive missile and drone strikes on our civilian targets and logistics,” the president stated.
It has opened Pandora’s box itself.
Russia’s retaliation struck Ukraine’s “most sensitive economic sectors,” including agricultural exports, which are its main source of revenue, Putin said.
He added that the diplomatic proposals Moscow is now receiving are sometimes “exotic and unacceptable.”
We are always ready for dialogue on peace, but only on the basis of the realities unfolding on the ground.
Moscow has long stressed that it prefers a diplomatic settlement to the Ukraine conflict, but will only accept a long-term and stable peace that removes its underlying causes.
Russia will continue to push toward its goals via military means as long as Kiev refuses to compromise, the Kremlin has said.
