ISTANBUL, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Tensions between Türkiye and Israel have intensified following Ankara's request for an Interpol Red Notice against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, days after Israeli strikes on a Syrian airbase near the Turkish border.
The Interpol request was made in connection with an ongoing Turkish criminal case over the interception of activists aboard the Global Sumud Flotilla, which set sail from Türkiye in May in a renewed attempt to break Israel's blockade of Gaza, according to Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek on Friday.
The flotilla was intercepted by Israel, and those on board were subsequently deported.
The Israeli Prime Minister's Office responded by accusing Türkiye of "hypocrisy" and referring to its President Recep Tayyip Erdogan as an "antisemitic dictator," saying Erdogan was seeking to extend what it called his "aggression" against Israel into Syria. The statement added that Israel would continue to act against what it described as threats to its security.
Türkiye's Communications Directorate hit back, describing the Israeli statement targeting Erdogan as "outrageous ravings" devoid of historical fact and political seriousness. It accused the Netanyahu government of using "cheap politics" for electoral gain and seeking to portray Türkiye as a new threat, warning that efforts to escalate tensions for domestic political competition posed risks to regional and global peace and stability.
The latest diplomatic exchanges followed Israeli airstrikes on Tuesday targeting the Abu al-Duhur military airport in Idlib province in northwestern Syria, which caused material damage but no casualties.
Israel said the airstrike was aimed at preventing what it described as a potential Turkish military deployment at the Syrian airbase, which it said would pose a threat to its security. Ankara has firmly denied any such deployment.
Canan Tercan, a Turkish political analyst of Istanbul Aydin University, said Israel's concerns over Türkiye's growing role in Syria were central to the latest tensions.
"Türkiye's presence in Syria for training purposes is entirely at the request of the Syrian government," Tercan said, noting that Ankara has no territorial ambitions and seeks to support Syria's unitary state structure.
Tercan also linked the escalating rhetoric to Israel's domestic political environment, saying Netanyahu faces increasing pressure ahead of the country's October election and may seek to maintain a hard-line security narrative.
In response to Türkiye's request for an Interpol Red Notice for Netanyahu, Tercan said the move could raise questions about the international standing of the Israeli prime minister.
"The issuance of an international Red Notice is a critically important development," she said, questioning how a political leader sought under an international Red Notice could continue to represent Israel on the international stage.
Omer Behram Ozdemir, an analyst at Ibn Haldun University, noted that despite the military provocations, Ankara is likely to maintain a strategy of restraint and focus on long-term institutional rebuilding in Syria rather than direct confrontation.
He argued that Israel's strikes are intended to expand the conflict and wear down its counterparts, while Türkiye's continued focus on rebuilding Syria's security institutions could strengthen Ankara's regional influence. ■

22:57:01 KST

HOHHOT, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- North China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region is stepping up efforts to expand its green computing industry and explore new ways of taking AI services global, with fresh projects and initiatives unveiled Saturday.
A total of 12 projects with a planned investment of 186.46 billion yuan (about 27.49 billion U.S. dollars) were signed at the 2026 Green Computing Power (Artificial Intelligence) Conference in Hohhot, capital of Inner Mongolia.
The projects involve leading companies including Volcano Engine -- ByteDance's cloud service platform, Cambricon Technologies, and China Telecom, covering green intelligent computing centers, token factories, and computing-power and electricity equipment manufacturing.
Also at the conference, construction officially began on a comprehensive service platform for digital services going global in the Hohhot Area of the China (Inner Mongolia) Pilot Free Trade Zone.
The platform will connect overseas developers with China's AI models and green computing resources while helping domestic AI companies expand overseas. It offers services including compliance assessment, computing-power scheduling, token measurement, cross-border settlement and developer support.
Inner Mongolia is leveraging its abundant wind and solar resources to build a large-scale green computing base. Horinger New Area in Hohhot has 62 computing centers with a total computing capacity of 150,000 PFlops, including 143,000 PFlops of intelligent computing capacity, according to local authorities.
PFlops (petaflops) is a unit used to measure computing speed for AI and data-intensive tasks, where 1 PFlop equals one quadrillion calculations per second.
In neighboring Ulanqab, operational computing capacity has reached 172,000 PFlops, with intelligent computing accounting for more than 95 percent.
The push comes as China's demand for AI computing continues to surge. Official data showed daily token calls in China rose from about 100 billion in early 2024 to 140 trillion in March 2026.
The new platform marks an effort to shift from exporting computing hardware and infrastructure to providing AI capabilities as digital services, linking China's green computing resources with the global AI market. ■

British PM sees Everton win

Arsenal has already won

Ukraine’s Minister for Veterans Affairs Vitaliy Kim outlined the ministry’s priorities under his leadership: establishing a State Support Service, digitizing services, and ensuring the economic independence of veterans.
"We have identified five priorities on which we are focusing our efforts: state support, honor and remembrance, transition from military service to civilian life, health and rehabilitation, and economic independence and opportunities," Kim said at the Ninth International Veterans Forum on Saturday in Kyiv.
He noted that there are plans to create a system of government support for veterans.
"Right now, there are individual programs in place. Some have even proven to be quite effective. There are excellent patrol services, there are NGOs, and there are veteran volunteers who are trying to help the government care for the veterans themselves. I don’t think that’s right. Or rather, it’s great. But it’s just one component. The government is obligated to provide this," he said.
The minister added that some brigades have ineffective support services.
"They’re fighting; they don’t have time to deal with anything else. The state has to do this. Today, the military already has a strong track record of supporting people. We’ll take all of this and create a single office that will handle all these functions," he added.
He said that one of the priorities is the digitization and standardization of the transition from military service to civilian life.
"Today, our concept is that a veteran must go through three steps: the Medical Examination Commission, surrendering their weapons, and registration at the Territorial Center for Social Reintegration. The state must handle the rest," the minister said.
In addition, he said the various aspects of the transition from military service to civilian life – medical treatment, physical rehabilitation, mental health, and sports – must work together as part of a single system, rather than in isolation.
"What happens to a person afterward is crucial. Do they have opportunities for self-fulfillment, employment, and economic independence? And this leads to the next priority. Even the best support system should not make a person dependent on the state. "I do not want to build a system in which a veteran is dependent on state support. Our goal is not to tie the veteran down, but to give them opportunities, to give them choices, so that they can move forward on their own," Kim said.
He said the government must work separately with the business community to create jobs for veterans.
As previously reported, on July 16, the Verkhovna Rada, upon the proposal of newly appointed Prime Minister Serhiy Koretsky, approved the new composition of the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine, specifically appointing Vitaliy Kim, head of the Mykolaiv Regional Military Administration, as Minister for Veterans’ Affairs.

One is not born, but becomes: India's drag story, from myth to modern stage

Unknown Publisher

22:49:43 KST

One is not born, but becomes: India's drag story, from myth to modern stage
Prisha Patnaik / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 22, 2026, 19:19 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
India has a rich but complex history of men performing femininity—one that modern drag queens are reclaiming with agency, drawing from both Indian tradition and global queer culture
The most heavily quoted feminist scholar, Simone de Beauvoir, launched entire fields of feminist theory by writing - one is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.To be a woman, to be feminine was never purely biological, it was also societal. You are shaped into a woman, piece by piece, experience by experience.In her rejection of the arbitrariness one would often attach to what femininity means, she made space for who some would argue is very much a queer icon and a scholar.Almost half a century later, RuPaul said: we’re all born naked, and the rest is drag.It's a strange thing, watching a philosopher and a reality show host arrive at the same conclusion from opposite directions, that gender was never the given, natural thing it pretends to be, just the costume everyone's already wearing. De Beauvoir got there through existentialism. RuPaul got there through sequins. Both arrived to the conclusion that the performance was the point all along.
The history of 'drag' in India
A common practice to define drag would be to trace its historic roots in the Indian subcontinent. Women were kept out of public spaces, be it India or the West. So when women roles had to be filled in theatrical production men would dress us as them and take up that role in the public eye.
India has its own unique lineage to give to this art form, be it through mythology or folk dance and other cultural performances. In the Natyashastra, men played goddesses, heroines, demonesses, styled into femininity through gesture, costume, and the trained emotionDance forms like Kathakali, Jatra and Yakshagana still carry that inheritance. These traditions though have never termed themselves as drag and only trace lineage through reductive definitions of drag being men becoming women convincingly enough to make an audience believe it.India's mythology also builds gender transformation directly into the stories being told. In the Mahabharata's Virata Parva, Arjuna spends a year of exile disguised as Brihannala, a court dancer and music teacher, cursed by the nymph Urvashi to live without his manhood after refusing her. Shikhandi was also born a woman, raised as a warrior, and eventually granted manhood by a Yaksha to fulfil a vow of vengeance against Bhishma.None of this stayed confined to myth and stage. In Ahmedabad, on the eighth night of Navratri, men of the Barot community drape themselves in saris and jewellery to dance garba. In Kottankulangara, Kerala, thousands of men dress as women each year for Chamayavilakku, offering prayers to the goddess Durga at a temple local legend says was born from a bleeding stone, with no women present at the founding moment, boys dressed as women to complete the ritual.Outside temple and epic, there is the tradition of Launda Naach, male dancers performing in women's dress at weddings, in the North Indian belt. It's argued to be India's oldest living form of vernacular drag but it shows no interest in being called "drag".India’s modern drag is a celebration of the feminine inside a being, a lot of what we try to say it draws its lineage from was never a celebration. In some instances it was perversion and in most it was erasure of women from public spaces.A man performing femininity is not automatically a drag queen.The historical circumstances matter. Who was performing? Why were they performing? Who was watching? Who was excluded from the performance? And, crucially, who controlled what that performance meant?
Contemporary drag
For Lush Monsoon, who was among the early generation of contemporary drag performers in Delhi, the relationship between these histories and modern drag is complicated by the question of agency.To her the art forms are exploitative, even if they are often posed as a celebration of queer history. She points to the gaze surrounding these traditions, and to the people who historically inhabit this gaze.
Drag queen: Lush Monsoon
“I always see them as an extension of that you are afraid of the feminine, so you are more okay with the masculine projecting as a feminine, and you putting their desire on that.”The issue, she says, is not only about the audience.A lot of the participants are queer. They are queer people from marginalised sections of society or spaces where the language of queer is not defined yet somehow exploited.A younger drag queen too, who has been in this space for around one year, held the same belief. They said that India has a culture of gender intermixing, something we can draw out as a rich queer heritage but modern drag is not a direct extension of this.“The reason that I got attracted to this form of drag, because I saw a certain amount of agency in it.”
The point is not to deny India’s rich queer history but to make space for its even more vibrant present.As of today, there are only a handful of venues and spaces for drag performers. Most of the queens interviewed said Indian drag still doesn't carry the same stature as its Western counterpart, which makes it hard to find venues, build audiences, and turn performance into a sustainable career.Venues like KittySu and the Lalit chain of hotels pioneered the space, and it's now getting a push from queer collectives like the GaySi family and smaller creators trying to build safer rooms for queens and their audiences.Yet, reaching a wider audience in the digital era will take a digital push. Every queen interviewed named the same first encounter with drag as an art form: RuPaul's Drag Race. The show cemented its place in queer history, but there's a need for an Indian platform that celebrates queerness and the art form on its own terms, instead of reducing it to comedy.Older drag queens have long faced the accusation of importing a Western culture that maligns Indian heritage. But that heritage has always had space for queer stories. It was colonialism that maligned it, criminalising hijra communities and policing gender through an imported Victorian morality, codified in 1861 as Section 377, a law that stayed on the books for 157 years until the Supreme Court struck it down in 2018.Getting there took decades of work the current generation didn't have to do from scratch. Earlier drag queens fought not just for legal recognition but for the art form itself – pulling it apart from the crass, punchline version of drag Indian television has long been comfortable with.Noor Sins, a younger queen, put it simply: that fight mattered because it meant queens her age could grow up with contemporary, Indian, queer icons to look up to, not borrowed ones.
Drag queen: Noor Sins
It is perhaps here that the history of Indian drag and what Indian drag is becomes more interesting. In some sense drag always existed but for a lot of contemporary queens what did not exist was the ability to see themselves in the person performing it.
The queens performing on stage are taking a form that has so often been used to make femininity into spectacle and making spectacle something they control. They are borrowing from the West without necessarily belonging to it, and drawing from Indian history without pretending that every man who ever wore a sari was a drag queen.The world is changing, the queens coming up now get to inherit something their predecessors had to build: a language, a community, spaces to perform, and most importantly, people who look like them already standing on a stage. But the stage has to become bigger, and the language more universal.De Beauvoir never wrote about drag. But she wrote the sentence that explains why it matters: one is not born, but becomes. For the queens performing in India today, that becoming is not simply about becoming a woman through makeup and dresses. It is about becoming visible to themselves, and then to one another, in a form that did not always give them someone to see.

With over two years of experience in social media and digital content, she is interested in how news, politics and culture are shaped for digital audiences. She holds a master’s degree in Media and Communications from Goldsmiths, University of London.

President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy signed a decree commemorating Hetman Ivan Mazepa and erecting a monument to him in Kyiv. This is reported by the Office of the President, UNN reports.
Details
Decree No. 781/2026 was signed by the president on August 21, 2026. The document stipulates that the Cabinet of Ministers must organize an open competition for the best design project for a monument to Ivan Mazepa.

-  organize an open competition for the best design project for a monument to Ukrainian Hetman Ivan Mazepa; 
-  ensure the design and construction of a monument to Ukrainian Hetman Ivan Mazepa based on the results of the open competition; 
-  jointly with the Kyiv City State Administration, resolve, in accordance with the established procedure, the issue of the location of the monument to Ukrainian Hetman Ivan Mazepa in the city of Kyiv and its erection; 
-  ensure, in accordance with the established procedure, the financing of the measures provided for by this Decree. 
The Decree enters into force on the day of its publication.

Ukraine’s Independence Shaping Our Collective Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Thirty‑five years ago, on Aug. 24, 1991, Ukraine’s Parliament adopted the Act of Declaration of Independence of Ukraine. Undeniably, this was one of the most important geopolitical moments of the 20th century.
The restoration of Ukraine’s Independence unchained the Ukrainian people from Russian colonial shackles and enabled them to enter the circle of free peoples of the world. Indeed, it ended three centuries of merciless Russian domination and exploitation, albeit punctuated by brief periods of Ukraine’s statehood. This grim period of Ukraine’s history included the Holodomor, now recognized by the international community as a genocide that took millions of Ukrainian lives.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Ukraine’s Independence also propelled the dissolution of the Soviet Union into 15 independent states and liberated many other enslaved peoples from what former US President Ronald Reagan correctly coined as an “evil empire.”
Therefore, the declaration of Ukraine’s Independence is a historic event that should be commemorated by Ukrainians and all freedom-loving people.
As for Russia’s current dictator, unsurprisingly, Ukraine’s Independence is fully unacceptable as it directly led to the collapse of the Soviet empire.
Since then, Russia has attempted in numerous ways, including with gas blackmail, to first reconquer Ukraine and, if successful, proceed to reconstitute the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact.
Modern Independent Ukraine at 35: Achievements and Problems
Realizing, though, that Ukraine was clearly heading in the direction of Europe and shedding its Soviet past, Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin had the same reaction as Soviet leader Joseph Stalin, when he wrote in 1932 to his henchman, Lazar Kaganovich: “If we do not start rectifying the situation in Ukraine now, we may lose Ukraine.”
That is why Russia invaded Crimea and a part of Donbas in 2014 and then started a genocidal all‑out war against Ukraine in 2022.
For over 12 years now, Ukraine has been heroically defending its independence and protecting the territorial integrity of Europe from Russia’s imperialist plans.
At the outset, NATO member countries condemned Russia’s military aggression. However, their support for Ukraine was cautious and incremental since they did not fully perceive the immediacy of Russia’s threat to their own security and erroneously calculated that restraint would prevent escalation.
Indeed, the CBC recently reported that, during his visit to Canada in May 2026, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, revealed that: “For more than 25 years, we all lived in a reality in which we believed there was no threat. We don’t need to do anything for our own defence.” He also conceded that, although the northern European countries reacted to Russia’s military invasion into Crimea, “Germany and other countries: they didn’t. They heard the alarm clock, but they pushed the snooze button and turned around”. Moreover, he warned that Russia could start a war against a NATO member country as early as three years, namely in 2029.
Then, on June 11, 2026, Politico published the following telling remarks of the Inspector of the German Army, the highest-ranking officer of German ground forces, Christian Freuding: “We have to be prepared […] We must be ready to fight […] All 32 NATO partners agree that Russia might have the capability to invade a NATO partner country in 2029.”
Fortunately, a Russian attack against a NATO member country, and its dramatic consequences on human lives, can still be averted if the West actively supports Ukraine now to ensure that Ukraine succeeds in defending its independence and liberating all its occupied territories.
Ukraine’s daily drone strikes against oil refineries deep into Russia and oil tankers in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov have already shattered the myth that Russia is a military superpower. Major media outlets have correctly noted that the tide has turned. For instance, on May 20, 2026, CNN published an article titled “Russia is losing in Ukraine. Xi has noticed – Trump should too,” which states that: “Thus far, it’s Ukraine – not Russia – that has achieved net territorial gains this year, together with inflicting massive losses on Russia’s invading forces.”
Putin is acutely aware of Russia’s current vulnerability and that is why its army has escalated deadly ballistic missile attacks on the civilian population, including children, and civilian infrastructure of Ukraine.
Under such circumstances, one would logically surmise that the West would supply Ukraine with additional effective air-defense interceptors to nudge the course of history in the right direction.
However, on Aug. 2, President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed that Ukraine has received only a third as many air-defense interceptors in 2026 compared to the same period in 2025. This revelation is bewildering as it exposes the West to a similar treatment in the foreseeable future.
This is a critical time and the perennity of Ukraine’s Independence will heavily impact on global security and stability.
On the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence, NATO member countries need to recognize this blatant reality for their own good and immediately provide Ukraine with the necessary tools, starting with effective missile defense ammunition, to ensure that we move towards a better, safer and more secure world.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

Why Assam wants to shrink Kaziranga National Park's eco-sensitive zone - explained
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:39:15 UTC
22:39:15 KST

Why Assam wants to shrink Kaziranga National Park's eco-sensitive zone - explained
Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 21:59 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
A one-horned rhinoceros grazes in the Burapahar Range of Kaziranga National Park (PTI Photo)
At dawn, Kaziranga wakes to mist rising over its tall grasslands. Elephants move through the wilderness as jeep tracks wind past marshes, while one-horned rhinos emerge from the grass.By afternoon, the landscape transforms into a trail of wildlife sightings, wild water buffalo, deer, elephants and, for visitors, glimpses of one of India's most celebrated natural habitats.But beyond the park's boundary, another debate is unfolding. How much space should be left between Kaziranga's protected landscape and the towns, homes and businesses that surround it?The Assam government has proposed replacing the existing default 10-km eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) around Kaziranga National Park and Tiger Reserve with a site-specific ESZ extending between one and three kilometres from the park boundary.The proposal has triggered a debate over how far conservation restrictions should extend beyond a protected area and how the needs of communities living alongside Kaziranga can be balanced with wildlife protection.The state government says the proposal will ease restrictions on housing, healthcare, infrastructure and local businesses while continuing to protect Kaziranga. It has also maintained that the move will not alter the boundary of the national park or its status as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The opposition and conservationists, however, have raised concerns that a narrower ESZ could weaken safeguards around an ecosystem whose ecological footprint extends beyond the park's legal boundary.
What is an eco-sensitive zone?
An eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) is a regulatory buffer around protected areas such as national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. It acts as an additional layer of protection for ecologically sensitive areas outside the protected area's boundary.ESZs are declared by the ministry of environment, forest and climate change based on proposals submitted by state governments and in accordance with the 2011 guidelines for declaring ESZs.The idea is to create a “shock absorber” around protected areas, providing a transition between areas requiring a high level of protection and those where human activity is more intensive.Importantly, an ESZ is regulatory rather than automatically prohibitive. Activities within an ESZ are classified based on their environmental impact and may be prohibited, regulated or permitted under the applicable rules.The declaration of an ESZ does not, by itself, mean that local communities can no longer carry out activities such as farming or building houses. The specific restrictions depend on the ESZ notification and the nature of the activity.
Assam has proposed a site-specific 1–3 km ESZ around Kaziranga instead of the default 10-km zone.
Why Assam wants a smaller ESZ
Chief minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has repeatedly argued that the 10-km ESZ around Kaziranga is a default arrangement, rather than a site-specific zone determined after assessing local conditions.On August 8, Sarma said the state government would submit a proposal to the Centre to reduce the ESZ from 10 km to 1 km, citing the need to facilitate development around Kaziranga, including the construction of a stadium.He later clarified that the existing 10-km ESZ would remain in force until the state's proposal is formally notified."The Supreme Court has said that around a wildlife sanctuary, the eco-sensitive zone will normally be 1 km, and if required, it can go up to three kilometres. Until the state notifies it, the eco-sensitive zone will remain 10 km. The moment it is notified, it will be reduced to 1 km," Sarma said.
If people living around Kaziranga are displaced, who will protect Kaziranga?
CM Himanta Biswa Sarma
Oriental darter birds seen at Kaziranga National Park, in Nagaon, on Tuesday. (ANI Photo)
Sarma has argued that retaining a uniform 10-km buffer would bring large populated areas under the regulatory framework and restrict development. "If we maintain 10 km all around Kaziranga, then everything in Kaliabor, Doboka, Jakhalabandha will be finished," he added."Local people have to run businesses to survive. Even the Numaligarh Refinery will have to be closed down if the 10 km area around Kaziranga is notified as ESZ," he said. "If people living around Kaziranga are displaced, who will protect Kaziranga?" Sarma added.The chief minister has also said residents should be able to pursue livelihood opportunities, including businesses involving GI-tagged products, while continuing to coexist with wildlife.Sarma has pointed to the geographical spread of Kaziranga and its adjoining areas, saying the park extends beyond the Kohora range towards Biswanath Ghat.A uniform 10-km zone from the park boundary, he said, could affect areas towards Gohpur and Biswanath Chariali.The government has similarly cited development requirements in Bokakhat, including a proposed modern stadium and other civic infrastructure, as examples of projects that could face restrictions under the existing arrangement."Since Kaziranga has not yet been finally notified, the default eco-sensitive zone is 10 km. Once the notification is completed, we will propose a scientifically defined 1-km eco-sensitive zone. That will remove unnecessary restrictions and allow us to undertake development works in Bokakhat while continuing to protect wildlife," Sarma said, according to local news reports.In June 2022, the Supreme Court directed that an ESZ of at least 1 km should be declared around protected forests, national parks and wildlife sanctuaries.The court subsequently modified aspects of that order after states and the Centre argued that a uniform approach was not practical in all areas.It also recognised that a rigid approach could create difficulties for people living around protected areas and potentially increase human-animal conflict.The one-kilometre figure, therefore, should not be understood as an automatic instruction that every protected area must have exactly a 1-km ESZ.The extent of an ESZ can vary according to local conditions. This is the basis on which the Assam government is seeking a site-specific approach for Kaziranga.Until the proposed ESZ is formally notified, however, the existing default 10-km arrangement continues to apply, according to the state government.
What is Assam government's stand?
The Assam government maintains that an eco-sensitive zone (ESZ) is not a blanket ban on construction or tourism. While activities considered environmentally harmful, including mining and certain polluting activities, face restrictions, other development can be permitted subject to prescribed regulations.The government also argues that ESZs need not be uniform and can vary according to the ecological and developmental conditions of a particular area. It has cited existing ESZs in Assam to support its case.Around Amchang Wildlife Sanctuary, for instance, the notified ESZ varies from 170 metres to 8.1 km from the sanctuary boundary. Around Hollongapar Gibbon Wildlife Sanctuary, it ranges from zero kilometres along the interstate boundary with Nagaland to 22.54 km in other areas.The state says Kaziranga should similarly have a site-specific ESZ based on its ecological characteristics and the needs of surrounding communities.The ESZ debate has also become intertwined with a separate controversy over tourism infrastructure near Kaziranga. CM Himanta Biswa Sarma has rejected allegations that the proposed reduction is aimed at facilitating a five-star hotel project near the park.“There is no connection between the hotel project and the ESZ debate. The ESZ framework primarily restricts mining and certain polluting and environmentally damaging activities, rather than prohibiting hotels or tourism facilities. If somebody is protesting against the hotel on the grounds that it will fall within an ESZ, they do not understand what an ESZ is,” he said.Sarma has argued that tourism is important to Kaziranga's economy and cited Jim Corbett as an example of tourism infrastructure around protected areas.However, the regulations do impose restrictions on certain tourism projects. A 2025 Gauhati high court record concerning tourism infrastructure noted that new commercial hotels and resorts are prohibited within one kilometre of the protected-area boundary or the applicable ESZ limit, whichever is nearer. Tourism projects beyond that distance but within the ESZ remain subject to applicable regulations and plans.
Kaziranga is recognised as the world's major stronghold of the Indian one-horned rhinoceros.
A balance between wildlife and people
At the heart of the Assam government's argument is the question of how conservation rules affect people living around Kaziranga.Thousands of residents live in the park's surrounding areas, with livelihoods linked to agriculture, tourism, local businesses and other economic activities. The state government has argued that the existing 10-km arrangement can make it difficult for communities to build homes and develop basic infrastructure.That argument has also found support among some residents. On August 18, hundreds of people from areas including Bagori and Kuthori rallied from Kuthori to Haldhibari in support of the proposed reduction. Residents said restrictions associated with the 10-km zone had affected their everyday lives and backed a site-specific approach.They argued that communities living alongside Kaziranga should have room to build homes, pursue livelihoods and improve basic infrastructure while continuing to coexist with wildlife.The rally came a day after Assam Congress workers held a demonstration near Kaziranga opposing the proposal, underscoring the wider debate over where to draw the line between protecting a fragile ecosystem and allowing communities around it to grow.
Congress raises mining concerns
The Assam Congress has strongly opposed the proposed reduction. State party president and Lok Sabha deputy leader of opposition Gaurav Gogoi led a protest at the Kohora range and demanded that the proposal be withdrawn.Gogoi alleged that the move could provide a "legal cover" for mining and weaken wildlife conservation."Rampant illegal coal, stone and sand mining patronised by the ruling dispensation has triggered catastrophic floods across upper Assam, destroying over 4,000 houses and claiming more than 100 lives," Gogoi alleged.He also claimed that deforestation and hill mining had pushed tigers and elephants towards human settlements, worsening human-animal conflict.The allegations have been rejected by the state government. Sarma has accused the opposition of politicising the issue and argued that criticism should be based on an assessment of the proposed ESZ's likely environmental impact.Mining is particularly significant in the debate because it is among the activities subject to strict restrictions within ESZs.The Gauhati high court's March 2026 order noted that mining was prohibited within the applicable 10-km ESZ under the prevailing arrangement.Reducing the ESZ could therefore change the regulatory framework applicable to areas that currently fall within the 10-km zone.
Why conservationists are concerned
Kaziranga's wildlife does not always remain within the park's legal boundary. Every year, when floodwaters rise, animals move towards higher ground outside the park.For conservationists, this makes the landscape surrounding Kaziranga an important part of the larger ecosystem.Wildlife conservationist Jadav Payeng said, "[Kaziranga National Park] is not just Assam’s pride, but it’s a world heritage site. The proposal, if implemented, would have a drastic effect on wildlife in the national park."He said rhinos, deer and elephants leave Kaziranga during annual floods and move towards nearby higher areas for safety.According to Payeng, reducing the ESZ could restrict these movements and leave animals vulnerable. He also questioned the need to reduce the ESZ to facilitate construction activities near the national park.
Terming it as trespassing into the animal territory would be fair as reducing the eco-sensitive zone from 10 km to 1 km is disheartening to the wildlife and local community.
Environmentalist Kavita Ashok
Environmentalist Kavita Ashok also raised concerns over the proposed reduction. "Terming it as trespassing into the animal territory would be fair as reducing the eco-sensitive zone from 10 km to 1 km is disheartening to the wildlife and local community," Kavita said.“The routes will be disrupted and animals would be displaced from their terrain. Traffic, development and maybe even construction of any sort will create imbalance in the otherwise peaceful Kaziranga zone,” she added.The concern is particularly relevant because Kaziranga is a flood-dependent ecosystem. Annual floods replenish its wetlands and grasslands, but severe flooding can also become deadly for wildlife.More than 130 wild animals, including at least six rhinos, died during the 2024 floods, according to the conservation assessment. The deaths included 117 hog deer, two sambar deer, a rhesus macaque and an otter.In 2017, more than 350 animals died during floods and vehicle collisions as wildlife moved through corridors towards higher ground.This makes the landscape outside Kaziranga more than just a development zone. For animals moving out during floods, the surrounding areas can become temporary refuge and passage routes to safer ground.
Nagaon: A herd of deers graze in the Burapahar Range of Kaziranga National Park. (PTI Photo)
Ecosystem that extends beyond boundary
The debate is therefore not simply about whether the ESZ should be 1 km, 3 km or 10 km. The larger question is what lies within those boundaries.Kaziranga is recognised internationally for its exceptional biodiversity. Unesco describes the park as an important habitat for the one-horned rhinoceros and other threatened species, including wild water buffalo, swamp deer, elephants and tigers.The 2025 Conservation Outlook Assessment also highlights Kaziranga's importance for rare and endangered mammals and birds. It describes the park as the world's major stronghold of the Indian one-horned rhinoceros and notes its significant populations of wild water buffalo, swamp deer and Bengal tigers.The assessment identifies several pressures on the landscape, including flooding, traffic along the highway bordering the park, tourism pressure, wildlife movement through corridors, invasive species, livestock grazing and human-wildlife conflict.Unplanned tourism infrastructure around the park has also raised concerns because construction can affect animal movement through wildlife corridors.This makes the exact mapping of the proposed 1–3 km ESZ critical. A smaller zone may not necessarily mean weaker conservation if it is scientifically designed to protect the most sensitive areas.Its effectiveness, however, will depend on whether important wildlife corridors, flood escape routes, wetlands, grasslands and other ecologically sensitive areas are included in the final notified zone.The Assam government has repeatedly stressed that reducing the ESZ would not reduce the area of Kaziranga National Park.Kaziranga was inscribed on the Unesco World Heritage List in 1985. The World Heritage property covers 42,996 hectares and is recognised for its exceptional biodiversity and its importance as a habitat for the one-horned rhinoceros.The proposed ESZ lies outside the protected-area boundary. A change in the ESZ therefore does not, by itself, change the boundary of the national park or its World Heritage status.At the same time, Unesco has historically stressed the importance of protecting areas around Kaziranga and encouraged India to provide a legal basis to protect the buffer zone south of the park, including the Mikir Hills and Karbi Plateau.
What happens next?
The Assam government has said its proposal will go through the prescribed process involving the Centre and scientific examination before a final ESZ is notified.Until then, the existing default 10-km arrangement will continue to apply. The final notification will be crucial because it will determine not just the width of the ESZ, but also which villages, roads, development projects, wildlife corridors and ecologically sensitive areas fall within it.
That is likely to be the real test of the proposal.For Kaziranga, the challenge is to protect a landscape that does not end at a line on a map while ensuring that communities living alongside one of India's most important national parks have space for homes, livelihoods and essential infrastructure.The debate over 1 km versus 10 km is therefore not merely about a number. It is about finding the point where the needs of people and the movement of wildlife can coexist without one coming at the cost of the other.

Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Indonesia bolsters troop numbers to combat Borneo wildfires
Fires between January and July burned more than 200,000 hectares of land, says the government.
The Indonesian government is sending 1,500 more soldiers to Borneo to help tackle wildfires that have burned through swaths of the island and created thick smog, choking some areas.
Fires this year have scorched at least 200,000 hectares (495,000 acres) of land – an area three times the size of the capital, Jakarta, the government said – as dry conditions, driven by a powerful El Nino weather pattern, take hold.

President Prabowo Subianto, on a visit to the region on Saturday, ordered increased troop deployment, Indonesian Cabinet Secretary Teddy Indra Wijaya said.
“An additional three Indonesia National Armed Forces battalions, or around 1,500 personnel, will be brought in from outside Kalimantan starting today,” Teddy said in a statement.
Kalimantan is Indonesia’s part of Borneo, which the country shares with Brunei and Malaysia.
Six helicopters are also being sent to boost waterbombing operations, Teddy said.
The government is monitoring the situation closely and mobilising resources to help contain the spread of the blaze, Prabowo told reporters in the Central Kalimantan provincial capital of Palangkaraya.
“We’re taking mitigation measures. The important thing is to immediately stop the spread of fire spots,” the president said.
Smog from the fires has prompted local governments in Borneo, home to pristine rainforest and vast plantations, to advise residents to wear masks and stay indoors.
The fires have sent smoke into Malaysian Borneo, with six areas of Sarawak state recording “unhealthy” air quality.
The area burned is already larger than during previous El Nino seasons in 2019 and 2023, but not as large as in 2015 during a particularly strong El Nino.
El Nino is a naturally occurring climate phenomenon that brings worldwide changes in winds, air pressure and rainfall patterns. It typically brings drought in Indonesia.
Climate change can amplify its effects because a warmer ocean and atmosphere make more energy and moisture available to feed extreme weather events.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum on Thursday defended her decision to abstain from an Organization of American States (OAS) vote on Nicaragua.
She said it was based on the constitutional principles of self-determination and non-intervention.
“It is a matter of self-determination,” said Sheinbaum.
The OAS Permanent Council approved a resolution Wednesday for an urgent meeting of foreign ministers to address the political situation in Nicaragua.
The measure received 29 votes, while Brazil voted against, and Mexico abstained. Haiti and Venezuela were absent from the vote.
Mexican representative to the OAS, Alejandro Encinas, defended the abstention during the session, saying “Nicaragua’s internal situation does not constitute a threat to hemispheric peace or security,” according to the Mexico Solidarity newspaper.
He argued that Mexico did not support convening a meeting on Nicaragua without clarity on what measures could be taken against a country that no longer belongs to the OAS, it said.
Sheinbaum ruled out seeking dialogue with the Nicaraguan government on democracy, saying Mexico “would have no reason to do so” because it is “a decision for Nicaraguans themselves,” said the Forbes Mexico publication.
The OAS initiative came after Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega announced July 19 that elections would not be held in 2026, despite general elections having been scheduled for November.
A constitutional reform approved in 2025 extended Ortega's presidential term and established his wife, Rosario Murillo, as co-president. The reform also moved the elections to November 2027.
The US, Argentina, Panama, Paraguay and Uruguay promoted the initiative after an earlier attempt to advance a similar measure failed to secure sufficient support on Aug. 5.
The OAS resolution adopted Aug. 19 said representative democracy, which the organization considers essential for the stability, peace and development of the region, “no longer exists in Nicaragua.”
Nicaragua’s withdrawal from the OAS took effect in November 2023, following years of tensions with the organization about democratic governance and human rights concerns.

Fatah moves to counter broad Hamas-Dahlan election alliance

Fatah moves to counter broad Hamas-Dahlan election alliance
An emerging electoral alliance bringing together Hamas, Mohammed Dahlan's Fatah Reform Current and other Palestinian factions is taking shape ahead of November's legislative elections, as Mahmoud Abbas's Fatah moves to prevent the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP) from joining the bloc.
Palestinian sources have told The New Arab that the proposed alliance would include Hamas, Palestinian Islamic Jihad, Dahlan's Reform Current, Nasser al-Qudwa's National Democratic Forum and the Popular Resistance Committees.
The development comes ahead of Palestinian legislative elections scheduled for 28 November, which would be the first such vote since 2006.
The emerging bloc brings together factions with sharply differing political and ideological positions, but which share opposition to the Palestinian Authority in Ramallah and Fatah under President Mahmoud Abbas.
It follows a series of meetings in Egypt over the past two weeks, including talks in El Alamein between Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya and Dahlan, the former senior Fatah figure expelled from the movement following a dispute with Abbas.
Sources told The New Arab that Dahlan played a role in persuading Hamas to move ahead with US President Donald Trump's plan for Gaza and had promised to seek US and European support for its participation in the elections.
The negotiations appear to have prompted a response from Fatah, with a senior delegation expected to arrive in Cairo on Sunday for meetings with Egyptian officials, Hamas and the PFLP.
Sources have said that the delegation will include Fatah deputy leader Hussein al-Sheikh, Central Committee member Majed Faraj and Executive Committee member Rawhi Fattouh.
One source said that the delegation "will meet the leadership of the PFLP and will press it not to participate in the political alliance being formed to contest the upcoming legislative elections in November.
The Fatah delegation is also expected to discuss arrangements for holding the elections in Gaza with Hamas, particularly as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza is not expected to have assumed responsibility for the enclave by November.
The discussions follow a meeting in Cairo on Thursday attended by representatives of Hamas, Islamic Jihad, the Reform Current and the PFLP.
Al-Qudwa, a former Palestinian foreign minister who heads the National Democratic Forum, told The New Arab that the meeting discussed forming a broad national list.
"All those who participated in the meeting agreed to the idea, with the exception of the PFLP, which asked for more time," al-Qudwa said.
"The idea behind the meeting was to propose forming a national list that includes all parties, without direct factional participation (...) We do not want to call it a factional list. There is considerable room for the participation of young people, women and all sections of society," he added.
Asked whether it amounted to a national alliance, al-Qudwa said: "I am not in favour of an alliance with any party against another party. What was discussed was simply the idea of a broad national list, not an alliance."
Islamic Jihad, however, has described the talks in different terms.
A senior source in the movement told The New Arab that "the movement has agreed in principle to participate in the national alliance project, which would form a national bloc," while stressing that consultations were continuing.
The source said Islamic Jihad had not abandoned its opposition to the 1993 Oslo Accords, "and for this reason there are points that remain under discussion".
Its participation would mark the first time the movement has agreed to take part in Palestinian legislative elections, although a final decision has not yet been made.
The Democratic Front for the Liberation of Palestine (DFLP) also attended Thursday's Cairo meeting but has postponed a decision on how it will participate until the proposal is discussed internally.
The manoeuvring comes as Fatah faces internal tensions following its eighth conference in May, which saw several veteran figures sidelined and figures close to Abbas rise through the movement, including his son Yasser Abbas, who was elected to Fatah's Central Committee.
A Palestinian official close to top political circles has meanwhile cast doubt on whether the November elections will take place as scheduled.
"The legislative elections will not be held on the announced date. There are many obstacles, and the alliance now being discussed could itself become a factor pushing towards postponement," the official told The New Arab.
"The justifications for such a postponement would certainly be different, and it would not be said that it was due to fear of the alliance or the results," the official added.

Scandal erupts over Ukraine's parliament move to block key EU integration bills

Scandal erupts over Ukraine parliament's move to block key EU integration bills
A parliamentary committee on Aug. 21 defended its earlier decision to block five bills intended to strengthen the country's fight against corruption.
The bills are requirements of the European Union, both to receive an estimated 2.1 billion euros ($2.45 billion) at the end of 2026, as well as to advance Kyiv's EU accession talks.
The reforms seek to expand anti-corruption agencies' authority, reform the Prosecutor General's Office and the State Investigation Bureau, and repeal legislation that impedes corruption cases.
The Ukrainian parliament's law enforcement committee on Aug. 19 blocked the bills by not including them in the agenda of parliament's current session, which is scheduled to end in January.
To become valid, the decision has to be approved by Ruslan Stefanchuk, speaker of the Verkhovna Rada.
The move has sparked outrage and drawn sharp criticism from pro-reform lawmakers and anti-corruption activists. They argued that the decision was a major blow to both Ukraine's EU integration and anti-corruption reforms.
Ivanna Klympush-Tsintsadze, chair of the European integration committee, told the Kyiv Independent that she was "absolutely appalled by this decision of the law enforcement committee."
"This is a revanchist attempt to reverse some of the most important reforms which are also interim benchmarks for (the EU's) Fundamentals Cluster," said Klympush-Tsintsadze, who represents ex-President Petro Poroshenko's European Solidarity party.
read also
Why were the bills blocked?
The decision to block the bills triggered a scandal because their substance was not even considered by the law enforcement committee.
The committee said in a statement on Aug. 21 that it had not "rejected" the bills but rather recommended not including them in the session's agenda. The statement was made in response to requests by the Kyiv Independent and other media outlets.
The committee also said that Vsevolod Chentsov, deputy prime minister for European integration, and parliament's European integration committee had not formally designated the bills as "European integration legislation."
Olha Savchenko, a committee member from President Volodymyr Zelensky's Servant of the People party, said at the Aug. 19 committee meeting that, instead of considering these bills, parliament should wait for alternative versions of the reforms from the Cabinet of Ministers.
The Cabinet has so far failed to submit any of the alternative bills.
Yaroslav Zheleznyak, a lawmaker from the liberal Holos party and a co-sponsor of the bills, told the Kyiv Independent that he deems the decision to block the bills to be illegal because it violates parliament's procedure.
Bills can be removed from the agenda only if they have lost relevance, but this is obviously not the case here, Zheleznyak said.
The committee has not responded to a request for comment on the accusation.
Zheleznyak also said that he would submit the bills again if parliament made a final decision on removing them from the agenda.
"These are bills that my colleagues and I submitted to strengthen the fight against corruption in the country," Zheleznyak wrote on Telegram. "These bills bring us closer to the EU. And around 2 billion euros in aid by the end of the year is tied to the passage of these bills."
The bills were co-sponsored by Zheleznyak, Anastasia Radina, head of parliament's anti-corruption committee, and other lawmakers.
They are part of a package of changes expected to be done by the end of 2026. Full completion of the reforms in that package would lead to Ukraine receiving 2.1 billion euros from the EU.
All five reforms fall under the EU's Ukraine Plan and its interim benchmarks on the rule of law.
For the EU to ever be allowed to consider any membership reforms as successfully completed by Kyiv, these interim benchmarks first need to be completely fulfilled.
read also
Which reforms were blocked?
One of the bills seeks to explicitly expand the National Anti-Corruption Bureau's (NABU) jurisdiction to officials of the President's Office and the head of the State Investigation Bureau.
There are loopholes allowing the bureau to investigate officials of the President's Office in some cases involving high monetary sums or officials from other institutions. However, the lack of direct jurisdiction still impedes the NABU's ability to investigate the President's Office.
According to the EU's requirements, Ukraine must expand "the jurisdiction of NABU and SAPO (Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office) to cover all high-risk positions."
The committee claimed that the bill expanding the bureau's jurisdiction "duplicates" existing legislation.
But anti-corruption activists interpreted the committee's move as an effort to obstruct the NABU's ongoing investigations.
On the same day as the committee meeting, the NABU raided the home of Zelensky's then Deputy Chief of Staff, Iryna Mudra. She was later charged in a large-scale money laundering and corporate raiding case.
Another bill seeks to select the prosecutor general in a transparent contest with the participation of international experts.
According to the EU reform roadmap, Ukraine should "conduct a comprehensive review of the selection and dismissal procedure of the prosecutor general, with a view to aligning it with European best practice." The plan also envisages reinstating transparent contests for other top prosecutor jobs.
However, the committee claimed that the bill on the prosecutor general "may be regarded as inconsistent with the Constitution."
Radina, a co-author of the bill, denied the allegation.
The package also includes a bill that would introduce a similar transparent contest for the State Investigation Bureau with the participation of international experts. According to the EU requirements, Ukraine should reform the bureau "in line with best European practices."
The committee claimed that the European Union Advisory Mission did not support the bill on the State Investigation Bureau.
The Kyiv Independent has requested the experts' conclusion from the committee, but has not received it so far.
Radina told the Kyiv Independent she had not seen the conclusion. But even if it is true, the experts' opinion does not have to coincide with the EU's official position, she added.
Zelensky pledged in January to submit to parliament an alternative bill to reform the bureau by the end of the month. So far, he has failed to do so.
Another bill concerns canceling the controversial 2017 amendments that dealt a major blow to corruption cases by severely limiting the terms of investigations and setting strict deadlines for sending cases to trial. Some of the amendments were repealed in 2023, but the main ones remain.
The committee claimed that the bill to cancel the amendments would contradict decisions made by the European Court of Human Rights.
There is also a bill that seeks to suspend the statute of limitations in top-level corruption cases when a defendant is mobilized. The legislation aims to ensure that mobilization is not used as a way to avoid prosecution.
The committee claimed that the bill suspending the statute of limitations would violate the "principle of legal certainty" required by the European Convention on Human Rights.
Ukraine's reform agenda is at a standstill
The governing party's inability or unwillingness to pass reforms has been notable for almost a year.
Ukraine failed to complete 11 reforms in the last three months of 2025, which were also required in order to unlock European funds.
That prompted the bloc's Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos to get more directly involved, drawing up an action plan in tandem with Taras Kachka, then Ukraine's deputy prime minister for EU integration. The plan, adopted in December, includes 10 urgently needed reforms to be completed by the end of 2026.
To date, Kyiv has yet to complete a single one of the ten items required by the Kachka-Kos plan.
One reform passed by the parliament in June, on integrity declarations for judges, might have even dismantled rules rather than strengthened them.
Judicial watchdog Dejure said that "instead of reviving a weak but important mechanism for vetting judges' integrity, lawmakers have chosen to dismantle it altogether."
And the man whose name features on the plan, Kachka, has been demoted by Zelensky and sent back to Brussels, but as Ukraine's ambassador to the EU.
In July, the EU made one last move to maintain the positive pressure to reform by ensuring the Kachka-Kos plan's reform list is explicitly tied to the disbursement of funds.
After that, the situation as it stands brings to mind the idiom that "you can lead a horse to water, but you cannot make it drink." And, in the minds of national EU leaders, nor should the bloc have to.
"An independent judiciary, solid democratic institutions, bodies effectively able to fight corruption, these are not just reforms designed to please Brussels," said Belgian Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot at a press conference in Kyiv on Aug. 18, the day before the law enforcement committee held its meeting.
These reforms are "designed to protect citizens, reinforce trust, and make your country more resilient," Prevot said.

====================================================================================================

'Jerusalem of the Balkans': Exploring Thessaloniki's lost Jewish history - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:33:36 UTC
22:33:36 KST

I’m standing with my husband at the port in Thessaloniki, a vital commercial hub on the Aegean Sea connecting Southern Europe with the Balkans.
I’m thinking of the Jewish stevedores who once worked these docks, and of those who later made aliyah and helped haul cargo on the waterfronts of pre-state Israel. Men from this community were also among the Sonderkommando prisoners who revolted at Auschwitz-Birkenau and destroyed crematorium IV.
When a proposed flight of two hours and 20 minutes appeared on my computer screen from Sun d’Or, El Al’s subsidiary, I booked tickets for my husband and me.
I had long wanted to visit the city where the port once closed on Shabbat, and where Jews were both longshoremen and leaders in commercial development. I didn’t know much more than that.
I was about to learn a great deal.
First, the name.
The Jewish community used a shortened form, spelled either Salonika or Salonica, and referred to this pretty city on the sea as “La Madre de Israel,” the Mother of Israel, and the “Jerusalem of the Balkans.”
Thessaloniki is the older name, and it commemorates a woman. Thessalonike was the half-sister of Alexander the Great and the wife of Cassander, who founded the city in 315 BCE. According to Greek legend, after Thessalonike’s death she became a mermaid who appeared before passing ships and inquired if her brother Alexander was still alive. The sailors had to answer, “He lives and reigns and conquers the world.” If they answered incorrectly, she would metamorphose into a monster and sink their ships.
There are legends, too, that Jews arrived with King Cassander, but no one knows exactly when Jews first settled in Thessaloniki. The city’s Jewish Museum describes an ancient Romaniote community, traditionally dated to around 140 BCE. They spoke a Jewish form of Greek known as Yevanic. They were joined many centuries later by the more than 20,000 Jews expelled from Spain in 1492, and from Portugal several years later.
Spain’s loss was Thessaloniki’s gain. The intellectual and commercial talents of the Golden Age of Spanish Jewry enhanced the seaside city. The newcomers prospered in business, printing, scholarship, and the arts.
Eventually, Jews made up half the population, and Ladino became one of the city’s principal languages. The port, which the Jews expanded and where they served as merchants, brokers, and longshoremen, naturally closed on Shabbat.
As a capellophile, I shopped in a hat shop called Stamion, “established 1914.” I learned that the proprietors weren’t Jewish, but that previous generations of the family had spoken fluent Ladino because so many of their hat-wearing customers were Jews.
In 1917, a cooking fire spread and ravaged Thessaloniki. More than 70,000 people were left homeless, approximately 52,000 of them Sephardi Jews. Many Jews left for Paris, New York, and pre-state Israel. Experienced Jewish longshoremen from Salonika played an important role in developing the ports of Haifa and Tel Aviv.
The day of rest was changed to Sunday. The Jewish Museum documents the rise and fall of one of the world’s outstanding Jewish communities, as well as today’s Jewish community.
The museum’s ground floor is surprisingly dominated by recovered tombstones.
Until December 1942, an enormous Jewish cemetery containing hundreds of thousands of graves occupied the land on which the city’s Aristotle University now stands. Some graves dated back to the 15th century. Empowered by the Nazis who conquered Greece, municipal workers arrived with pickaxes to topple the graves and take the land. Marble was used for a swimming pool for German soldiers, for church renovations, for pavements, and for private courtyards. The Hebrew lettering was scratched away, or the stones were turned over.
Recovering the gravestones remains an ongoing process.
This reminded me, of course, of the devastation of the Jewish cemetery on the Mount of Olives between 1948 and 1967. I have often visited the grave of Hadassah founder Henrietta Szold, who died in 1945. Her headstone was used as road pavement. After the Six Day War, the cemetery caretaker found it and returned it to her grave.
Thessaloniki's Jews were forced to remove bodies from gas chambers at Auschwitz
AT THE Monastirioton Synagogue, which survived because it was used by the Red Cross during the German occupation, we were privileged to hear Elia Matalon, a retired surveyor and civil engineer, recount the history of the community through both public events and the experiences of his family and those of his wife, fellow guide Hella Kunio Matalon.
Long ago, on a tour of Auschwitz-Birkenau, I heard that Jews from Thessaloniki, known for their physical strength as longshoremen, were forced into the Sonderkommando units. These prisoners had the horrifying task of removing bodies from the gas chambers and bringing them to the crematoria.
I knew about the mighty Jewish boxer Salamo Arouch, a longshoreman about whom a movie was made. I had never understood how an entire community of more than 50,000 people, including so many tough, experienced port workers, could have been transported to Auschwitz with so little organized resistance.
Matalon explained how thoroughly the community had been deceived.
Hard as it is to imagine in today’s world of instant communication, the Jews of Thessaloniki didn’t know about the concentration camps and death camps of Poland. Using a modified strategy, the Germans initially avoided sealing them inside the kind of starvation ghettos found in Eastern Europe. The boundaries of the ghettos were porous. Matalon’s mother-in-law, then a schoolgirl, would leave in the afternoon to meet her non-Jewish Greek friends and return at night.
The Germans promoted the fiction of a “New Europe” in which unemployed and hungry Jews would supposedly find jobs, education, and abundant food in Poland.
Rabbi Zvi Koretz, the city’s chief rabbi, remains a contentious figure. He had been arrested by the Germans and imprisoned near Vienna before being returned to Thessaloniki. Matalon believes that Koretz came back a manipulated and manipulative man.
Koretz preached at the many city synagogues that the Jews should embrace relocation. The community was led to believe that families would travel together by train and be resettled together. Instead, they were forced into cattle cars, and it was too late to turn around.
More than 53,000 members of the Jewish community, out of a population of 56,000, were murdered.
Matalon’s mother-in-law came from a large family that had experienced an earlier confrontation with the Nazis. That experience led some family members to suspect that the promises of resettlement were a ruse. Even so, of the 23 members of the extended family, only his future in-laws and the daughter who would become his wife went into hiding. The others were murdered at Auschwitz.
“They felt it inconceivable that their entire community could be destroyed,” Matalon told us.
His own family survived because Righteous Gentiles hid them in Albania.
Thessaloniki has begun acknowledging the Jews who contributed to its history
Later, walking through the port, my husband mused that perhaps we should not have come. Too many residents of Thessaloniki had been complicit. Too many had taken possession of Jewish apartments, shops, furnishings, and property. We had not understood the full scope of the tragedy that had befallen this magnificent Jewish community.
Last year, we visited Chalkida, another Greek city, where non-Jewish residents helped save their Jews.
But then, we thought, staying away would leave its Jewish history even more invisible. How will we know if we don’t come and see?
In more recent years, Thessaloniki has begun acknowledging the Jews who contributed so much. Holocaust memorials have been erected, and signs identify Jewish contributions to the city’s commercial and architectural life.
Greece is making a huge investment in Israeli defensive technology. Our Uber driver praised Israel for objecting to the sale of advanced fighter planes to Turkey.
At the Monastirioton Synagogue, we heard Elia Matalon sing the popular Ladino song “Adio Kerida,” Goodbye, Beloved. It’s a haunting song of wounded love and departure. Matalon told us that Jews sang it to their city as they stood beside the railway tracks.
The beloved had betrayed them.
“I’ll go find another love. I hope there is a real love there,” the song proposes.
An estimated 55,000 descendants of Greek Jews live in Israel today, many of them with roots in Thessaloniki.■
The writer is the Israel director of public relations at Hadassah, the Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Her latest book is A Daughter of Many Mothers, cowritten with Holocaust survivor and premier English-language witness Rena Quint.

'The ABY' hotel brings new life to Tel Aviv’s historic Zamir Cinema site
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
13:33:34 UTC
22:33:34 KST

On one of Tel Aviv’s most recognizable corners, a building that once drew generations of moviegoers is beginning its next act.
The ABY, a new 40-room boutique hotel, has opened at the intersection of Allenby and Ben-Yehuda streets, on the site of the historic Zamir Cinema.
Developed by hospitality entrepreneur Danny Tamari in an equal partnership with the Eilat-based Astral hotel chain, the approximately NIS 40 million project brings new life to a preservation building with deep roots in Tel Aviv’s cultural history.
For decades, Zamir Cinema was part of the city’s entertainment landscape and a gathering place for generations of moviegoers. The building also played a role in the wider Israeli film industry, with films distributed from the site to cinemas throughout the country.
Designed in the International Style of the 1950s, the building stands at Mugrabi Square, once an important center of Tel Aviv life. After years of decline and neglect, the square and surrounding area have been undergoing a renewal, with the area expected to become a vibrant pedestrian zone.
Even the hotel’s name is tied to its location. “Aby” is derived from the initials of Allenby and Ben-Yehuda, reflecting its position at the meeting point between central Tel Aviv and the sea.
Preserving the building’s history was central to the hotel’s nearly eight-year planning, preservation, and renewal process, led by architect Yoav Messer, who also served as the building’s preservation architect.
The road to opening came with an unexpected setback. The hotel’s debut was delayed a year, after the building sustained damage from a missile blast. Its eventual opening marks both the completion of a lengthy preservation project and another step in the ongoing revitalization of this stretch of central Tel Aviv.
'A place that tells a Tel Aviv story'
“The ABY was born from a deep love for Tel Aviv and from a desire to create a place that tells its story,” Tamari said. “It was important to us to honor the history of the building and the memories it carries, while at the same time opening a new chapter for it.”
For Tamari, The ABY follows the hospitality philosophy he established with The Vera, his boutique hotel on Lilienblum Street, which opened around eight years ago. Israeli creativity is at the heart of both properties, with an emphasis on local artists, manufacturers, suppliers, and products.
At The ABY, that approach can be seen throughout the hotel. With interiors by Dan Troim, the design draws inspiration from the property’s location between the city and the sea, incorporating warm walnut wood, exposed concrete, naturally finished copper, mashrabiya screens, and marble in sandy and Mediterranean stone tones.
Local artists, manufacturers, and suppliers are incorporated throughout the property, from faucets specially manufactured domestically to art and design pieces found across the hotel.
The hotel lobby also houses the flagship store of Aroogot, an Israeli natural cosmetics brand whose skin-care products are based on natural ingredients grown in fields surrounding the Gaza border communities.
Local wines are offered to guests in the lobby, while breakfast is served on ceramic tableware created by Israeli ceramic artist Adi Nissani.
Breakfast will also be open to the general public, giving Tel Aviv residents a reason to experience the property without staying overnight.
These partnerships form part of The ABY’s broader emphasis on local sourcing and its “minimal waste” philosophy. The approach is intended to incorporate sustainability into the hotel’s everyday operations, from its design choices and collaborations with local manufacturers to its preference for Israeli-made products.
For Tamari, the connection to local creators and businesses is fundamental to the experience the hotel hopes to offer.
“We believe that true hospitality begins with a connection to a place, to the people, culture, art and community around it,” he said. “The ABY is designed to allow guests not only to visit Tel Aviv, but to be part of it, even if just for a moment.”
For the remainder of the year, a two-night weekend stay for two, from Thursday to Saturday, ranges from around NIS 1,600 to NIS 3,000.
My pick is the Garden Room, one of the priciest options but also the most serene, with a plush king-size bed dressed in 400-thread-count Egyptian cotton linens and a private terrace complete with a bathtub.
Rooms are best suited for two guests, although a couple of room categories can accommodate an extra bed for a child.
Coming soon
Some of The ABY’s most interesting features are still to come, with the hotel planning programming intended to bring together visitors and Tel Aviv residents alike.
Among them is a biweekly running club that will depart from the hotel and conclude with cocktails on the rooftop.
In the near future, the property will also organize local art and cultural tours and pay homage to its cinema roots, with plans to host film screenings under the open sky. It’s a fitting connection between the site’s past and what The ABY hopes to become.
Rather than functioning solely as a hotel for visitors, The ABY is positioning itself as a neighborhood hub for locals and travelers alike. After decades of bringing Tel Aviv residents together through film, its next chapter feels closely tied to both that cultural legacy and the continuing revival of Allenby Street.
The writer was a guest of the hotel.
She is an avid traveler, travel writer, and VP of communications at travel tech start-up Faye Travel Insurance. Her travel tips have been featured in The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Fox News, and more. Follow her on Instagram @Gumport.
