It’s a miracle: Natalie Harp has turned Republicans into feminists | Arwa Mahdawi
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:00:03 UTC
21:00:03 KST

Jon Ossoff is quite the miracle worker. Perhaps the Democratic senator can’t turn water into wine, but he has managed to turn whining conservatives into impassioned feminists.
During a rally last Sunday, the Georgia senator delivered a takedown of Donald Trump, which included a reference to his aide Natalie Harp. “He doesn’t want to do the job,” Ossoff said of the president. “He wants to build his ballroom and travel with Natalie on their apparently defenseless flying palace gifted by the Emir of Qatar.”
Those three words – travel with Natalie – were deliberately loaded. Harp was in the spotlight at the time because of the decoy plane story. The 35-year-old was one of a handful of people Trump had taken onto a different plane via a catering truck when he was worried about a potential assassination attack targeting Air Force One. Intrigue as to the exact nature of the relationship between Harp and Trump was heightened by the fact that Melania Trump, the president’s third wife, hadn’t been seen in public for weeks at the time. (Funnily enough, she magically reappeared on Thursday, a few days after Ossoff’s comments, for a press conference where she lovingly held hands with Trump. Very cute.)
Ossoff’s remarks about “Natalie” might have been something of a cheap shot, but it’s hilarious to watch the right discover misogyny and decry the remarks as sexist. Suddenly, everyone from Fox News to prominent conservatives are very worried about a professional woman not being taken seriously.
The former House speaker Newt Gingrich, for example, said on Twitter/X that Ossoff owes Harp an apology. “If a conservative Republican had attacked a liberal Democrat working professional woman the way Ossoff smeared Natalie Harp there would be cries to kick them off the ticket and reject this kind of misogynistic language diminishing and smearing someone who is simply doing their job.”
The conservative commentator Scott Jennings, who is rumoured to be a potential replacement for Karoline Leavitt as White House press secretary, was also appalled. “[Ossoff] unleashed a comment so vile against a young Republican woman working in politics that every woman in this country, no matter your ideology, ought to listen carefully and never forget it,” Jennings said on his podcast.
Meghan McCain also clutched her pearls at the coverage Ossoff’s comments sparked. “The egregious sexist attacks on Natalie Harp are absolutely insane – and they’re coming from prestigious journalists,” she wrote on X. “What is wrong with everyone?! Every president has close aides and sometimes they are females. Like what year is this?!”
It’s 2026, Meghan. And in the year 2026 I think the masses have generally understood that simply criticizing a woman is not in itself misogynistic. I’m not saying there hasn’t been any misogyny in the Harp coverage, but the main reason there has been so much attention on the story is because the White House has had a completely unhinged response to Ossoff’s comments and kept it in the news. More importantly, the reason so many people aren’t taking the Trump aide seriously isn’t because she’s a woman; it’s because she’s not a serious person.
And I’m being diplomatic with that choice of language. After all, we’re talking about someone whose nickname is “the human printer” because, while working on Trump’s re-election campaign, she reportedly ran around after him with a portable printer, handing him hard copies of flattering coverage. You could write that off as a canny career move from someone who understands flattery gets you everywhere with Trump, but that’s also one of the least weird things Harp has done. Per a CNN report, which has pictures of the incident, back in 2023, Harp jumped in the trunk of an SUV because she wanted to be close to Trump and there was no room in his motorcade. Once Trump won re-election and Harp joined him in the White House, she apparently worked for a year without security clearance. According to reporting by MS NOW, she declined to complete the clearance process for unknown reasons.
And then there are the “adoring letters” Harp sent Trump, first mentioned in the book Regime Change, by the New York Times reporters Maggie Haberman and Jonathan Swan. Two were later published in the Daily Beast. “You are all that matters to me,” she wrote in one letter. Other memorable lines included “I want to bring you joy, to feel like we can get through a day without ever having to talk ‘work’”; she also called Trump her “Guardian and Protector in this Life”.
To state the obvious: these are deeply weird things to say to your boss. (It’s also weird that Harp shares Trump’s unconventional approach to capitalization.) I should note that Harp, who says she is a cancer survivor, seems to believe that Trump saved her life by signing legislation that gave her access to experimental bone cancer treatment when she was younger. While that might make her obsession with Trump more understandable, it does not make her general conduct any more professional. So spare me all the lectures from the right about sexism, please. If you’re worried about how women in politics are treated, you should probably focus your attention on the adjudicated sexual abuser who is president.
Donald Trump attacks another female journalist
Trump can’t seem to stand it when a woman doesn’t fawn over him and has a history of attacking female journalists. The latest object of his ire is the CNN reporter Kristen Holmes, who asked the president about Ossoff’s comments regarding Natalie Harp. Trump called Holmes a “loud boisterous person” and instructed her to be “quiet”. Meanwhile, the White House’s social media account posted about Holmes multiple times. In one post they wrote: “Someday, your children will come across your disgusting and inhumane question. They will be sickened and embarrassed to have a parent be so callous and vindictive.”
New York gives parents a ‘night out’
New York mayor Zohran Mamdani hosted the city’s first Parents’ Night Out. The city provided free childcare for nearly 300 kids so parents could have a little time off. This is what “family values” and being pro-life actually look like: supporting parents, not forcing women to give birth.
Sudan’s humanitarian crisis grows, with 200,000 newly displaced people
Increased fighting in the Kordofan region and flooding has made one of the world’s largest displacement crises even worse.
Chanel has made pricey ‘barefoot sandals’ for the well-heeled
Margaret Qualley was spotted stepping out in the sole-less shoes. Somehow I do not think I will be wearing these around the filthy streets of Philadelphia.
‘Heated Rivalry’ author donates $300,000 to rural libraries facing closure
“I had to do it because I don’t know what the point is of being a successful author in Nova Scotia if you’re not going to use it for good,” Rachel Reid told CBC News. Wouldn’t it be nice if Elon Musk thought like that?
Israel launches an ‘investigation’ into killing of Hind Rajab
In January 2024, 335 bullets were fired into a car containing five-year-old Hind and six of her family members in Gaza. When paramedics came to help, they were killed too. IDF vehemently denied responsibility for this atrocity, despite investigations making it obvious that its military was responsible. This week, Israel finally admitted its troops fired into the car and said there would be an investigation. Which is not particularly reassuring: Israel’s investigations into itself rarely result in any sort of accountability. Wesam Hamada, Hind’s mother, is demanding an independent inquiry, which is the least Hind deserves.

Diamonds for sale: lab-grown gem auctions are all over TikTok right now, but some aren’t happy about it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:00:02 UTC
21:00:02 KST

The first time Andrea Greenhill came across a livestream auction for lab-grown diamonds while scrolling on TikTok, she was stunned. While the diamond engagement ring her husband proposed with years ago had cost thousands of dollars, these loose lab-grown diamonds were selling in seconds at a fraction of the price.
“I have two rings that are both natural diamonds and cost a fortune,” she said. I saw the prices they were going for in the auctions, and I was like, “This is insanity.’”
For years, lab-grown diamonds did not have the same cultural cache as natural diamonds, even though the chemical composition of both are the same. Now they are more accepted, and live auctions for lab-grown diamonds that last as little as 10 or 15 seconds have exploded on TikTok in recent weeks, drawing a mix of curious spectators, bargain hunters and new enthusiasts.
Typically, the diamonds are sold on their own at a price point of $100 to $200 a carat, offering consumers a lower barrier to entry than ever before to the diamond market.
“It was only the rich and high class who could afford diamonds, and now they’re accessible to anybody and everybody, and that’s very exciting,” said Kenzie Cisneros, a jeweler and the owner of Diamond Hideout. “There’s a rush in being able to say ‘I bid on this and I got it for a couple hundred bucks.’”
The live streams have become so common on TikTok that they’re easy to find at any hour of the day. Lively auctioneers streaming from places such as Florida, New York and Los Angeles often play the part of the salesperson in shock about what a good deal bidders are getting. Many of the auctions start at just $1. The auctioneers root for bidders, shouting refrains as simple as “go, go, go” as well as chiding them sometimes for not bidding high enough (“chat, we’re too low, we’re too low,” they sometimes say). The effect is a spirited, interactive shopping experience that draws in hundreds of viewers at a time.
The auctions are a thrill even for people who haven’t been as tempted to enter their credit card information on the platform and click the button to make a bid.
Isabella Stolberg, a 21-year-old wardrobe stylist, said that her whole family has gotten into watching the auctions. Sometimes they even project them on a screen in their home for a wider viewing. Stolberg said that she gets drawn in by the instant gratification of people buying a diamond in such a short time frame, often wondering what else the auctioneers will put up for sale.
“There’s this feeling of once it’s gone, it’s gone, and you have that anticipation of what’s coming next – if it’s going to be bigger, if it’s going to be better, even if you’re not directly buying or bidding or consuming it,” she said.
Though Stolberg said she watches the auctions in bed before she goes to sleep, she’s held off from buying any so far.
“It’s become a bit of an addiction, but if I find the right piece that speaks to me, I have a bunch of visions in my head of jewellery that I do want to create for myself – something special,” she said.
Others have purchased more enthusiastically. On the first night that Greenhill stumbled on the auctions, she was so impressed by the offerings that she bought two diamonds. Since then, she’s continued to purchase more loose stones, citing a pink cushion and a blue emerald as among the favorites in her collection. She has bought more than 30 diamonds through TikTok live auctions since early June, she said.
Even when she isn’t bidding on new diamonds, Greenhill has grown attached to watching the streams in the evening, telling her husband “my show is on” as they sit together on the couch. “I’ll be in there cheering people on because I enjoy it. It’s my nightly routine,” she said.
For buyers in the market for a smaller lab-grown diamond, it’s not difficult to find one for $100 or less. Still, the price can obscure the cost of setting them in a piece of high-quality gold or silver jewellery. The price of gold, especially, has fluctuated wildly in the past year and can be several times the cost of the stone.
Most TikTok sellers stick to shipping loose diamonds, though some will work with buyers to find a jeweller that can set the stone in a pendant or a ring. Marie Ann Altuve, a content creator based in New York, has bought two loose diamonds on TikTok auctions, including a heart-shaped diamond for $151.
“My plan is to either go to Chinatown or the diamond district here in New York City to see what can be done with them,” said Altuve.
So far, Greenwell has taken a couple of her diamonds for setting to a local jeweller where she lives in northern Mississippi. She turned a recent purchase of a 3.78-carat lab-grown diamond into a ring. The stone cost about $500 while the 14-karat gold band with white gold prongs cost about $1,100, she revealed in a TikTok video. That’s still a steal, said Greenwell, who got the ring appraised for $5,700.
Most auctioneers show the certification of the lab-grown diamond during the sale to ensure their authenticity. Experienced jewellers, however, caution that the speed of the auctions and fluorescent lighting in the video can hide some of the imperfections of a diamond.
“The certificate doesn’t really tell you the whole story of the diamond,” said Kim Shaul, the owner of Virtue Diamonds, based in Idaho. “If it’s a legit diamond, it could be poorly cut or not have good light performance.”
While there are plenty of reputable sellers on TikTok, consumers don’t always know what to look for, Shaul explained, adding: “You can get some pretty fantastic deals on loose stones, but you might get a really garbage diamond too.”
Cassandra Cadwell, a beauty content creator who discovered the auctions while scrolling on the platform, said she’s not too worried about the quality of the diamonds because of the relatively low price point. When the auctions come across her feed, she keeps an eye out for a particular style.
“If I’m gonna get a lab diamond on TikTok Shop, I want it to be big – give me the big ones,” she said. Cadwell, who is partial to pear-shaped diamonds, said she’s stuck to a formula of not buying something more expensive than $200 per carat to keep her purchases in check. For her, the appeal of the auctions is obvious: “I mean who doesn’t love diamonds, right?”

Inside Coca-Cola’s secretive innovation labs: How the beverage giant wants to automate dirty soda and refreshers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:00:01 UTC
21:00:01 KST

ATLANTA — Coca-Cola is branching out into new customizable drinks and trend-driven equipment as consumers — and food service operators — increasingly want more options.
Tucked away in an anonymous office park not far from its global headquarters here, Coke has been working on a flood of innovation at its secretive labs, including a way for its Freestyle drink dispensers to make dirty sodas, which combine pop with flavored syrups, cream or other ingredients. In partnership with AMC Theatres, it is testing a Micro Matic dispenser that can make brightly colored refreshers. And Coke has more white-label beverage options on the way, like an energy drink that can be customized by color and flavor.
For many restaurants, handcrafted drinks like refreshers or iced coffee have become an important way to drive traffic and sales, even as diners broadly cut their spending. In the second quarter of this year, beverage servings at restaurants outpaced both servings of food alone and food with beverages, according to Circana data. When consumers are away from home, a drink often represents more than hydration, particularly for Generation Z.
"Oftentimes these beverages are an opportunity to take a break, get some energy or protein, have a treat, at a lower price point," David Portalatin, Circana senior vice president and food service industry advisor, told CNBC.
From McDonald's to Wendy's, longtime Coke customers have been expanding their beverage offerings to meet the shift in consumer behavior and boost their profit margins. As operators seek to add more drinks to their menus, Coke must add more convenient beverage options — or risk losing sales to a competitor.
"It's our job to ensure that we're providing unique experiences and beverages because it's not a bonus now with consumers — it's the norm, they expect it," said Megan Tallman, Coke's vice president of dispensed equipment and innovation for its North American business. "When you think about Gen Z, they are okay paying $10 for a drink that is craveable and that they can show on their Instagram or on TikTok, which is helping our customers drive margin and also beverage attachment."
Beyond Freestyle
This July, Coca-Cola's Freestyle drink dispenser celebrated its 17th anniversary.
"Honestly, if you fast forward to today, Freestyle is more relevant today than probably it was over a decade ago," Tallman said, crediting the machine's dozens of flavors.
Even with the variety it offers, Coke is still trying to evolve to keep up.
In the time since the Freestyle was introduced, the number of specialty beverage chains has exploded, offering customers nearly unlimited ways to customize their drinks, from sugar content to toppings. Market research firm Technomic tracks more than 100 different chains, with more than 41,000 locations across the U.S. combined, selling everything from coffee to juice to boba.
Ever since Freestyle began popping up in restaurants and movie theaters, the dispensers have poured more than 67 billion 8-ounce servings of beverages; Coke has been able to track them all, thanks to the equipment's real-time data collection. That data is coming in handy now.
Inside its Equipment Innovation Center in Atlanta, a massive television screen displays real-time data showing what drinks dispensed by the Freestyle are trending, what time of day and where — from the region to the type of business. AHA sparkling water, for example, is trending up at office buildings and hospitals.
Insights from Freestyle dispensers also help the company discover new drinks that it can launch in grocery stores, like the limited-time Coca-Cola Orange Cream, which combines its namesake soda with vanilla and orange syrup.
"If we see that the flavors that we're offering to consumers in food service are actually resonating — it's the largest testing platform out there," Tallman said.
But Coke has more ideas in store.
First is the Freestyle Mini, which initially launched in Europe. Intended for bars and restaurants with limited space, the dispenser holds up to 16 drink options, more than double the choices available in a traditional soda gun. Coke unveiled the new smaller machine at the National Restaurant Association Show in Chicago this spring, but the company has not yet sold it to customers in the U.S.
And then there are other equipment ideas that aren't as far along, inspired by Coke's desire to branch out into dirty soda, refreshers and coffee.
To automate dirty soda, Coke has created a prototype that adds a dairy module to the classic Freestyle dispenser. Utah-based chain Swig takes credit for its invention of the dirty soda, although the trendy drink has now spread far and wide, from KFC restaurants to grocery store shelves.
The trend has helped to change soda's image from a tired, mass-market drink to a handcrafted beverage that can be a treat.
"Gen Z is the first generation raised to believe that nothing you consume is neutral, so everything is either helping you or costing you," said Matthew Greer, food, agribusiness and beverage analyst for Truist. "So, traditional soda does nothing for me, and it gives me 40 grams of sugar, so that fails the test."
The rise of a dirty soda is boon for Coke, because pop is still its number one category. Coke's sparkling soft drinks business, which houses soda brands like Sprite, Schweppes and Fanta, still accounts for 69% of the company's overall unit case volume, even as other ventures like coffee and dairy-based beverages have grown. Coke's namesake soda alone accounted for 47% of global unit case volume and 42% of U.S. unit case volume in 2025, according to a company filing.
Coke's prototypical dispensed dirty soda comes with a preprogrammed recipe, allowing for little customization but eliminating mess. The prototype, which took roughly three weeks to create, keeps the recognizable drip down the sides of the cup, giving the dirty soda its trademark visual appeal.
Refreshing its offerings
Beyond the Freestyle, Coke is also testing Micro Matic "mixology" dispensers to make refreshers and iced coffee drinks.
Starbucks created the refresher back in 2012 to appeal to non-coffee drinkers who wanted a boost, especially in the afternoon, when traffic to its cafes slowed. Customers can pick their bases, flavors and even caffeine level. Refreshers now represent about $2 billion in annual sales for Starbucks.
Other restaurant chains, such as Panera Bread to Dunkin', have taken note. Refreshers can be found on 8.1% of menus at national restaurant chains, according to Datassential.
"It's almost, I think, a compliment, the fact that our Refresher business is being imitated in so many places," Starbucks CEO Brian Niccol said on the company's earnings conference call in late April.
For its part, Coke is hoping to make its mark on the refresher category — whatever that means.
"There's no real definition for what a refresher is, so we're trying to take a stand on what that can be and what function that we believe it should deliver to the guest," said Sarah Kate Sims, director of dispensed innovation for Coca-Cola North America.
To Sims, a refresher is a "healthier" beverage that delivers some kind of pick-me-up without a traditional coffee caffeine base, instead using a green tea or a natural coffee extract as a base. And a refresher must look good, too, she said.
"So that's what I'm working on for next year," Sims said.
Inside 'The Vault'
Coke's innovation efforts aren't restricted to equipment either. Across the parking lot from its Global Equipment Platforms office is "The Vault," where the company tests new drinks.
"We bring a lot of our top customers here to showcase our innovation and mixology, but also to collaborate and problem-solve and tackle the biggest challenges in the business," said Caroline Zambataro, collaboration architect at Coke.
One of those customers is Whataburger. Coke worked with the Texas-based burger chain for about 18 months on its line of "Whatafreshers," which launched in July.
In some cases, consumers might not even realize that they are drinking a Coke product. For example, the company considers itself a "pioneer" of premium lemonade after launching a white-label version more than a decade ago.
More than 40,000 bubbler dispensers carry the drink, according to Tallman. That number includes Wendy's, which sells it under "Dave's Craft Lemonade," after founder Dave Thomas.
These days, lemonade is a popular base for a lot of refreshers and other brightly colored drinks. So, too, is Sprite, which ranked fifth among U.S. carbonated soft drink brands by 2025 sales volume, according to Beverage Digest.
But Coke is also working on a new blank slate for handcrafted beverages: a colorless, relatively unflavored energy drink that comes in frozen or liquid form. The company plans to launch the beverage with food service operators in the first half of 2027.
Energy drinks are a much smaller category than sparkling beverages, but the segment has the highest expected growth projections for the next 10 years, according to Tallman.
"We believe this solution really meets many consumers because more female consumers are interested in energy if it's a handcrafted solution," Tallman said.
Starting with Celsius, the conversation around energy drinks has changed, widening their audience and the number of occasions where they can be consumed, Truist's Greer said. Rather than a beverage that you buy at the gas station for a pick-me-up, now energy drinks can become a part of some consumers' workout routines.
Coke's take on energy drinks will be designed to be served by employees to "limit consumption," according to Tallman. A 12-ounce serving of Coke's version contains 106 milligrams of caffeine, roughly the same amount as the same size can of Red Bull and half of the caffeine content of a Celsius can. Excessive caffeine consumption has become a liability concern after Panera Bread's Charged Lemonade was named in at least two wrongful death lawsuits.
A golden opportunity
Broadly, Coke has been fielding more inquiries from food service partners these days about customizable drinks, according to Melinda Pritchett, director of innovation for Coke's North American business.
"If you're looking at what McDonald's is doing with the handcrafted beverages, all of our customers are saying, 'We should be in that as well,'" she said.
As the largest U.S. restaurant chain by system sales, McDonald's playbook is often replicated elsewhere. In May, the fast-food giant expanded its McCafe menu in the U.S. to include refreshers and crafted sodas, including Coke's Sprite and Hi-C, as part of its broader strategy to lean into beverages.
"In the U.S., [drink] sales are ahead of plan. Guest checks are higher, and we're seeing new occasions emerge throughout the day," McDonald's CEO Chris Kempczinski said on the company's earnings conference call earlier in August. "We've also seen strong food attachment rates on these orders."
But the drink launch arrived during what was otherwise a lackluster quarter for McDonald's U.S. business, which reported same-store sales growth of just 0.8%. The company has replaced its U.S. president in the hopes of accelerating its domestic division.
On Monday, McDonald's further expanded its beverage options with the Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer. Red Bull is privately owned, with no connection to Coke. The chain's choice to partner with a competitor rather than using an energy drink affiliated with Coke, like Monster, has sparked speculation about the state of the companies' more than 70-year-long relationship.
"We have a fantastic and very long-standing partnership with McDonald's, and that's intact, right? We continue to be very happy with that partnership," Coke CEO Henrique Braun said on the company's earnings conference call in late April, answering an analyst question about the partnership. "… We do respect the decisions on other choices about their relationships with other companies."
Ultimately, the most important part of any business relationship is the effect on sales.
When testing a new beverage with a food service partner, Coke tracks a couple of different performance metrics, like "incremental volume." In other words, would a customer buy one of the new refreshers even if they wouldn't otherwise buy a drink?
A survey of several dozen U.S. McDonald's franchisees conducted by Kalinowski Equity Research found that more than half of operators said the specialty drinks are performing in line with their expectations.
"They are selling great, but most of it is a trade-off from other beverages," one anonymous franchisee said in the survey. "Not many new transaction counts."

US golfers and ‘coolcations’ push Up Scottish vacation prices
- Hotel prices in rural Scotland rose 9.2 per cent to over £167 (S$289) per night, driven by strong demand from US golfers and British tourists seeking cooler "coolcations".
- Scotland’s attractions like golf, whisky, castles, and improved airport links are drawing more American visitors, boosted by celebrity endorsements such as LeBron James.
- Booking patterns have shifted with shorter lead times, and the broader UK hospitality sector has benefited from the rise in demand for cooler domestic holiday spots like Scotland.
AI generated
Hotel rooms in rural Scotland have surged in price over the summer, the latest sign of growing interest from American tourists and domestic travellers seeking “coolcations”.
The average daily rate of a hotel room there rose 9.2 per cent in the three months through July from 2025. according to data from CoStar Group. That is the fastest growth of any rural British holiday destination.
The cost of a night’s stay there climbed to above £167 (S$289) in July, making it by far the UK’s priciest rural location of the regions analysed.
The data show how Scotland is benefiting from a surge in interest from travellers at home and abroad. The country’s historic golf courses, whisky, castles and lochs are drawing US visitors, helped by better airport connections.
Meanwhile, British tourists seeking cooler domestic breaks, or “coolcations”, to avoid the heatwaves in parts of England are also driving demand.
“You are seeing people choosing to come to somewhere that gives them the same kind of experience at the seaside and rural coastal locations, but without the intense heat that you’re getting in the south of the country or southern Europe,” said Kate Nicholls, chief executive officer of lobby group UK Hospitality.
Celebrity endorsements are also boosting tourism in Scotland. Basketball star LeBron James recently hailed it as “God’s country” after a golfing trip to a 400-year-old castle in the Highlands.
Phil Scott, managing director of Links House at Royal Dornoch, a five-star boutique hotel in the Highlands popular with American golfers, said it was experiencing the highest occupancy in his seven years at the property.
Trips to the region, he said, are resonating with tourists seeking a “little bit more of an escape” from higher temperatures farther south.
Elsewhere, to the southwest of Scotland, the five-star Knockinaam Lodge hotel in Dumfries and Galloway suffered an “incredibly difficult year” in 2025 when it generated little profit, according to general manager Callum McCann.
“But this year has been totally different,” he said in an interview. “We’ve had a lot more bookings.”
People are leaving it much later to book, with lead times falling to two weeks this summer from roughly two months previously, McCann said.
The broader British hospitality industry has thrived this summer. Strong performances from the accommodation and amusement and recreation sectors were among the reasons why the UK economy grew unexpectedly in June.
The increase in “coolcations” is a factor in the rising demand for destinations like Scotland, said Cristina Balekjian, CoStar’s senior director of UK hospitality analytics. Hotels in Edinburgh and Glasgow have also performed well in recent years, she added.
“It definitely doesn’t take away from the fact that people will still want the sun and sea and beaches and everything,” she said. “But it’s definitely the trend that more people are gravitating towards these cooler destinations as well, and in Scotland, for example.” BLOOMBERG

NATO weighs allied support for Strait of Hormuz navigation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:58:56 UTC
20:58:56 KST

NATO's top military commander convened senior defense officials from allied countries this week to discuss possible contributions to keeping the Strait of Hormuz open, but the alliance stressed that it is not planning a NATO military mission in the strategic waterway.
U.S. Air Force Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, NATO's Supreme Allied Commander Europe, hosted a videoconference Wednesday with defense chiefs from interested allied countries to explore ways they could support freedom of navigation in the strait, a spokesperson told Reuters on Friday.
“Given NATO's unique strengths in its ability to bring together Allies and understand the capabilities they bring to bear, it makes sense for NATO to facilitate in this way,” the spokesperson said, while emphasizing that the effort was not a NATO mission.
The discussions come as NATO members seek to avoid direct involvement in the nearly six-month-old conflict between Iran, the United States and Israel while preparing for a possible effort to restore commercial shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The narrow waterway, which connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman, is one of the world's most important energy routes. Before the conflict disrupted shipping, roughly one-fifth of globally traded oil passed through the strait.
France and Britain have been leading efforts to assemble a coalition of about a dozen countries to help guarantee safe passage once tensions ease or the conflict ends. Any lasting arrangement, however, would ultimately depend on Iran allowing international shipping to resume freely.
The NATO discussions came as tensions between Washington and Tehran showed no sign of easing.
Iran warned Friday that any new U.S. threats would trigger a “devastating” response after Washington said it planned to impose some of the toughest financial penalties in its history in an effort to pressure Iran's leadership.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said he would provide details of the new sanctions Monday. President Donald Trump has warned that countries providing “any type of lifeline to Iran” could face economic consequences.
Iran's Armed Forces chief of staff, Maj. Gen. Ali Abdollahi, said Tehran was prepared to respond across multiple domains.
“With preparedness across land, sea, air, air defense and cyberspace, Iran's armed forces will respond to the enemy's new threats with crushing, punishing and devastating responses,” Iranian media quoted him as saying.
The exchange of threats comes as both sides continue to claim momentum in a war that has killed thousands of people, damaged Iran's economy and military capabilities, drawn in other countries in the Gulf region and pushed global energy prices higher.
Although U.S. strikes have significantly weakened Iran's conventional forces and economy, Tehran retains missiles and drones capable of threatening oil tankers and regional infrastructure.
Trump has also yet to achieve several of the objectives he outlined when the conflict began, including dismantling Iran's nuclear program and creating conditions for Iranians to overthrow the country's clerical leadership.
The war has contributed to higher gasoline prices in the United States and has weighed on Trump's political standing. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released this week showed his approval rating at its lowest level of his current term.
Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf, who has been involved in mediated negotiations with Washington, said the United States appeared to have concluded that it could not prevail through direct military confrontation.
“We must make plans to deal with the unjust sanctions so that we can overcome them,” Qalibaf said in neighboring Iraq.
But he also acknowledged the growing pressure on Iran's economy.
“No matter how much military power we have, we won't survive if people are hungry and we don't have financial turnover, economic growth and national production,” he told Iranian and Iraqi businesspeople Thursday, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
Oil prices rose Friday after Washington threatened sanctions against Iran's trading partners, raising concerns that tighter restrictions could further reduce supplies in the global market.
Bessent told CNBC that he would outline the new measures Monday and said the administration intended to “collapse this regime.”
Iran has lived under extensive international sanctions for nearly five decades, but the latest pressure comes as the country struggles with high inflation, a weakening currency, energy shortages and infrastructure damage.
The consequences could extend well beyond Iran.
Bessent said China obtains about half of its energy from the Gulf and should cooperate with Washington's pressure campaign. China buys more than 80% of Iran's seaborne oil, according to 2025 data from analytics firm Kpler.
Beijing has pushed back against the sanctions threat. China's embassy in Washington said sanctions and pressure would not resolve the crisis and called for diplomacy.
The conflict also poses serious risks to U.S. allies in the Gulf, where Iranian attacks have targeted energy facilities and desalination plants that provide drinking water.
The United States and Iran have twice announced ceasefire agreements, in April and June, aimed in part at restoring the movement of commercial vessels through Hormuz. Iran and Oman, which sits across the narrow waterway, have also held separate talks focused on reopening navigation.
Washington, however, has opposed any agreement that would require ships to pay a toll.

Flights disrupted at southern France airport after critical weather system fails

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
Air traffic at Marseille Provence Airport in southern France was disrupted Saturday due to a failure of a critical weather system used to provide atmospheric pressure data to aircraft, BFM TV reported.
The failure was detected at around 6 am local time (0400 GMT) at the airport in Marignane, near Marseille, according to airport authorities.
The system is considered “critical and vital” for aircraft landings and, depending on the aircraft and airline, departures, an airport spokesperson told Actu Marseille.
The cause of the failure was not immediately known.
The airport said operations had been gradually returning to normal since around 10 am local time (0800 GMT) and advised passengers to follow updates from their airlines.
Of 35 flights scheduled to depart between 6 am and 10 am, 21 were able to take off, although with delays, according to an airport spokesperson.
Fourteen flights were still awaiting departure at around 11 am local time (0900 GMT), France 3 reported.
Some flights scheduled to land in Marseille were diverted to Nice and Montpellier. An Air France flight from Paris Charles de Gaulle and another flight from Nantes were canceled.

No more boarding pass stamps: New immigration rule for international flyers from Sept 1

No more boarding pass stamps: New immigration rule for international flyers from Sept 1
Edited by: Pranjal Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 22, 2026, 17:25 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
International travelers will soon need e-boarding passes on smartphones for immigration clearance. Physical boarding passes will no longer be stamped by immigration authorities from September one. This change aims to streamline the process and reduce passenger inconvenience. A pilot project is also underway to eliminate immigration stamping for Indian passport holders. The Bureau of Immigration is implementing these modernization efforts across airports.
Passengers travelling abroad will reportedly need an e-boarding pass on their smartphones for immigration clearance from September one, as immigration authorities plan to replace the physical boarding pass, officials said.The decision was taken after the Bureau of Immigration (BOI) under the ministry of home affairs (MHA) found that the physical stamping of boarding passes, required for immigration, was inconvenient for passengers."The matter has been examined by the BOI and it has now been decided to do away with the mandatory requirement of physical boarding passes and the stamping of boarding passes at immigration counters at all international airports in the country", according to officials who spoke to PTI.“Improper or incorrect” stamping also led to errors in reading boarding passes, prompting the decision to do away with this procedure, they added.However, while physical boarding passes will continue to be accepted, they will not be stamped by the immigration authorities from September 1.
Security officials said international travellers were also no longer having their boarding passes stamped by the Central Industrial Security Force (CISF) during individual frisking. The passes were instead required to be produced only for clearance by immigration authorities.
Notably, CISF had stopped stamping boarding passes for both domestic and international passengers several years ago.According to the officials, a pilot project is also underway to eliminate the stamping of immigration entry and exit for Indian passport holders. The process is expected to be implemented across Indian airports soon after the pilot exercise is complete.

Even if the government wishes to conduct the two-tier exam, including mains, for BPSC, they should do it from TRE-5 because aspirants have already lost too much time,” student leader Dileep Kumar told PTI on Thursday.He also demanded the withdrawal of the 25 per cent bonus weightage given to existing contractual employees in BSSC exams, calling it an “unfair advantage to contractual employees”.Protesters have warned of further escalation. One of the protesting groups said it would gherao the Bihar chief minister's official residence on August 25 if the government failed to hold a meaningful dialogue by August 24.TRE-4 protesters have also threatened to call a Bihar bandh if their demands are not considered.

Victim of sword attack at a Swedish school was a 17-year-old girl
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:53:02 UTC
20:53:02 KST

Student killed in sword attack at a Swedish school was a 17-year-old girl
STOCKHOLM (AP) — The victim of a deadly sword attack at a school in central Sweden was a 17-year-old girl, police said Saturday.
An 18-year-old man armed with a sword carried out the attack at the Brinell School in Fagersta, northwest of Stockholm, while classes were in session on Friday. One person was killed and three others were wounded, two of them severely.
Police said the suspect had been arrested and that the case was being investigated as murder and attempted murder. The police said they have no reason to believe there were more perpetrators.
Vastmanland County, where the town is located, said that the two seriously injured boys were ages 12 and 17. A third person, also under 18, was slightly injured and has been discharged from a hospital, Swedish news agency TT reported.
The school principal told local media P4 Västmanland on Saturday that the attacker was a student at the school.
The police said they fired shots during its action on Friday but the attacker was not hit.
On Saturday morning, around 70 people gathered at the memorial site that the municipality prepared, carrying flowers and lighting candles, TT reported.
Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, who visited the site on Saturday, expressed solidarity with the families affected by the attack and with those impacted by previous school attacks in Sweden.
“What must never happen has happened again,” Kristersson said.
Kristersson was joined in Fagersta by Magdalena Andersson, leader of the main opposition Social Democrats. With Sweden’s parliamentary election due in September, political parties suspended campaign events on Saturday. Kristersson also invited all party leaders to a meeting to discuss the progress of the investigation.
There was no official information on the attacker’s possible motive.
Sweden’s national police said that investigators have already carried out two house searches in connection with the suspect. Many witnesses were expected to be interviewed as part of the investigation.
The region went into a state of emergency on Friday, but it had ended by Saturday.
Sweden has seen a series of violent school attacks over the years.
Last year, 11 people, including the gunman, died after an attack at an education center in Örebro in central Sweden, leading the government to propose tougher gun laws. It’s considered to be the worst mass shooting in the country’s history.
In 2022, an 18-year-old man attacked two female teachers with a knife and an ax in a school in Malmo, killing them.
In 2015, a 21-year-old local man rampaged through a school in the southern industrial city of Trollhattan, stabbing three people to death before being fatally shot by police. Authorities called it a racist hate crime, saying he methodically selected dark-skinned victims at Trollhattan’s Kronan school, where most students are foreign-born.

Europe’s Gray Zone of Non-Peace:
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:52:00 UTC
20:52:00 KST

As NATO’s eastern flank prepares for a potential conflict, defense can no longer be reduced to weapons, soldiers and shelters. States are increasingly turning toward a model of comprehensive defense, in which civilian institutions, local governments and ordinary citizens all play a role in national resilience. Kyiv Post spoke with Dr. Weronika Grzebalska, a sociologist at the Institute of Political Studies of the Polish Academy of Sciences and editor of the Batory Foundation report on women in Poland’s comprehensive defense, about resilience, preparedness and the changing role of society in times of crisis.
Michał Kujawski: On NATO’s eastern flank, defense is the number one issue, particularly when it comes to weapons and, more recently, shelters. But it seems that this is not the whole picture.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Weronika Grzebalska: No, it is not. But from the first years of the war, starting in 2014, Poland really did focus on modernizing the military arm of its defense. Defense spending was increased, the Territorial Defense Forces (WOT) were established, and weapons have been modernized.
Societies have a sense that they pay taxes and see military equipment being purchased, and as a result they believe there is some professional army that will defend them. Do we forget that it is the entire country that has to be defended, and that war is not simply a brief interruption of normal life?
Poland Officially Confirms Russian Kh-101 Missile Crashed on Its Territory
The initial rebuilding of mainly hard power eventually began to change and diversify. Work started on strengthening population protection and societal resilience within the framework of comprehensive defense, sometimes referred to as total defense. Decades of relative peace after joining NATO caused people to detach themselves from security. Conscription was suspended, among other things. This even happened in Sweden, which had been something of a poster child for total defense. After the Cold War, its system was also rolled back to some extent. Finland was the main exception, with Estonia also retaining some elements.
Did we experience a brief end of history?
We all believed that Europe was “prosperous, secure and free.” Armies became professionalized and increasingly took on an expeditionary character. The assumption was that the role of society was to pay taxes and support military spending, rather than participate directly in security. All of this led to the expectation that security was the responsibility of “some services,” rather than us as citizens. This applies across the West.
Perhaps societies that are relatively affluent, bourgeois and consumer-oriented are paralyzed by the very word “war”?
Prosperity, democratization and progress lead societies more toward self-realization and emancipatory values. We have seen this across Europe.
I have the impression that Western societies, after seeing millions of refugees in 2022 – mostly women, children and elderly people – and seeing the front line, tend to assume that all men of military age are going to the front. There are many volunteers, many mobilized soldiers, and also people who want to avoid military service without leaving the country. But war and fighting are not limited to the front. They also affect the economy and demography. What does defense actually look like?
Perceptions of war, particularly in countries such as Poland, are primarily shaped by the memory of the Second World War, as conveyed both through family stories and popular culture. This creates an image of war as purely a kinetic, military conflict involving the literal occupation of an entire country. Images from Bucha and the waves of refugees seen by Western societies have only reinforced this perception.
And then those same people see parties in Kyiv and Odesa on social media and are surprised. They cannot understand that during a brutal war, and in between missile and drone attacks, people also lead ordinary lives. Sometimes this even results in denial.
Societies do not fully understand that we are already in a state of non-peace. This is where we encounter what we might call the paradox of resilience: the more resilient our institutions are, and the more effectively they sustain cyberattacks, hybrid operations or acts of sabotage without people being killed, the weaker our sense of the reality of war can paradoxically become. On the one hand, we expect resilience; on the other, the seriousness of the threat becomes increasingly abstract.
Have cyberattacks and other hostile activities become commonplace? Have we simply become accustomed to them?
Yes. This is one reason why it is difficult to understand some aspects of the war in Ukraine, where everyone comes into contact with the reality of war. In a country like Poland, that is in a gray zone state of non-peace, it is more difficult for people to fully internalize the threat and understand what it looks like. Many people ask themselves how, in a situation of undeclared warfare, democratic elections and the logic of election campaigns, we can build wide-scale defense awareness and engagement. There is no immediate threat in the conventional sense. The only answer is to convince society and seek public support.
So we need to make society aware that resilience has many dimensions – from going to work and keeping the economy functioning to resisting disinformation or putting on a uniform?
Exactly. We are building resilience as we go. Take Poland, for example. There is no fully integrated system yet, but there are areas that function effectively. One of them is the Territorial Defense Forces, which serve as a kind of link between society and the military. Thanks to the WOT, the state and national defense have become tangible for people – for example, during various natural disasters, floods and the Covid-19 pandemic.
There is also significant progress in strengthening the resilience of state institutions to threats – procedures, resources and so on. Poland is also energetically laying the foundations for a system of civil protection and civil defense which, following the Swedish model, is based on local governments. Local authorities are in turn required to cooperate with other social actors, services and institutions.
Institutionalizing cooperation at the local level is fundamental. Poland’s comprehensive defense recently came under test during the wave of refugees from Ukraine in 2022 and the 2023 flood. The problem is that nobody had ever practiced this cooperation on such a scale. In such situations, people may be afraid to make decisions or may not know exactly what their responsibilities are. But that is understandable – crises have their own logic.
That is difficult in a situation where peacetime law remains in force. Not everything can be tested.
Yes, but Poland, Sweden, the Netherlands and other countries have begun working on preparedness. In Poland, for example, a crisis manual was distributed to every citizen. There are also various campaigns and training programs for civilians, organized by the MOD as well as Ministry of Interior in cooperation with NGOs such as the volunteer fire service or the Red Cross.
Such initiatives mobilize people who are not attracted to the military. Interestingly, women accounted for 70 percent of participants in the recent Polish Red Cross training programs.
This brings me to my next question. When we look at popular culture, we see war as something in which men participate. Mobilization and conscription apply to men. War is portrayed as a male occupation. At the same time, many armies have large numbers of women, including in professional military service. Around 37,000 women serve in the Polish Armed Forces. In the Territorial Defense Forces, women make up around 21 percent of personnel. So is the military and national defense really something only for men, or is that no longer the case?
In Poland, we are building comprehensive defense, and the defense system is undergoing a transformation. This requires the involvement of civilian institutions and civilians themselves. The social contract between citizens and the state is also changing.
The division of roles into male protectors and female objects of protection is being reconsidered as well, because total defense is broadening defense beyond a male obligation into a whole-of-society endeavor. This is particularly visible in Scandinavian countries that introduced gender-neutral conscription.
So what is the role of women in resilience and national defense?
We certainly need different people with different skills. I am not talking only about the military, but about society as a whole. The military is not a solution to every problem. We need different paths to mobilization – both military and civilian. I mean medical, humanitarian, cyber and other areas.
As for women, in Poland they constitute the majority of sectors responsible for societal resilience. This is clearly visible in areas such as healthcare, volunteering and humanitarian work, social assistance and local administration.
Should this ultimately lead to a situation where, when there is a genuine threat – not only a military one, but perhaps a natural disaster – everyone performs tasks according to their own skills and competencies?
That is what it should lead to. The mistaken assumption that defense is limited to the armed forces still persists in parts of the society. However, there is growing awareness that we need a single, integrated system for registering defense resources, not only military ones.
A comprehensive defense system must also rely on civilian actors, including businesses and NGOs. Civilian women have an enormous role to play there, although contrary to what some might think, defense mobilization of women is nothing new. History shows this clearly. Female camp followers in Napoleon’s army were responsible for vital support, while when men in Britain went off to fight during the Second World War, women replaced them in factories.
What is new, and what we argue in our report, is the need to formally recognize and institutionalize these feminized, civilian actors within the defense system, granting them representation and resources. What matters is that different civilian sectors become an integral part of the overall system. We need to institutionalize whole-of-society defense and resilience.

12 killed as wrong-way driving alarms England, Ireland
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:51:52 UTC
20:51:52 KST

Twelve people have been killed in less than a week in separate wrong-way driving crashes in England and Ireland, intensifying concerns over a dangerous trend in which motorists deliberately drive against traffic and, in some cases, record the stunts for social media.
Seven people, including two police officers, died early Saturday when a Volkswagen Passat traveling the wrong way on the A66 near South Bank in Middlesbrough, northeastern England, collided head-on with a marked Cleveland Police vehicle.
The crash happened at about 3:39 a.m. local time after officers had been pursuing a suspicious vehicle. The Passat, traveling against the flow of traffic, struck the police car, killing the two officers inside and five people in the Volkswagen.
All seven victims died at the scene.
Emergency crews sent 14 ambulance resources, a specialist paramedic team, a hazardous area response team and a doctor from the Great North Air Ambulance Service to the crash site.
The Independent Office for Police Conduct launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the collision, including the police pursuit.
The A66 was closed in both directions between Normanby Road and Church Lane in Eston as investigators examined the scene.
The deaths came less than a week after a separate wrong-way crash in Ireland killed five teenagers and seriously injured four other people.
On Aug. 16, a black BMW traveling the wrong way on the northbound M9 motorway near Moone in County Kildare, west of Dublin, collided head-on with a Hyundai.
Five teenagers in the BMW died. They were identified locally as Kamil Pustkowski, 17, of Limerick; Joey "Joe" Carthy, 15, of Athy, County Kildare; Alex McCarthy, 17, of Carlow; Jack Kennedy, 17, of Athy; and Jeremy O'Brien, 18, of Carlow.
Four people traveling in the Hyundai, including a 7-year-old boy, were seriously injured. The group included three women from the same family who were traveling toward Dublin Airport for a family wedding in Britain. Two of the women were reported to be in critical condition.
Garda Siochána, Ireland's national police force, determined that the BMW had been linked to suspected break-ins or burglaries in the Carlow and Athy areas earlier that night. Gardai had attempted to stop the vehicle after it was reported to have been involved in the incidents, but it failed to stop.
Investigators believe the BMW traveled the wrong way on the M9 more than once. Gardai had prepared measures, including stinger devices, near an exit ramp, but the vehicle continued before the fatal collision.
Police were not pursuing the BMW at the moment of impact. Garda policy generally prohibits officers from chasing vehicles traveling against traffic on a motorway because of the extreme danger posed to other motorists.
The Garda investigation has also examined social media activity connected to some of the teenagers. Authorities said some of those involved had previously posted or been linked to videos showing reckless driving, including wrong-way driving.
The M9 crash was not an isolated incident.
A week earlier, on Aug. 9, a stolen vehicle carrying eight teenagers was driven the wrong way, including down an entrance ramp, on Dublin's M50 motorway near Junction 12 at Firhouse. The vehicle collided with another car, injuring all nine people involved. One of the teenagers suffered critical injuries.
Authorities have increasingly pointed to social media as a factor in a series of dangerous driving incidents involving young people.
Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly described the M9 crash as "horrific" and said the behavior was even more disturbing because some drivers appeared to be committing the offenses for social media attention.
He also linked the crash to the recent M50 collision and warned that driving against traffic on a motorway can have devastating consequences.
Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said there could be "no tolerance" for the reckless behavior, describing wrong-way motorway driving as an irresponsible and dangerous act that must stop.
Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan condemned what he called "outrageously dangerous criminal behaviour" and said the government was considering whether wrong-way motorway driving should become a specific offense.
Irish authorities have described a pattern involving groups of predominantly teenage males stealing vehicles, driving them recklessly and sometimes deliberately entering motorways in the wrong direction after failing to stop for police.
Some of the activity has been filmed and shared on platforms such as TikTok, with videos showing high-speed driving, damaged ignition systems, police encounters and other dangerous behavior.
Police have also raised concerns that offenders understand the limitations placed on officers during motorway pursuits. Gardai generally cannot pursue a vehicle traveling against traffic because doing so could put innocent motorists at even greater risk.
The Garda Representative Association has called for improved training for officers dealing with motorists who refuse to stop, while Ireland's media regulator, Coimisiún na Meán, and an Oireachtas committee have sought explanations from TikTok about content that may glorify illegal and dangerous driving.
TikTok has said it removes content that violates its rules and is monitoring material connected to the incidents.
Wrong-way crashes are among the most dangerous collisions on high-speed roads because vehicles can approach each other at extremely high closing speeds, leaving drivers little or no time to react.
Wrong-way driving can occur because of impairment, confusion or mistakes, but Irish authorities are increasingly concerned about cases in which drivers appear to enter opposing lanes deliberately and record the behavior for online attention.
The A66 crash in England has raised a separate set of questions about police pursuits and the risks officers face when a suspect vehicle begins traveling against traffic.

Russia struck Kyiv and Boryspil, its main airport hub, twice in 24 hours with ballistics Ukraine can’t stop without US Patriots, days before Independence Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:51:42 UTC
20:51:42 KST

Russia has struck Kyiv and its suburbs with ballistic missiles for a second consecutive day, killing civilians. Meanwhile, Ukraine lacks enough interceptors to stop them because deliveries from the US have halted.
The strikes land at a moment when Ukraine's ability to shoot ballistic missiles down has been cut off at the source. Ukraine intercepts ballistic missiles mainly with US-made Patriot systems. During the recent Oval Office meeting, President Donald Trump declined President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's request for hundreds of additional Patriot interceptors, according to the Financial Times.
At the same time, when Ukraine sought to destroy Russia's ballistic launchers on Russian territory, US billionaire Elon Musk did not allow Ukraine to use Starlink to guide strikes on those launchers, The Atlantic reported. Ukraine can neither shoot the missiles down at the rate it needs nor freely strike the launchers that fire them.
A railway worker was killed in Kyiv
The overnight attack hit Ukraine's railway. On the night of 22 August, a Russian ballistic missile struck a railway enterprise in Kyiv's Darnytsia area, killing a Ukrzaliznytsia worker, the railway's board chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said.
He described a strike timed to the threat.
"In Darnytsia, ballistic strikes hit one of the railway enterprises, at the same moment as, or even a second before, the ballistic threat appeared. One of our workers, a foreman, was killed on the spot. The rest we managed to evacuate quickly after the first strike," Pertsovskyi reported.
Russia launched about six ballistic missiles, with launches recorded from three directions, Kursk, Bryansk, and Millerovo, according to monitoring channels.
A morning strike on Boryspil killed two civilians
Russia struck again in daylight. In the morning, six to eight ballistic missiles attacked the Boryspil area in the Kyiv agglomeration, likely with cluster warheads, according to monitoring channels. Boryspil city is home to the Boryspil International Airport, Ukraine’s main and largest international passenger airport.
The strike killed civilians and hit infrastructure. Two civilians, a man and a woman, were killed, and the number of wounded rose to eight, including a child, with the daytime strike hitting a truck parking lot along with warehouses, a fuel station, a private household, and vehicles. Two trucks caught fire, and a blaze spread across 700 square meters of open ground, the State Emergency Service (DSNS) said.
The strikes come days before Independence Day
The attacks landed two days before Ukraine marks its Independence Day. The Security Service (SBU) has already urged citizens to be especially vigilant before and during the 24 August holiday because of the threat of attacks, warning that in wartime, Russia may use mass events for strikes, provocations, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other crimes.
The service has also warned against recruitment. It reminded Ukrainians not to publish photos or videos of military objects, critical infrastructure, checkpoints, or air-defense systems, nor to share information on the consequences of strikes or the movement of Ukrainian forces.
Russian special services may try to recruit Ukrainians to prepare attacks and sabotage, the SBU said, urging anyone offered money for arson, property damage, planting unknown objects, or collecting information on military sites to report it immediately.

Myanmar military airstrike kills 14 at Buddhist monastery: reports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:49:00 UTC
20:49:00 KST

Myanmar airstrike kills 14 at Buddhist monastery: reports
August 22, 2026
At least 14 people were killed when a military airstrike hit a Buddhist monastery in Myanmar's central Sagaing region, an opposition group and local witnesses said Saturday.
Friday's attack, by the ruling military regime that seized power in a 2021 coup, is the latest deadly assault on pro-democracy forces in the Southeast Asian country's ongoing civil war.
What do we know about the airstrike on the monastery in Myanmar?
The strike happened in Swel Le Oh village, Myaung township, in central Myanmar, said Nway Oo, a spokesman for an anti-government resistance group.
The village is about 75 kilometers (45 miles) west of Mandalay, the country's second largest city.
Nway Oo, from the Civil Defense and Security Organization of Myaung Township, or CDSOM, said the dead included three women and that 20 others were wounded.
The Associated Press spoke to a villager who confirmed the death toll and said that a military jet dropped two bombs 15 minutes apart.
The villager said the second strike damaged a nearby house.
Victims were civilians attending a retreat
More than 100 people were taking part in a weeklong meditation retreat to mark Buddhist Lent, the villager added.
AFP news agency cited Nway Oo Myaung, a pro-democracy rebel, as saying: "It wasn't a mistaken target; they intentionally attacked a monastery."
The military government has yet to confirm the strike.
Myanmar's military has often used airstrikes to counter opposition forces, especially in Sagaing region, a stronghold of armed resistance.
UN flags sharp rise in airstrikes
A United Nations investigation team said last week it had observed a notable increase in aerial attacks over much of the past year.
The UN's Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM) accused the military-backed government of "indiscriminate and intentional aerial attacks against civilians."
Last month, conflict monitoring group ACLED accused the regime of adopting "a terror strategy" that it said focuses on "civilian infrastructure and social gatherings, such as weddings and religious festivals, to maximize psychological impact."
Myanmar government defends strikes
On Sunday, Myanmar’s foreign ministry rejected the IIMM report, insisting that its operations were in response to insurgents and terrorist groups.
The ministry said it uses maximum restraint to avoid civilian harm.
Myanmar's army took power from the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi in February 2021.
Suu Kyi, a Nobel Peace Prize laureate, was detained and sentenced to lengthy prison terms on multiple charges widely viewed as politically motivated. She was moved to house arrest in May.
After a brutal crackdown on peaceful demonstrations, many opponents of military rule armed themselves and plunged large parts of the country into conflict.
More than 100,000 people are estimated to have been killed on all sides over the past five years, according to ACLED.
Myanmar held elections this year, which were widely condemned as a sham.
The polls culminated in the chief of the former junta, General Min Aung Hlaing, being appointed president, as the military regime sought to present itself as a civilian government.

Trump’s ‘peacemaker’ promise faces growing test as Iran war drags on
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:46:00 UTC
20:46:00 KST

With the Iran war now locked in a costly standoff and conflicts from Ukraine to Gaza still unresolved, President Donald Trump's ambitious foreign policy agenda appears increasingly stalled as he heads toward November's midterm elections.
The setbacks are striking for a president who returned to office last year promising to be a "peacemaker" and made resolving international conflicts a central pillar of his second-term agenda.
Trump has grown increasingly impatient with questions from reporters and criticism from U.S. allies. This week, he lashed out at journalists pressing him about his foreign policy record and renewed his threat to bomb Oman, a U.S. ally involved in negotiations with Iran over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Labor Day, which falls on Sept. 7 this year, traditionally marks the point when U.S. election campaigns accelerate. Republicans now face the prospect that unresolved conflicts abroad, along with their economic consequences at home, could threaten the party's hold on Congress.
Trump has called off talks with Tehran after pushing for weeks for a diplomatic solution and announced Wednesday a new campaign of "economic warfare" against the Islamic Republic, in an apparent acknowledgment that months of military attacks have not forced the concessions the U.S. wants to see.
As inflation persists and the Iran war drives up gasoline prices, Trump's approval rating has fallen to another low point, with just 33% of Americans in the latest Reuters/Ipsos poll approving of his performance.
Other efforts to broker peace have also stalled.
On Monday, Trump's negotiator and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, left empty-handed from talks aimed at advancing a Gaza peace deal. An expected visit to Kyiv by Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff to revive long-stalled negotiations to end Russia's war in Ukraine has yet to happen.
After a string of early foreign policy achievements, including a Gaza ceasefire and the capture of Venezuela's leader, Trump's record has become increasingly defined by stalled diplomatic efforts.
"Trump has successfully challenged and disrupted the comfortable foreign policy consensus in Washington, but has not translated that disruption into a strategy with deliverables for Americans," said Asli Aydintasbas, a fellow at the Brookings Institution in Washington.
The conflict with Iran has weighed "intensely" on the president, and there is no consensus inside the White House on how to resolve it, one Trump ally said on condition of anonymity.
The pressure could increase if investors conclude the war will drag on, driving up U.S. borrowing costs and further constraining Trump's domestic agenda. Trump has said the economic costs are worth it to ensure Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon, despite Iran's denials that it seeks one.
"President Trump has successfully made America respected again, and the results speak for themselves: Nine wars have ended, hostages have been freed from Gaza, trade deals are fairer, and now, Iran will be prevented from ever possessing a nuclear weapon," said White House spokesperson Anna Kelly.
A senior Trump administration official said U.S. sanctions and a naval blockade had crippled Iran's economy and left it "completely broke," adding, "There are many levers the president can crank harder in the weeks ahead."
Some experts give Trump credit for a willingness to grapple with issues they believe other presidents have been unable or unwilling to solve.
"The president wants a more stable world, and that means attempting to resolve disputes, whether hot like Ukraine or cold like trade and overcapacity," said Nick Snyder, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute, adding that Trump also worked to settle conflicts between Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of Congo and between Thailand and Cambodia.
Trump has upended traditional diplomatic norms of peacemaking, relying on America's economic and military might, including against U.S. allies, but that unorthodox style has yielded mixed results.
He brought parties to the table with the aim of ending Russia's invasion of Ukraine, but the longest war in Europe since World War II is nowhere near ending, with the latest Russian airstrikes killing 16 people in the Ukrainian capital on Thursday.
In Gaza, mediators fear intensifying Israeli strikes on the enclave are undermining efforts to end the conflict as both Israel and Hamas balk at conditions needed to advance a peace plan Trump forged in October last year. In Lebanon, Israeli airstrikes killed 11 people Sunday even as a U.S.-mediated peace framework between the two countries remains in effect.
One notable success came in Venezuela, where the U.S. military captured President Nicolás Maduro without U.S. casualties. Analysts say the operation helped convince Trump that joining Israel in attacking Iran would also proceed smoothly.
But they say that proved to be a miscalculation. They argue Trump has relied too heavily on applying coercive pressure even though Iran's leaders have little incentive to back down and reopen the Strait of Hormuz despite the country's weakening economy.
"He is obsessed with applying coercion, and sometimes flattery, to bend others to his will, but oblivious to their strategic goals and domestic politics. As a result, he keeps flailing and failing," said Stephen Wertheim, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
Meanwhile, the political clock is ticking, with Trump's Republican Party facing elections that could cost it control of one or both chambers of Congress and sharply curtail his ability to advance his agenda during his final two years in office.
Analysts say Trump's reliance on coercive pressure can bring adversaries to the table but often fails to produce lasting settlements, a dynamic that may encourage rivals to wait him out.
"U.S. adversaries understand that his political clock is shorter than theirs, and that while the United States can apply enormous coercive pressure, it may eventually lose patience," Aydintasbas said.
"Putin, Xi and Iran may therefore want to wait out Washington. After November, the incentive to wait out Trump will become even more pronounced."

Latvia Detains 28 Migrants Who Crossed From Belarus Through Underground Tunnel
Latvian border guards detained 28 people who attempted to cross illegally from Belarus into Latvia through an underground tunnel, Delfi reported, citing Latvia’s State Border Guard.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
While investigating the circumstances of the illegal border crossing, officers searched the surrounding area and discovered a concealed underground passage approximately 20 meters (66 feet) from the border.
According to the report, the entrance to the tunnel had been carefully camouflaged with moss.
All 28 people detained after crossing the border were returned to Belarus.
Latvia’s State Border Guard said this was the second recorded case in which migrants had used an underground tunnel in an attempt to enter the country illegally.
Similar underground passages have also been discovered along neighboring Lithuania’s border with Belarus. On August 5, Lithuania’s State Border Guard Service reported finding an unfinished four-meter-long tunnel extending from Belarus beneath the border fence near the village of Latežeris in Druskininkai municipality. The passage had been dug at a depth of approximately 1.5 meters.
Lithuanian border guards located the tunnel using specialized equipment provided by their Polish counterparts. The passage had been reinforced with logs and wooden planks, while its entrance on the Belarusian side was concealed with camouflage fabric.
The discoveries come as Lithuania takes broader measures to strengthen its preparedness along the border with Belarus. The country plans to relocate civil defense reserves currently stored near the Belarusian border to more secure locations by 2027, according to Aurimas Guščius, head of the Planning Bureau at the National Crisis Management Center.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Akhtubinsk Airfield, Damaging Su-34 Fighter-Bomber
Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck the Akhtubinsk airfield in Russia’s Astrakhan region on August 20, damaging a Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, an assessment of the strike confirmed damage to the Su-34 aircraft, as well as a fuel spill on the territory of the airfield.
Akhtubinsk airfield hosts the Russian Defense Ministry’s 929th State Flight Test Center, one of Russia’s primary facilities for testing and evaluating new military aircraft and aviation weapons.
The airfield is also used to base Su-34 aircraft, which Russian forces employ to launch guided aerial bombs against targets in Ukraine, according to the General Staff.
The facility is located approximately 650 kilometers (404 miles) from the frontline.
About Su-34 fighter-bomber
The Su-34 is described by Ukrainian intelligence as one of Russia’s primary platforms for deploying guided aerial bombs fitted with glide and correction modules, including universal gliding and correction modules. These weapons have been used extensively against Ukrainian ground targets.
The fighter-bomber has played a central role in Russia’s aerial campaign during its full-scale war against Ukraine, allowing Russian forces to strike targets at tactical and operational depths while enabling pilots to remain beyond the range of many Ukrainian air defense systems.
The Su-34’s production also remains partly outside Western sanctions restrictions. Nearly one-third of Russian companies involved in manufacturing components for the aircraft have not been targeted by Western sanctions, potentially allowing them continued access to foreign technologies and parts.
On March 16, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) published additional information through its War&Sanctions portal identifying manufacturers involved in the production of Russia’s Su-34 fighter-bombers.
