Stalin also accused Vijay's government of concentrating on changing the names of old schemes.
NEW DELHI: DMK chief MK Stalin on Saturday took aim at Tamil Nadu chief minister C Joseph Vijay over his "conduct" in the state assembly, accusing the actor-turned-politician of treating the House like a film set and using it to deliver "punch dialogues".Speaking at a DMK executive meeting, Stalin also accused Vijay's government of concentrating on changing the names of welfare schemes introduced during the DMK's previous tenure."The present chief minister is busy changing the names of all the schemes we introduced. He is treating the legislative assembly like a cinema set and delivering punch dialogues. As far as we are concerned, whether we win or lose, we are people who remain deeply connected with the day-to-day lives of the people," MK Stalin said.
Stalin's remarks came as the DMK executive meeting also focused on changes to the party's organisational structure, including measures aimed at bringing more young people into key positions.
Stalin says election defeat is not permanent setback
Addressing the party's recent electoral defeat, Stalin said the DMK had lost an election but should not view the result as a permanent setback."Let us consider this as an opportunity we have been given to plan the future of the party.
This is going to be a very important Executive Committee meeting in the history of the party. With your approval, we are going to make major and significant changes to the organisational structure of the party," said Stalin.He acknowledged that the performance of party office-bearers had contributed to the defeat and said the organisation needed to recognise its shortcomings instead of simply replacing individuals."Even if the mistake is committed by an individual, it is the 75-year-old party that suffers because of it. After a defeat, many reasons are put forward. Instead of examining each constituency individually, identifying shortcomings and simply replacing people, I decided that we need to undertake a comprehensive self-assessment," he said.
DMK sets age and term limits for party posts
The executive meeting passed a series of resolutions aimed at changing the party's organisational structure and increasing the participation of younger members.The resolutions fixed the maximum age for a Branch Committee Secretary at 45 years. The post was initially limited to two terms, although the term limit was later increased to three terms following discussions with members of the DMK Executive Committee.The party also decided to create Branch Committees in Chennai, Coimbatore, Madurai, Tiruchirappalli and Salem corporations, as well as in other corporations wherever required, to strengthen Ward Committees.In Chennai Corporation, ward committees will cover an average of 10,000 voters, while the corresponding figure will be around 5,000 voters in other corporations.For Municipal, City and Town Panchayat Ward Committee Secretaries, the maximum age has been set at 50 years, with a maximum of three terms following the revised decision.The maximum age for Town Panchayat Committee Secretaries has been fixed at 60 years, with the same three-term limit.
DMK redraws local organisational structure
Under the new structure, Area Committees in Chennai Corporation will cover an average of 40,000 voters, while those in other corporations will cover around 30,000 voters.The maximum age for Area Committee Secretaries has been fixed at 60 years, with a maximum of three terms.
City Committees will also cover an average of 40,000 voters. Their Secretaries will have a maximum age of 60 years and a three-term limit.The party has further decided that one Union Committee should be formed for every average 30,000 voters. Union Committee Secretaries will have a maximum age of 60 years and can serve for up to three terms.The organisational changes are part of Stalin's broader effort to restructure the party following its electoral setback, with greater emphasis on youth participation, fixed tenure and a wider internal assessment of the party's functioning.

Bills on fast track: Over half of 18th Lok Sabha bills passed in same session, shows data

Bills on fast track: Over half of 18th Lok Sabha bills passed in same session, shows data
TOI News Desk / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 22, 2026, 17:04 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Parliament Bills passed without discussions
NEW DELHI: More than half of the bills introduced in the 18th Lok Sabha so far have been passed by both Houses in the same session, with the pace of passage accelerating sharply over the past year, an analysis of data from PRS Legislative Research shows.Of the 64 bills introduced since the 18th Lok Sabha was constituted, 34, or 53%, were passed by both Houses in the session in which they were introduced.The 18th Lok Sabha initially recorded a slower pace. During the Budget Session of 2026, five of the 10 bills introduced were passed by both Houses in the same session. The pace accelerated during the Monsoon Session, which ended on August 13, with 11 of the 12 bills introduced being passed before the session concluded. The Indian Statistical Institute Bill, 2026, was the only bill left pending.
Bills passed without being on original agenda
The government's original legislative agenda had listed five new bills for introduction and passage and two pending bills for consideration and passage. However, six of the 11 bills eventually passed during the Monsoon Session were not included in the original agenda.Neither of the two pending bills listed for consideration and passage — the Viksit Bharat Shiksha Adhishthan (VBSA) Bill, 2025, and the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment (FCRA) Bill, 2026 — was passed.
The parliamentary committee examining the VBSA Bill has not yet submitted its report, while the FCRA Amendment Bill was referred to a Joint Committee following Opposition demands for its withdrawal.
Seven bills cleared in minutes
The rapid passage of legislation has raised concerns over the time available for parliamentary scrutiny. PRS has previously pointed out that a short gap between introduction and passage gives MPs less time to examine proposed laws and limits opportunities for consultation with stakeholders.
The Monsoon Session data illustrates the trend. According to PRS, nine of the 11 bills passed were cleared without any MP other than the minister piloting the legislation speaking on them. Seven bills were passed in five minutes or less. Held from July 20 to August 13, monsoon session had 19 sittings. Lok Sabha functioned for only 15% of its scheduled time, while Rajya Sabha worked for 33%, according to PRS.The trend towards faster passage became more visible in 2025. Three of the five bills introduced during the Budget Session of 2025 were passed in the same session, followed by eight of 13 bills during the Monsoon Session and seven of nine during the Winter Session.

Canada fires back at Trump’s 50% tariffs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:27:57 UTC
20:27:57 KST

Canada fires back at Trump’s 50% tariffs
Ottawa will introduce reciprocal “dollar-for-dollar” measures in response to the 50% tariffs the US has imposed on Canadian goods, Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement on Friday, after trade talks with Washington broke down.
The latest round of intense negotiations lasted three days and was aimed at wrapping up months of talks between Washington and Ottawa, with mutual tariffs threatening to escalate into an all-out trade war.
“Canada will match those tariffs dollar for dollar to protect our workers and businesses,” the statement reads.
The prime minister stressed that “last-minute changes in the US-proposed terms were unfair, uneconomic, and called into question the reliability of any deal.”
Earlier in the day, the Trump administration invoked Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930, a rarely used provision that allows the head of state to impose duties of up to 50% on imports from countries deemed to have subjected US commerce to unequal or discriminatory treatment.
The tariffs, which came into effect just after midnight on Saturday and cover about 5% of Canada’s US-bound exports, target goods ranging from plywood and cement to wine and hockey sticks, Western media outlets have reported.
The dispute, which dates back to Trump’s first term, was rekindled after he returned to office last year and imposed sweeping tariffs on imports from a wide range of countries, including Canada, Mexico, China, the EU and Japan. Trump once again accused America’s trading partners of unfairly benefiting from access to the US market.
Earlier this week, Trump delayed the 50% levies, originally scheduled to take effect on August 19, to give negotiators additional time to reach a deal.
At the time, Trump said Washington and Ottawa had agreed to revive the Keystone XL pipeline project, which was intended to transport Canadian oil to the US, while Carney noted significant progress made by the two sides in trade talks.
AP has cited a senior Trump administration official as saying that Canada had been seeking concessions from Washington on tariffs previously imposed by the US president on steel, aluminum, automobiles and lumber, but the US has so far shown no willingness to make such concessions.
US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement shortly after midnight that despite the US offer to give Canada “the best treatment of any major exporter to our market,” new demands and walk-backs of other commitments by Ottawa had “upended the careful balance” reached in recent days.
Commenting on the US tariffs, Candace Laing, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, called the collapse “a body blow to North American competitiveness in this self-defeating trade saga.” She warned that “Americans will see their costs go up, and Canadians will see customers, investment and small businesses disappear.”
Carney has, however, pledged to introduce additional measures to support Canadian workers and businesses in the coming days, as well as to diversify the country’s partnerships abroad.

Major Asian exporter tests Russian Arctic shortcut to Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:27:36 UTC
20:27:36 KST

Major Asian exporter tests Russian Arctic shortcut to Europe
South Korea has launched its first trial container ship voyage to Europe via the Northern Sea Route (NSR), as disruption to traditional shipping lanes drives growing interest in Russia’s Arctic trade corridor.
The NSR stretches roughly 5,600 km along Russia’s Arctic coast, mostly through waters under its jurisdiction. The route relies on domestic port and navigation infrastructure. State atomic energy corporation Rosatom oversees its development and operates the world’s only nuclear-powered icebreaker fleet.
The PanStar Acro departed from Busan New Port on Saturday and will sail through the NSR before calling at Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and Gdansk in Poland.
The ship is expected to reach Felixstowe in around 18 days. The journey between Busan and Rotterdam via the Arctic is around 13,000 km, 35% shorter than the roughly 20,000 km route via Suez, with South Korean estimates suggesting the NSR could cut around ten days from a typical Asia-Europe voyage.
According to Reuters, Western diplomats have raised concerns over South Korea’s plan, which involved consultations with Russia and permits for the ship’s passage. The agency cited a European diplomat as saying Western governments want to isolate Moscow over the Ukraine conflict, not pursue “engagement” with it.
There are questions over sanctions risks linked to payments for Russian navigation and other services. Seoul says consultations with relevant countries and agencies have been completed, and Korean media report that the sanctions risks have been resolved.
The country’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries has said it aims to establish a new trade corridor, with the voyage marking the country’s return to the Arctic after a decade-long hiatus and its first use of a container ship on the NSR.
South Korean companies conducted five trial voyages along the NSR between 2013 and 2016, but regular services did not follow due to limited cargo volumes and a less developed route. Russia has since significantly expanded its Arctic infrastructure and navigation capabilities.
Moscow has sought to turn the NSR from a corridor primarily serving its Arctic projects into a major international trade artery linking Asia and Europe. China has already launched a regular container service to Europe via the NSR, while India is considering sending its first cargo vessel along the route in 2027 and Japan has shown interest as well.
Earlier this month, Rosatom CEO Aleksey Likhachev linked growing demand for the NSR to the “persistently difficult situation” in the Persian Gulf. The Iran conflict has also fueled instability affecting Red Sea shipping, with Houthi attacks and threats around the Bab el-Mandeb strait prompting some operators to avoid the Suez Canal route.

As Russia turns to jet-powered drones, Ukraine scrambles for new interceptor tech

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22

As Russia turns to jet-powered drones, Ukraine scrambles for new interceptor tech
A serviceman of Ukraine's 116th Mechanized Brigade watches a Ukrainian-made P1-Sun interceptor drone fly in Kharkiv Oblast, Ukraine, on May 20, 2026. (Yevhen Titov / Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images)
For residents of Kyiv, it was a particularly dark day. Already reeling from a massive Russian aerial bombardment overnight on Aug. 20 that killed 15 people, the daylight hours saw a steady stream of drones target the capital, claiming the lives of a further two.
A grim soundtrack of air raid sirens and periodic explosions marked what appears to be one of the latest stages in the ever-evolving air war — Russia's escalating use of jet-powered Shahed-type drones.
"In July, there were five times as many as in June," Colonel Yurii Ihnat, head of the Communications Department of the Air Force Command of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, told the Kyiv Independent.
"Sometimes, two-thirds of all drones launched during the day are jet-powered," he added.
Russian drones over Ukraine are nothing new, and the country's military has become the global pioneer of downing piston-engine versions using first-person view (FPV) interceptor drones.
But equipped with jet engines and in ever-increasing numbers, Russia's attack drones are now outpacing Ukraine's interceptors.
read also
The evolving threat
As the threat changes, Ukraine's drone producers are scrambling to develop newer and faster models of the interceptor drones that proved so effective in neutering Russia's older and slower drones.
Simultaneously, Russia is racing to scale production of newer versions, redirecting resources once poured into production of piston-engined models into faster but more complex jet-powered models.
Russia first started importing assembled piston-engined Iranian Shahed 131 and Shahed 136 one-way attack drones in 2022, which were known in Russian service as the Geran-1 and Geran-2 respectively.
Production was quickly localized and scaled at the Yelabuga drone factory in Tatarstan, where Russia employs child labor to produce the suicide drones en masse. Assembly lines in Yelabuga were soon churning out thousands of drones per month.
"Russia's use of Geran-2 drones started to escalate massively from the summer of 2024," Kyle Glen, a researcher at the Centre for Information Resilience who monitors the drone campaign on both sides, told the Kyiv Independent.
"The Ukrainian Air Force went from reporting around 400 drones a month to around 700, and then around 1,300, 2,000, 2,500. This escalated up until May 2026 when nearly 7,500 drones were launched in a single month," Glen said.
May represented a peak of Russia's use of the piston-engined drones against Ukraine. Despite the massive numbers launched at the country, the combination of Ukraine's new interceptor drones and years of experience in downing Russian drones helped interception rates peak around 95%.
"Interceptor drones are the main focus," Ihnat said. "Ukraine has achieved high shoot-down rates for conventional Shahed-type drones,"
A Ukrainian innovation, drone interceptors turned cheap commercially available hobbyist drones — a typical Ukrainian drone interceptor, such as the Wild Hornets STING, costs around $2,300 — into extremely effective air defense systems.
"We’ve established mobile fire teams and equipped them with modern systems, which have significantly improved our effectiveness. Automated systems have even begun to appear," Ihnat added.
Ukrainian effectiveness in dealing with Russian and Iranian drones was starkly demonstrated during the continuing war in the Persian Gulf. As Iranian drones penetrated sophisticated American air defenses, causing billions of dollars' worth of damage, Ukrainian interceptors and Ukrainian anti-drone specialists were called in to help bolster the defenses of U.S. bases in the region.
read also
Jet power
Facing the decreased effectiveness of its piston-engined drones, Russia has pivoted toward producing ever larger numbers of jet-powered drones. In a statement on June 4, then-Ukrainian Commander in Chief Oleksandr Syrskyi claimed Russia planned "to increase the share of jet strike drones to 50%."
"This poses new challenges for us that require a timely response," he said.
Ukraine's Military Intelligence (HUR) assesses Russia produces "around 3,000" jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 kamikaze drones per month, Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi reported on Aug. 12.
HUR also assesses that by August 2026, production of Russia's jet-powered one-way attack drones had surpassed production of the piston-engined Geran-2 model.
The newer jet-powered models are significantly faster than piston-engined models, making them much more difficult to shoot down with FPV interceptors and mobile fire teams.
While the piston-engined Geran-2 has a maximum speed of around 185 kph, the jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 can reach 500 kph and 600 kph respectively.
Jet-powered drones are more expensive and more complex to build than piston-engined variants, leading to an overall drop in the numbers of drones being launched against Ukraine, according to Glen.
"The total number of Russian drones reported launched at Ukraine by the Ukrainian Air Force has dropped off in recent months," he said. "Less than 6,000 for June, less than 5,000 for July, and less than 2,500 for August so far."
read also
The defensive arms race
"Interceptors capable of intercepting jet-powered drones are currently being developed," Ihnat told the Kyiv Independent.
"Ukrainian developers are aware of this problem; jet-powered drones and the Banderols (a small, low-cost Russian cruise missile) didn’t just appear yesterday, but their use has now increased," he added.
One senior engineer working on one of Ukraine's interceptor programs, and who spoke on condition of anonymity due to the sensitive nature of his work, told the Kyiv Independent the slow introduction of Russia's jet-powered drones had given Ukraine's engineers advance warning of the threat.
The engineer said his team had already been modifying their existing drone interceptors to increase their flight speed, and that they already had prototypes that were capable of reaching the speeds necessary to engage jet-powered drones.
"It's an engineering problem, to which there's an engineering solution," the engineer said, pointing out that their newer prototypes were not significantly more expensive than their current interceptor models that were in serial production.
Meanwhile, the jet-powered drones they were designed to intercept were significantly more expensive for Russia to produce than piston-engined drones.
This favorable economic differential is important for the long-term sustainability of Ukraine's air defense, the engineer said, as relying on expensive, mostly Western-sourced surface-to-air missiles to defend against jet-powered drones would be unsustainable, both due to the cost and the limited production of such interceptors.
Ukraine is also developing jet-powered interceptors. On August 14, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov announced the first jet-powered interceptors which can reach speeds of 600kph are "undergoing combat testing."
A few days later, on Aug. 21, the first jet-powered interceptor, the Alexa Spatium, officially entered Ukrainian service, Ukraine's Defense Ministry announced.
The manufacturer of the small and sleek turbojet-powered aircraft has not been disclosed, but the interceptor is capable of "high speeds" and can be reused if no target is engaged.
The aircraft can also engage ground targets and helicopters, the Defense Ministry said.

Israel must stop Erdogan’s military expansion before Turkey reaches its borders - opinion

Unless Israel draws concrete red lines in Syria and the eastern Mediterranean, the Turkish army and navy will further encroach upon Israel’s northern and maritime borders.
Israel could find itself facing Turkish tanks on the Golan Heights and Turkish frigates off the coast of Caesarea.
This is the warning I heard this week from a very senior Israeli intelligence official.
The warning echoes the alarm expressed in the 2025 Nagel Commission report (which evaluated Israel’s security budget and force buildup) about the Turkish drive toward an Islamist-jihadist regional order with Ottoman-era hegemonic ambitions.
Israel must be prepared, the commission’s report cautioned, for direct confrontation with Ankara and with Syrian proxies and armies aligned with Turkey.
“The threat from Syria could evolve into something even more dangerous than the Iranian threat,” the report stated.
This threatening reality explains the Israeli air strike several days ago on an airbase near Idlib in northern Syria, where the Turks apparently were setting up a radar and air defense system that was meant to interfere with the IAF’s operations in the north.
The Israeli strike sent a stark signal to Turkey’s radical Islamist dictator Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his Syrian satrap, the former ISIS terrorist named Ahmed al-Sharaa (a.k.a. Mohammed al-Julani), to back off.
Understand: Erdogan is a true-blue believing old-school antisemite, who considers classic antisemitic myths like the Protocols of the Elders of Zion (where Jews control the global banking and media conglomerates) as truth.
He honestly hates Jews and Israelis, and he openly seeks to lead a pan-Islamic coalition to crush Israel – while remaining a member of NATO.
Erdogan is anchoring a Sunni alliance of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Qatar (with some Egyptian role too) that has a malodorous anti-American and anti-Israeli scent. Erdogan has even drafted a model constitution for an Islamic confederation meant to replace NATO.
According to US President Donald Trump, Erdogan’s military was prepared to join Iran’s war against Israel this year until Trump “asked” Erdogan not to do so.
But that has not stopped Erdogan from siding with Russia against the West in defense of Iran and in support of the Iranian economy and Iranian war effort, and from hosting Hamas military headquarters.
All the while, he petitions gullible Europeans for goodies, and lobbies his friend Trump for engines for Turkey’s homegrown fighter jet and for advanced American F-35 fighter jets.
Trump and his special envoy to Turkey and Syria Tom Barrack (who is wildly solicitous towards Erdogan and al-Sharaa) have stuffed their mouths with cotton balls and have nothing to say about Erdogan’s much-too-close alignment with Russia, China, and Iran; his long-term military occupation of northern Cyprus and northern Syria; and the diplomatic and military war he is waging (for the moment, mainly behind the scenes) against Israel.
Israel has not declared and does not want to consider Turkey an enemy country, but it cannot ignore Turkey’s military buildup and its encroachment – nay, its essential takeover of Syria and attempt to extend its military reach to Israel’s borders.
This week’s Israeli strike was designed to push back against Turkish air intrusion, and Israel will certainly strike again if Erdogan insists on expanding his military presence in Syria or attempts to rebuild the Syrian air force.
But the more immediate Turkish threat comes from its large navy, since Erdogan repeatedly threatens to wage war with Israel over gas fields in the Mediterranean.
The Turkish Navy has tens of frigates, destroyers, and amphibious landing craft, as well as 12 submarines. It is now building six more submarines along with 24 new frigates and destroyers.
By comparison, the too-small Israeli navy has 15 missile ships, six submarines, and a dozen cruisers. Israel will soon add naval helicopters to its defensive arsenal.
It is no surprise that the Nagel Commission recommended a massive build-up of the Israeli navy as a priority expenditure.
Applying standards to Turkey
At the moment, NATO cannot afford a complete rupture with a country that controls the Turkish Straits and hosts US nuclear weapons.
But at the very least, a “reciprocity standard” should be applied to Turkey. Contracts with that country must be tied to its foreign policy and military conduct.
Human rights standards should pertain to Turkey too. Erdogan has jailed more journalists, judges, generals, and academics than any other country in the world, including China.
He is building 40,000 new jail cells to handle the overload. He is creating an authoritarian system to suit his imperial purposes.
Erdogan needs to be cut down to size, and his madly ferocious foreign and military policies put in a box. American and European leaders who prioritize stability in the region ought to weigh in against his overly ambitious and aggressive schemes.
They should not be censuring Israel when it necessarily acts to drive Erdogan back from the brink.
Remember: the past three years of devastating enemy attacks on Israel taught Israelis an important lesson – the need to maintain a proactive defense posture, including strategic ascendancy against enemies near and far.
Consequently, Israel will not return to the containment policies of recent decades that prioritized restraint and diplomacy over enemy degradation and military triumph.
This approach allowed enemies to develop attack capabilities under the cover of diplomatic breathing time, which some Western officials mistakenly called periods of “stability.”
That approach blew up in Israel’s face, with terror and invasion from the West Bank, Gaza, and from Syria and Lebanon, and with the march of Iran’s nuclear bomb program to near completion and Iran’s ballistic missile array to near-annihilation-of-Israel potential.
The lessons Israel has learned apply to Turkey as well. From Idlib to Istanbul, Israel will attack, if necessary, not defend.
It will insist on jihadist-free buffer zones along its borders with Lebanon and Syria. It will not tolerate the placement of equilibrium-breaking strategic weapon systems on its doorstep nor abide the advance of threatening foreign armies and navies.

Israel 'baited' Turkey with Abu al-Duhur airbase 'pre-election' strike, US Envoy Tom Barrack says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:26:02 UTC
20:26:02 KST

The Israeli strike on the Abu al-Duhur military base in Syria on Tuesday, which nearly led to a direct military confrontation with Turkey, may have been intended to provoke Ankara and could have been linked to political considerations ahead of Israel’s elections, US Special Envoy to Syria and Ambassador to Turkey Tom Barrack suggested on Saturday.
In an interview with Mario Nawfal on X/Twitter, Barrack stressed that this was only one possible theory, not an intelligence-based conclusion.
According to Barrack, one possibility is that “the Israelis were baiting the Turks,” partly against the backdrop of a previous incident in which Turkey shot down a Russian fighter jet that approached its border. He described a situation in which fighter jets operate near a border without coordination or warning as a “very dangerous game.”
Barrack directly linked this possibility to Israeli politics, saying that the strike may have been a “very aggressive but maybe a well-received pre-election concept.”
Later in the interview, Barrack discussed how domestic politics can shape the rhetoric of regional leaders.
“What you're hearing in rhetoric amongst the senior leaders of these countries is they have to, during a political campaign, which everybody is in, right?” he said.
“Prime Minister [Benjamin] Netanyahu is moving toward October," Barrack noted. "He knows what his constituency wants.”
Barrack: Erdogan may soon call early elections
He added that Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan is also approaching a decision on whether to call early elections and must consider his voters, who are particularly sensitive to developments in Gaza.
Barrack also presented a second theory regarding the circumstances that led to the strike: that Israel received intelligence indicating Turkish military personnel or military assets could be stationed at the Syrian base.
According to Barrack, Israel raised the concern with the United States about six days before the strike.
“We have some intelligence that there might be Turkish movement into this site, which we would be very concerned about,” Barrack said, describing the message delivered to Washington.
However, according to Barrack, the US reviewed the intelligence with relevant officials and received a clear response: “No, that's not happening.”
The comments come amid reports of behind-the-scenes contacts before the strike. According to Barrack’s account, the issue was examined through diplomatic channels, including a backchannel conversation lasting about two hours between Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and the Mossad chief.
Despite those contacts, Israeli Air Force aircraft appeared and struck the base’s runways without Turkey receiving advance warning of the operation.
According to Barrack, the incident then escalated from another Israeli strike in Syria into a moment that could have triggered a far more dangerous regional confrontation.
Barrack emphasized that the Turkish military is strong, well-equipped, and possesses significant intelligence capabilities.
“When they see these jets coming towards the border, and they don't know what the purpose, direction, or intent is, they start to say 'we're going to have to scramble our own.'” he said.
Such a scenario could have led to a possible aerial encounter between Israeli and Turkish aircraft and a direct confrontation between Israel and Turkey, a NATO member and one of the United States’ most important allies in the region.
Barrack was asked whether such an incident could have escalated into “World War III.” He said that almost any unintended incident could lead to broader escalation, but stressed that, in his assessment, neither side intends to reach such a confrontation.
“Thank goodness, palm heads really came to the moment of the day, and we unwrapped it,” he said.
According to Barrack, it was one of those moments when “for many of us, our whole life went in front of us,” leading to the conclusion: “There's got to be a better way, guys.”
Barrack emphasized that, in his understanding, Ankara is not seeking a war with Israel.
“I know that the Turks, their intelligence agency, their hierarchy, their foreign minister, the president, the head of intelligence, all are concentrating on restraint,” he said.
“They're not predatory," he added. "They're not interested in attacking or even engaging in any kind of kinetic or adversarial relationship with Israel. It's not good for the region.”
Barrack said both sides are ultimately looking for a way to de-escalate, but that from Turkey’s perspective, the Palestinian issue is even more important than Iran. According to him, developments in Gaza are a major concern for both the Turkish public and the broader Muslim public.
Behind the immediate confrontation lies a much broader strategic struggle over the future of Syria following the fall of the Assad regime, according to Barrack.
Syrian territory provides Israel with 'a clear line of sight to Iran,' Barrack says
Israel wants Syria to remain free of military systems that could limit its freedom of action in the region, particularly against Iran. Barrack previously described Syrian territory as providing Israel with “a clear line of sight to Iran.”
Turkey, meanwhile, is expanding its military and political position in the new Syria. Barrack said Turkey’s growing influence as a regional power is raising concerns among other actors, but expressed hope the sides can maintain restraint.
According to Barrack, US President Donald Trump recently asked Erdogan why Turkey did not simply “take” Syria for itself, given the role it played in developments there.
According to Barrack, Erdogan responded: “Because we don’t want it. We want Syria to be a sovereign and independent country."
Barrack also addressed mutual concerns over territorial ambitions. According to him, maps are published in Turkey showing what is allegedly a vision of “Greater Israel,” while in Israel, maps appear warning of “Ottoman Empire 2.0.”
“We don't think any of those things are true,” he said.
Despite the severe crisis, Barrack revealed that behind the scenes there is also security cooperation between Turkey, Israel, and Syria over a shared threat.
“Every evening... we have coordination between Turkey, Israel, and Syria, hunting ISIS terrorists,” he said.
According to Barrack, the group is attempting to exploit the governing vacuum created in Syria to rebuild itself.
Barrack recalled that in the early 2000s, Israel and Turkey enjoyed a period of “honeymoon” relations and hoped the two countries could eventually return to a similar relationship.
However, this week’s incident highlighted how dangerous the path toward such a relationship remains. According to Trump’s envoy, Israeli aircraft approached the Turkish border without warning; Ankara began considering scrambling its own fighter jets, and for several moments two key US allies came close to a confrontation that, according to Barrack, neither side truly wants.
Defense Minister Katz: Barrack's statements 'full of inaccuracies'
After Barrack's statements, Defense Minister Israel Katz said they were "full of inaccuracies" and argued they contradicted US President Trump's positions.
"The attempt by opposition figures and parts of the media to paint the operation in Syria in political colors stems from a combination of ignorance, a lack of understanding of Israel’s security interests, and a constant desire to attack the government, and deserves every condemnation.
"The response of US envoy Barrack is full of inaccuracies and positions that contradict Trump’s own position regarding the Golan Heights.”
Katz also claimed that the IDF issued a direct warning to senior Syrian officials before strikes on the Abu al-Duhur airfield "in an attempt to prevent the move."
"After the request went unanswered, the prime minister and I authorized the IDF to carry out the strike, and it was carried out successfully. Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down," Katz said.

The Middle East’s ‘peace architecture’ may be giving rise to an anti-Israel bloc - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:25:55 UTC
20:25:55 KST

Israel has always known how to deal with hostile governments one at a time.
What should worry it now is something more dangerous: a growing network of countries that increasingly act together, pressure together, and may soon help decide when Israel must withdraw, whether Hamas or Hezbollah have really disarmed, and when Israel is permitted to defend itself.
That danger became clearer this week.
Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Pakistan, and Indonesia issued a joint statement pressing Israel to move ahead with the latest Gaza framework and calling for continued American involvement to ensure Israeli compliance.
The problem is not diplomacy. The problem is the direction of the pressure.
Israel is being pushed to withdraw while Hamas remains armed.
Hamas can announce that it accepts a roadmap. That is not the same as surrendering weapons, dismantling tunnels, ending military command structures, and proving that it will not rebuild.
October 7 should have ended any illusion that Israel can afford to trade hard security for promises.
If Hamas is required to disarm, then disarmament should come first. Israel should not make an irreversible withdrawal while Hamas offers a reversible commitment.
Yet Turkey, Qatar, Egypt, and now the UAE are increasingly speaking through the same diplomatic framework and pushing Israel in the same direction.
That matters because these countries were never meant to function as a collective referee over Israeli security.
Egypt is the clearest example.
Israel and Egypt signed peace in 1979. For almost half a century, that agreement turned Israel's most dangerous military frontier into one of its most stable borders. It worked because it was bilateral.
Egypt acted according to Egyptian interests. Israel acted according to Israeli interests. The United States served as guarantor. Egypt did not need Turkey or Qatar to maintain peace with Israel.
Now Cairo is increasingly operating inside a wider Gaza mechanism together with Ankara and Doha, while the UAE is joining the same coordinated statements.
The danger is not that Egypt suddenly abandons peace. The danger is that a strong bilateral relationship becomes absorbed into a regional bloc where Turkey, Qatar, and others help shape the collective position.
Imagine the next crisis.
Israel discovers Hamas rebuilding tunnels, weapons depots, or armed units after an Israeli withdrawal. Israel acts. Turkey condemns it. Qatar condemns it. Other governments join them.
Egypt comes under pressure to align with the regional position. The UAE does too.
Suddenly, Israel is no longer dealing with one mediator or one peace partner. It is confronting a coordinated diplomatic front.
That is the risk we should be discussing now, before it becomes permanent.
The same pattern is appearing in Lebanon.
Britain, Italy, Switzerland, and Indonesia have been discussed as possible participants in a mechanism to verify whether Hezbollah has disarmed.
Again, the concept sounds reasonable; Israel needs Hezbollah disarmed.
But who gets to decide when Hezbollah has complied enough?
Britain has already shown a growing willingness to use sanctions and economic pressure against Israelis and Israeli policies in Judea and Samaria. Italy has created more distance in defense cooperation with Israel. Indonesia has long taken strongly pro-Palestinian positions.
Why should governments that are willing to pressure Israel become judges of whether Israel's enemies are sufficiently disarmed?
That is the larger issue.
The basic imbalance
Each initiative sounds harmless when viewed alone: a Gaza peace board. A stabilization force. Arab mediation. A Hezbollah verification mechanism. European sanctions. Reconstruction financing.
But together they form something much more powerful.
They create a network with money, military personnel, diplomatic recognition, economic leverage, and American backing.
That network can eventually influence whether Israel withdraws, whether it can strike, whether Hamas has complied, whether Hezbollah has complied, and whether Israeli actions in Judea and Samaria deserve punishment.
That could become more consequential than the United Nations.
Israel knows how to survive hostile UN resolutions. Most of them have limited practical effect.
These newer mechanisms are different. They can affect the battlefield. They can affect borders. They can affect sanctions. They can affect reconstruction money. They can affect Washington.
And there is a basic imbalance in all of this.
Israel is easy to pressure. It has banks, companies, diplomats, tourists, trade agreements, and international relationships.
Hamas does not.
Hezbollah does not.
A European government can sanction an Israeli. It cannot meaningfully sanction a terrorist hiding in a tunnel.
Turkey and Qatar can pressure Washington.
Hamas pays almost no price for rejecting international expectations until someone forces it to.
That means the democratic state becomes the easiest target.
We are already watching that happen.
Hamas remains armed, yet international pressure increasingly focuses on when Israel will withdraw. That is backwards.
Hamas started this war. Hamas carried out October 7. Hamas built the tunnels. Hamas took the hostages. Hamas created the military infrastructure that made this war possible. The burden should be on Hamas to prove that the threat is gone. Not on Israel to withdraw first and hope.
Peace requires partners, and Israel should continue strengthening peace with Egypt, expanding the Abraham Accords and building relationships across the Arab world.
But peace agreements should remain peace agreements. They should not quietly evolve into multinational structures that police Israel.
Egypt should be Israel's neighbor at peace. The UAE should be Israel's normalization partner. Turkey and Qatar can mediate when useful.
But none of them should be given a collective veto over Israel's security decisions.
The US should be building a regional architecture that restrains Hamas, Hezbollah, and Iran. It should not accidentally build one that is far better at restraining Israel.
The test is simple.
Before Israel is pressured to withdraw, Hamas should disarm.
Before Israel is told Hezbollah no longer poses a threat, Hezbollah should actually dismantle its military infrastructure.
Before international monitors tell Israel that the danger has passed, the danger should actually be gone.
Otherwise, we are not building peace. Instead, we are building a system in which Israel's enemies keep their weapons while Israel's friends gain the power to tell Israel when it may use its own.
That is not a peace architecture.
That is a bloc.
And Israel should recognize it before it is too late.
The writer is founder and CEO of the Orthodox Jewish Chamber of Commerce.

Hong Kong-built greenhouse gas tracker device ‘functioning well’ on space station
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:22:40 UTC
20:22:40 KST

Hong Kong-built greenhouse gas tracker device ‘functioning well’ on space station
Tech minister Sun Dong says Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory has ‘successfully captured images with good clarity’
A greenhouse gas monitoring instrument developed by a university in Hong Kong is operating successfully aboard the Tiangong space station and is expected to contribute to sustainable development, the city’s technology minister has said.
Secretary for Innovation, Technology and Industry Sun Dong also revealed more details in a blog post on Saturday about the life of the city’s first astronaut, Lai Ka-ying, who he said had a busy schedule at the space station.
The Multi‑Spectral Imaging Carbon Observatory (Musico), developed by a team led by scientists at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology and funded by the city government, has been deployed to China’s space station.
“Musico is equipped with four sensors for detecting carbon dioxide, methane, oxygen, and aerosols. They have all successfully captured images with clear imaging quality and demonstrated good overall performance,” he said.
“Over the next two years or more, the instrument will provide autonomous, controllable, and highly accurate greenhouse gas (carbon dioxide and methane) emission monitoring data, contributing to efforts to address climate change and promote global sustainable development.”
Musico is considered the world’s first lightweight, high-resolution, high-precision synergistic observatory for carbon dioxide and methane.

                                    MINSK, 22 August (BelTA) – Belarus prevented the rise of “predatory capitalism” and the plundering of the country, and President Aleksandr Lukashenko deserves immense credit for this. The military observer with the Russian newspaper Komsomolskaya Pravda, Colonel (retired) Viktor Baranets offered the opinion in a recent episode of BelTA’s project On Point.
 
“True to my habit of speaking the unvarnished truth and nothing but the truth, I state: part of Belarus’ greatness lies in the fact that it has not allowed predatory capitalism to take root. From this point of view we also have something to learn from Belarusians,” said Viktor Baranets.
 
He noted that he had visited Belarus on more than one occasion, and each time he had been pleasantly impressed by his visits to the republic. “As I traveled across its vast expanses, I often found myself thinking about the cleanliness of your cities, towns, and villages. On the whole, I have always considered Belarusians to be a very talented people,” added Viktor Baranets.
 
The observer pointed out that after the collapse of the USSR, Belarus managed not only to preserve its Soviet potential but also to significantly expand it by preventing factories and plants from being sold off for a song. “This is also a reflection of your sound policies,” he stated.
 
Viktor Baranets is convinced that Aleksandr Lukashenko deserves immense credit for this, as he quashed attempts to sell off domestic enterprises in the early years of his presidency, thereby preventing the plundering of the country. “We must give credit to the government, at the center of which stands the president of Belarus. He managed to rein in this genie. And judging by the statements I often read and hear, he still keeps in check those who would like to ‘grab a quick buck.’ This is the right policy,” the observer emphasized.

What Russia learned from Putin and Trump in Anchorage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:20:06 UTC
20:20:06 KST

What Russia learned from Putin and Trump in Anchorage
The meeting between the Russian and US presidents in Alaska last year caused a sensation in both form and substance. Expectations were so high, whether expressed as hope or alarm, that the Anchorage summit was almost certain to disappoint.
The conflict surrounding Ukraine is too deep and complex to be resolved at a single meeting, even one involving the leaders of Russia and the United States. Negotiations to end the Vietnam War dragged on for years, despite both sides understanding from the beginning that the conflict would eventually have to end.
The real question was whether Anchorage could provide the starting point for a peace process; it didn’t. Much has since been said about why, although the conditions for such a breakthrough probably didn’t exist in the first place. Yet rather than dismissing the summit with the usual sarcasm about the “spirit of Anchorage,” it’s worth considering what the meeting did achieve.
First, it exposed the widening divergence between the United States and Western Europe as the old world’s leaders remain committed to seeking a military victory over Russia, but Washington, by contrast, doesn’t want to become directly involved in pursuing that objective.
Donald Trump’s claim that the United States is merely a mediator rather than a participant is plainly disingenuous, given that Washington remains deeply involved, but American involvement could be far greater, even allowing for the apparent limits on its resources and its growing obligations elsewhere.
This divergence doesn’t mean the transatlantic alliance is about to collapse; however, it does suggest that the Atlanticism established during the second half of the 20th century will not survive in its old form. Whether its replacement will prove more advantageous to Russia remains unclear, but, nevertheless, Moscow has long wished to see the end of NATO as we have known it, and the chances of that happening are increasing.
Anchorage also demonstrated that the United States isn’t all-powerful, as Trump was unable to secure from Western Europe and Ukraine what he wanted at the time. In that instance, Washington’s failure worked against Moscow, but the broader recognition that American power has limits should be regarded as a positive development.
Taken together, these lessons show that the West is becoming more diverse and internally divided, so its remaining unity must increasingly be maintained by political pressure and institutional inertia. Russia must therefore develop a more sophisticated and flexible policy towards Western countries, exploiting their growing differences rather than continuing to treat them as a single bloc.
Finally, Anchorage offered a revealing model of modern diplomacy, in which personalities increasingly matter more than institutions, and character more than principles. There are no longer any “magic” agreements and a gentleman’s agreement lasts only until another gentleman arrives with different priorities.
What retains value is composure and reliance on one’s own capabilities, combined with a sober assessment of their limits. Russia’s mistake before Anchorage was to imagine Trump as an external force capable of fundamentally changing the situation, but he didn’t play that role, nor could he have done so.
That disappointment returned everyone to the reality of the conflict in that no outside power can impose its resolution. During the year since Alaska, the Russian-Western European military confrontation has acquired a clearer direction and an internal logic of its own and it’s within that logic that Russia must seek a way to end the present war and prevent the next one, without waiting for magical solutions or grand bargains imposed from abroad.
This article was first published by Kommersant and was translated and edited by the RT team.

12 countries condemn Israeli strikes on Syrian military base
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
19:19:40 CST
20:19:40 KST

AMMAN, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Foreign ministers of 12 countries have condemned the Israeli airstrikes targeting the Abu al-Duhur military airport in northwestern Syria, calling the attacks a dangerous escalation and a "flagrant" violation of Syria's sovereignty and territorial integrity.
In a joint statement on Friday, the ministers of the countries, including Türkiye, Algeria, Indonesia, Jordan, Lebanon, Malaysia, Mauritania, Pakistan, Palestine, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and Somalia, expressed deep concern over the continued targeting of Syrian territory and infrastructure, warning that such actions risk undermining efforts to restore security and stability, rebuild national institutions and address the humanitarian consequences of the country's long-running conflict.
The statement said Israel's continued violations threaten to further escalate regional tensions, undermine regional peace and stability, and weaken respect for international law and the UN Charter.
The ministers called on the international community to adopt a firm and principled position against what they described as ongoing Israeli aggression in Syria and urged concrete measures under international law to end such violations, calling for full compliance with the 1974 Disengagement Agreement and the withdrawal of Israeli forces from occupied Syrian territories.
Syria's state-run Al-Ikhbariya TV reported, citing a military source, that Israeli warplanes carried out eight airstrikes early Tuesday on the runway of the Abu al-Duhur military airport in Idlib province, causing material damage but no casualties.
The Abu al-Duhur military airport, a major Syrian airbase, is situated near routes linking parts of Idlib, Aleppo and Hama provinces.
Following the attack, Syria's foreign affairs authority and the Turkish Foreign Ministry condemned the strikes in separate statements, describing them as violations of Syria's territorial integrity and unity. ■

Israeli security officials have also reportedly warned against an “unnecessary” escalation with Türkiye, expressing concern that public statements by Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz could further inflame tensions.
The reported disagreement with the military comes as Netanyahu faces a difficult electoral landscape, with recent opinion polls showing his governing bloc falling short of the parliamentary majority needed to form a government.

Syrian media reported Saturday that an Israeli drone struck a vehicle near the village of Beit Jinn in the Damascus countryside, wounding one person. The IDF has not confirmed carrying out the attack.
The report comes during a week of sharply heightened tensions following an unusual Israeli strike on Syrian territory that damaged the Abu al-Duhur military airfield in Idlib, including runways and other facilities.
Israel said that operation was carried out after receiving information that Turkey intended to deploy forces at the site.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu addressed the strike this week, warning that Israel would not tolerate a Turkish military presence expanding farther south in Syria.
“We will not tolerate Turkish military entrenchment moving south, because it threatens us, and we made that clear in general,” Netanyahu said. “We saw that Turkey intended to establish itself at an airfield south of its line, near Aleppo, and we sent a message: Don’t. The message was delivered, but apparently they didn’t hear it. So we made sure they understood.”
Meanwhile, U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoy to Syria and ambassador to Turkey, Tom Barrack, did not rule out the possibility that Israel’s unusual strike this week was intended to provoke a Turkish military response.
In an interview with content creator Mario Nawfal, Barrack said: “One theory is they simply tried to bait Turkey. It’s a very aggressive move, but one that might play well going into elections. That’s one theory.”
Barrack also referred to Turkey’s downing of a Russian warplane in 2015 and said that election periods can sometimes produce “irrational judgment.”
The latest reports also come as relations between Israel and Turkey continue to deteriorate. On Friday, Ankara asked Interpol to issue a Red Notice for Netanyahu over what Turkey describes as “genocide” in connection with the Gaza flotilla affair.
Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said the request followed an arrest warrant issued on July 14 and was part of ongoing legal proceedings in Turkey.

'Sometimes dynastic politics has its benefits': Akhilesh on how 5 family MPs helped SP
Edited by: Rajeev Singh / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 18:33 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
"Sometimes dynastic politics has its benefits," Akhilesh Yadav said with a laugh.
NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav on Saturday said the party had an "advantage" in avoiding a possible split as five members of his family are among its MPs, adding that "sometimes dynastic politics has its benefits".He suggested that even if some MPs left, the party would retain enough numbers to remain intact."Have you ever wondered why the entire party did not split? Because there are five MPs from the same family. We also have several Muslim MPs, and some staunch socialists, so our numbers would not decrease," he told news agency PTI.
Yadav also sought to put to rest any speculation about the SP breaking its political alliances, saying the party had consistently stood by its commitments."The Samajwadi Party never breaks alliances. When the Samajwadi Party agrees to move forward with others, it stands by them, and we have always honoured our commitments."The SP chief said his party's broader goal was to form a government based on socialist ideology and social justice, with the PDA, referring to 'pichhda' or backward classes, Dalits and 'alpsankhyak' or minorities, at the centre of its politics."They are scared of the PDA, that is why they are trying to misrepresent the PDA.
The greater the suffering, the stronger the PDA will become," Yadav said.
Yadav attacks BJP over rising prices
Yadav then turned his criticism towards the BJP government over the rising cost of essential commodities, particularly with festivals approaching."Everything is becoming expensive today. Diesel, petrol, everything," he said, while questioning the government over the rise in sugar prices.He also questioned the use of sugarcane for ethanol production, alleging that the policy was benefiting businesses while consumers were facing higher prices."They are mixing ethanol in petrol for profit, and also hiking sugar prices to maximise their gains. The question is: whose pocket is this money going into?"The former Uttar Pradesh chief minister also questioned claims of rising per capita income, pointing to the number of people still dependent on subsidised rations."What is the per capita income of these 15 crore people?" he asked.

Türkiye hosts STRATCOM forums on AI, global order in Tokyo

Türkiye’s Communications Directorate held the STRATCOM Roundtable and Public Forum in Tokyo with the Embassy of the Republic of Türkiye, bringing together officials and experts to discuss emerging technologies, strategic communication and economic security.
The roundtable examined “Changing Global Order in the Age of Emerging Technologies”, while the public forum focused on “Managing Economic Security in the Age of Geopolitical Competition”.
Economic security
Participants discussed AI’s impact on global governance, digital sovereignty, information security and international cooperation, as well as critical technologies, trusted supply chains, data security and the digital economy.
Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said geopolitical, technological and social changes were reshaping global power. He warned that digital technologies were also creating vulnerabilities through manipulation, polarisation and uncertainty.
“Today, we are facing a situation that can be described as both a crisis of truth and a crisis of communication,” Duran said, calling for international cooperation and shared principles.
Türkiye’s Ambassador to Tokyo Oguzhan Ertugrul said Türkiye and Japan could play a constructive role in supporting global peace, stability and prosperity. Deputy Communications Director Ferhat Pirincci highlighted AI’s transformation of international relations and public diplomacy, as well as disinformation’s effects on economic stability, investment and public confidence.
Disinformation and critical technologies
AK Party Deputy Chair Omer Ileri said geopolitical and technological transformations were occurring simultaneously, with protectionism, domestic production, AI, data and market concentration reshaping competition.
University of Tokyo academic Akira Igata discussed disinformation targeting companies involved in critical mineral supply chains and data centre infrastructure. Professor Kazuto Suzuki examined the role of critical technologies and strategic minerals in geo-economic competition.
Kunihiko Miyake of the Canon Institute for Global Studies said effective strategic communication required a clear strategy and strong narrative, adding that technology alone could not guarantee success.
The events aimed to strengthen Türkiye-Japan dialogue on strategic and crisis communication and promote cooperation on communication risks and opportunities in the age of AI.
Strategic communication dialogue
The events contributed to strengthening institutional dialogue between Türkiye and Japan in the fields of strategic communication and crisis communication, evaluating common approaches to communication risks and opportunities emerging in the age of AI, and increasing the sharing of international information and experience.
Held annually with international participation, STRATCOM continues to serve as a global consultation platform where current issues in strategic communication are discussed from different perspectives, bringing together public institutions, international organisations, academia, the media and the technology sector.

Anadolu staff

- Britain weighs further sanctions as Western governments demand accountability from Tel Aviv
- Israeli officials reportedly view some international moves through lens of upcoming election
Israel is facing mounting diplomatic pressure from several of its traditional partners over its policies in the occupied Palestinian territories and military actions in the region, with Israeli media describing the country’s international standing as increasingly strained.
Israeli news outlet Ynet reported Friday that a series of statements and measures from Australia, Britain, Canada, Germany and other countries in recent days had highlighted Israel’s growing international isolation, particularly in its relations with Europe.
The report pointed to criticism over Israel’s settlement plans in the occupied West Bank, its decision not to pursue a criminal investigation into the killing of seven World Central Kitchen (WCK) aid workers in Gaza, and its latest military action in Syria.
Six European countries condemned Israel’s plans for construction in the E1 area near the illegal Ma’ale Adumim settlement, according to Ynet.
The E1 project has long drawn international criticism because construction in the area would further fragment the occupied West Bank and undermine the territorial continuity of a future Palestinian state.
Britain, meanwhile, is considering additional measures against Israel over the settlement plans, the report said.
European officials have warned that construction in E1 poses an “existential threat” to the two-state solution, though some have also expressed concern that punitive measures ahead of Israel’s Oct. 27 election could strengthen Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his right-wing allies.
Western countries condemn decision on WCK killings
Australia, Britain and Canada also issued a joint condemnation after the Israeli military decided not to open a criminal investigation into the April 2024 strikes that killed seven WCK employees in Gaza.
The three countries described the decision as “shameful” and said the victims and their families deserved justice and accountability.
Australian Foreign Minister Penny Wong separately expressed “outrage” over the decision, while Canada called it “unacceptable” and Britain said it was “appalled and angry” on behalf of the families of three British nationals killed in the attack.
Poland, whose citizen was also among those killed, expressed disappointment and called on Israeli authorities to cooperate with a Polish investigation.
The aid workers were killed when Israeli forces repeatedly struck their clearly marked convoy in the Gaza Strip.
The Israeli military acknowledged failures in the operation but concluded that the commanders’ actions did not raise reasonable suspicion of criminal conduct.
US criticism over Syria strike
The diplomatic pressure has also extended to Israel’s actions in Syria amid rising tensions with Türkiye.
Ynet highlighted criticism from the US following an Israeli strike on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur military airbase, which has fueled tensions between Israel and Türkiye.
US Ambassador to Türkiye and Special Envoy for Syria and Iraq Tom Barrack said Washington’s intelligence agencies had found no evidence supporting Israeli claims that Türkiye was moving military assets into the Syrian base.
The developments come amid growing debate inside Israel over Netanyahu’s foreign policy as the country heads toward parliamentary elections.
Recent Israeli analyses have increasingly focused on whether military and diplomatic confrontations could become part of Netanyahu’s election strategy. 
Ynet has reported that concerns are growing that military escalation could be used for political gain, while another analysis said Netanyahu may have an incentive to portray resistance to international pressure as a political asset ahead of the vote.
Israel’s parliamentary elections are scheduled for Oct. 27.

Kaarel Tarand: A beggar's bag still has room for matches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
11:01:00 UTC
20:01:00 KST

Kaarel Tarand: A beggar's bag still has room for matches
Revised GDP figures showing Estonia's economy performed better than previously thought should prompt the government to reconsider past spending cuts and restore funding disproportionately taken from culture, Kaarel Tarand writes.
Statistics Estonia recently published revised national accounts figures for the past four years. With additional data incorporated, the results showed that Estonia's economy performed better than previously thought and that real gross domestic product is higher than had been estimated.
Predicting and rapidly measuring the impact of all manner of external influences, crises and shocks is a thankless task, as analysts have emphasized in commenting on the new figures. Things can go one way or another; this time, the result is encouraging.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal was also quick to seize on the message, saying that "this also changes the story we have been telling about the Estonian economy. It is no longer entirely accurate to speak of an economic downturn lasting nearly two consecutive years." The message is aimed primarily at his political opponents: It is high time they stopped the incessant complaining that the government has destroyed Estonia's economy, does not know how to manage it and has plunged the people into poverty, because the facts show otherwise — things are not rosy, but the heading is right.
Statistics Estonia's work proceeds according to schedule, but the timing of the release could hardly be more convenient for the government as it prepares next year's state budget. The new data will have to be reflected in the Ministry of Finance's summer economic forecast, on which the draft budget is based and which is traditionally released in late August.
If GDP is larger and growth faster, that means additional money becomes available to spend. Having that money on hand matters more in the run-up to a Riigikogu election than in other years, particularly for a coalition that has only just technically become a minority government and whose opponents in parliament can presumably be expected to use every means at their disposal to make life difficult for its bill.
A word problem simple enough for an elementary school student might go something like this: If the country's GDP turned out to be larger than previously thought and the indicator used as the basis for budgeting — the overall tax burden as a share of GDP — remained the same or actually increased, did the state, in retrospect, collect less or more tax revenue available for spending than had been projected in recent years' state budgets? This assumes that the Tax and Customs Board's collection capacity remained stable and that it did not simply sit on its hands after new taxes or tax rates were introduced. The answer is that there was more money, which means fiscal conservatism was taken too far.
As always, there is another side to the coin. If the better figures transformed the story of recession into a story of growth in the prime minister's eyes, they must at the very least also call into question the almost biblical tale of suffering that has come to be known collectively as "cuts."
At least the Parempoolsed party will undoubtedly continue marketing its obsession. The April version went like this: "Estonia's public finances are in such disarray that much more painful decisions lie ahead. That is true regardless of who forms the government after the 2027 election. Cuts will have to be made in every sector. The only questions are how and by how much."
Hopefully, competitive politics will nevertheless produce some who want to put an end to this fixation on cuts, which is sowing deep pessimism at least in the public sector. As a side effect, it also entrenches the utterly detached-from-reality myth of an efficient and frugal private sector and a lax and profligate public sector. The former is supposedly locked in an uncompromising struggle with the latter, to the point of amputating every last limb.
Ending the fanatical fixation on cuts that is holding the future hostage is one thing. But we also need to look back at the recent past and ask whether and how the suffering caused by reliance on poor data can be remedied, so that the injustice and inequality created by the cuts do not become permanently embedded in improved circumstances and future budgets.
If one area of government lost a larger percentage of its budget to cuts than others and therefore now has a correspondingly lower base, then giving everyone the same percentage increase will simply cause those losses to continue accumulating in the years ahead.
I am thinking first and foremost of cultural spending. As we may recall, the culture minister's zeal for cuts (or ineptitude in negotiations) resulted in the cultural sector accounting for more than 10 percent of the state's total cuts in 2025, even though cultural spending represented just 1.8 percent of the state budget.
This injustice led cultural workers to demonstrate on Toompea — even if the protests had no impact on the budget — and prompted many rather bleak statements about the bright future supposedly awaiting professional arts and culture. Even the current state budget provided cultural workers with a smaller percentage pay increase than employees in other areas of government.
To spell it out in the simplest possible terms: There was once an understanding in this country that education and cultural workers with higher education qualifications performed work of comparable complexity and should therefore receive comparable pay. But then their paths diverged. This year, the minimum starting salary for a teacher is €1,970, compared with €1,720 for a cultural worker, even though many cultural workers also do educational work.
The difference is €250 a month. On top of that, cultural work has no so-called career model, meaning there are no coefficients guaranteed by law or agreement to compensate for increasing experience and professional mastery, as there are for senior and master teachers.
If the minimum salary in both categories were raised by 10 percent next year, the gap would widen by €25 and with each subsequent year it would grow by ever larger increments.
Restoring fairness therefore begins by first putting back into the cultural budget the money that has been disproportionately cut from it over several years and only then multiplying that restored amount by whatever percentage increase may be possible. That is the minimum. It still would not provide managers of public-sector cultural institutions with a guaranteed way out of a wage-policy situation that has by now completely collapsed, while many institutions also need to restore budget lines for training, business travel and employer-provided benefits that were cut to zero out of sheer necessity.
I will skip the endlessly repeated defense of culture, which Maarja Kangro recently summed up nicely in Sirp. It cannot compete anyway with the public relations machinery of the more powerful ministries, which they use to garnish their slices of the budget pie at every opportunity.
When a defense industry company's building caught fire in Lasnamäe a week ago, everyone, starting with the prime minister, immediately pointed an accusing finger toward Russia. (The detectives Vera, Grace and Lynley, familiar to everyone from TV, not to mention the young Morse, would hardly be satisfied with such a simple explanation: It all seems a little too convenient, with a vigilant citizen and the main suspects apprehended and ready-made for the plot.)
Security officials offered recommendations on how companies could further improve their protection and increase security. And what that means, of course, is that defense spending must increase as well because companies can hardly be expected to fight a war against Russia with their own money.
During the Soviet occupation, Russia once attacked Estonia's cultural institutions with matches as well: Devastating fires broke out within a short span of time at St. Nicholas' Church (1982), the Estonian Drama Theater (1983) and the Sassi-Jaani farmstead at the Estonian Open Air Museum (1984). Regardless of the official findings of the investigations, people at the time were convinced that Moscow was behind them and that they were attacks on our national culture. This caused a nationwide sense of despair, although money and manpower were scraped together from wherever possible to compensate for the damage and restore what could be restored.
It is tempting to ask: If no defense of culture will do the trick, must we really stage a false-flag operation even in a free country and make a burnt offering to secure adequate funding for the cultural budget? Or is it possible to reach mutual understanding and agreement before it comes to that, knowing that, in retrospect, there has always been more money than the forecasts predicted?
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

Ministers keep quiet on laser weapons beyond DragonFire
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
12:00:44 BST
20:00:44 KST

The Ministry of Defence has declined to say what directed energy weapons it is developing alongside DragonFire, telling Parliament only that further announcements will be made when appropriate, in a written answer published this week.
Luke Pollard, the Minister of State for Defence, was responding to Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative MP for Huntingdon, who asked with reference to paragraph 93 of the Defence Investment Plan what other systems were in development.
Mr Pollard said: “The Defence Investment Plan commits £490 million to Directed Energy Weapons over the next four years. This investment will deliver DragonFire and help ensure the UK remains at the forefront of this technology within NATO, while laying the groundwork for the next generation of DEW capabilities in collaboration with UK industry.”
He said: “This forms part of a longer-term investment programme. The DIP also sets out plans to invest at least £20 billion in new weapons and munitions between 2030 and 2035, including DEW for both land and maritime platforms.”
He added: “Further announcements on DEW will be made when appropriate.”
The reference to land platforms is the detail that carries most weight. DragonFire has been developed as a naval system and is due to be fitted to a Type 45 destroyer, but a land-based directed energy weapon would address a different problem, namely the drones and loitering munitions now used in volume against ground forces and fixed installations.
The British Army has already trialled a separate laser system mounted on a Wolfhound armoured vehicle, and has tested a radio frequency directed energy weapon designed to disable multiple drones at once rather than engaging them individually. Neither has been announced as a programme of record.
The economics are what drive interest in the technology. A laser engagement costs a few pounds in electricity against targets that cost thousands, which reverses the cost exchange that has troubled Western forces since Houthi drone attacks in the Red Sea saw multi-million pound missiles fired at aircraft worth a fraction of that. The constraints are power generation, cooling, and performance in poor weather.
DragonFire itself is being developed by MBDA with Leonardo and QinetiQ under a Defence Science and Technology Laboratory contract, and demonstrated high-power firings against aerial targets at the Hebrides range in 2024. The Ministry of Defence subsequently brought forward the planned in-service date, aiming to have it aboard a Royal Navy ship before the end of the decade.
The £490 million figure covers four years, which places directed energy some way down the list of Defence Investment Plan commitments. The plan allocates £26 billion to naval base infrastructure alone.
