Türkiye's Communications Directorate hosts STRATCOM events in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:43:18 UTC
19:43:18 KST

The STRATCOM Roundtable and STRATCOM Public Forum, organized by Türkiye's Communications Directorate in cooperation with the Embassy of the Republic of Türkiye in Tokyo, were held in Japan's capital, Tokyo on Saturday.
According to a statement by the Communications Directorate, the STRATCOM Roundtable, held under the theme Changing Global Order in the Age of Emerging Technologies, and the STRATCOM Public Forum, titled Managing Economic Security in the Age of Geopolitical Competition, were organized in Tokyo as part of the International Strategic Communication Summit (STRATCOM Summit).
The forum addressed the multidimensional effects of emerging technologies -- particularly artificial intelligence -- on global order, strategic communication and economic security.
At the STRATCOM Roundtable, held under the theme Changing Global Order in the Age of Emerging Technologies, the effects of emerging technologies on global governance, strategic communication, digital sovereignty, information security and international cooperation were evaluated from a policy perspective.
Participants exchanged views on the impacts of artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging technologies on international power balances, technological competition, combating disinformation, the use of new technologies in strategic communication, the transformation of public diplomacy and technological applications in crisis management.
Economic security
As part of the program, the panel titled Managing Economic Security in the Age of Geopolitical Competition, held during the STRATCOM Public Forum, discussed the effects of intensifying geopolitical competition on economic security policies, critical technologies, trusted supply chains, data security and the transformation of the digital economy from different perspectives.
Communications Director Burhanettin Duran also addressed the program in a video message.
Duran said the world is going through a period of profound geopolitical, technological and social transformation, adding that alongside economic power, military capacity and diplomatic influence, the ability to build narratives, shape perceptions, communicate with global audiences and build trust is becoming an increasingly important dimension of national and international power.
Pointing out that digital technologies expand access to information and communication opportunities while also creating new vulnerabilities such as manipulation, polarization and uncertainty, Duran said: "Today, we are facing a situation that can be described as both a crisis of truth and a crisis of communication.”
“These crises operate through perceptions, emotions, fears and expectations,” he said, adding: “They can affect societies before governments have the opportunity to fully understand what is happening.”
“That is why a comprehensive and multidimensional approach is needed. No country, institution or organization can achieve this alone,” Duran stated.
“We need greater international cooperation, the sharing of experience and the development of common principles," he stressed.
Stronger cooperation between Türkiye and Japan
Türkiye's Ambassador to Tokyo Oguzhan Ertugrul and Deputy Communications Director Ferhat Pirincci also delivered speeches during the panel.
Ertugrul drew attention to the uncertainties and multiple crises increasing pressure on the international order.
Emphasizing that global challenges require stronger cooperation based on justice, diplomacy and multilateralism, he pointed to the importance of regional ownership and the reform of global institutions.
Stating that Türkiye and Japan are two countries located at the western and eastern ends of Asia with complementary strategic capacities, Ertugrul said the two countries can play a constructive and proactive role in supporting global peace, stability and prosperity.
He also stressed that the event provided an important platform for raising awareness of the need for stronger cooperation and coordination between Türkiye and Japan in the face of ongoing geopolitical transformations.
Fight against disinformation
Pirincci further said emerging technologies, particularly AI, are transforming not only the economic and technological fields but also a wide range of areas from international relations to public diplomacy and strategic communication.
Emphasizing that information security and a trusted information ecosystem are among the fundamental elements of economic resilience, he noted that disinformation can have direct effects on economic stability, the investment environment and public confidence.
He said strategic communication is of critical importance for protecting accurate and reliable information, combating disinformation and strengthening societal resilience, adding that international cooperation and the development of common policies in this field are becoming increasingly important.
Pirincci also noted that Ankara and Tokyo possess significant and complementary expertise in technology, innovation, strategic communication and crisis management, adding that joint initiatives between the two countries will contribute to regional and global stability.
AK Party Deputy Chair and Head of Information and Communication Technologies Omer Ileri also spoke at the panel.
Ileri pointed out that simultaneous transformations are taking place in the geopolitical and technopolitical spheres.
He said protectionism and an emphasis on domestic production are gaining strength in geopolitical dynamics, while developments such as AI, the growing importance of data and market concentration are reshaping the technology field.
He also underlined the potential of Türkiye and Japan to contribute to the development of more consistent and human-centered approaches to these transformations.
Information manipulation
Akira Igata, project associate professor at the Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology at the University of Tokyo and director of the Economic Security Intelligence Laboratory, focused on the growing relationship between economic security and information manipulation.
Giving examples of disinformation and influence operations targeting companies operating in critical mineral supply chains and data center infrastructure, Igata emphasized the importance of public-private cooperation, information sharing and education in strengthening societal resilience.
Kazuto Suzuki, professor at the Graduate School of Public Policy at the University of Tokyo, discussed the role of critical technologies, rare earth elements and strategic minerals in geo-economic competition.
Noting that interdependencies among major powers, particularly the US and China, continue to shape economic security policies, Suzuki said diversifying critical supply chains and reducing strategic vulnerabilities are becoming increasingly important.
Kunihiko Miyake, director and special adviser at the Canon Institute for Global Studies, stressed that effective strategic communication requires a clear strategy and a strong narrative.
Pointing out that technological tools alone cannot guarantee successful communication, Miyake highlighted the importance of developing messages aligned with strategic objectives and tailored to target audiences.
Participants also exchanged views on protecting a trusted information ecosystem, ensuring the flow of accurate information during periods of economic crisis, the impact of digital platforms on the global economy and models of public-private cooperation.
Türkiye-Japan strategic communication dialogue
The events contributed to strengthening institutional dialogue between Türkiye and Japan in the fields of strategic communication and crisis communication, evaluating common approaches to communication risks and opportunities emerging in the age of AI, and increasing the sharing of international information and experience.
Held annually with international participation, STRATCOM continues to serve as a global consultation platform where current issues in strategic communication are discussed from different perspectives, bringing together public institutions, international organizations, academia, the media and the technology sector.

Sallaum Lines and Sallaum Logistics launch dedicated European automotive logistics company

2026-08-22

19:42:04 KST

Sallaum Lines today announced the launch of Sallaum Logistics Ltd, a dedicated European automotive logistics company that extends Sallaum’s ocean vehicle-transport network onto the road- giving manufacturers and dealers a single accountable partner from port to dealership across Europe.
Backed by Sallaum Lines’ experience, relationships and global network in maritime vehicle transportation, Sallaum Logistics will operate as an independent road logistics company focused on the movement of finished vehicles. The company is built for automotive manufacturers, OEMs, dealership groups, fleet operators, shipping companies and logistics partners that need dependable inland transport with visibility and professional execution.
The launch connects Sallaum’s ocean and inland operations into a single vehicle-transport chain, extending its expertise from sea to road. While Sallaum Lines continues to focus on global Ro-Ro Ocean transportation, Sallaum Logistics will support the next stage of the journey: moving vehicles from ports, compounds and distribution hubs to dealerships and final destinations across Europe.
“For years, customers have trusted Sallaum Lines to move vehicles across oceans with reliability, discipline and care. Sallaum Logistics carries that commitment further inland, giving automotive partners a road logistics company built on the same principles of safety, transparency and customer commitment. This is a natural continuation of the vehicle logistics journey from sea to road.” — Sami Sallaum, Chairman, Sallaum Lines.
A Focused Road Logistics Platform for Europe’s Automotive Industry
Sallaum Logistics has been created around a clear market need: automotive customers require an inland vehicle logistics partner that can deliver the same quality, accountability and communication standards expected in maritime transport.
Rather than competing as another general road carrier, Sallaum Logistics is being built as a focused automotive logistics platform- one that combines fleet-based execution, professional vehicle handling, cross-border capability and digital visibility.
The company’s services will encompass comprehensive Finished Vehicle Logistics solutions, covering vehicle transportation from European factories and inland terminals to ports for global shipment, cross-border transport, fleet distribution services, port-to-dealer and port-to-distribution center deliveries & vice versa. Sallaum Logistics will also offer vehicle processing, pre-delivery inspection and storage at selected sites, building on existing operations at the Port of Antwerp.
Built to Reduce Complexity After the Port
In automotive logistics, the inland handover after port arrival is often where pressure increases. Customers need to coordinate transport capacity, timing, vehicle condition, route planning, delivery visibility and final-mile communication.
Sallaum Logistics is designed to take responsibility for that stage of the journey. Its role is to help customers reduce fragmented coordination, improve delivery visibility and maintain consistent standards as vehicles move across European corridors.
Scalable Fleet, Operational Discipline and Long-Term Growth
Sallaum Logistics will launch with an initial fleet of 50 truck-and-trailer units, with a plan to expand toward 300 owned trucks by 2029. The fleet will use modern multi-car transporter configurations capable of carrying up to 10 vehicles, depending on vehicle type, route and each country’s road regulations.
The company will operate a mixed fleet model combining owned and strategically leased vehicles, allowing it to scale with customer demand while maintaining professional service standards and operational control.
Fleet reliability will be supported by strict European compliance, preventive maintenance, regular inspections, driver safety policies and manufacturer service standards.
Technology Designed for Visibility and Confidence
Sallaum Logistics will use integrated fleet management systems, transport monitoring tools and logistics software to support routing, fleet optimization and operational reporting. GPS tracking, telematics, route optimization and driver monitoring will give customers improved visibility over vehicle movement and delivery coordination.
As the company grows, Sallaum Logistics plans to continue investing in digital customer visibility and reporting platforms, supporting a more transparent and responsive finished vehicle logistics experience.
European Network and Growth Vision
Headquartered in Lithuania, Sallaum Logistics will begin operations across key European automotive markets including Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Spain, France, the Czech Republic and Poland, with further expansion into key port-connected European markets.
The network will be designed around major port-to-dealer and port-to-distribution center corridors across Western and Central Europe, connecting automotive gateways such as Antwerp, Bremerhaven, Rotterdam, Marseille and inland distribution hubs.
Over time, Sallaum Logistics plans to expand across major European automotive trade corridors, supported by operational depots for vehicle handling, staging and regional fleet distribution.
Responsible Growth and Sustainability
Sallaum Logistics is being developed with a responsible growth mindset. The company aims to reduce operational emissions while improving fleet efficiency, route planning and transport reliability.
Its sustainability priorities include Euro-compliant fleet standards, route optimization, fuel efficiency programs and future electrification for suitable shorter routes.
“Sallaum Logistics was created to make inland vehicle movement simpler, more visible and more dependable. We are building a road logistics company with professional drivers, clear communication, real-time visibility and a fleet plan designed for long-term scale. Our ambition is to give customers confidence in every stage of the inland journey.” — Edvinas Rybelis, CEO, Sallaum Logistics

Why trauma changes how our memory engages with our conscious experience
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:41:30 UTC
19:41:30 KST

When survivors of trauma recount their experiences, they are often questioned because of how they relay their stories. They may have problems remembering what happened, or their memories may be jumbled or even contradictory. People hearing those stories—attorneys, reporters, healthcare workers or friends—may expect a clearer, linear narrative.
Those unaffected by trauma may also be surprised to hear how the person acted in the moment. It’s easy to assume that someone experiencing a traumatic event would have a “fight or flight” response, instinctively fighting off a perpetrator or fleeing the scene—but that might not be the case.
Understanding the science of how trauma affects memory and behavior reveals why these responses can actually be expected and are not contradictory.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
In both my academic and clinical work as a psychologist, I have witnessed the impact trauma has on people’s memories and behaviors, especially when an event in their present life triggers something from their past.
Research shows that taking a trauma-informed approach, which prioritizes understanding and curiosity about someone’s experience as opposed to judgment or critical evaluation, increases empathy for survivors’ thoughts, feelings and behaviors.
How trauma affects the brain
According to the World Health Organization, approximately 70 percent of people worldwide report experiencing a traumatic event in their lifetime. The majority of these people do not develop PTSD, a clinical diagnosis of symptoms, such as having nightmares and flashbacks about the event, avoiding places that are reminders of it, and increased arousal that can make concentration and sleep difficult. Many survivors don’t meet criteria for PTSD but struggle with feeling distressed, depressed or anxious.
In traumatic situations, people often respond in unexpected ways, and they may second-guess themselves. This may happen particularly when someone experiences a repeated trauma, which is more likely than not due to how many people experience traumatic events.
Trauma also distorts how memories are stored and retrieved.
Research indicates that people experience traumatic memories differently than memories of other significant events, such as sad or positive experiences. Two of the main brain structures scientists believe are involved in storing traumatic memories are the hippocampus—responsible for memory storage—and the amygdala, which is responsible for processing emotions.
During trauma, the amygdala becomes highly active, processing emotions such as fear, and the hippocampus becomes overwhelmed by stress, leading to problems with memory storage.
Traumatic memories do not follow a neat, linear story. Instead, people may experience the memory as disconnected fragments of sensations, emotions, smells or images. Such memories cause the body to reexperience the past threat as if it is happening in the moment. This may cause a person to feel like running away or fighting back—flight or fight. Or they may freeze.
In other words, people don’t have the distant perspective they often feel with other memories from the past. Rather, they may feel they are reliving the original experience.
Misinterpreting victims’ behaviors
With this understanding, consider someone who experiences a trauma at the hands of a professional during an appointment. They may appear outwardly calm while it happens and then leave the session as they typically would—checking out, providing payment and possibly even scheduling the next appointment. While their response to act normally may seem odd, such behavior makes sense for someone trying to escape a threat.
Fight, flight or freeze responses have become widely known in popular culture. In a freeze response, a person’s mind goes blank and they may be unable to speak, leading to a “deer in the headlights” behavior.
On the other hand, a person may act paradoxically—perhaps by going on about their day as if nothing happened. They may not report the event or may question whether the incident even occurred. This represents another survival response—the lesser-known fawn response. This way of handling stress occurs when someone acts calm, appeases the threatening person and retreats to de-escalate the situation. Instead of literally backing away, in this example, the person metaphorically backs away by completing the session and exiting as expected without further conflict.
Outsiders may misconstrue these behaviors as evidence that a trauma did not actually happen or that a survivor lacks credibility. But that logic reflects common misconceptions about how people “should” remember or respond to trauma.
If this was the person’s first experience with a traumatic situation, afterward they are likely to feel afraid, disoriented or hyperalert. However, if they had previous similar experiences, this scenario may trigger past memories in the moment. This can muddy the experience even further, making it difficult to recall the incident later, especially under stressful circumstances.
When a survivor reports an incident and ultimately testifies against someone who harmed them, memory recall might be uniquely affected. Most people in this situation would be highly stressed, especially if the perpetrator were in the room.
To make matters worse, the feeling that the recalled memory is actually happening in the moment and not in the past may cause a survivor to convey a more fragmented story. They may also have either a more intense or detached emotional experience, depending on their own trauma responses.
Legal and other professionals unaware of the range of natural responses to trauma can easily misinterpret these behaviors as signs of lying or malingering.
In reality, the percentage of people who falsely report sexual assault, for example, is low—between 2 percent and 10 percent.
Providing better support
Research shows that people who better understand nuances of trauma and mental health in turn are more empathetic toward survivors. Some healthcare settings have adopted a trauma-informed approach to prevent retraumatization and build safety. Studies show that even being attentive to word choice can help ensure effective care for patients that avoids victim blaming.
A trauma-informed approach can also improve legal and justice systems so victims are better supported. This includes understanding why accounts aren’t linear and not equating memory inconsistencies with lying.
Research also shows that trauma-informed responses are equally important in everyday relationships. In friendships and close relationships, or in the workplace, patience and empathy convey a sense of respect, safety and trustworthiness. These offer a strong foundation for positive social and working relationships, which can lower a survivor’s distress and support their healing.
When people have a greater understanding of how trauma affects the brain, they gain insight into how survivors think, act and process their memories. What initially looks confusing or inconsistent is actually behavior that flows logically from a traumatized brain.
Having a trauma-informed perspective helps people to be better friends, co-workers and professionals. By extension, responding from this awareness may even help survivors understand their own reactions and experiences, which may ultimately aid their healing and ability to lead fulfilling lives.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

Death Toll Mounts After Russian 'Barbaric Double-Tap' Strike On Ukrainian Shopping Mall
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:37:30 UTC
19:37:30 KST

Search-and-rescue operations continued at the site of a devastating Russian drone attack on a shopping mall in the Ukrainian city of Kryviy Rih, as Russia continues to launch strikes across Ukraine.
Two Russian jet-powered drones struck the largest shopping mall in the south-central city on the afternoon on August 21, as many residents were out shopping at the end of the work week.
The attack killed at least 16, leaving more than 130 others injured, including 23 children, some of whom are in critical condition. A day later, four people remained unaccounted for.
"There was smoke. Everyone was shouting," Yuliana, a mall employee, recalled of the first moments following the attack in an interview with RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service.
She said the attack caused parts of the ceiling to collapse in a parking garage where some shoppers and staff had sought shelter during an air-raid alert, and that a car was blocking the entrance, forcing people to climb over metal barriers.
The fire at the site engulfed over 9,000 square meters and took hours to extinguish.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiha said Russia deliberately struck the site twice, and that the second wave of drones came after emergency responders arrived at the scene.
"Such barbaric double-tap strikes are intended to maximize civilian casualties. They prove Russia's status as a terrorist state," he wrote calling for “criminals responsible for such atrocities” to be brought to account.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, a native of Kryviy Rih, reiterated his call for air defense support -- new supplies of ballistic and other missile interceptors -- from international partners.
"Every day that Ukraine lacks air defense is a sacrifice that could have been avoided," he wrote on August 22.
European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc's defense and foreign ministers would discuss Ukraine's air defenses during their first meeting after the summer break in September.
The attack "shows the absolute and utter depravity of Moscow's war," Kallas wrote on X. "This is terror by design. Russia wants to make Ukrainian cities unliveable."
She also vowed to unveil "the most far-reaching Russia sanctions listings since the start of the war" to further increase pressure on Russia to end the war.
On August 22, Russia's air attacks continued to pound places across Ukraine, leaving at least 4 people killed and more than a dozen of others injured.
Zelenskyy said the Odesa, Dnipropetrovsk, Kharkiv, Donetsk, Sumy, Kherson, Chernihiv, and Mykolayiv regions came under attack overnight, with damage reported to residential buildings, energy and railway infrastructure facilities, and civilian enterprises.
Moscow has gained little ground at the front line in Ukraine since the beginning of the year, and has intensified its strikes against the country, often hitting civilian infrastructure and causing civilian casualties.
Ukraine has sought to bolster its air defense capabilities with help from the United States and its European partners but is struggling with a lack of US-made Patriot missiles. Washington has sent mixed signals about a potential agreement to grant Kyiv a license to produce Patriots.
Separately, since the beginning of summer, Kyiv has been actively responding to Russian attacks by targeting oil and military infrastructure inside Russia, leaving the country facing its worst fuel crisis in years.
Early on August 22, Ukrainian drones hit an oil refinery in Novokuybyshevsk in Russia's Samara region, 900 kilometers away. One person was killed, the local governor said.
The day before, the Ukrainian military targeted a Russian oil facility in Perm, more than 1,600 kilometers from Russia's border with Ukraine, and a military air base in the Volgograd region.
Kyiv's forces also hit a warehouse of major e-commerce retailer Ozon on August 22, expanding its attacks on the sector after weeks of strikes on facilities belonging to Russian online giant Wildberries.
Ozon confirmed the strike, saying 500 employees were evacuated "within minutes," but added that some had sustained injuries.
"We continue, through our long-range sanctions, to bring the consequences of the war back to where it came from," Zelenskyy said on August 21, referring to the campaign.

'Judges are not gods, won't get every judgment right': Outgoing SC Judge Sanjay Karol in farewell speech
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:34:42 UTC
19:34:42 KST

'Judges are not gods, won't get every judgment right': Outgoing SC Judge Sanjay Karol in farewell speech
Edited by: Kanchan Yadav / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 16:10 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
NEW DELHI: Retiring Supreme Court judge Justice Sanjay Karol in his farewell address on Saturday, said judges "are not gods and they will not get every judgment right." He also urged other judges to look beyond the facts of a case and see the person behind every litigant.The Supreme Court bid farewell to Justice Karol on his last working day, with Chief Justice of India Surya Kant and senior members of the Bar, including Solicitor General Tushar Mehta and Supreme Court Bar Association president Pradeep Rai paying tribute to the outgoing judge.“We, as judges, are not gods. We will not get every judgment right. What was always in our hands was simple: to see the person, not just the petitioner. A petition can only tell you the facts of a case, but it cannot tell you what the person has already lost or what he is hoping to seek from the courts. And perhaps that is why I have always said that judging requires a certain level of humility,” Justice Karol said.“The Constitution does not ask us merely to apply the law correctly. It asks us to apply it justly. That is perhaps why the responsibility of judging has always seemed larger to me than simply deciding who is legally correct,” he added.
Justice Karol, who was elevated to the Supreme Court on February 6, 2023, reflected on his nearly four-decade journey in the legal profession. He said the courtroom had never been merely a workplace for him, but a vehicle for something “greater and more important” than himself.“I will not pretend that this journey has been mine alone. This courtroom has not left me; it has supported me,” he said.Karol spent 40 years in courtrooms, initially as an advocate and later, for 19 years, as a judge. He said judges must learn to listen not only to arguments but also to the “eloquent silences” in courtrooms.“In the silence of the Bar, there is a way of listening,” he said, stressing that the judicial process was also about understanding what people were seeking “in the spaces between the words”.Recalling his first visit to Courtroom No. 1 of the Supreme Court in 1996, Justice Karol said the Bench appeared to him to be almost six feet above the ground.“Judging from there has taught me something about this courtroom's symbolism. From below, the height of the bench can appear to signify authority. From the comfort zone, it signifies something quite different, and that is responsibility with dignity and honesty,” he said.Justice Karol said the Supreme Court's true significance lay in the faith of ordinary citizens who approach it believing that someone would listen.“But we must also remember those who never reach those doors because justice is too distant, too expensive, too intimidating,” he said.Reflecting on constitutionalism and justice, Karol said concepts such as law, due process and constitutional legality could be understood through the idea of “dharma”, which he described not as ritual but as duty.“The duty of a judge is to respect justice and see that the person standing before the court, however small, however wretched, is seen and heard,” he said.Addressing the Bar, he said the principles of judging extended beyond courtrooms and judicial robes, with every individual responsible for judging their own choices, conduct and use of power.“There may be no courtrooms, no robes, no technical grounds, but in these small choices, each of us dispenses the measure of justice that we take,” he said.“A judge is a judge before he dons and after he takes off the robes,” he added.Referring to a point made by CJI Surya Kant a day earlier, Justice Karol said India had not only a living Constitution but also had to “live the Constitution”.“The greatness of our Constitution is tested not only in great cases. It is tested in ordinary conduct,” he said. Concluding his farewell address, Justice Karol said he was returning to “the most distinguished constitutional office," that of the ordinary citizen.
Born on August 23, 1961, Karol studied in Shimla and obtained his law degree from Himachal Pradesh University. He became advocate general of Himachal Pradesh in 1998 and served until 2003, and was designated a senior advocate in 1999.He was appointed a judge of the Himachal Pradesh high court in March 2007 and became chief justice of the Tripura high court in November 2018. He was later transferred as chief justice of the Patna high court in November 2019 before being elevated to the Supreme Court in February 2023.
Kanchan Yadav is a writer at The Times of India, where she covers business, politics, international affairs and social issues. Her reporting also focuses on policy, governance and economic developments, with a close lens on how decisions in corridors of power affect everyday lives and community well-being.

Man hospitalised after bamboo scaffolding collapses in Sham Shui Po
Victim suffers head injuries after being trapped under scaffolding on Nam Cheong Street, police say
A Hong Kong man has been hospitalised after being trapped by fallen bamboo scaffolding at a building in Sham Shui Po, prompting authorities to launch an investigation.
Emergency services were called to 105-107 Nam Cheong Street at around 3.49pm on Saturday following reports scaffolding measuring about 15 metres by 33 metres (49 feet by 108 feet) had partially collapsed and trapped the victim.
According to police, the victim, who is believed to be in his fifties or sixties, suffered head injuries but was conscious when taken to Princess Margaret Hospital in Kwai Chung for treatment.
Police have classified the case as an industrial accident, and an investigation into the cause of the collapse is ongoing.
The Hong Kong and Kowloon Bamboo Scaffolding Workers Union said that according to workers interviewed at the scene, the scaffolding collapsed after heavy construction materials were stored on an upper platform, causing the supporting base poles to snap.
A worker at the site told the union that his colleague on the upper platform was using ropes to lower bags of construction waste to other labourers below just before the incident.

This yeast supplement may boost cancer-fighting immunity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:34:22 UTC
19:34:22 KST

This yeast supplement may boost cancer-fighting immunity
- Date:
- August 22, 2026
- Source:
- Trinity College Dublin
- Summary:
- A simple yeast-based food supplement may help restore the immune system’s ability to fight cancer, according to new research in mice. Scientists found that yeast beta-glucan reprogrammed early immune cells in the bone marrow, leading to stronger, longer-lasting cancer-fighting responses against colorectal, skin, and breast cancer cells.
- Share:
Researchers at Trinity College Dublin and University College Dublin (UCD) have found that a yeast-based dietary supplement can strengthen immune cells involved in fighting cancer in mice.
In experiments with obese laboratory mice, the researchers found that adding the supplement to the animals' diets changed the way immune cells developed and produced stronger cancer-fighting responses.
Obesity can interfere with immune function, making it more difficult for the body to respond effectively to tumors. The new findings suggest that a yeast-based supplement could potentially help restore some of that lost immune activity.
The research was published in the scientific journal Cell Reports. The study was led by Frederick Sheedy, Associate Professor in Immunology in Trinity's School of Biochemistry and Immunology, and Helen Roche, Professor in Nutrigenomics, UCD School of Public Health, Physiotherapy and Sports Science and Director of the UCD Conway Institute.
Training Immune Cells Through Diet
Dr. Anna Ledwith, postdoctoral researcher in Prof. Roche's group and first author of the research paper, said: "We wanted to investigate whether a common dietary supplement, yeast beta-glucan, could reprogram early-stage immune cells in the bone marrow to produce long-lasting, enhanced anti-tumor immune responses.
"Mice were fed a standard or high-fat diet supplemented with yeast beta-glucan for 4-12 weeks, and then their immune system was challenged by different types of cancer cells: colorectal, skin, and breast cancer. The study also tested whether yeast supplementation could overcome immune dysfunction caused by obesity and whether protective effects persist after weight loss."
The researchers wanted to determine whether consuming yeast beta-glucan could produce a form of lasting immune training by changing early immune cells in the bone marrow. They also examined whether the supplement could counter the immune problems caused by obesity.
Prof. Roche said the findings show for the first time that consuming yeast beta-glucan in the diet is enough to trigger trained immunity by altering bone marrow stem cells. Earlier studies achieved similar effects using injections.
Commenting on the significance of the findings, Prof. Roche added: "This is the first demonstration that dietary delivery of yeast beta-glucan is sufficient to induce trained immunity through reprogramming of bone marrow stem cells. Previous research required injections.
"Crucially, this dietary intervention restores anti-tumor innate immunity in obese mice and reverses long-term immune memory defects that persist even after weight loss, a major unmet clinical challenge."
Reversing Immune Problems Linked to Obesity
Obesity affects millions of people around the world and can significantly disrupt immune function, increasing susceptibility to both infections and cancer. These immune changes can continue even after a person loses weight.
That persistence is an important challenge because weight loss does not necessarily erase all of obesity's long-term effects on the immune system. In the mouse experiments, yeast beta-glucan helped reverse immune memory problems that remained after weight loss.
Cancer, meanwhile, continues to be one of the leading causes of death worldwide. Researchers are therefore looking for safe, widely available approaches that could help restore immune function and potentially work alongside existing cancer treatments.
Yeast beta-glucan is already sold as a dietary supplement and has a strong safety record. That makes it a practical candidate for future studies in people.
A Potential Addition to Cancer Treatment
Looking to the future, Professor Sheedy said: "This research paves the way for dietary intervention studies in people living with obesity, chronic infections and other immunocompromised populations. The yeast beta-glucan used, WellmuneTM, from Kerry Group, is already food-grade and commercially available, facilitating rapid clinical trials.
"Ultimately, a simple dietary supplement could help boost the immune system's cancer-fighting ability, complementing existing treatments such as chemotherapy and immunotherapy, with the potential to improve vaccine responses and resistance to infection."
The researchers say the findings could now support dietary intervention studies involving people with obesity, chronic infections, and other conditions associated with weakened immune function.
Because the specific yeast beta-glucan used in the study is already commercially available as a food-grade supplement, researchers believe it could move relatively quickly into clinical testing. Future studies will need to determine whether the immune benefits seen in mice can also be reproduced in humans.

Materials provided by Trinity College Dublin. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

- Anna E. Ledwith, Hannah Prendeville, Cian JH. Horneck Johnston, Stephen P. Cunningham, John P. McGrath, Carrie Corkish, Aaron M. Walsh, Fatma Koc, Hugo Charles-Messance, Vasile Mihai Sularea, Caitlín Ní Chasaide, Heike C. Hawerkamp, David K. Finlay, Lydia Lynch, Kingston H.G. Mills, Catherine Stanton, Helen M. Syria requests to join anti-chemical weapons partnership

Breadcrumb
Syria requests to join anti-chemical weapons partnership
Syria on Friday said it had requested to join the International Partnership Against Impunity for the Use of Chemical Weapons on the anniversary of a 2013 chemical attack on a suburb of the capital Damascus.
In a joint statement with France commemorating the attack during former leader Bashar al-Assad's rule on rebel-held areas, Syria announced its bid to join the partnership of dozens of countries, launched by Paris in January 2018.
France welcomed the step as "a clear demonstration of Syria's commitment to strengthening accountability and justice and combating impunity" following its more than decade-long civil war.
Damascus and Paris also said they "commemorate the victims, extend their deepest sympathies and solidarity to their families, and reaffirm their joint commitment to supporting efforts to uncover the truth, ensure justice, and hold those responsible for these crimes accountable".
In August 2013, the Syrian army under Assad was accused of using chemical weapons to target areas then under rebel control.
According to US intelligence and rights groups, more than 1,400 men, women and children died as a result.
With Syria at the height of its civil war, the Assad government denied responsibility, but agreed to hand over its chemical arsenal in order to avert US strikes.
Assad went on to remain in power for more than a decade, only to be ousted in 2024 by Islamist-led rebels, headed by now President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Survivors of the attacks, including medics, at the time risked their lives by posting dozens of videos online, and spoke to journalists about the horror they had witnessed.
The footage showed dozens of corpses, many of them children, outstretched on the ground.
Other images showed unconscious children, people foaming at the mouth and doctors trying to help them breathe.
The scenes provoked revulsion and condemnation around the globe.
'Painful chapter'
A United Nations report later said there was clear evidence sarin gas had been used.
Syria agreed to join the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) and disclose and hand over its toxic stockpile under Russian and US pressure, averting the threat of strikes by Washington and its allies.
But that was not the last of the chemical attacks: the OPCW went on to blame Assad's forces for others later in the civil war.
Marking 13 years since the attack, Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani called it "one of the most painful chapters in Syria's history".
"Tomorrow, the Syrian Arab Republic begins a new phase in dealing with the legacy of these weapons. We have initiated the necessary technical and logistical procedures for their disposal, in cooperation with our international partners," he added, also vowing to pursue those involved in the attack.
Several Syrian officers linked to the attack have been arrested since Assad's fall.
Syria's civil war began in 2011, with a brutal crackdown on dissent that yielded an armed rebellion. More than half a million people ended up being killed, with millions more forced into exile.
The OPCW reinstated Syria last month, five years after taking the unprecedented step of stripping it of its voting rights.

It Is Not Putin’s War. It’s Russia’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:31:00 UTC
19:31:00 KST

In a recent issue of The Economist, one of Russia’s richest men set out why the West should worry less about Ukraine and more about Russia. In an opinion piece and nearly 60 hours of interviews, the sanctioned oligarch Andrey Melnichenko argues that “broken Russia” would be bad for the world.
In his account, the war did not begin because Russia chose to invade; it began when trust between great powers broke down, at which point “politics does not direct events; it is led by them.” Ukraine appears mostly as scenery. That is a sophisticated version of long-established trickery allowing Russia to escape accountability for its crimes.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Western media have developed a weird habit. Russia invades Ukraine, but headlines often say “Putin” did. Russian missiles kill civilians, but are then called “Putin’s missiles.” And the pattern continues. This is a factual error, a moral dishonesty, and a strategic mistake.
Putin ordered the invasion. But he is not personally flying fighter-bombers, developing lethal drones, and celebrating murderous missile strikes on TV. Russians do that: Russian officers, Russian engineers, and Russian journalists.
This is Russia’s war. Meekly calling it “Putin’s war” is preposterous and negligent.
Putin does not wage war alone
“Putin’s war” may sound fitting because Russia is a dictatorship. It is inaccurate because, for all the tawdry uniform posturing by Putin, wars are not fought by dictators. Russia’s war is fought by its army, and depends on millions of Russian men and women who keep the war machine running. Moreover, a seemingly victorious initial onslaught drew undeniable public support, with only cracks in the triumphant narratives causing visible discontent (more on that later).
Russian Strikes Damage Infrastructure and Utilities in Odesa Region, Injuring 1
This does not mean that every Russian bears the same guilt as a war criminal in Bucha. Criminal guilt is individual, but political and historical responsibility is broader. Nations can be responsible for wars even when individuals differ in their degree of culpability.
We say Nazi Germany invaded Poland. We do not reduce that war to Hitler. Nor did responsibility end with him. Germany paid reparations, lost territory, was occupied and partitioned, and saw hundreds of thousands investigated and tried. Yet for Russia, Western discourse grants a conspicuous exemption.
The euphemism gives Russia an indulgence – at home and abroad
At home, a criminal war does not require every citizen to be a fanatic. It requires enough willing participants and supporters, and enough people who choose comfort over conscience. For the latter, “Putin’s war” provides an easy moral escape route. It tells them: this is not really about you. It is one man’s responsibility.
Abroad, the myth of an inculpable and almost holy Russia is preserved: a Russia of ballet, literature, and the mysterious Russian soul. Meanwhile, Russian troops level Ukrainian cities. This is how the “good Russians” narrative works: they oppose the war in words while defending Russia as an entity that must remain intact.
Of course, there are Russians who genuinely oppose the war. But they are exceptions to a national pattern, not proof that the pattern does not exist. And if Russia as a nation is not responsible for a war fought by its own state, army, and citizens, the concept of responsibility in international relations becomes void.
The bet on ‘ordinary Russians’ has failed
Apparently, one reason for the “Putin, not Russia” formula is tactical. The idea was to avoid alienating ordinary Russians in the hope that they might eventually turn against the war. After more than four years of mass slaughter, that hope looks naïve and oblivious. Bucha, Mariupol, the stolen children, and missile strikes on Ukrainian apartment blocks did not produce national unrest. The endless funerals of Russian soldiers did not produce one either.
Russia’s polling environment is obviously distorted. Still, Levada published a defense of the center’s methodology, arguing that response rates have not meaningfully changed since before the war. The available data do not support the notion of a hidden anti-war majority. Russia Matters, summarizing Levada’s February 2026 data, reported that 72.2% of respondents supported the actions of the Russian army, with opposition at only 16.7%. That same survey, ostensibly, found 67.2% wanting negotiations to begin. However, most of that 67% want the war ended only on Russia’s terms. Other research using Gallup and Levada data found evidence of strong public support for the war.
What has produced tangible irritation in Russia is not the murder of Ukrainians, but inconvenience at home: fuel shortages, Internet outages, and other consequences of the growing reach of Ukrainian drones.
Months of Ukrainian strikes on targets inside Russia have done something four years of war never managed: produced visible public anger, caught on camera and in social media posts. They have even translated into a marginal dip in Putin’s approval rating.
“It is not just the fuel shortages and internet outages that make people angry, but the widening gap between reality and the Kremlin’s rhetoric,” writes The Economist. In other words, as long as they were comfortable and realities aligned with the government’s narratives, the people largely accepted the war.
This contrast is revealing. Four years of Ukrainian suffering did not shake Russian society. Disruption to Russian comfort did.
The case of Melnichenko as elite whitewash
The Economist’s package around Melnichenko is a fine specimen of Russian elite demagoguery. Russia starts a war, commits atrocities, threatens Europe. Yet somehow the warning offered is not about a broken Ukraine and the menace Russia poses, but about the danger of a broken Russia.
The essay’s word choices are revealing. Melnichenko writes that Russia concluded diplomacy had run its course and then “acted” – not invaded. He calls the 2014 popular revolution in Kyiv a “political upheaval.” He traces the war’s origins to a familiar claim: that Moscow’s security concerns went unheeded.
Melnichenko writes that it is “in Russian eyes, a war against the West as a whole.” He does grant Ukraine a paragraph – with a passing acknowledgement that it is more than a battlefield, but a “society and a political will” that has paid a heavy price – yet that sentence organizes nothing else in the essay. Moreover, that paragraph ends with a sweeping claim about a negative relationship between Ukrainian security and “Russia’s sovereign agency.”
The argument from start to finish concerns Russia’s relationship with the West. What Ukraine’s security actually requires is left out. The victim becomes secondary. The aggressor becomes a system whose integrity must be handled with utmost care.
Worth noting, too, is what is absent. In an essay of over 3,000 words, countless war crimes go unmentioned. There is just a line about a “terrible price.” Everything else is written in the register of an engineer: sovereignty, fertilizer flows, nuclear risk. He presents himself as a neutral system-thinker rather than a political actor. A sanctioned oligarch – that essentially means a part of the Russian exhaustive state system – presenting a political and moral crisis as disinterested physics is yet another round of profoundly dishonest and dangerous manipulative rhetoric.
This is why the West must stop using language that narrows responsibility to Putin. The “it’s Putin” formula is not merely an innocent journalistic blunder. It helps Russia’s elites whitewash Russia, evade national responsibility, and persuade Western audiences that the supreme post-war priority is keeping the Russian imperial polity intact.
But why should the West be fixated on preserving the very entity that has brought war and nuclear blackmail back to Europe? A stable peace cannot be built on comforting the aggressor. It must be built on guaranteed security for the victims and assertive prevention of future aggression.
Damage to deterrence and accountability
If the war is understood as Putin’s personal project, then the lesson for Russia’s institutions is simple: wait him out. One day Putin will leave or die, and everyone else can claim they were merely trapped inside his system. That destroys deterrence. For deterrence to work, Russian elites must understand that aggression carries consequences.
It also complicates post-war accountability. It becomes harder if the West accepts the ludicrous fiction that the war is somehow detached from Russia itself. Who is responsible? If the answer is “Putin,” then Russia escapes yet again. And if Russia escapes, it will learn nothing except that it can repeat it all under another ruler.
Say what happened
Saying that every Russian is guilty of every Russian crime would be false and unjust. But saying “Putin” instead of Russia distorts reality, comforts the passive, assists Russian soft power, weakens deterrence, and enables future evasion of responsibility. Putin gave the order. But Russia is waging the war. When discussing the war, the better term is Russia’s war against Ukraine. Because that is what it is.
A country that destroys another country cannot be allowed to hide behind the name of one man. History should not record this as Putin’s aggression. It should record the truth: Russia invaded Ukraine, Russia devastated Ukrainian cities, Russia murdered Ukrainians, and Russia must be held responsible.
The views expressed in this opinion article are the author’s and not necessarily those of Kyiv Post.

The SNP MSP for Inverclyde has questioned why management at Ferguson Marine failed to secure additional work, describing the announcement of job losses at the Port Glasgow yard as a wake-up call for the company’s leadership.
Stuart McMillan, whose constituency covers the yard, posted his response on Tuesday after Ferguson Marine opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave.
He said: “There have been many well documented challenges at Ferguson Marine and the yard needs to become competitive.
“Today’s announcement must be a wake-up call for management. The order book remains empty until the Scottish Government finalise the direct award.
“Why have management taken their eye off the ball and not secured additional work?
“I have concerns about the loss of skills and knowledge as many of the older workforce have been with Fergusons for many years. Their experience is important for training apprentices.”
The framing puts him at odds with others who have commented on the announcement, who have directed their criticism at ministers rather than at the yard.
Paul Sweeney, the Labour MSP for Glasgow and a former shipyard worker, told the UK Defence Journal that the award of phase one of the Small Vessel Replacement Programme to Remontowa in Gdansk rather than to Ferguson Marine had directly caused the job losses.
He said: “They can’t secure additional work because Scotland doesn’t provide shipbuilding project finance through its state investment bank. Every other shipbuilding nation does this. That leaves Ferguson dependent on government contracts, but they have been awarded to foreign shipyards.”
Mr Sweeney said the Scottish Government has placed £550 million of orders with foreign shipyards since 2022 with none going to Scottish or UK yards, and that Caledonian Maritime Assets had recently drawn up tendering requirements for a ferry contract in terms that excluded British yards from bidding.
GMB Scotland, the largest union at the yard, called the losses a betrayal of a blameless workforce and blamed ministers for failing to deliver new contracts while sending work overseas. Louise Gilmour, the union’s Scotland secretary, said: “Shipbuilders needs ships to build so where are those promised to Ferguson Marine? If they ever come, who will build them?”
Ferguson Marine’s own account attributes the reduction to the completion of Glen Rosa rather than to any failure to win work. Graeme Thomson, the chief executive, said the yard faces “an inevitable gap in workload while we work with the Scottish Government to make the relevant preparations to enable us to proceed with contract negotiations.”
Mr McMillan’s point about the order book is not disputed by any of the parties. The Scottish Government announced in March 2026 that it intended to make a strategic direct award covering four vessels, two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel, and due diligence on that award remains under way.
Where the accounts diverge is on whether the yard could realistically have won commercial work in the meantime. Ferguson Marine has held subcontract work from BAE Systems on the Type 26 frigate programme, fabricating structural units for assembly at Govan, and Mr Sweeney said that subcontract has now come to a conclusion.
Stephen Flynn, the Economy Secretary, said the redundancies would put the yard on a more competitive footing and were necessary to help secure a viable future, adding that he had been assured they would not affect Glen Rosa.

Your Expired Visa Card Could Be ‘Zombified’ to Make Contactless Payments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

As the controversial vehicle surveillance giant Flock Safety continues to expand, WIRED got the code for the company’s new AI policing tool and reconstructed the software to show that its capabilities go far beyond reading license plates and tracking vehicles. We also published the story this week of a Rhode Island police officer who was subjected to five internal affairs investigations in less than two years after he publicly questioned his department’s use of Flock cameras.
Following incidents of high-profile rogue activity by some of its AI agents, OpenAI said this week that it is halting model training runs and overhauling internal safety protocols. The company said that its upcoming Astra model may represent a turning point of “critical” cyber capabilities.
A reverse-lookup identification service exposed millions of photos of people’s faces in a database accessible through the open internet. Meanwhile, Meta ran advertisements for an app that promised to nudify female politicians, including one ad featuring a pornographic video that included a deepfake resembling a well-known US politician. Apple removed the app from the App Store after WIRED’s inquiry.
And WIRED spoke with Andy Yen, CEO of the privacy-focused digital services company Proton, about the privacy implications of AI and how access to encryption can continue to expand in this new technological era.
But wait, there’s more! Each week, we round up the security and privacy news we didn’t cover in depth ourselves. Click the headlines to read the full stories. And stay safe out there.
Fraudsters Could Use “Zombified” Expired Visa Cards to Make Contactless Payments
Many people know that any active credit card represents a fraud risk the minute a card is lost, stolen, or otherwise gets out of their hands. Less expected is that an expired Visa card, too, could serve as an errant key into their bank account if it’s left unattended or discarded intact, discovered by a fraudster, and “zombified” using a new technique researchers recently revealed.
At the Usenix Cybersecurity Conference last week, researchers at the University of Massachusetts Amherst warned that fraudsters could make contactless payments using expired credit cards issued by Visa by proxying them through a man-in-the-middle app that relays the credit card’s data through a pair of phones. Due to issues in the authentication chain of contactless payments, the researchers found that whether an expired card’s transaction would be disallowed was left to cryptography implemented differently by various card issuers. Visa’s had a particular flaw allowing out-of-date cards to pass its check. (Visa didn’t respond to requests for comment from tech news outlet the Register, which reported on the research this week.)
In fact, as the researchers describe it, Visa’s essentially passed on the task of authenticating these transactions to the cardholder’s bank—and while some banks prevented the use of the zombified cards, others didn’t. The result is that fraudsters could in some cases dumpster dive for an expired card and use it to make payments from the unwitting owner’s account—particularly at point-of-sale terminals where no human is present to look askance at their phone-based proxy setup.
The lesson: When that Visa card expires, a pair of scissors can ensure it doesn’t reanimate in someone else’s hands.
Apple Sent Out an “Unprecedented” Number of Hacked-Device Warnings
Apple has long sent out notification to the owners of iPhones and other devices it’s detected may be the target of what it calls “mercenary spyware”—sophisticated, stealthy malware installed by a government or state-sponsored hacker-for-hire. Last weekend, the number of those alerts sent to potential victims spiked to an “unprecedented” number, according to TechCrunch, which spoke to security analysts who investigate potential spyware intrusions. The alerts, which were sent out to potential hacking targets in 110 countries, reached numbers of users more than 30 percent higher than previous rounds of these alerts, by the estimate of Mohammed Al-Maskati, who leads a team of security investigators at Access Now, a digital rights group that Apple refers victims to in its spyware alerts. At least one target, TechCrunch noted, was a Ukrainian soldier, who said that others in the Ukrainian military had also received the alert. Sophisticated iPhone hacking campaigns may well be on the rise: Just this year, researchers at iVerify and Google uncovered two iOS mass-hacking tools known as DarkSword and Coruna.
Ukraine Says It Hit Russian Ecommerce Giant With a Cyberattack—and Drones
In Russia’s decade-plus cyberwar against Ukraine, it has at times experimented with combined physical and digital attacks, such as triggering a hacker-induced blackout in a Ukrainian city in the midst of an air raid. Now, as Ukraine increasingly strikes back against Russia in an effort to impose cost on its invaders, it appears to have tried a similar tactic. The Ukrainian military this week claimed to have carried out a disruptive cyberattack against Russian ecommerce giant Wildberries—by some measures, the Russian equivalent of Amazon—in the midst of drone attacks that have also destroyed parts of the company’s warehouse infrastructure, according to cybersecurity news outlet The Record. While Wildberries is largely a consumer retail business, The Ukrainian Main Intelligence Directorate also claimed that it is part of Russia’s sells military logistics and played a role in financing the war in the Ukraine. The Record couldn’t confirm the exact effects of the cyberattack on Wildberries, but it notes that Russian media has reported that the company has lost nearly 13 million square feet of warehouse space to drone attacks.
US Agencies Warn of AI-Aided Hacking Targeting American Infrastructure Systems
Hackers’ exploitation software, like all software, is now rarely written one keystroke at a time. So perhaps it’s little surprise that hackers targeting US infrastructure equipment are among those using AI to automate their work. A group of US agencies including the NSA, the FBI, the Department of Energy, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency warned in an advisory this week that AI-assisted exploitation software was targeting Siemens programmable logic controllers, or PLCs, devices used to digitally control physical systems. Among the industries that use the targeted devices, the advisory warns, are manufacturing, chemical, energy, water, food, and agriculture facilities. “Using AI to generate exploitation scripts represents an evolution in threat actor capabilities, dramatically reducing the technical expertise and time required to develop working ICS exploitation scripts and malicious tools,” the advisory reads, using the term ICS to mean “industrial control systems.” This inevitable adoption of AI-coded hacking tools comes in the midst of an unprecedented campaign of likely-Iranian hacker disruptions targeting US water and wastewater facilities in dozens of utilities across seven US states.

Feature: China-LatAm youths craft localized solutions to global poverty
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
18:27:03 CST
19:27:03 KST

by Xinhua Writer Lu Junyu
RIO DE JANEIRO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- An "offline AI box" for classrooms without internet access and a smart platform optimizing waste-cooking-oil collection routes to tackle river pollution were among practical solutions presented by young innovators at the Brazilian finals of the 2026 China-Latin America Challenge to Alleviate Poverty.
Launched in 2024 by Tsinghua University alongside leading Latin American institutions, this year's competition brought together 666 participants across 88 universities and organizations from China, Brazil, Chile and Peru. Of 119 cross-border teams, 12 gathered in Brazil and Chile, bringing fresh perspectives to local poverty reduction.
Joining the initiative reshaped the perspective of Leonardo Vaz, a computer engineering student at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ). When Tsinghua team leader Zhang Henan got in touch, Vaz saw a hands-on way to tackle educational challenges in underserved regions of his own country.
As part of Team "Lighthouse," they collaborated to engineer an "offline AI box" designed for remote rural schools lacking electricity and internet connectivity. Educators load digitized course materials onto the portable device in connected areas, and students in isolated communities can then access resources and interact via a local hotspot on their mobile phones.
"This week, we did a field visit to an educational program in a favela, interviewed a math teacher to present our project, and tried to gather information and ideas to improve," Vaz recalled.
Navigating an 11-hour time difference between Brazil and China was no easy feat. "Our calls had to be scheduled at dawn in Brazil or late at night in China, but we overcame it. Collaborating with my Chinese teammates to tackle real-world challenges has been an absolute honor," he said.
Deploying technology across borders demands not just technical capability, but deep empathy and local knowledge.
"Poverty is complex, and solutions can not simply be copy-pasted from one nation to another," said Chen Taotao, director of Tsinghua University Latin America Center. "The core of China-LatAm cooperation lies in mutual learning. Chinese technology faces realistic localization challenges when adapted to Latin America's unique infrastructure and social landscape. Only through field testing and joint on-the-ground teamwork can these barriers be bridged," Chen said.
Ana Celia Castro, director of the UFRJ Institute for Advanced Studies, emphasized the need to move from concepts to action. "Innovative ideas only gain transformative power when they truly land on the ground," Castro said, highlighting the importance of building long-term mechanisms that engage businesses and civil society.
Addressing real-world issues was central to this year's items, which featured 26 practical prompts submitted by the participating organizations.
To tackle river pollution in Rio's Pavuna-Meriti basin, one team developed an AI-powered app connecting waste pickers with local businesses to collect used cooking oil -- drawing inspiration from China's mature supply chain for converting waste fats into biofuel.
"We realized that existing recycling programs in Brazil rarely reach informal waste pickers or low-income neighborhoods," said Wu Zongqin, a master's student at Tsinghua University. "We wanted our project to tackle deep-seated challenges like fatbergs, rather than just scratch the surface."
As global challenges grow increasingly interconnected, international collaboration among the next generation offers a beacon of hope.
"Young people from China and the Latin American region are learning how to listen to each other, understand different realities, and work together to solve real problems, from education and healthcare to agriculture and sustainable energy. This is what makes this challenge truly special," said Lv Xingcan from Envision Group, a key corporate supporter of the project.
Reflecting on the evolution of the program, Chen sees a promising road ahead.
Looking ahead, Chen envisions a collaborative ecosystem uniting academics, enterprises, and governments. But for students like Vaz and Zhang, the impact is already real -- measured by call by call across an 11-hour time zone. ■

Mexico resumes livestock sales to US under tight controls over screwworm risk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
10:23:01 UTC
19:23:01 KST

Mexican ranchers prepare to resume livestock sales to US under tight controls over screwworm risk
HERMOSILLO, Mexico (AP) — At daybreak, rancher Martín Alfonso Ibarra takes advantage of the cooler hours in northern Mexico’s desert to oversee the milking of his cows and tend to 16 prized calves. Soon, he hopes, they will be headed north to the United States as a yearlong ban on Mexican cattle imports comes to an end.
The ban, imposed over concerns about a flesh-eating parasite known as the New World screwworm fly, dealt a blow to cattle and beef industries on both sides of the border, exacerbating a livestock shortage in the U.S. and hurting a Mexican ranching sector already weakened by drought and a cattle export business that generated $1.2 billion for Mexico last year.
Now, the U.S. is set to resume livestock imports from Mexico beginning Aug. 24 at the Douglas, Arizona, border crossing, which borders Agua Prieta in Mexico’s Sonora state. If the reopening goes smoothly, the U.S. Department of Agriculture could allow imports through additional ports, though shipments will initially be subject to restrictions aimed at preventing the spread of the parasite — which has already crossed the border, with authorities battling cases in Texas and New Mexico.
The screwworm gets its name from the maggots’ habit of burrowing — or screwing — into a wound, according to the USDA Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service. Any warm-blooded animal, including wildlife, pets and occasionally even humans, can be infested.
In Mexico, the screwworm outbreak was detected in November 2024 and has spread to 30 of the 32 states — most recently in Sonora, where the first case was reported Wednesday in the community of Munihuasa, near the borders with Chihuahua and Sinaloa, states where infections have also proliferated.
To date, Mexico has 1,969 active screwworm cases, which represent less than half of the infections reported a year ago, a decline that authorities say shows progress in containing the outbreak. Still, they acknowledge eradication will take time.
New US controls are expected to slow shipments
Against that backdrop, Ibarra and thousands of other ranchers in the northern state of Sonora are preparing to resume live cattle exports. But optimism is tempered by new U.S. controls expected to slow shipments across the border.
“This is not over yet,” said the 58-year-old rancher, adding that the export halt cut his income by 40% last year.
According to the protocol defined by U.S. authorities, in the first week of reopening, only 700 cattle per day will be allowed through; this will rise to 900 in the second week and will gradually increase until reaching 1,300 cattle per day, veterinarian Arturo Ruiz, responsible for animal health for the state of Sonora, told The Associated Press.
The new rules also require cattle to be fitted with radio-frequency identification tags in their ears and screened by electronic readers and trained dogs. Officials from the U.S. Department of Agriculture will conduct the inspections before allowing the Mexican cattle to cross into Arizona, Ruiz explained.
Mexico accepted the U.S. protocols, but the restrictions have frustrated some local ranchers.
“We are at a complicated moment when we need authorities to think less politically and more technically and reasonably,” said Juan Carlos Ochoa, president of the Regional Livestock Union of Sonora, referring to tensions between the Mexican and U.S. governments when the ban was first imposed in May 2025.
Ochoa said the new U.S. restrictions would limit shipments and argued that a greater flow of cattle across the border is needed to address supply shortages in both countries.
A cautious optimism as imports resume
Although both countries felt the effects of Washington’s decision, the impact was greater in the U.S., particularly for consumers facing record-high beef prices that led some to cut back on meat.
Juan Carlos Anaya, general director of agricultural consulting firm Grupo Consultor de Mercados Agrícolas, said U.S. ranchers were unable to make up the supply shortfall, contributing to closures at some meat-processing plants and hurting feedlot operations.
Before the border closure, Mexico exported about 1.2 million head of cattle to the United States each year, mainly from its northern states. When exports were suspended, Mexican ranchers turned to the domestic market, where they sold their cattle for nearly 40% less than they had received in the U.S. — a loss of income that forced many to sell some of their cattle or cut spending and investment.
Back in Sonora, in the stifling August heat of the capital, Hermosillo, Ibarra was cautiously optimistic about finally sending his 16 calves to the U.S. But he said he would temper his expectations until October, when the cattle have gained enough weight and the sale could be finalized.
“There’s no need to get too excited,” he said.
