Why this is end of the line for Trump in Iran war?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:49:10 UTC
17:49:10 KST

Donald Trump's declaration of an unprecedented economic war against Iran cannot be seen merely as a sign of the start of new economic pressure. This decision shows, more than anything else, that Washington, after months of military and sanctions pressure, is facing the narrowing of its effective options. Instead of finding new and decisive targets inside Iran, the United States has now shifted the scope of pressure beyond Iran's borders and is targeting countries, banks, and companies that still allow Tehran to trade and maintain financial access. In fact, Trump's new policy can be seen as an attempt to compensate for the failure of previous pressure; a shift from direct pressure on Iran to pressure on the network that allows Iran to circumvent sanctions.
Over the past years, the United States has placed almost all major sectors of Iran's economy on the sanctions list; from oil and petrochemicals to shipping, metals, the automotive industry, the Central Bank, financial networks, and various economic institutions. The Atlantic Council has also emphasized, in its review of sanctions on Iran, that almost all sectors of Iran's economy have been targeted by US sanctions.
Therefore, Washington's problem is no longer finding a sector of Iran's economy that has not been sanctioned; the problem is that each new sanction, compared with previous sanctions, does not necessarily create new and decisive pressure.
This is why Trump now speaks of an unprecedented economic war, but the main arena of this war is no longer only Iran. The United States wants to pressure foreign banks, shipping companies, oil buyers, trade intermediaries, and even governments that cooperate with Tehran.
This policy shift must also be seen in the context of recent military developments. Washington has turned to intensified economic pressure at a time when military pressure has failed to achieve the political goals the United States expected. If military power alone could have forced Tehran to accept Washington's demands, there would have been no need to declare a new "economic war."
It can therefore be said that Trump's new policy is a kind of change of playing field; the United States has not retreated from the military field to the economic field, but it is trying to complement insufficient military pressure with economic pressure.
In the view of Western experts, the problem is that Iran's economy, over several decades of sanctions, has gradually developed mechanisms to cope with these pressures. Informal trade networks, oil sales, financial intermediaries, the use of local currencies, and cooperation with non-Western partners are part of these mechanisms.
The biggest challenge to the new US policy is China. According to data from the company Kpler, cited in a recent Al Jazeera report, more than 80 percent of Iran's oil exports in 2025 have gone to China. A significant portion of this oil also goes to small Chinese refineries, and payments are made through small banks, trading companies in Hong Kong, and settlement in yuan.
This creates a serious problem for Washington. Sanctioning an Iranian company is fundamentally different from sanctioning a major Chinese bank. In the first case, the main cost falls on Iran; but in the second case, the United States enters into direct confrontation with one of the world's largest economies.
For this reason, as Bloomberg has reported, the United States has previously warned two major Chinese banks about the risk of secondary sanctions related to Iran, but has not yet sanctioned them directly.
Here one of the most important contradictions of Washington's sanctions policy becomes apparent. The power of US sanctions stems largely from the dominance of the dollar and broad access to the US financial system. But the extensive use of this very tool has encouraged target countries to find alternative paths.
Chatham House analyses show that the expansion of sanctions has contributed to deepening cooperation among countries such as Iran, China, and Russia and has pushed them toward creating payment and settlement routes that are less dependent on the dollar.
This means sanctions may create pressure in the short term, but in the long term they increase the incentive of target countries to reduce their dependence on the US financial system.
As a result, the tool Washington uses to preserve its economic power can gradually increase the incentive to create rival tools.
The main problem with Trump's new policy lies precisely here. The more the United States expands the scope of secondary sanctions, the greater the likelihood of colliding with the economic interests of major powers. Sanctioning buyers of Iranian oil can affect global oil supply and raise energy prices. Pressure on China can lead to a reaction from Beijing. Targeting foreign companies can also deepen the rift between the United States and its trading partners.
Washington therefore faces a difficult equation: to increase pressure on Iran, it must shift pressure onto other countries; but the larger this circle becomes, the higher the cost of implementing the policy for the United States itself.
The ultimate goal of US sanctions is not merely to reduce Iran's income; the main goal is to change Tehran's political behavior. But the experience of past years has shown that economic pressure does not necessarily lead to a change in political behavior. Iran can pay higher costs, change its trade routes, and expand economic cooperation with countries such as China and Russia. Even Chatham House has warned, in its examination of the consequences of sanctions, that broad pressure can help form parallel financial and trade networks; networks that ultimately reduce the effectiveness of the US sanctions tool. For this reason, the main question for Washington is no longer "what can be sanctioned against Iran?" but rather "how many other countries is the United States willing to enter into conflict with in order to close each of Iran's economic routes?"
If we place Trump's new policy alongside the military developments of recent months, a clearer picture emerges. After the experience of military pressure, the United States has now returned to sanctions; but this time almost all of Iran's economy has already been sanctioned, and to find new targets, Washington is forced to go after Iran's external network. This is the very point at which "maximum pressure" can turn into "costly pressure." The United States can increase economic pressure, but it cannot expand it indefinitely without cost. China stands in the way of this policy, Russia has greater incentive to cooperate with Tehran, and Iran itself has gained considerable experience over the years of sanctions in creating alternative routes.
Ultimately, Trump's new policy is less a sign of the discovery of a new economic weapon against Iran than a sign of the narrowing of Washington's previous options. After military pressure failed to produce the expected result, the United States is now trying to continue the same pressure in the economic arena.
But this time there is one fundamental difference: the target is not only Iran. To isolate Tehran, the United States must also pressure China, financial networks outside the West, oil buyers, and international companies.
And this is precisely where the tables may turn; the sanctions that were supposed to isolate Iran can deepen Iran's cooperation with the East, increase the use of non-dollar currencies, and reduce the dependence of some countries on the US financial system.
Under such conditions, Trump's unprecedented economic war may be less the beginning of a new phase of pressure on Iran than a sign that US sanctions policy has reached the limits of its own power.

Türkiye, Japan discuss AI risks, economic security in Tokyo

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:44:36 UTC
17:44:36 KST

Turkish and Japanese officials and experts met in Tokyo to examine how artificial intelligence and geopolitical competition are reshaping strategic communication, economic security and global supply chains.
The STRATCOM Roundtable and STRATCOM Public Forum, organized by Türkiye’s Presidential Communications Directorate and its embassy in Tokyo, brought together representatives of public institutions, international organizations, technology companies, think tanks and universities.
The roundtable focused on the effects of emerging technologies on global governance, digital sovereignty, information security and international cooperation. Participants also discussed disinformation, the changing role of public diplomacy and the use of technology in crisis management.
A separate public forum on managing economic security examined critical technologies, reliable supply chains, data security and the transformation of the digital economy.
In a video message, Presidential Communications Director Burhanettin Duran said digital technologies had widened access to information but also created new vulnerabilities through manipulation, polarization and uncertainty.
“Today, we are facing what can be described as a crisis of truth and a crisis of communication,” Duran said.
He called for greater international cooperation, exchanges of experience and the development of common principles, saying no country or institution could address such challenges alone.
Türkiye’s ambassador to Japan, Oğuzhan Ertuğrul, said multiple crises and growing uncertainty were placing further pressure on the international order. He called for stronger cooperation based on diplomacy and multilateralism, alongside reforms to global institutions.
Ertuğrul said Türkiye and Japan possessed complementary strategic capabilities and could work together to support international peace, stability and prosperity.
Deputy Communications Director Ferhat Pirinççi said information security and a reliable information environment were central to economic resilience. Disinformation could directly affect economic stability, the investment climate and public confidence, he said.
Pirinççi added that the two countries could deepen cooperation in technology, innovation, strategic communication and crisis management.
AK Party Deputy Chair Ömer İleri said protectionism, the growing emphasis on domestic production and the increasing importance of AI and data were transforming both geopolitical and technological competition.
Akira Igata of the University of Tokyo’s Research Center for Advanced Science and Technology drew attention to disinformation and influence operations targeting companies involved in critical-mineral supply chains and data-center infrastructure.
He called for closer cooperation between governments and businesses, as well as greater information sharing and education.
Kazuto Suzuki, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Graduate School of Public Policy, said interdependence among major powers, particularly the United States and China, continued to shape economic security policies.
Diversifying critical supply chains and reducing strategic vulnerabilities were becoming increasingly important, he said.
Kunihiko Miyake of the Canon Institute for Global Studies said technological tools alone could not ensure effective communication, which also required a clear strategy and messages tailored to their intended audiences.

Who Is Lev Shlosberg, the Russian Politician Jailed for Opposing Russia’s War?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

Russia has sentenced Lev Shlosberg, the 63-year-old deputy chairman of the liberal Yabloko party – and one of the few prominent opponents of Russia’s war against Ukraine who chose to remain in the country – to 11 years and one month in a penal colony for participating in a debate and reposting a newspaper cover.
On Aug. 17, a court in the northwestern city of Pskov found him guilty of repeatedly “discrediting” the Russian military and spreading “false information” about it. The court also prohibited him from administering websites for six years,Reuters reported.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
On the same day, Russia’s Supreme Court rejected Yabloko’s appeal against its exclusion from the Sept. 18-20 parliamentary election. Yabloko was the only registered Russian party openly campaigning for an end to the war.
The two rulings removed both an anti-war party from the ballot and one of its best-known politicians from public life. Dozens of people who gathered near the Supreme Court were detained.
Eleven years for a debate and a repost
One part of the case concerned Shlosberg’s January 2025 online debate with historian Yuri Pivovarov.
Shlosberg argued that Russia and Ukraine should agree to an immediate ceasefire. Pivovarov warned that a premature settlement could produce another war and supported Ukraine fighting until victory.
Investigators claimed that a recording of the debate posted on the Russian social network Odnoklassniki “discredited” the military. Shlosberg said he did not control the account and had not uploaded the recording.
Russian Emigration Interest Doubles Amid Fears of Mobilization This Fall
The second charge concerned a repost from Feb. 25, 2022 – the day after Russia launched its full-scale invasion. It showed a Daily Mirror front page featuring an injured Ukrainian woman alongside Russian leader Vladimir Putin.
The law criminalizing “false information” about the Russian military was signed on March 4, after the repost had already appeared. The court nevertheless used the publication to help impose a sentence of more than 11 years.
The proceedings were troubling even by the standards of a Russian political trial. According to Deutsche Welle, closing arguments began without any of Shlosberg’s three lawyers present. The court refused to postpone the hearing and imposed a state-appointed lawyer whom he had rejected.
The sentence incorporated an earlier punishment of 420 hours of compulsory labor for allegedly failing to comply with the requirements imposed on a so-called “foreign agent.”
Amnesty International called the prosecution retaliation for exercising freedom of expression. Human Rights Watch demanded his release and noted that the offending “false information” included the image of a wounded Ukrainian civilian.
Pskov politician who investigated Russia’s secret war
Shlosberg was born in Pskov in 1963 into a family of teachers. He studied history at the Pskov Pedagogical Institute, later worked as a teacher and social worker, and helped establish the non-state Pskov Free Institute in the early 1990s, according to a biographical account published while he was in pretrial detention.
He joined Yabloko in 1994 and led its Pskov branch from 1996 until 2023, when he became one of the party’s deputy chairs.
Unlike opposition figures whose careers were made in Moscow, Shlosberg built his reputation through local politics, journalism and civic work. He was twice elected to the Pskov Regional Assembly, first serving from 2011 to 2015 and then from 2016 to 2021.
He was also the publisher and editor of Pskovskaya Guberniya, a regional newspaper whose reporting brought him national attention, and nearly cost him his life.
In August 2014, while the Kremlin denied that regular Russian troops were fighting in eastern Ukraine, the newspaper investigated the funerals of service members from Pskov’s 76th Guards Air Assault Division.
The soldiers had officially died in unclear circumstances. The evidence indicated that they had been killed during Russia’s undeclared intervention in the Donbas.
The issue was particularly sensitive in Pskov. The division was one of the region’s most important military institutions, and reporting on its losses punctured Moscow’s claim that the war was a purely Ukrainian conflict involving local “separatists” and Russian volunteers.
On Aug. 29, 2014, unknown assailants attacked Shlosberg near his home. He was hospitalized with a concussion, facial injuries and temporary memory loss. The assault followed a wider series of threats and attacks on journalists trying to establish how Russian soldiers had died in Ukraine, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists.
No one was held accountable for the attack.
In 2015, fellow regional deputies stripped Shlosberg of his mandate after he represented a civic organization contesting its designation as a “foreign agent.” He considered the decision political retaliation. The following year, he received the inaugural Boris Nemtsov Prize for his defense of democratic values and returned to the regional assembly in an election.
Opposition to Crimea seizure
Shlosberg opposed Russia’s seizure of Crimea from the beginning. In a 2016 essay titled “The Crimean Dead End,” he described how Russian troops blockaded Ukrainian military facilities before a referendum held under occupation.
Yabloko’s subsequent election platform stated that Crimea belonged to Ukraine, that its annexation was illegal and that it should be reversed. This was an unusually direct position for a party still permitted to operate legally in Russia.
After the full-scale invasion began, Shlosberg continued to oppose the war publicly. He described the war as a game of “bloody chess” and argued that peace had to precede political change.
“We must first stop killing people,” he said in the debate that later became part of his criminal case. “If we achieve peace, we will regain freedom.”
The repression accumulated gradually.
Russian courts repeatedly fined Shlosberg and his wife, Zhanna, for allegedly “discrediting” the military. In June 2023, the Justice Ministry designated him a “foreign agent,” a label used to stigmatize critics and exclude them from political life.
In 2024, he was fined for reposting Arnold Schwarzenegger’s March 2022 appeal to Russians about the war. Authorities searched his home and the home of his elderly father.
In June 2025, he was detained over the debate with Pivovarov and placed under house arrest. When investigators opened the separate “false information” case in December, he was transferred to pretrial detention, where he remained until his conviction.
Despite other prominent anti-Putin figures like Maxim Katz, Shlosberg refused to leave Russia and compared himself to Antaeus, the figure from Greek mythology who lost his strength when separated from the earth.
Anti-war position that Ukrainians strongly disputed
Despite Shlosberg’s opposition to some of the Kremlin’s actions, his stance toward Russia’s war on Ukraine still raises an eyebrow.
His position after the full-scale invasion centered on a form of radical pacifism and an immediate, unconditional ceasefire. In a December 2024 Yabloko essay, he argued that shooting should stop first and questions of territory, borders, sanctions and European security should be negotiated afterward.
For Ukrainians, the problem is obvious. A ceasefire that does not require Russian withdrawal may freeze an occupation achieved through aggression, give Moscow time to rearm and leave millions of Ukrainians under Russian rule.
That year he also made another controversial statement. He argued that Ukraine ceased to be a victim when it began resisting, saying that the “myth that Ukraine remains a victim” did not correspond to history.
After Ukraine’s operation in Russia’s Kursk region, he attacked exiled Russian opposition figures who supported Kyiv and called them the “party of other people’s blood.” Critics accused him of focusing on Ukrainian military action while failing to recognize Ukraine’s right to strike the forces and infrastructure used to attack it.
Why the Kremlin chose this moment
Four and a half year into the full-scale war, the Kremlin has tightened its grip on all opposition. Even parties without wide support like Yabloko.
Shlosberg’s Fellow Yabloko deputy chair Maxim Kruglov was also sentenced to seven years in June for allegedly spreading “false information” about the military. Other party members have been imprisoned, declared “foreign agents” or excluded from elections.
On Aug. 10, the Supreme Court removed Yabloko from the ballot following a complaint by the ultranationalist Rodina party. A week later, the court rejected Yabloko’s appeal while Shlosberg was being sentenced in Pskov.
In his final statement, Shlosberg called the war a catastrophe and warned that Russia would eventually have to confront the full list of its dead. He said military cemeteries were expanding faster than maternity wards, kindergartens and schools.
The judge repeatedly interrupted him, and in the end granted the 11 year sentence that epitomizes modern Russia’s zeitgeist: that of a state edging on totalitarianism as the Russian authorities continue to ban social media, interfere with the private lives of its citizens, and silence all criticism.

Is India falling short on sugar supplies ahead of festive season?
While the mammoth Indian festivals of Dussehra and Diwali are still weeks away, a sharp rise in sugar prices is setting off alarm bells. That's despite the government’s assurances that it is taking measures to assuage concerns.
The all-India modal retail price of sugar rose to Rs 65 per kilogram on Friday from Rs 45 on July 21 and Rs 50 on July 31, according to the Department of Consumer Affairs. The rise has been attributed to lower-than-expected sugar production and stocks at a nine-year low.
Indian Sugar & Bio-energy Manufacturers Association had initially estimated gross domestic sugar production for the 2025-26 season at 343.5 lakh tons, the Indian Express reported. After diversion of 34 lakh tons for ethanol production, net output was projected at 309.5 lakh tons.
Opposition Congress President Mallikarjun Kharge questioned Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government over rising prices and declining stocks, highlighting the decision to divert sugarcane toward ethanol production.
India is one of the world's largest sugar producers and exporters. However, current exports have been halted, and the government has allowed the duty-free import of 1 million tons of sugar.
Neeraj Chopra back with second place at Lausanne Diamond League
Indian javelin superstar Neeraj Chopra snagged second place at the 2026 Lausanne Diamond League, close behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage.
The Sri Lankan took the top spot with a throw of 88.14 meters, nine centimeters ahead of Chopra's season-best throw of 88.05.
"I didn't realise it was only nine centimetres (apart), it was really close, but I'm happy with the 88-metre throw," the Indian Express quoted Chopra as saying after the competition on Friday night. "To be honest, it didn't feel like it went 88 metres because I felt very relaxed. I tried really hard and later focused on my technique. With every competition, I feel that I’m coming back."
The two-time Olympic medalist spent nine months out of the sport over an injury before making a comeback at the Doha Diamond League in June this year, where he finished fourth.
Indian foreign minister S. Jaishankar set for Russia visit
India's External Affairs Minister, S. Jaishankar, is set to make an official visit to Russia on August 23-24, the ministry said in a statement.
In addition to co-chairing a session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation, he is also expected to meet his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov during the trip.
India and Russia share a relationship that spans decades and is deeply rooted in history, trade and defense. Since Russia began its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, India has been under pressure from Kyiv's Western allies over its unwillingness to disengage with Moscow.
In June, Russian President Vladimir Putin, speaking to reporters at the St. Petersburg Economic Forum, called India a "great country" and a "reliable partner."
Confusion surrounds Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman's reported visit to India
Bangladesh has not decided whether Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will visit India later this month, his press secretary said Friday, after Indian media reported he was expected in New Delhi on August 23-25.
Press secretary Saleh Shibly told Reuters "no decision has yet been made on the visit," saying Dhaka is waiting on New Delhi's response to requests for the extradition of former PM Sheikh Hasina and other "absconding offenders."
India's foreign ministry spokesperson said he had nothing to share on the visit.
Adding to the confusion, Rashtrapati Bhavan, the official residence of the President of India, published a statement on Friday afternoon canceling Saturday's routine Change of Guard ceremony for rehearsals tied to Rahman's "ceremonial welcome," the Indian Express reported.
As the visit was not formally confirmed, the office withdrew the statement less than an hour later without explanation.
This would be Rahman's first India visit since taking office in February after his party's landslide win.
It comes as the neighbors try to rebuild ties that became strained after Hasina fled to India following her 2024 ouster after a student-led uprising. Dhaka has repeatedly sought her extradition; India says the request is under review.
Last week, Rahman's government signaled that conditions needed to improve before the trip, especially after Hasina held a press event which Dhaka condemned.
Hasina was sentenced to death in absentia in November over the deadly crackdown on 2024 protests. She denies the charges and has said she'll return to Bangladesh in December.
Gandhi's personal notes sell for $1.7 million, setting auction record
A collection of handwritten notes by Mahatma Gandhi has sold for $1.7 million in Mumbai, the highest price ever paid for an Indian historical document at auction, auction house Saffronart said.
The 688 notes were written by Gandhi to his close associate Anand Hingorani between 1944 and 1946, following the death of Hingorani's wife, Vidya. Later compiled into a book titled "A Thought for the Day," the writing touched upon a number of themes including truth, God and non-violence, offering personal insights on principles that Gandhi was closely associated to publicly.
The collection, preserved by Hingorani's family, was sold under the title "Gandhi: From the Collection of Anand T Hingorani." Gandhi's portable spinning wheel, notes on the discipline of spinning, manuscripts, letters, photographs and other personal items were also part of the auction.
Hingorani first met Gandhi in 1930 and later joined him on the Salt March, a campaign of peaceful resistance against Britain's salt monopoly.
"What makes this collection particularly compelling is the opportunity to see one of the most significant figures in India's history through the lens of a close, personal relationship," Saffronart co-founder Dinesh Vazirani said.
Gandhi led India's non-violent struggle for independence from British rule and influenced similar movements worldwide. He was assassinated in January 1948.
Welcome to our coverage
Hello! This is Seerat Chabba from DW's Studio Delhi, bringing you the latest from across India.
After a night of incessant rain in the capital, I am back in the hot seat, but not making nearly enough to buy a collection of notes by India's "Father of the Nation," Mahatma Gandhi, which was sold for a record $1.69 million (about €1.47 million) at a Mumbai auction.
Meanwhile, New Delhi and Dhaka have been offering mixed signals about Bangladeshi Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's reported visit.
India is grappling with a potential sugar shortage ahead of the upcoming festive season, as prices soar and production as well as stocks fall.
Arguably one of India's favorite athletes, Neeraj Chopra, seems to be regaining his mojo, finishing second behind Sri Lanka's Rumesh Pathirage at the men's javelin event at the 2026 Lausanne Diamond League.

Central Bank ends physical gold conversion scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:40:15 UTC
17:40:15 KST

The Central Bank has repealed a regulation that allowed physical gold held outside the banking system to be converted into lira-denominated deposit and participation accounts.
The decision, published in the Official Gazette on Aug. 22, entered into force on the same day. The regulation had been in place since March 14, 2022.
New accounts and renewals under the scheme had already been halted on Aug. 23, 2025. Accounts opened before that date remained valid until maturity.
Under the repealed rules, savers could take physical gold to authorized jewelers or bank branches for transfer to gold accounts. At the account holder’s request, the balance was converted into liras at a price set by the Central Bank.
The funds were placed in deposit or participation accounts with maturities of three, six or 12 months, while banks sold the corresponding gold to the Central Bank at the conversion price.
At maturity, account holders received the principal together with interest or a profit share. If the increase in the gold price exceeded that return, the Central Bank covered the difference through the relevant bank.
The scheme also allowed an additional return under rules set by the Central Bank.

U.S. Marine Corps accepts first Ancillary Surface Craft prototype
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:38:42 UTC
17:38:42 KST

- The Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory completed technical acceptance of its first Ancillary Surface Craft prototype, built by Birdon America under a 2024 contract.
- The 150-foot landing craft can carry 46 tons of cargo and 40 Marines and is rated for Sea State 5 operation, surviving up to Sea State 7.
The U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory has completed technical acceptance of the first Ancillary Surface Craft prototype, moving the roughly 150-foot vessel into a new phase of testing at Quantico, Virginia, the laboratory said in a release.
The ASC is a roll-on/roll-off landing craft designed to carry personnel, equipment, and fuel directly onto unimproved shorelines, delivering what the Marine Corps calls the “last tactical mile” of logistics support. The laboratory said the craft can transport up to 46 tons of cargo and 40 combat-loaded Marines. It is rated for full operation in Sea State 5 and designed to survive conditions up to Sea State 7.
The craft is equipped with forward-looking sonar intended to let operators navigate uncharted, shallow littoral waters and assess beach gradients before landing.
The Marine Corps awarded the ASC contract to Birdon America, the U.S. arm of Australian shipbuilder Birdon, in 2024. Birdon partnered with C&C Marine and Repair in Belle Chasse, Louisiana, to build the vessel, with construction beginning in 2025 at C&C’s facility near New Orleans. Birdon has said the ASC design, which it also refers to as the Ancillary Surface Craft-Medium, was built for rapid, automation-driven production intended to shorten the time needed to build each craft.
“Achieving technical acceptance is a crucial first step in our rigorous testing regimen,” said Aaron Hatfield, Maritime Program Manager, Science and Technology Division, U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory.
“This validation assures that the craft’s advanced systems and robust design are ready for MCWL to begin hands-on technical experimentation, ensuring we can meet the extreme operational demands of the Indo-Pacific theater.”
The ASC now enters limited technical assessments, in which Birdon America craft masters and engineers will work alongside Australian Army crewing support under Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory oversight. The laboratory said the craft will initially be operated by a hybrid crew pairing Marines with contracted mariners as the Marine Corps trains its own personnel toward independent operation of small surface craft.
The ASC is intended to complement the Medium Landing Ship, a larger amphibious vessel the Marine Corps and Navy have been developing to move forces between islands. The Medium Landing Ship program has faced repeated delays, and the Marine Corps has described the ASC and similar smaller craft as part of an interim “bridging strategy” to sustain distributed forces in the Pacific while that program continues. Where the Medium Landing Ship moves forces at a larger scale, the ASC is built with a shallow draft meant to reach landing sites beyond the reach of bigger vessels, including shorelines without ports, piers, or causeways.
“To support Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations (EABO), our forces must remain highly mobile and sustained without relying on fixed, vulnerable ports,” said Col. Kenny Jones, Science and Technology Division Director at the Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory.
“This prototype allows MCWL to immediately execute hands-on experimentation, test tactical concepts, and put real hardware in the hands of Marines. By exploring the ASC’s traditional bow-first beaching physics alongside other experimental platforms, we are actively reducing programmatic risk and perfecting the requirements for the future naval fleet.”
Expeditionary Advanced Base Operations is the Marine Corps concept for positioning small, mobile units at temporary locations across contested maritime areas, including islands in the Pacific, to support sea denial and fleet sustainment missions. The concept relies on units that can move between locations without depending on fixed infrastructure that would be vulnerable to attack.
The Marine Corps has ordered two ASC prototypes from Birdon under the current contract. Upcoming testing phases will evaluate force protection and self-defense configurations for the craft, whose primary mission remains logistics and maneuver rather than direct combat.

Explainer: What abrupt cut to joint drills means for U.S.-S. Korea alliance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
16:34:43 CST
17:34:43 KST

SEOUL, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- A major U.S.-South Korea military exercise ended earlier than planned Friday after U.S. President Donald Trump unexpectedly ordered a substantial reduction in its scale, raising fresh questions over the stability of the U.S.-South Korea alliance, Seoul's plans to assume wartime operational control and the reliability of U.S. security commitments to its allies worldwide.
The Ulchi Freedom Shield (UFS) military exercise, originally scheduled to run through next Thursday, was cut to five days from 11, with both the duration and scope of training significantly reduced.
The move came after Trump called on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to scale back the drills in a social media post just hours before the exercise was due to begin. South Korean officials said they had not been informed of the decision in advance.
A SURPRISE THAT SHOOK SEOUL
The abrupt change was unusual because large-scale U.S.-South Korea exercises are normally coordinated months in advance between the two militaries, according to South Korean media. The two countries also scaled back drills in 2019 amid efforts to promote dialogue with the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), but that decision was jointly coordinated beforehand.
This time, South Korean officials said they were caught off guard. Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Defense Minister Ahn Gyu-back said Wednesday that they had not been informed beforehand.
The move also came amid broader friction between Washington and Seoul. Trump has repeatedly complained that the United States does too much for South Korea while receiving too little in return, and recently criticized Seoul for refusing to join U.S. efforts related to Iran's "denuclearization."
NEW UNCERTAINTY RAISED OVER COMMAND TRANSFER
According to local media analysis, the shortened exercise is also significant because South Korea has regarded combined drills as an important mechanism for assessing its readiness to assume wartime operational control of its forces.
Seoul has potentially aimed to complete the transfer in 2027. Commander of the U.S. Forces Korea Xavier Brunson, however, has stressed that any transfer must be based on military readiness.
South Korean officials have insisted that the latest reduction will not delay the process. Ahn said the two issues were unrelated, while Cho said the exercise cut should not be used as a reason to postpone the transfer. President Lee Jae Myung has also reaffirmed his intention to pursue the transfer during his term.
Wang Son-Taek, adjunct professor at Sogang University, noted in an interview with Xinhua that the first phase of UFS, which focused primarily on defense operations, had already been conducted. The part that was mainly reduced was the second phase, involving counteroffensive operations after the defense phase.
Still, South Korean defense and geopolitical expert Do Jin-ho warned that reducing combined drills could delay the command-transfer process and affect the frequency of future U.S. strategic asset deployments to the peninsula.
Yoo Ji-hoon, a research fellow at the Korea Institute for Defense Analysis, said the reduction may not put the command-transfer process on hold, but could expose broader coordination challenges within the alliance.
ALLIANCE TRUST UNDER PRESSURE
South Korean analysts have warned that repeated unilateral adjustments by Washington could weaken mutual trust and make the joint defense system less predictable.
Wang said that the episode could deepen unease among South Koreans over whether Washington would reliably uphold its security commitments, potentially putting additional pressure on the South Korean government.
At the same time, Wang cautioned against drawing the conclusion that Seoul should simply reduce its reliance on Washington.
Analysts said the Trump administration has used U.S. security commitments as leverage in dealing with allies. It has pressed Seoul over defense cost-sharing of U.S. troops stationed in South Korea, and pressured NATO allies over military spending. The latest move has renewed concerns about the reliability of the U.S. security umbrella.
Wang said the episode could contribute to a perception in Northeast Asia that trust within alliances was weakening and could reduce public confidence in the United States in South Korea. In the longer term, he said, such a trend could even become self-defeating for Washington's efforts to maintain its dominant position. ■

BJP passes resolution condemning Congress’ decision to sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram
NEW DELHI: BJP on Saturday condemned the Congress' decision to sing only the first two stanzas of Vande Mataram at party programmes, saying the move undermines the national song’s legacy and significance.The party passed a 10-point resolution asserting that it would protect the honour, national character and prestige associated with the complete version of Vande Mataram.
"No compromise on honour, legacy of Vande Mataram will be accepted for political convenience or appeasement," the resolution read.
It further "resolved to strongly condemn and unequivocally oppose the Congress Working Committee’s decision of 19th August 2026 to reaffirm its 1937 resolution and restrict Vande Mataram to its first two stanzas at Congress programmes."Further labeling it as "anti-imperialist cry", the BJP further resolved "to recall and disseminate Mahatma Gandhi’s own testimony that Vande Mataram had become an “anti-imperialist cry” and that he associated it with “the purest national spirit”, demonstrating its larger national meaning beyond the literary or religious context of particular stanzas."The BJP also said it would launch a nationwide campaign to highlight the history, meaning and significance of the national song and counter what it described as attempts to diminish its importance.
After the resolution were passed, BJP leader Sambit Patra held a press conference slamming Congress and highlighting significance of the national song. "This is the 150th anniversary of Vande Mataram. On August 15, 2026, the complete Vande Mataram, which has six stanzas, was sung from the Red Fort. But on August 15, an indecent act took place at the Congress office. In the presence of Congress MP Sonia Gandhi and Leader of Opposition in Lok Sabha and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi, when the Tricolour was being hoisted, Sonia Gandhi signalled to stop Vande Mataram after two stanzas," he added.
"On August 19, a proposal came in at the CWC meeting stating that we will sing only two stanzas of Vande Mataram. We all know why this decision was taken in 1937," he added.
Earlier, Union home minister Amit Shah had also attacked the Congress Working Committee’s resolution, calling the decision “anti-national” and accusing the party of reviving what he described as its decades-old “politics of appeasement”.

GMB Scotland has called job losses at Ferguson Marine a betrayal of a blameless workforce, blaming ministers for failing to deliver new contracts while sending shipbuilding work overseas, after the Port Glasgow yard opened a voluntary redundancy programme expected to see up to 70 employees leave.
Louise Gilmour, GMB Scotland secretary, said the jobs are at risk while the Scottish Government refuses to sign off contracts promised before the Holyrood election in May.

She said: “Its reputation has been battered for ten years because of two calamitous contracts decided and driven by those in charge of our ferry network. Their hubris and incompetence have failed a blameless workforce that deserves the chance to turn the page.”
GMB is the largest union at the publicly owned yard, and describes the losses as draining skills and experience from the last commercial shipyard on the Clyde.
Ferguson Marine announced the programme on Tuesday, saying the workload is naturally reducing as Glen Rosa moves into final outfitting and commissioning ahead of delivery in the fourth quarter of 2026. Formal consultation has begun.
Graeme Thomson, chief executive of Ferguson Marine, said: “Our immediate focus remains the safe, high-quality handover of Glen Rosa in Q4 2026. “Shipbuilding capability relies on continuity and while changes of this nature are difficult, taking proactive action now ensures we protect the long-term viability of the yard and remain lean, modern, and ready to cut steel on the new fleet as quickly as possible.”
He said: “We take our responsibility to our workforce and community incredibly seriously. By offering a voluntary redundancy path, we want to support team members who have given so much to shipbuilding on the Clyde as they consider their next steps. At the same time, we are doing everything in our power to ensure the yard is structured to offer secure, long-term careers once the new build programme gets underway.”
Stephen Flynn, the SNP Economy Secretary, defended the decision. He said: “The action that the leadership team at Ferguson Marine is taking today is necessary to help secure a viable future for the yard, and that of commercial shipbuilding on the Clyde. This is alongside their efforts to upskill workers, bid for new contracts and opportunities with partners.
“I am assured that a reduced workforce will not impact the build of the MV Glen Rosa, which is on track to be delivered in quarter four 2026. Our intention to directly award four vessels continues to undergo full due diligence further to next steps which will be announced to Parliament in due course.”
Ferguson Marine currently employs 238 staff, including 34 apprentices, meaning the departure of up to 70 people would account for close to a third of the workforce.
Opposition parties have directed their criticism at the Scottish Government.
Martin McCluskey, the Scottish Labour MP for Inverclyde and Renfrewshire West, called the situation economic vandalism of the highest order. He said: “These redundancies will be deeply concerning for workers, their families and the wider Inverclyde community. Ferguson Marine is an important part of our industrial heritage and a hugely significant part of the economic future of this sector. The UK cannot afford to lose any shipbuilding capacity.
“The Scottish Government promised work for the yard when they wanted people’s votes at the election and we are still waiting. Trade unions and workers have been calling for ferry contracts for years. It should never have come to this point, with skilled workers facing redundancy while the Scottish Government continues to deliberate over orders it has already said it wants to place with the yard. It is economic vandalism of the highest order.”
He said he had spoken to local trade union representatives and would be speaking to BAE Systems about the work at Govan and the pipeline there, adding: “My hope is that anyone who is no longer employed at Ferguson Marine can find work elsewhere on the Clyde. More than 1,500 jobs have now been lost in Inverclyde in just a few years. Calls for direct support have been made repeatedly to the Scottish Government but have been ignored.
“This is a local jobs crisis. The Scottish Government needs to step up, move faster and do everything within its power to secure the future of Ferguson Marine and the skilled jobs that depend on it.”
Daniel Johnson, Scottish Labour’s economy spokesperson, said: “This news will be causing significant anxiety for the workers at Ferguson Marine and the wider community. The skilled workers at this yard have been continually let down by the chaos of the SNP government.
“The SNP must listen to this wake-up call and ensure the pipeline of work promised moves forward with the urgency needed so we can protect these crucial jobs. We need a real long term plan to support Scotland’s iconic shipbuilding industry and secure jobs at this site for generations to come.”
Willie Rennie, the Scottish Liberal Democrat transport spokesperson, said: “These workers have been let down by the SNP over and over again. The yard needs a pipeline of work to flourish but that has not been forthcoming.
“Meanwhile, there can be little doubt that the chaos around its ownership and management have made it a less appealing prospect for those wanting to build commercial ships. All of this can be traced back to the SNP yet despite so many transport ministers coming and going no one has ever taken responsibility. It has been a case study in how not to do a government intervention.”
The contracts at the centre of the dispute were announced in March 2026, when the Scottish Government said it intended to make a strategic direct award to Ferguson Marine covering four vessels: two ferries for Caledonian Maritime Assets under the Small Vessel Replacement Programme, along with a marine protection vessel and a marine research vessel. Due diligence on that award is still under way.
Ferguson Marine says the changes are designed to address the size of the business and align skills across the yard so it is ready to begin work as soon as the contracts are settled, and that the consultation will not affect the remaining work or the delivery schedule for Glen Rosa. A phased transition plan is in place across active projects.
Glen Rosa is the second of two dual-fuel ferries ordered for the Clyde and Hebrides network in 2015, a contract that ran years late and far over budget, and which led to the yard being taken into public ownership in December 2019 after Ferguson Marine Engineering went into administration. Her sister ship Glen Sannox was handed over in early 2025.
The yard also carries out fabrication work for BAE Systems on the Type 26 frigate programme, producing structural units that are shipped up the river to Govan for assembly, and is partway through a transformation project intended to modernise the site.
Ferguson Marine has operated at Port Glasgow since 1903.

U.S. Marines to use Accrete’s Argus AI for information ops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:30:05 UTC
17:30:05 KST

- Accrete won a sole-source U.S. Marine Corps contract for Argus for Cognitive Advantage, an AI platform for analyzing narratives across social and broadcast media.
- The company previously deployed Argus with the Department of War in 2022 and won a multi-million dollar U.S. Army contract for the technology in 2024.
The U.S. Marine Corps has awarded Accrete a contract to deliver an artificial intelligence platform designed to track and analyze narratives across social media, broadcast outlets, and messaging platforms in near real time.
The contract covers Argus for Cognitive Advantage, a system built on Accrete’s Knowledge Engine platform. Accrete describes Knowledge Engines as tools that convert the expertise of experienced analysts into AI agents capable of surfacing relevant information across large volumes of open-source data. The company did not disclose the contract’s dollar value or duration.
Argus for Cognitive Advantage pulls from open-source intelligence, the open web, social media, broadcast media, messaging platforms, and foreign-language outlets, according to Accrete. The company said the system can process hours of video content in minutes, transcribing and translating speech, identifying objects and scene content, and inferring location details, including from video in languages the analyst does not read.
The platform includes several component tools, Accrete said. A narrative intelligence function tracks how conversations evolve and spread using stance detection and predictive simulation. A separate audience simulation tool models how different audience segments might react to a message before it is released. The system also generates automated measures of effectiveness intended to quantify mission outcomes, and includes a chat interface, called Argus Chat, that lets analysts query data using plain language.
Accrete said the platform draws on content from Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, X, YouTube, Reddit, Telegram, Weibo, and VKontakte, with real-time translation and transcription across 243 languages. The company said every inference the system produces is traceable to its source, within what it described as auditable, accreditation-ready boundaries.
“Cognitive advantage is a warfighting requirement, not a support function, and this award reflects the Marine Corps’ clear recognition of that,” said Bill Wall, CEO of Accrete AI Government.
“Furthermore, this sole-source award demonstrates the trust Accrete has built across the Department of War services. Accrete is proud to expand its reach within the Department of War by supporting the U.S. Marine Corps.”
Accrete first deployed the Argus platform with the Department of War in 2022. The company won a multi-million dollar contract from the U.S. Army in 2024 to develop the technology further for Army information operations. Argus for Cognitive Advantage was also selected for a 2025 AFWERX STRATFI award, a Department of War funding mechanism intended to move technology from prototype to operational use.
“Knowledge Engines are dynamic context recorders, and the advantage begins the moment an organization presses record,” said Prashant Bhuyan, founder, CEO, and chairman of Accrete.
“The most valuable context in any institution is the know-how trapped in the heads of its best people. Organizations that never capture it are ceding compounding advantage to adversaries and competitors that do. Argus for Cognitive Advantage is one of the most sophisticated applications of the Knowledge Engine platform, and Accrete is proud to extend it to the Marine Corps as it counters adversaries operating against the United States every day through digital channels.”
Accrete’s announcement frames the tool as a response to adversaries operating below the threshold of armed conflict, using coordinated narratives, synthetic media, and inauthentic social media activity to shape public perception. The company said this kind of information competition moves faster than human analysts working through open-source material by hand.

What’s so bad about a planned Hong Kong economy? Just look at Singapore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:30:04 UTC
17:30:04 KST

What’s so bad about a planned Hong Kong economy? Just look at Singapore
Dismissing economic planning out of hand is a mistake. The market does not always get it right
Having been in Asia for 50 years – in Singapore, which I consider a planned economy, and Hong Kong – and having travelled in and written about China while also living in Japan, perhaps I might offer a few observations.
The first is that people who take up extreme positions on either side of the market-vs-planned economy argument are often sadly misinformed, if not naive. The second is that those who passionately espouse the virtues of a market economy need to look more closely and clearly at the recent performance of these unplanned systems, both economic and financial.
It is absurd to argue that economic planning is undesirable per se. I have long hewn to a somewhat leftist view on such matters but that view was reinforced when I arrived in Singapore in 1976 to join the Business Times as a founding writer. Then under the leadership of Lee Kuan Yew, a Cambridge graduate, newly independent Singapore was busy implementing a plan to carve out a small nation state with industry at its core, and to free it from colonial dependency as an entrepot for East-West trade.
I was impressed by this endeavour, as were many others, including former British prime minister Margaret Thatcher. No one could accuse Thatcher of being a dangerous leftist. She was pragmatic enough to realise that a partially planned or state-cum-market economy like Singapore’s was a realistic and workable alternative to leaving things entirely to the private sector.
I then moved on in 1979 to Hong Kong to become business editor of the sadly now defunct Far Eastern Economic Review. There, I found a very different economic and social ethos. To espouse a planned economy in Hong Kong at that time was to utter the ultimate heresy.

South Africa uncovers major drug lab
Two Mexicans were among five people arrested at a crystal meth lab worth more than half a billion rand (nearly $30 million) on a farm in Musina, Limpopo, the South African Police Service (SAPS) reported on Friday.
The lab was raided late on Thursday night. The blitz was carried out by the US Drug Enforcement Administration and Homeland Security, alongside the Hawks, SAPS, the South African Narcotics Bureau, Crime Intelligence and the Special Task Force. Hawks spokesman Colonel Avele Fumba said drugs and laboratory equipment worth an estimated R600m were seized, along with an undisclosed amount of cash.
The five men are aged between 20 and 47. Two are Mexican, two are Zimbabwean, and one is Malawian. Fumba said the raid followed a two-month investigation into drug manufacturing on the farm, and that the lab was set up for industrial-scale production. It is the third clandestine drug lab shut down in Limpopo.
Limpopo Hawks head Major General Gopz Govender said the operation had gone after the machinery behind the drug trade. “This R600 million seizure is not merely a quantity of drugs taken off the streets. It represents the disruption of an entire criminal enterprise,” Govender said. “We will follow the money, the networks and every person connected to this operation.”
Limpopo police commissioner Lieutenant General Jan Scheepers said communities would not be left to become markets for syndicates. “Those who manufacture and distribute these dangerous substances must know that law enforcement is closing in on them,” he said.
Officers were still working the scene on Friday morning. Photographs released by police show officers in masks and surgical gloves moving through a low structure roofed with corrugated iron and walled with green shade netting. Industrial steel pots stand on the concrete floor beside a gas cylinder and a digital floor scale.
Musina sits on the Beitbridge border post with Zimbabwe, the busiest land crossing in southern Africa. The five face charges of manufacturing and possessing illicit drugs and are due in the Musina Magistrate’s Court on Monday.

DR Congo receives 1st batch of vaccines to contain Ebola outbreak

Unknown Publisher

17:24:21 KST

James Tasamba
22 August 2026•Update: 22 August 2026
The Democratic Republic of Congo has received the first batch of 16,520 doses of the Ervebo Ebola vaccine to contain the Ebola virus, health authorities said late Friday.
Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said more than 50,000 doses are expected by Monday.
“These doses would strengthen the government’s response to Ebola and contribute to the protection of populations, with the support of our partners,” Kamba told reporters in Kinshasa.
The World Health Organization announced on Thursday that 70,000 vaccines would be supplied to Congo from the global Ebola virus disease vaccine stockpile for a Phase 3 clinical trial to better understand the impact of the vaccine on the Bundibugyo virus and to be used for frontline and health workers.
To date, no vaccine or specific treatment has been approved against the Bundibugyo virus.
The Ervebo vaccine is licensed and recommended for use in outbreaks of Ebola virus disease, previously called Zaire ebolavirus.
Confirmed infections in the current Ebola outbreak have reached 5,290 cases, including more than 2,500 deaths, according to the latest Health Ministry situation update.
On Friday, Doctors Without Borders (MSF) warned that communities in Congo are not receiving adequate support to contain the Ebola virus.
MSF said in a statement that training for health workers and community leaders on case detection, referrals and infection prevention and control measures must be urgently bolstered within communities affected by the outbreak.
The latest epidemic has affected 56 health zones across six provinces: Haut-Uele, Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Bas-Uele and Tshopo since the outbreak was declared in mid-May.

Congo receives more than 16,000 doses of Ebola vaccine as it grapples with unprecedented outbreak
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
08:23:02 UTC
17:23:02 KST

Congo receives more than 16,000 doses of Ebola vaccine as it grapples with unprecedented outbreak
BUNIA, Congo (AP) — Congo has received more than 16,000 doses of the Ervebo vaccine as the country grapples with the fastest Ebola outbreak in history, the country’s health minister said.
The 16,250 doses arrived at the N’djili International Airport in the capital, Kinshasa, late Friday, as part of 70,000 doses expected from the World Health Organization and partners that were announced on Thursday. More doses are expected early next week.
The current Ebola outbreak in Congo is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which currently has no approved treatment or vaccine. It can spread easily and go undetected because some of its symptoms are similar to other illnesses, such as malaria. The Ervebo vaccine is licensed to treat Ebola and has been effective in past outbreaks. The WHO said it may provide some protection against the Bundibugyo virus.
The latest outbreak, which has recorded 2,557 deaths out of the 5,375 confirmed cases across six affected provinces, is spreading at an unprecedented rate and is on track to surpass the deadliest outbreak on record, which killed over 11,000 people across West Africa between 2014 and 2016. Data from the Africa Centre for Disease Control shows that transmission has not yet peaked and could reach three times its known rate.
Efforts to contain the outbreak have been hampered by armed conflict between the government and rebel groups, which control key cities in the hot spot; attacks on medical personnel and facilities; an itinerant labor population and people displaced by the armed conflict; and a lack of critical infrastructure.

Wall Street week ahead: Reports on consumer confidence and inflation on tap

Wall Street week ahead: Reports on consumer confidence and inflation on tap
NEW YORK (AP) — Wall Street will get key updates next week on closely-watched measures for consumer confidence and inflation.
The latest consumer confidence report from business group The Conference Board will be released Tuesday. Wall Street expects the report to show that confidence in the U.S. economy fell again in August after slipping in July.
Consumer confidence has been weak most of the year as inflation remains stubbornly high. The U.S. war with Iran helped fuel inflation by stifling oil supplies worldwide. That raised gasoline prices, squeezing household budgets. It has also raised costs for shipping a wide range of products, from groceries to clothing.
Wall Street will get another important inflation update on Wednesday when the U.S. releases its report on personal consumption expenditures, or PCE, for July. It is the Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation. Much like the consumer price index, it has shown that the rate of inflation remains stubbornly above 3%.
The Fed has been struggling to get inflation back to its target rate of 2%. It came close in early 2025 but then inflation started creeping higher as the U.S. imposed a wide range of tariffs globally. The rate of inflation leaped higher in early 2026 as the Iran war curtailed global oil shipments from the Strait of Hormuz.
The Fed is expected to continue holding its benchmark interest rate steady at its upcoming meeting in September.

Age limit, two-term cap: DMK passes nine resolutions for sweeping organisational overhaul
Edited by: Karan Manral / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 22, 2026, 14:53 IST

Stalin acknowledges that the changes would be “stringent” and difficult for some to accept.
NEW DELHI: The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) on Saturday unveiled a structural overhaul of its organisation following its defeat in the Tamil Nadu Assembly elections in April, when it lost power after a single term.DMK’s executive committee, headed by party supremo and former chief minister MK Stalin, met at Anna Arivalayam, the party’s state headquarters in Chennai, and passed nine key resolutions aimed at radically restructuring the organisation.
Addressing the meeting, Stalin acknowleded that the changes would be "stringent" and even "difficult" for some to accept."The functioning of our party office-bearers is also one of the reasons for our defeat. We must first acknowledge our mistakes. We are going to make several changes in the party’s organisational structure. They will certainly be stringent, and for some, they may even be difficult to accept,” the former chief minister said.“Going forward, we are going to introduce age limits and terms of office for various organisational posts, according to the responsibilities involved. We are going to give a larger number of organisational responsibilities to newcomers.
We can regain political success only by restructuring the party. We must carry out the organisational reforms as quickly as possible,” he added.Under the new blueprint, the DMK leadership has introduced strict age limits, a mandatory two-term cap for all posts and a major expansion of organisational districts, with the aim of professionalising party operations and facilitating generational succession.The DMK will increase the number of organisational districts from 78 to 110, with each district broadly covering two assembly constituencies to ensure more localised administration. Once Stalin formally releases the boundary maps for the 110 revamped districts, district executive committees will have to convene within 15 days under the supervision of the party headquarters to implement the transition.The standalone post of “city secretary” in major urban centres such as Coimbatore and Tambaram has also been abolished. Instead, urban zones will be redrawn based on voter density, with Chennai Corporation Area Committees averaging 40,000 voters and those in other corporations averaging 30,000 voters per committee.
Following Stalin’s defeat in his Kolathur Assembly constituency in Chennai, the DMK is now being led in the Tamil Nadu assembly by his son and former deputy chief minister Udhayanidhi Stalin, who is now serving as the leader of the opposition.

Germany news: Friedrich Merz to visit area struck by fires

Germany news: Friedrich Merz visits area struck by fires
Published August 22, 2026last updated August 22, 2026
What you need to know

-

This is a roundup of the main headlines in and about Germany on the weekend of August 22-23, 2026:
IN DEPTH: Industry and residents clash over water near Berlin
The state surrounding Berlin is drying out, but local Tesla and Red Bull plants are looking to expand. Is Brandenburg running out of water to share?
Learn more about the drought affecting Berlin and the surrounding areas in this report by DW's Anne-Sophie Brändin.
Merz says forest fires 'a consequence of climate change'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz thanked local firefighters for their efforts battling last week's dramatic forest fire in western Germany's Eifel region and stressed that such fires are a consequence of climate change.
"We have to expect such events more often," he said during a visit to the communities affected by the fires. "This is climate change."
"I want to tell all those climate change deniers: Look at what's happening here," he added.
Merz said he would do everything possible to combat climate change but stressed that "we also have to live with climate change."
When it comes to climate policy, Merz's CDU has stressed the importance of market-based strategies rather than bans to protect the environment.
He was met with whistles and boos from people holding signs and saying Merz's government has not adequately addressed the climate crisis.
The chancellor thanked the firefighters and all other local groups that helped fight the Hürtgenwald fire that raged for a week, forcing the evacuation of entire villages before it was finally extinguished late last week.
It was Merz's first public appearance since July 29, when he left for his summer vacation. He previously thanked emergency workers for their "tireless effort" on X.
Opposition parties criticized his prolonged absence while the country was grappling with heat waves and forest fires and suggested he was not taking climate change seriously.
Magdeburg marks Pride parade ahead of crucial election
Under the slogan "Vote for Love," around 3,000 people took part in a pride parade in the eastern German city of Magdeburg. The city is the capital of Saxony-Anhalt, which will hold state elections on September 6 that the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) is expected to win.
The AfD promotes a traditional heterosexual family model and is at times critical of the LGBTQ+ community.
The parade's organizers said Saturday’s event was a show of support for democracy, diversity and an open society.
While it was Magdeburg’s 30th Pride parade, this year was the first time it was held on a central square in front of the state parliament, in part to increase political visibility ahead of the election but also to help with security measures.
Last month, a deadly attack on the Berlin Pride Parade left one person dead and injured many others.
Several other cities in Germany also held their pride parade on Saturday. In Bremen, around 33,000 people marched under the slogan "Generations Full of Pride — Happy, Visible, Strong."
Conservative local candidate sparks controversy with 'MILF' necklace
Corinna Jodeit, a candidate from Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) in local elections outside Bremen, has caused a stir with her official campaign portrait.
Jodeit is running for a seat on the Wildeshausen city council and can be seen wearing a gold necklace prominently featuring the English-language acronym MILF on posters for the September 13 vote.
The term is an abbreviation for the phrase "Mother I'd like to f--k."
The candidate herself said that although the term is "naturally provocative," the necklace is "just a piece of jewelry" that emphasizes her independence.
"I'm happy to be a mum, but there's more to me than that," she told the Wildeshausener Zeitung newspaper, admitting that she had considered removing the necklace for the photo but added that she felt it would have been inauthentic.
Comments below an Instagram post by the paper garnered strong opinions, offering both support and critique, with some readers calling the situation "embarrassing" and "inappropriate" and others saying they found it "hot" and "funny."
German finance minister calls for windfall tax on oil profits
German Finance Minister and Vice Chancellor Lars Klingbeil on Saturday called for a tax on windfall profits currently being racked up by large multinational oil companies.
"We must address the problem of high energy prices by discussing an EU-wide framework for taxing windfall profits," Klingbeil wrote in an open letter also signed by several European counterparts.
Klingbeil said he has often raised the issue of energy company rip-offs at the Finance Ministry in Berlin and has now joined his colleagues to call on Ireland's Finance Minister Simon Harris to put the topic on the EU agenda "as soon as possible."
Ireland currently holds the EU's rotating presidency.
The next meeting of European finance ministers is scheduled to take place in Dublin on September 18 and 19.
Although finance ministers acknowledge that the main price driver at the moment is the US-Israeli war on Iran, they point out that "oil companies are reporting strong overall profitability and margins on refined products, which — albeit possibly influenced by product-specific bottlenecks — exceed the rise in crude oil prices."
"Dissatisfaction with the rising cost of living is growing not only in Germany and Europe, but worldwide," as government interventions fail to ease the burden of higher fuel prices on taxpayers, the ministers wrote.
The ministers are now calling on those who profit from the current crisis in the Middle East to "pay their share to ease the burden on the public at large."
Klingbeil and his colleagues say the EU should make available its findings from 2022 research on "targeting the foreign profits of multi-national oil companies" and how they can be taxed.
According to aid organization Oxfam, the world's six largest fossil fuel companies — BP, Chevron, Eni, ExxonMobil, Shell and TotalEnergies — registered €40 billion in profits in the second quarter of 2026. Total profit is forecast to hit €147 billion for the year.
Germany's federal government, like those of Klingbeil's partners, has so far refused to level windfall oil profit taxes.
The European Commission has also poured cold water on the concept, saying it has no plans to introduce any scheme on excessive profits.
Massive pay gap between German, foreign workers in Germany
Germany's Labor Ministry released data on Saturday showing a 23.6% pay gap between German and foreign full-time workers in 2025.
The data was released in response to a parliamentary inquiry posed by far-right opposition Alternative for Germany (AfD).
Accordingly, although wage growth grew across the board, median full-time monthly pay for Germans was €4,396 ($5,138), whereas foreign full-time employees pulled in €3,358.
The numbers track with trends seen since 2020.
Overall, Labor Ministry stats show that 30.6% of foreign workers earned low wages as compared to 12.3% of Germans.
The AfD launched its query to poke holes in Berlin's immigration policies, which it claims are smothering wage growth, though that is not made clear by the data.
A separate study by the Institute for Employment Research said the gap could be because "immigrants are less likely to be employed in high-paying sectors or positions."
The Federal Employment Agency said earnings depend heavily on a person's education, qualifications and professional job experience.
In 2025, workers without vocational qualifications earned a median wage of €3,133, while full-time employees with recognized vocational qualifications earned €4,069 and college graduates earned €6,146.
Germany's FAZ newspaper slams Russian arrest warrant for correspondent
Germany's Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung (FAZ) on Saturday slammed a Russian Interior Ministry arrest warrant for the paper's Balkans correspondent Michael Martens, as "an attempt to intimidate a German journalist and the free press."
The paper accused Moscow of seeking to curtail free speech through threat of criminal punishment.
"Freedom of the press is non-negotiable," said the FAZ, "It applies even when questions or reports provoke criticism."
The paper said it flatly rejects any attempt to obstruct independent journalism.
Russia issued the warrant over Martens' phrasing in posing a question to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during an August 8, 2026, press conference in the Serbian capital, Belgrade.
Mertens asked Zelenskyy what Europeans could do "to help you kill more Russians," which FAZ management says could have been formulated differently, acknowledging that the phrasing left the issue open to "misinterpretation."
The paper said, "We have clarified this and expressed our regret at the wording."
Last week, Russia issued its warrant for Martens' arrest for "public incitement to hatred and hostility." If found guilty, he would face six years in prison.
The Russian Embassy in Berlin has asked public prosecutors in the German capital to look into the situation, saying Martens' remarks "regarding the possibility of 'aiding and abetting the murder of Russians' as well as the lack of a public apology," suggest the wording "was chosen deliberately and intentionally."
Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova described Martens' words as "unacceptable" and "criminal."
Germany mulls constitutional protections for LGBTQ+ people after Berlin Pride attack
Germany's Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig is calling for an amendment to the country's constitution, known as the German Basic Law, to specifically protect LGBTQ+ people.
"I am in favour of amending Article 3(3) of the Basic Law to include a ban on discrimination on the grounds of sexual identity," Hubig told the Rheinische Post newspaper in an interview published on Saturday.
Hubig, a member of the center-left Social Democratic Party, said there were reservations within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservatives, but there were also encouraging signs.
German Basic Law prohibits the disadvantage or preferential treatment of people on grounds such as their ancestry, language, homeland or origin, their faith, religion or political views. "It is only logical to also prohibit unequal treatment on the grounds of sexual identity," said Hubig.
Hubig's comments come after a man drove his car into a crowd on the sidelines of Pride festivities in Berlin, one of the largest LGBTQ events in Europe.
The suspected attacker, Abdul Ballout, a German citizen of Lebanese background, was shot dead by police the day after the attack following a major manhunt.
Germany's antisemitism commissioner calls for tougher laws for Hamas supporters
Germany's Federal Antisemitism Commissioner Felix Klein on Saturday called for harsher laws and punishment for those supporting militant Palestinian groups such as Hamas.
In an interview published in the Saturday edition of the daily Kölner Stadt-Anzeiger newspaper, Klein said he hopes Chancellor Merz and Justice Minister Stefanie Hubig will strengthen existing laws and called for anyone demonstrating in support of the Palestinian militant group Hamas — considered a terrorist group by Israel, the US, Germany and many other nations — to face at least six months in jail.
"If the person is a foreign national without secure residence status," added Klein, "they should be deported after being convicted and serving their sentence."
He also demanded customs authorities be given expanded powers to disrupt the financing of terrorist organizations.
While praising the work done combating antisemitism through education, Klein also called for rigorous, mandatory teacher training. "Anyone susceptible to antisemitism has no place in the teaching profession," he said, calling for disciplinary consequences for teachers expressing antisemitic sentiments.
Klein said Jewish life in Germany must be presented in a positive light and that Judaism is about more than antisemitism, the Holocaust and the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.
Felix Klein is leaving his current post, which he has held since 2018, to serve as Germany's ambassador to the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in Paris.
Over 100 injured in mass soccer brawl at German Cup match
Some 35 police officers and 85 fans were injured in a massive brawl during a soccer match on Friday evening in the southwestern city of Mannheim say local officials, with several people hospitalized.
More than 1,400 police and security officers were on hand for the German Cup game between local rivals Waldhof Mannheim and 1. FC Kaiserslautern. Officials say 23,500 fans were at the sold-out game, 3,500 of them supporters of visiting Kaiserslautern.
Those fans began shooting fireworks at Mannheim players at the end of normal time with the match goalless. Mannheim fans rushed onto the pitch in response, which in turn brought out mounted police and security officers.
"The intense preparations by all participating institutions and the close cooperation among all those involved paid off. Our tactical plan worked perfectly," said Mannheim Police Chief Michael Reichert after the melee.

That is exactly how we will treat these individuals in order to enforce law and order in our stadiums."
Police say they have launched investigations into "insults, various assault charges, property damage, breach of the peace, physical assault on police officers, and violations of the Explosives Act."
Several football fans were detained, German news agency DPA reported.
The German Football Association (DFB) has promised a full report into the incident.
Ibrahim Kanate scored in the last minute of extra time to give Kaiserslautern a 1-0 win. The second-division side advances to the second round of the Cup.
