NEW DELHI: Punjab chief ministerBhagwant Mann’s wife, Gurpreet Kaur, on Saturday sent a legal notice to former Punjab and Haryana high court judge Ranjit Singh over his allegations that she attempted to suppress a rape case and sought Rs 5 crore in exchange for doing so.According to an official communication from the ruling Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), Ranjit Singh, brother-in-law of Congress leader Sukhpal Singh Khaira, has been asked to respond to the legal notice within 24 hours of receiving it. The notice warned that failure to respond within the stipulated deadline would invite legal proceedings and require Singh to appear before a court.Gurpreet Kaur’s move came after the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC) took cognisance of the matter and directed the Punjab chief secretary and director general of police to inquire into the allegations.Earlier, NHRC member Priyank Kanoongo said the commission had received the complaint from Justice Ranjit Singh (retd).“We have received a complaint from former Punjab and Haryana High Court Justice Ranjit Singh alleging that the wife of Punjab CM Bhagwant Mann attempted to hush up a rape case in exchange for a bribe of Rs 5 crore. It is a matter of concern when such an allegation is levelled against a person holding a top position in a state regarding a case involving the safety of women and children,” Kanoongo told ANI.
He further noted that the NHRC had sought a report from the state administration.“We have directed the chief secretary and the DGP of Punjab to investigate the matter and submit a report to us. We have also informed the Women’s Safety Division of the Union Ministry of Home Affairs. We will be able to proceed with further investigation only after receiving the report,” Kanoongo added.He also warned officials against acting under “political pressure”, cautioning that action could be taken against them if they succumbed to such pressure.The NHRC has given Punjab 15 days to submit an Action Taken Report and will decide on further action based on the report.

Wehrmacht motorbike from the Danube brings siege of Budapest to life
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:14:01 UTC
16:14:01 KST

Wehrmacht motorbike from the Danube brings siege of Budapest to life
Which unit did the Wehrmacht motorbike found near Budapest belong to, and how did it end up in the Danube? Euronews asked Lt Col Norbert Számvéber, a military historian at the Institute and Museum of Military History, about this rare find.
At the beginning of August, a Second World War-era German DKW NZ-350-1 motorcycle was found in the Danube, right in the heart of the capital, by Batthyány Square.
Since then it has fascinated archaeologists, historians and military-history enthusiasts. It is extremely rare anywhere in the world for a relic from the past to surface in such condition.
The German motorcycle draws attention to the period when almost 100,000 German and Hungarian soldiers became casualties in Budapest, so that Nazi Germany's Third Reich could buy time against the Soviets.
Until the spring of 1944, Hungary was not considered a theatre of operations, partly because the war had not yet reached its borders, and partly because the Allies had not begun systematically bombing it. All that changed on 19 March 1944, when the armed forces of the Third Reich occupied Hungary.
This was not only a tragedy for Hungary's Jews and the civilian population in general, but also for all the soldiers who were deployed in Hungary in the service of Hitler's plans.
SS soldiers in the Danube: Not necessarily linked to the motorcycle
According to Lieutenant Colonel Norbert Számvéber, director of the Military History Archive at the Military History Institute and Museum (HM HIM), the motorcycle belonged to one of the most important units among the German forces encircled in Budapest.
"This was the armoured division Feldherrnhalle (commonly abbreviated to FHH), which had an armoured pioneer battalion bearing the same name," the lieutenant colonel told Euronews. "The motorcycle may have entered the inventory of this unit, then in the process of being re-formed, in September 1944, when it was still called Pionier-Bataillon (mot.) Feldherrnhalle. At the end of that month, or at the latest in early October 1944, it was renamed Panzer-Pionier-Bataillon Feldherrnhalle. The motorcycle and the vehicles that had already been marked with the unit insignia were not repainted one by one, perhaps for lack of time."
Anti-tank mines, ammunition and the remains of two German soldiers were also found near the bike. The military historian recalls that during the siege of Budapest, after the surrender of the Pest bridgehead on 18 January 1945, the battered remnants of the German 22nd SS Volunteer Cavalry Division defended the Buda embankment of the Danube. The two soldiers discovered next to the motorcycle belonged to this SS unit, as indicated by their identity tags (in everyday parlance: dog tags), so they were probably not directly connected to the motorcycle.
"Here they may have fallen in combat, or they may have been executed on the spot by the Soviets. The latter was by no means uncommon in the case of SS members, but since the Soviets typically removed identity tags before executions, the former scenario is more likely," explains Norbert Számvéber.
Dumped in the Danube during clearance operations?
Examination of the vehicle showed that its gearbox was in second gear, or stuck there. Curators at the HM HIM also established that the motorcycle was definitely involved in a crash 81 years ago, but it cannot be determined whether that happened at the moment it entered the Danube.
"At this stage it is impossible to reconstruct reliably how the vehicle and the bodies of the two SS soldiers found beside it ended up there. I rule out the possibility that a ferry may have been crossing the Danube and was sunk by the Soviets, because neither the tactical situation nor the heavily iced river would have allowed that during the siege of Budapest," the historian said. "This type of motorcycle was used mainly for liaison tasks, for example to carry reports and orders. I assume that it became a loss near the riverbank while performing such a mission, but that it may only have found its way into the Danube after the end of the siege, during debris-clearing operations."
The Corporal and the Others
One thing is certain, however: in the 1965 film A tizedes meg a többiek (The Corporal and the Others), a legendary work of Hungarian cinema about ordinary Hungarian soldiers trapped between the German and Soviet armies and switching sides from one to the other, Imre Sinkovits did not sit on a bike of this kind. His was a Soviet copy of a BMW.
About 12,000 examples of the DKW model raised from the Danube were produced in 1944–45, already with grey cast-iron engine blocks because of the shortage of aluminium. After the Second World War the Soviets dismantled the entire production line and shipped it to Izhevsk as reparations. There, up to 1951, they manufactured a further 127,000 under the name Izs-350.
Of the German-produced machines, only a few dozen – an estimated 30 to 50 – are thought to have survived, some of them in partly original condition.
The German motorised pioneer companies were not only technical support sub-units, they also had considerable combat value. Each such company was equipped with two heavy machine guns, 18 light machine guns, two 8 cm mortars and six backpack flamethrowers. In the armoured companies, flamethrowers were fitted mainly to their infantry fighting vehicles.
"These were excellently equipped assault battalions designed for attacks against fortified positions and for fighting in built-up areas. In a major city such as Budapest, units of this kind became particularly important."
Elite unit – but what was its link to the notorious SA?
The history of the Feldherrnhalle armoured division goes back to 1935, when Viktor Lutze, head of the Nazi Party's paramilitary organisation, the brown-shirted Sturmabteilung (SA, in Hungarian Rohamosztag), wanted to create a regiment with weapons similar to the SS's "Leibstandarte". In September 1936 Hitler granted the SA Guard Regiment the name "Feldherrnhalle", which soldiers then wore on their uniforms, embroidered in silver thread on a brown background on the lower part of the left sleeve of their tunics. During the Second World War the unit shuttled between the western and eastern fronts, suffered heavy losses and also took part in the occupation of Hungary.
"Some of the soldiers in the Feldherrnhalle division came from the SA," explains Számvéber. "The organisation had a large mass base, which is one reason it survived at all, but the SA itself had no military armament and played hardly any role in the war – except for the Feldherrnhalle units, one of which included the motorcycle found at Batthyány Square."
As an example, the historian mentions one Feldherrnhalle commander who, as a reservist officer, left his dental practice to join the army and went on to become a decorated armoured general.
The losses of the siege of Budapest
Between Christmas 1944 and mid-February 1945 around 100,000 German and Hungarian soldiers defended the Hungarian capital. This force was practically wiped out: those who were not killed in combat were taken prisoner of war. When the breakout was attempted, only 705 German and 36 Hungarian soldiers, together with 44 civilians, reached the German lines.
The total losses of the Soviet forces and the Romanian troops fighting alongside them may have been around 38,000.
Because of the bloody fighting during the siege, the residents of the then one-million-strong capital retreated to air-raid shelters. Illustrating the intensity of the clashes, there were cases where one wall of a cellar was broken through by the Soviets, the other by the Germans, who then fired at each other over the heads of terrified civilians. Civilian deaths are estimated at around 23,000.
The siege also ended tragically for the surviving part of Hungary's Jewish community. While the Soviets besieged the city, the Arrow Cross militia terrorised the inhabitants of Europe's last ghetto. By the end of the siege around 15,000 Jews had died in Budapest.
The significance of the siege of Budapest and the fighting in Hungary
"It was a pointless, horrific bloodletting," says Norbert Számvéber. "Hungary fell victim to the Germans' strategy of buying time."
According to the military historian, it was Hungary's utterly botched, poorly prepared and even more poorly executed attempt to break away from the war that led to prolonged fighting in the country. As a result, the German high command diverted virtually all its armoured reserves to Hungary from the Warsaw–Berlin axis, even though the Red Army was advancing on the German capital at a tremendous pace. Operations here were intended in part to protect the oilfields in Zala, as domestic production roughly covered the fuel needs of the German troops fighting in Hungary.
But that was not the most important reason, Számvéber sums up.
"Hitler refused to allow Budapest to be abandoned because he wanted to launch an offensive from the Pest side towards the north-east. The Feldherrnhalle division would also have had a role in this," he says. "Another reason was that Budapest acted as bait in the defence of the Vienna industrial region. If the Soviets took the bait and became bogged down around the Hungarian capital, the German command could thereby protect the Vienna Basin and gain time to build what was called the 'Alpine Fortress'. It was a grandiose plan to gain time. Budapest, along with German troops and, of course, the city's innocent inhabitants, was deliberately allowed to be encircled, and in this way the Germans succeeded in imposing their will on the Soviets."
On 29 October 1944, Soviet troops tried to take Budapest on the move. This meant they attacked without prior preparation or an operational pause – and suffered heavy losses. They then attempted to encircle the capital, and once the 3rd Ukrainian Front had arrived, they began the systematic siege of Budapest, which lasted until 13 February 1945, mainly because of German attempts to relieve the city. Hitler's plan to gain time thus succeeded.
The two German soldiers may finally receive a burial
The director believes that the motorcycle recovered from the Danube has become a symbol of this protracted struggle and the suffering it caused.
"Like a time capsule, it confronts us with our past at close quarters. From the point of view of military history, the vehicle and the associated finds have now also confirmed, from a conflict-archaeology perspective, the data that research had pieced together from other sources over recent decades. In principle, the two German soldiers can be identified by name, so for their families they are no longer relatives who disappeared without trace. After 81 years they can be granted the last honours and laid to rest."
The extremely fierce fighting on the Hungarian battlefield has left numerous traces. However, partly because of the country's physical geography – Hungary has no extensive marshes – and partly because of post-war metal-collection campaigns, these traces very rarely take the form of complete combat vehicles or aircraft.
In that light, the discovery of this intact motorcycle is particularly welcome.
(The first full-length documentary about the siege of Budapest was made in 2015 and can be viewed here (source in Hungarian).)

pyramids and maya forms shape coco brun and sten studio’s stone vessels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:13:11 UTC
16:13:11 KST

French artist and designer Coco Brun joins forces with Mexico City-based Sten Studio for Echoes of Mexico, a collection of sculptural vessels rooted in the country’s lapidary traditions. Hand-carved from red travertine, veined marble and multicolored onyx, the pieces translate references to ancient Mesoamerican architecture and ornament into a contemporary design language. Developed with support from the Institut Français d’Amérique Latine (IFAL), Mobilier National and Galerie Territorio, the project was recently recognized in the fourth edition of Le French Design 100 at Art Paris.
The collaboration unfolds through two capsule collections, each limited to a maximum of 10 pieces. Rather than sourcing new blocks, Brun and Sten Studio work with remnants from the workshop’s existing production, including red travertine, white Venetian marble, black Orizaba marble, and pink and green onyx. Variations in veining, translucency and color are therefore not treated as imperfections to be corrected, but as part of the final composition — which is fortunate, considering stone rarely agrees to repeat itself.
marble and onyx define the sculptural vessel series | all images courtesy of Sten Studio and Coco Brun
PYRAMIDS, MASKS AND POLISHED MASS
The Místicos series takes its geometry from the structural logic of Mexican pyramids. Faceted silhouettes, sloped surfaces and flattened summits abstract architectural forms into compact vessels, balancing the visual weight of polished marble against the translucent depth of onyx. Rather than reproducing specific monuments, the pieces distill their proportions and mass into a smaller, more domestic scale.
A different set of references informs Abstracted Ancestry, which looks to the layered geometry of Maya ceremonial masks and, in particular, the oversized ear ornaments worn by dignitaries. The resulting vessels feature oval bodies, sweeping curves and two straight perforated fins that extend from either side. These openings reference the form of historical ear ornaments while also introducing voids into otherwise dense stone objects, shifting the pieces somewhere between vessel, sculpture and architectural fragment.
each piece is shaped from reclaimed stone fragments
LEFTOVER STONE GOES ON TOUR
Material reuse runs through both collections. By working with offcuts from Sten Studio’s primary production, Echoes of Mexico gives fragments that might otherwise remain unused a new formal role. The project therefore connects a highly traditional craft process with a contemporary concern for material efficiency, while preserving the irregularities that make each vessel distinct. The result is not so much recycling disguised as luxury as a demonstration that the leftover piece can occasionally be the most interesting one.
The collection is also conceived as a traveling dialogue between France and Mexico. Following its presentation in Europe, the works are set to appear at the Lake Como Design Festival, before continuing to Mexico City Design Week as part of Inmersiones Creativas at Casa Ortega, an exhibition marking 200 years of diplomatic relations between France and Mexico. The journey concludes in Paris at 1000 Vases, staged at Espace Commines during Art Basel week, extending the project’s conversation between craft, geography and cultural memory across several very different contexts.

the vessels combine dense marble with translucent onyx
each object is produced as a limited-edition piece
geometric forms reference pyramids and ceremonial ornament
upcycled stone gives every vessel a unique material character

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says

Somalia child hunger crisis deepens after aid cuts, UNICEF says
The drought-stricken country has recorded a 32 percent jump in the number of children treated for severe malnutrition.
Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
Life-threatening malnutrition among children is spiking in Somalia as more than 200 health and nutrition facilities were forced to shutter following cuts to international aid, the United Nations has warned.
The East African country has seen a 32 percent jump in the number of children admitted to facilities with severe acute malnutrition and complications in the first six months of 2026, UNICEF said on Friday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Thousands flee drought in Somalia amid sharp aid decline
- list 2 of 3Suspected Somali pirates seize tanker near Yemen amid wave of hijackings
- list 3 of 3Somali army clashes with rebel forces for control of key city Baidoa
Nearly 1.9 million children are projected to be malnourished this year.
“In Somalia today, aid cuts are closing doors to healthcare, shutting down nutrition services, and pushing water, education and protection further out of reach,” UNICEF spokesman James Elder told reporters in Geneva, speaking via video from Nairobi.
As many as 618 health facilities could close nationwide under “severe funding scenarios”, Elder said. “This is the wrong moment to retreat.”
Somalia faces a severe drought that has killed livestock, ruined harvests and destroyed livelihoods. Aid groups estimate that drought displaced about 500,000 people between January and April, adding to roughly 3.3 million Somalis already uprooted.
One-third of Somalia’s population of 19 million people is facing severe food shortages.
Yet funding for addressing acute malnutrition in parts of Somalia has dropped by more than 80 percent this year, Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, said earlier this month, with the United States and several other Western countries slashing aid.
Somalia was also excluded from the $2bn global humanitarian aid pledge announced by the US for this year due to allegations of aid diversion and corruption.
The cuts have compounded the effects of the current drought, curtailing access to water even as prices in rural and pastoral areas have quadrupled, according to UNICEF.
At the same time, fuel and fertiliser costs have risen because of the US-Israel war on Iran, while a record-strength El Nino climate pattern is forecast to worsen the humanitarian crisis with severe flooding, Elder said.
Nearly a million children below five, adolescent girls and women risk losing access to nutrition services.

Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents

Unknown Publisher

Hospital sees daily child injuries from electric scooter accidents
80 percent of serious electric scooter accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but because the rider loses balance and falls, said ER doctor‑resident Kadri Ustav.
According to Ustav, most adults involved in such accidents have consumed alcohol.
"I can give examples from the North Estonia Medical Centre (PERH) and Tallinn Children's Hospital, and lately it seems that at least one child arrives at the children's hospital every day due to an electric scooter accident. At PERH, there were nearly 400 such accidents last year, and that number includes adults," Ustav said.
All serious cases, according to Ustav, are caused by excessive speed and not wearing a helmet. "Statistics show that 80 percent of these accidents do not happen because of a collision with another vehicle or person, but simply by losing balance or falling," Ustav said.
Among adults, there are also too many cases where several people ride on one scooter. "Adults have other substances involved that impair their decision‑making. In the PERH context, most riders involved in accidents have consumed alcohol."
Working in the ER, you see everything. "Elderly people with chronic illnesses, severe traffic accidents, poisonings, everything," Ustav said. "In the ER workflow, the most important role is the triage nurse, who must understand which patient needs the fastest help."
"People should also know more about their own health. Most things people want to come to the ER for can be treated at home. If you have a tick, fever, cough or cold. If nothing helps anymore, only then should you go to the ER. There are some specific things that require immediate attention, such as strong chest pain radiating to the arm, severe trauma, or a deep cut," Ustav noted.
"We at PERH's ER only see very severe accidents involving children; we do not see the smaller accidents involving children," Ustav said.

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says

Full fee waivers rise 20-fold to 280,000 after healthcare reform, minister says
Health chief defends higher charges for less urgent services in Hong Kong as full fee waivers increase from 14,000 since new regime began on January 1
About 280,000 patients have secured full fee waivers since Hong Kong’s public healthcare charges were overhauled at the start of the year, a 20-fold increase from the previous figure of 14,000, the health minister has said.
Secretary for Health Lo Chung-mau revealed the figures on Saturday as he defended the reform, which raised user fees for non-urgent and less serious services to reduce the government subsidy rate. He said the changes were intended to optimise the use of existing resources and strengthen protection for vulnerable groups.
“Since its implementation, just in eight months the number of people benefiting from full medical fee waivers has increased from 14,000 to 280,000 – a growth of over 20-fold,” Lo said.
The new public healthcare fee regime was introduced on January 1 to ensure the sustainable development of the healthcare system amid challenges posed by an ageing population.
Under the new structure, a visit to an accident and emergency department at a public hospital costs HK$400 (US$51) for less urgent cases, up from between HK$50 and HK$150 per visit.
The number of people eligible for subsidised or free healthcare will also expand significantly, from 300,000 to 1.4 million, following the relaxation of income and asset limits.

Ukraine's Air Force claimed that it downed 182 out of 217 drones, as well as destroyed nine missiles, launched by Russia overnight.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said in a morning statement that it launched a massive strike against transportation infrastructure facilities and a logistics center in Kyiv and the surrounding Kyiv region.
It said that the strike hit the “Darnytsia” locomotive depot, where “technical maintenance and repair of the locomotive fleet was carried out, ensuring the transportation of weapons and military equipment for the Armed Forces of Ukraine.”
It also claimed strikes on a logistics center in the city of Brovary in the Kyiv region, as well as on “warehouses with military equipment and fuel tanks intended for the Ukrainian Armed Forces” in the Chornomorsk and Pivdennyi ports in the Odesa region.
Strikes in Russia
A later Defense Ministry statement said Russian air defenses shot down 457 Ukrainian drones overnight over 15 regions, as well as over the Black Sea, the Sea of Azov, and Crimea, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
Vyacheslav Fedorishchev, governor of Russia’s Samara region, said that his region was targeted in a “massive” Ukrainian drone strike, claiming several dozen drones were shot down during the attack.
“Damage was sustained at one industrial facility. Additionally, a hit was recorded at the Ozon logistics complex,” Fedorishchev said, noting that several casualties are known, all of whom are receiving medical assistance.
Ozon, a Russian e-commerce company, confirmed the strike on its logistics complex in the Samara region, saying a fire broke out in its warehouse and that over 500 employees were evacuated from the site.
"Unfortunately, there were casualties. We will certainly provide them with all the necessary support," the statement said, adding that the warehouse has been closed indefinitely.
Separately, Krasnodar Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said civilian infrastructure and residential buildings in the southern region's Yeysky district came under attack, noting two children were killed and two others injured as a result.
Kondratyev said drone debris also fell on an enterprise located on the territory of the district's administrative center, and that firefighters are currently extinguishing a fire that consequently broke out.
Ukraine's General Staff claimed it struck and caused a fire at the Novokuibyshevsk oil refinery in the Samara region during an overnight attack, alleging that the facility's products are “used to supply the needs of the Russian Armed Forces.”
Moscow and Kyiv have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining that their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

Belarus to present project in St. Petersburg ahead of 85th anniversary of Siege of Leningrad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:04:00 UTC
16:04:00 KST

An archive photo
                    MOSCOW, 22 August (BelTA) – A unique Belarusian project – the requiem concert Every Third – will be presented in the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall in St. Petersburg on September 8 and 9, BelTA learned from the Standing Committee of the Union State of Belarus and Russia.
 
8 September 2026 marks the 85th anniversary of the start of the Siege of Leningrad – one of the most tragic pages of the Great Patriotic War of 1941-1945. On the Day of Remembrance for the Victims of the Siege of Leningrad, more than 100 Belarusian artists will take the stage at the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall to honor the memory of the victims and heroes of the Great Patriotic War and to speak out against the resurgence of Nazism.
 
The project Every Third presents an unusual fusion of concert, theatrical performance, and documentary narrative based on photographic and video documents related to various periods of the Great Patriotic War and the postwar era as well as figures and information refined by modern research. For a long time it was believed that one in four residents of Belarus perished during the war. However, data refined in recent years indicates that Belarus lost one in three of its population during the war.
 
The requiem concert will feature both well-known musical works from the Soviet era and new compositions by contemporary Belarusian composers: Valery Shmat, Anna Seluk, Yevgeny Oleinik, Anna Blagova, and others. The poetic foundation of the concert is Anatoly Vertinsky’s Requiem for Every Fourth. The requiem concert was created on the initiative of OOO Musical Media Company with the support of Belarus’ Defense Ministry and Culture Ministry. The project’s director is Vladislava Artyukovskaya, artistic director of the Youth Variety Theater. The script was written by Vladislava Artyukovskaya and Anna Seluk.
 
Between 2024 and 2026, the requiem concert Every Third was seen by thousands of viewers in Belarus and was performed twice each in Moscow and Kazan. In 2025, the project was awarded the Belarus president’s prize For Spiritual Revival for preserving historical memory and strengthening spiritual values.
 
During the days of the requiem concert the foyer of the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall will host thematic exhibitions that have become iconic for Belarus. The photo exhibition Fates Folded into a Triangle is based on the joint online project of the same name by BelTA and the Belarusian State Museum of History of the Great Patriotic War. The exhibition tells the stories of those who perished and those who survived the entire war through authentic personal letters, postcards, and greeting cards sent from the front lines to loved ones as well as archive photographs. Visitors will have a rare opportunity to write and fold a triangular letter themselves, following the front-line model.
 
The exhibition Partisans of Belarus – a joint project of the publishing house Belarus Today and the National Archive of Belarus – consists of an archival database of award sheets, personal files, and combat records of partisans. Using the interactive display of the Partisans of Belarus project, every visitor will be able to find a relative among the partisans and underground resistance fighters of Belarus and learn new facts about the partisan movement during the Great Patriotic War.
 
Performances of the requiem concert at the Oktyabrsky Grand Concert Hall are organized as part of the Year of St. Petersburg Culture with the support of the St. Petersburg government.

‘The worst part is the guilt’: the owners who fear dog food caused pets’ eye problems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:00:57 UTC
16:00:57 KST

“It’s been horrible – Chester developed sudden red and gunky eyes in May,” said Elizabeth, whose six-year-old cavachon “can’t open his eyes” on many days.
The 29-year-old civil servant is one of a number of people who contacted the Guardian because they are concerned about a potential link between a recalled dog food and their pet’s eye condition.
Elizabeth, who did not want to give her surname, said she and Chester had been to see vets more than 10 times in recent months, and they had all been “totally stumped”. Chester was initially treated for conjunctivitis, before Elizabeth was told it could be hay fever because of the lack of rain and high pollen count, and then the vet thought her pet might have an autoimmune disorder.
Then came the news this week that the dog food brand Years was recalling all its fresh meals after reports that a recipe change may have caused some animals to develop a condition called sudden bilateral dry eye. Also known as keratoconjunctivitis sicca, or KCS, dry eye occurs when a dog is unable to produce tears, making their eyes very sore. If left untreated, it can lead to sight loss.
The company said its investigation was “currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply”. Buckwheat was added to the company’s meals several months ago.
Years said it began receiving reports late last month of dogs experiencing sudden bilateral dry eye and, as of Tuesday evening, 192 customers had reported “potential, as yet unverified, eye issues”.
Chester had been fed on Years food for about 18 months, and Elizabeth said her vet had told her “they are fairly confident of a link” between the recalled dog food and Chester’s eye condition.
She said one theory was that there had been “a toxic chemical reaction” of some sort, adding that the vets “are unsure if just taking him off the food is going to be sufficient”.
Elizabeth, who lives in north London, said the vet trips and treatments had cost her hundreds of pounds “and Chester has been miserable for months”, adding: “I fear what long-term damage has been done and whether this is reversible.”
Marie Carter-Robb’s seven-year-old cavalier King Charles spaniel, Phoebe, was formally diagnosed with dry eye – the condition linked to the Years recall – during a visit to the vet on Thursday.
Phoebe is one of her three dogs. All three have eaten Years meals regularly as part of their diet since her subscription with the company began in April 2025, but Phoebe is the only one who has developed these eye problems.
“Her symptoms began in June,” said Carter-Robb, who is the editor of Pets Magazine. “She had never suffered from allergies before this summer and, until discovering the Years recall, I had assumed we were dealing with some sort of new allergy or an ordinary eye problem.”
Since then, Phoebe has had repeated vet examinations and treatment.
Speaking just before Thursday’s vet examination, Carter-Robb said that, having reviewed the Years recall information, “my vet has subsequently told me that the information is concerning and could suggest the food as a possible cause. He said that if the timing of the introduction of buckwheat correlates with the onset of Phoebe’s symptoms, he would be suspicious of it as the inciting cause.”
The emotional impact has been considerable, she added.
“The worst part is the guilt. I had absolutely no reason to suspect her food. I thought we were dealing with an allergy or an ordinary eye problem, and I carried on feeding Years to all three dogs. Finding the recall by chance at 11pm at night and suddenly looking back at everything Phoebe has been through was horrible.”
She said that as a first priority she wants Phoebe to recover fully, and then she wants to understand exactly what happened and whether the condition is linked to diet.
Phoebe has now been prescribed an eye ointment to treat the dry eye and will need treatment for at least the next few months, meaning examination and medication costs, Carter-Robb added.
Adele Chaplin, 50, who lives in Suffolk, said her eight-year-old greyhound, Lettuce, was first diagnosed with bilateral dry eye and eye ulcers in March this year. He has been eating Years dog food for “a good couple of years”.
Chaplin said: “He has undergone treatment from our local vet and was referred to a specialist vet ophthalmologist in April with the severe warning that he may well lose his eyes. The specialist vet has been seeing him since and, fortunately, his eyes are safe for now, but he still had zero tear production when he was last tested and vast amounts of discharge.
“Frankly, he’s miserable. His eyes itch and are painful; he rubs them against anything he can (sofas, legs, curtains), and now he has a gruelling daily regime of oils, cream and drops which are administered hourly. Add to that the sudden need to switch him to an entirely new food (something you are always recommended to avoid – you should always do that gradually) and he’s a very confused dog.”
Chaplin said that since the details of the recall had emerged, she had been in communication with the vet ophthalmologist, who told her to immediately stop feeding the Years food to Lettuce.
“I’m hopeful we’ll get a reduction in symptoms, but it’s too early to say,” she added.
“So far, this has cost thousands in treatment and medication, not to mention the travel back and forth to the specialist vet, which is an hour away from our home … Greyhounds live to about 14, so we could have another six years of treatment and medication costs, along with the increased insurance (which has already doubled as a result of this issue).”
A Years spokesperson said: “Years exists for one reason: to give people more time with their dogs, and the reports we have received are deeply upsetting to everyone here. As a result of the reports, we took the step to voluntarily recall our fresh meals because, while the evidence is still developing, we are not prepared to take chances with the dogs people trust us to feed.
“Our investigation is currently focused on potential contamination within a portion of buckwheat supply, rather than buckwheat itself, although a definitive cause has not yet been established.
“Independent laboratory testing is under way, alongside our wider investigation, to understand exactly what has happened. We want to give customers clear, evidence-based answers rather than speculate while that work continues, and we will communicate the findings as soon as the investigation is complete. In the meantime, customers are encouraged to visit www.years.com/pages/care for more detailed information.”

Subterranean salad: underground farmers seek solution to food crisis in disused UK mines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:00:56 UTC
16:00:56 KST

It has the vibe of a Bond villain’s underground lair but the workers in hi-vis and helmets aren’t weighing and packing hard drugs or parts for a death laser. It’s pak choi and lettuce.
More than 1,000 metres down, researchers in North Yorkshire have created the world’s deepest underground farm and are running trials for a project that could transform UK food production.
They want to use disused mines to grow crops, believing the stable environment and ability to use existing infrastructure could reduce the high energy costs associated with conventional vertical farming.
It’s a game-changing idea, but the team behind it need evidence that it will work – and the clock is ticking.
“We need to double food production by 2050 to support the world’s population,” says Jacob Nickles, a University of Sheffield research fellow and one of the project’s leaders. “That is the long and the short of it. Is it possible? Maybe if we start using mines.”
While Nickles and his colleagues might in previous years have been talking about the food crisis looming far in the future, this year’s extreme weather has shown it could be even closer.
In England, the dry, hot summer has led to crops dying and livestock using winter feed because there is no grass. “The crisis is less looming,” says Nickles, “it’s here … now.”
The underground farm operation has been set up in a science facility at Boulby mine, near Saltburn. The mine itself is a working one: the world’s only commercial producer of polyhalite, which is used as an agricultural fertiliser.
Drive through the ICL-UK mining operation and you will come to offices of the UK government-funded science facility, which hosts mind-blowing experiments – often involving the search for dark matter.
This week, the Guardian accompanied Nickles two-thirds of a mile (1.1km) underground as he and colleagues harvested pak choi and lettuce from vertical towers in the mine.
Getting there involves two detailed health and safety inductions, a change into bright orange hi-vis and an eight-minute descent in the original lift, constructed more than 50 years ago.
Once there, it feels strangely warm. “You’re experiencing a million times less radiation than you were 10 minutes ago. Does it feel nice?” asks the lab’s engagement officer, Jonny Gutteridge.
The experiments take place in the salty tunnels and also the air-conditioned lab facilities where, away from the extensive research going on, you feel you could be anywhere.
The kitchen kettle boils water to make tea, although it boils it hotter than it would on the surface. The toilet flushes, although it is the deepest flushing toilet in the UK.
The farming project is a partnership between Sheffield University and Farm Urban, a socially conscious food producer.
“We’re not here to replace conventional farming,” says Nickles. “We’re here to work alongside it and there are some things that are just uniquely better suited to controlled environment agriculture. Lettuce is a really good example.”
The aim is to gather the first real-world evidence that uniform, marketable crops can be grown underground.
During our visit to the site, there were mixed results. Some crops appeared spectacular, with lettuce bigger than a human head. Others looked less impressive but Nickles is consoled by the fact it is a technical, engineering issue rather than a scientific one.
“It’s sad when it doesn’t work … but I have to keep reminding myself that this is only the first growth.”
Overall, the 12-month study is going well and Nickles is optimistic about the possibility of samphire and tomatoes being trialled next.
As well as producing food at scale that can be sold and eaten, the project is about reusing the thousands of redundant mines that exist in the UK, creating new jobs and improving access to fresh produce in economically deprived areas.
It is backed by the government, with Patrick Vallance, the then science minister, last month saying: “Growing fresh food while using less energy and land – and being less reliant on changeable British weather – could strengthen food security across our country and protect our environment.”
The farm research is taking place in a facility that, its supporters say, should be better known.
“We are in a hole in North Yorkshire,” says Gutteridge. “We’re a small team of 20-25 people. But the science that goes on … In the past we’ve hosted the world’s most sensitive dark factor detector. We’re doing the world’s first deep underground quantum mechanics experiment. We should be so proud as a country to have a place like this.”
The lab’s full name is Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC) Boulby Underground Laboratory. It is the only place like it in the UK and is regarded as internationally important, one of only 12 in the world.
Among the work going on is Durham University’s Quasar project, which involves supercooling atoms and aims to “open a completely new frontier for quantum technology in the UK”. Nearby is Birmingham University’s Bond-sounding DarkSphere.
The success of the lab means expansion is already under way with stage one: a new cavern providing a factor 5 increase in space, scheduled to be completed in 2030.
Further expansion will happen if Boulby is chosen as the site for a project known as XLZD – the construction of a giant, next-generation liquid-xenon observatory to search for dark matter.
A decision could come next year. “We would love to host XLZD,” says Gutteridge. “The socio-economic benefits, the skills, the outreach, the education, the investment, the industry partnerships, the advanced manufacturing, all of it that would be coming inwards to the north east, to the UK. The impact of hosting a detector like that in the region would be phenomenal.”

‘I think in Lithuanian’: the Azerbaijani girl who aced the Lithuanian national exam
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

When Zeinab Mamedova arrived in Lithuania at the age of nine, she spoke no Lithuanian whatsoever. Within a few months, she was fluent. This summer, she scored 100% on Lithuania's school-leaving Lithuanian language and literature exam – and won a place to study medicine.
Zeinab was born in Almaty, Kazakhstan's largest city, to an Azerbaijani family. Her first language is Russian, the dominant language of Almaty; she also speaks Azerbaijani.
Lithuanian was acquired in a classroom, in the small northeastern Lithuanian town of Utena, where she moved with her mother in November 2015.
"I didn't know anything about Lithuania," she recalls. "A few days after we arrived, I started school."
Learning by pointing
The school her family chose – Krašuona middle school – had a teacher experienced in working with children who spoke little or no Lithuanian. This was a practical consideration, since nine-year-old Zeinab understood nothing of what was said around her, except in maths lessons.
But she was, by her own account, unbothered. "I was a child, so I didn't really worry about it. I just wanted to make friends. And since none of the other children spoke English or Russian, we tried to communicate in Lithuanian. My classmates taught me words – they'd hold up a pencil and say 'pieštukas'. That's how the language slowly stuck."
Her very first Lithuanian word, she says, was 'pienas' – milk – learned before she left Kazakhstan, from her stepfather, an Azerbaijani man living in Lithuania.
"I didn't even know where Lithuania was at that point. But I asked him how to say 'milk'."
She found Lithuanian difficult at first, particularly its complex system of grammatical case endings – Lithuanian is one of the most grammatically intricate languages in Europe, with seven noun cases.
"I never liked the locative case," she says, referring to a grammar case that turns the noun into a location. "At home I'd guess at how words should sound. But eventually it just settled in. Lithuanian became very beautiful to me."
Reading helped. Zeinab had been a keen reader since childhood, and worked her way through Lithuanian books as her vocabulary expanded. But Zeinab herself believes communicating with others in Lithuanian was most helpful in learning the language.
By the time she returned to school after her first summer holiday, she was speaking fluently and without an accent.
Her speech therapist, who had been assigned to help her when she first arrived, was astonished. "She told me: 'I think you're very bright, you should become a doctor. My daughter got into medicine, and Lithuania needs good doctors.'"
Zeinab laughed it off at the time, saying she would never pick medicine. Ten years later, she changed her mind.
"I couldn't let myself celebrate"
Scoring 100% on a national language exam is unusual enough for native speakers. For someone who arrived in the country speaking none of it, it is remarkable.
Lithuania's school-leaving exams – taken at the end of secondary school, roughly equivalent to A-levels in the UK – are graded on a national scale, with Lithuanian language and literature among the most demanding.
Zeinab sat five exams in total: Lithuanian, history, biology, chemistry and mathematics, plus an earlier international English qualification. Her results across all of them were high enough to secure a place at the Lithuanian University of Health Sciences in Kaunas.
But the Lithuanian result came at a cost. The exam requires a written essay based on readings drawn at random from a mandatory syllabus, meaning candidates have no way of knowing in advance which texts will come up, and must work through the entire list for the best result.
"In years 11 and 12, I didn't really live a normal life – I mostly just studied. I read every book on the syllabus. I watched every documentary. Even when I was eating, exercising, just walking around, I'd listen to audiobooks. I wanted to go into the exam knowing I'd have something to write about, whatever the question."
She even skipped her high school's end-of-year farewell ceremony – a significant occasion in Lithuanian school culture – because the Lithuanian exam was two days later.
"I couldn't let myself celebrate, knowing the exam was coming," she said.
Though initially hoping to get 100% due to her love for literature, after sitting the paper, she was convinced she'd done badly, and rang her teacher in distress.
"She wrote to comfort me. That night I barely slept," Zeinab recalls.
When results day came, she was visiting her father and grandparents in Kazakhstan. The results system initially wouldn't load – something she attributes to accessing it from abroad.
"After 15 minutes it finally opened and I saw 100. I couldn't believe it. I started screaming, grabbed everyone around me, and said: 'That's it. Thank God.'"
"I think in Lithuanian"
Zeinab's family speaks several languages at home – Azerbaijani, Russian and Lithuanian. When her younger brothers were born, the family made a deliberate shift. "We wanted them to learn Lithuanian well, so we started speaking Lithuanian at home too. My mum doesn't really speak it, but she understands a lot."
She is matter-of-fact about where her sense of identity now sits. "I think in Lithuanian," she says. "Ten years ago I would never have imagined things would turn out this way. When I arrived as a small child, my mum was even worried I might not learn the language and we'd have to move to Vilnius and put me in a Russian-language school. I'm very glad that didn't happen."
She is considering specialising in gynaecology – the field she associates most closely with life itself, she says – though nothing is fixed yet.
One last trip to the mountains
LRT.lt spoke to Zeinab on the last day of her summer visit to Kazakhstan, as she was preparing to return to Lithuania and move to Kaunas, a city she barely knows, to begin her degree.
That morning, she and her grandmother had driven to the mountains outside Almaty. "We are mountain people. Even though we live in Kazakhstan, we are Azerbaijani, and Azerbaijan is deeply connected to the Caucasus mountains. Mountains have always been part of our culture. If we have nothing to do, we just get in the car and drive up."
One of the biggest differences between her old life and her new one, she says, is simply the landscape: Lithuania is flat. "When I first arrived, that felt very strange."
She will miss Kazakhstan, she admits – but she already misses Lithuania more. "I miss Utena. I miss home." Starting university in an unfamiliar city, she says, feels both daunting and overdue. "School is behind me now. Twelve years is a very long time. I'm ready for something new."

Economic Watch: Chinese robotics fair draws crowds as industry brews innovation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
14:55:17 CST
15:55:17 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Unitree Robotics' blockbuster IPO, the bustling World Robot Conference (WRC), and the upcoming World Humanoid Robot Games, amount to a string of high-profile events which have combined to make this week a "super week" for Chinese robotics.
Underpinning these events is a clear trend: China is swiftly becoming a global epicenter of robotics innovation, which is poised to reshape the way products are manufactured and the way people live.
The numbers confirm China's significant rise in robotics. Data from the country's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology show that revenue of industrial enterprises above designated size in China's robotics sector had exceeded 300 billion yuan (about 44.24 billion U.S. dollars) in 2025, with an average annual growth rate of more than 20 percent over the past five years.
Also, a report by California-based research firm Smart Analytics Global indicates that global humanoid robot shipments totaled approximately 19,100 units in the first half of 2026, with Chinese-made units accounting for over 97 percent of the total.
More broadly, exports of industrial robots increased 13.2 percent in the January-July period, while shipments of surgical robots surged 3.3-fold year on year in the first half of 2026.
Robots, AI products and innovative drugs are three new drivers of China's export growth, according to Science and Technology Minister Yin Hejun.
This momentum has played out at this year's WRC, which is being held in a southeastern technology hub in Beijing.
On weekday mornings, traffic ground to a halt for kilometers around the WRC exhibition hall, forcing the organizers to issue daily "travel advisories," a task that speaks volumes about the sector's red-hot vitality in China. Inside the venue, crowds are so dense they rival the throngs at CES in Las Vegas.
WRC exhibitors this year have topped 300, up 69 percent from 2025, with the event featuring over 3,000 products, and roughly 300 making their debuts. Additionally, many are powered by large AI models, cloud computing and big data.
China's vast and sophisticated manufacturing sector is providing a massive testing ground for embodied AI technologies, which are now being deployed on a large scale in factories and training facilities.
According to an industry research report, by June this year, China had launched over 70 training grounds for robots, with another 46 either under construction or in the planning pipeline.
"This week's IPO is just the start of the journey," said Aron Kisdi, managing director of Autodiscovery and Unitree Robotics' U.K. distributor, at the company's WRC booth. Unitree Robotics, based in Hangzhou in east China, went public on China's A-share market on Wednesday, the same day the WRC opened, and its shares skyrocketed 629.44 percent to open at 1,100 yuan.
"It signals that the time in the lab is nearing an end, and we're pushing robots into the real world," Kisdi explained.
On the exhibition floor at the WRC, many booths are displaying robots operating in real-world work scenarios. A logistics robot sorts parcels at a rate of more than 1,000 items per hour, while nearby, a pair of dexterous robotic hands smoothly folds a cardboard sheet into a packaging box.
At UBTECH's display zone, robots perform automated loading and unloading of automotive sheet metal parts with zero human oversight, building on earlier trials at several car plants. Chinese robotics firms have, notably, already put robots into factories to test their capability of doing more sophisticated jobs beyond just basic handling.
Elsewhere at the show, automakers like Xiaomi feature their own humanoid robots, underscoring how industry demand is fueling robotics innovation.
The bustling expo floor in Beijing also features robots designed for emotional companionship, housework, convenience-store retail and coffee brewing, which can tap into China's massive consumer market, the world's second-largest in terms of commodity consumption for more than 10 consecutive years.
"Robots are no longer only about flashy concepts and specs. They're increasingly focused on tackling real-life challenges," said Ren Jingwei, a manager at Zhiyuan Research Institute in Hangzhou.
Also, this year's WRC fair is no longer just for curious onlookers. Industry players up and down the supply chain are busy exchanging business cards and phone numbers there in bids to forge new partnerships.
One noteworthy shift this year is the considerable presence of dexterous-hand sensor makers, joint module suppliers and chip manufacturers at the WRC. These component suppliers, once supporters behind finished robots, have now also taken center stage in their own niche sectors -- a sign that China's robotics industry is maturing into a more sophisticated ecosystem.
Humanoid robots could spur investment across precision transmission, smart sensors, AI chips and intelligent software, generating a huge market from R&D to after-sales service, said Xu Xiaolan from the Chinese Institute of Electronics.
To many attendees, Beijing's robot show points to an upcoming transformative change in the industry. The "ChatGPT moment" for embodied AI will come in two to three years under an optimistic outlook, or within five to ten years at the latest, said Wang Xingxing, Unitree Robotics founder and CEO, when speaking at a WRC forum. ■

TOKYO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- The torch relay for next month's Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games began Saturday at Nagoya Castle, with three-time Olympic wrestling champion Saori Yoshida carrying the flame on its opening leg.
The official Games flame was formed shortly before the relay by combining three fires collected in Tokyo, Hiroshima and Nagoya. Former Japan football star Homare Sawa and retired tennis player Kimiko Date brought the fires kindled at Tokyo's National Stadium on August 18 and in Hiroshima two days later.
Takeru Goto, a member of Japanese boy band INI and an official ambassador for the Games, kindled the Nagoya fire with a concave mirror before the three fires were merged.
Yoshida, who competed at four Asian Games and won gold, said the continental event holds special memories for her.
"I hope the feelings of every torchbearer will give strength to the athletes competing at the Games," she said before setting off from the castle.
The flame was then handed to local torchbearers and carried through central Nagoya. Saturday's route included Meijo Park, Hisaya-odori Park, the Oasis 21 complex and the Nakagawa Canal. The flame will be divided after the opening-day relay and carried along two routes across Aichi Prefecture.
Around 1,000 torchbearers, including members of the public and prominent figures, will carry the flame through 40 local government areas and a number of schools before it arrives at Nagoya City Mizuho Park Athletic Stadium on September 19 for the Games' opening ceremony.
Japan will host the Asian Games for the third time, following Tokyo in 1958 and Hiroshima in 1994.
The 20th Asian Games will be held from September 19 to October 4, featuring 43 sports and athletes from 45 countries and regions across Asia. ■

Its editor-in-chief, Alexandra Nazarova, said many requests are now urgent, with people seeking “to have time to leave before September-October.”

In search of peace
The most popular destinations for relocation were Serbia, Armenia and Georgia, where tens of thousands of Russians have flocked in recent days.

She described the trend as a possible new wave of emigration, although many people are still “testing the waters” rather than leaving immediately.
Mobilization this fall?

Japan's FY 2027 budget requests may exceed 130 trln yen, hitting new record high
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
14:54:51 CST
15:54:51 KST

TOKYO, Aug. 22 (Xinhua) -- Budget requests from Japanese government ministries and agencies for fiscal 2027 are expected to exceed 130 trillion yen (around 818 billion U.S. dollars), a significant increase from the current fiscal year's initial budget of 122.31 trillion yen, Kyodo News reported on Friday.
The report said that the actual budget could rise further when finalized at the end of this year, as spending for many items is yet to be determined.
Among the requests, the Ministry of Defense plans to seek a record of about 8.9 trillion yen. Previous media reports said key spending areas will include procuring large numbers of interceptor drones, introducing artificial intelligence into command-and-control systems, and further deploying long-range missiles with what Japan calls "counterstrike capabilities."
Expenditures on social security, such as pensions and medical costs, are expected to rise by around 390 billion yen due to the country's continued aging of the population.
Ministries and agencies are required to submit their budget requests for fiscal 2027, which runs from April 2027 to March 2028, by the end of this month, after which the Ministry of Finance will compile the budget by the end of the year.
It is worth noting that the Japanese government has previously imposed caps on budget requests to control the scale of spending. This time, however, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's government launched a major budget drafting reform by not setting limits on some of the investment projects it is promoting. This is seen as a major factor behind the unusually large increase in overall budget requests.
The report said that with the Japanese government forecasting tax revenue of about 83 trillion yen for fiscal 2026, budget requests topping 130 trillion yen will likely lead to new debt issuance, further straining the debt-ridden country's fiscal health.
Amid growing concerns over the country's deteriorating fiscal situation, Japanese government bond yields have continued to rise recently, increasing the government's debt-servicing burden and putting further pressure on public finances. (1 yen equals 0.0063 U.S. dollars) ■

MANNHEIM, Germany (AP) — A German Cup match between Waldhof Mannheim and Kaiserslautern was halted for about half an hour on Friday as fans threw fireworks and other objects and invaded the pitch.
The match was tied at 0-0 and heading into extra time when fans at both ends of the ground threw flares and objects, narrowly missing some of the players as they ran from the field.
Some Mannheim supporters made it on to the pitch before officers in riot gear and mounted police fanned out to push them back.

Beyblade battles drive up sales at Hong Kong malls, but how long will the trend last?
Struggling to attract patrons, shopping centres are embracing resurgent popularity of Japanese toy, drawing fans who stay and spend – at least for now
The sharp clatter of spinning metal tops, cheers, sighs of frustration and shouts of “three, two, one … Go shoot!” echo across a shopping centre in Hong Kong’s New Territories on a weekday.
In shops across Tuen Mun Town Plaza, children, teens and young adults hunch over small plastic battle arenas, unleashing their tops into the “Beystadiums” in head-to-head competitions where the top that remains spinning the longest wins.
The toy popularised by Japanese anime in the early 2000s made a comeback in Hong Kong and elsewhere in Asia early this year, and gatherings are attracting crowds of local players eager to put their models to the test.
Spotting the economic potential behind the hobby, shopping centre operators across Hong Kong are converting open spaces into free battle zones to drive up foot traffic and sales.
Tuen Mun Town Plaza went a step further by scaling up the concept into a mall-wide strategy ahead of a major Beyblade tournament in August, encouraging shop operators to take part in the game and offer discounts to shoppers who present their tops.
“The strategy is about how a tenant can engage with customers through a shared interest, instead of directly selling to them,” said Bella Chhoa Peck-lim, chief commercial officer of Sino Group, which owns the plaza.
“It’s a soft-selling approach that allows staff and shoppers to start a conversation, drawing people into the store before making a sales pitch.”

Excavations to resume at Antalya’s ancient city of Rhodiapolis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:47:51 UTC
15:47:51 KST

Excavation work at the ancient city of Rhodiapolis in Antalya’s Kumluca district is scheduled to resume next year, following a period of suspension, as efforts continue to uncover and preserve the site’s archaeological heritage.
Kumluca District Governor Bahadır Güneş recently visited the ancient city with a delegation, describing Rhodiapolis as “a window into Kumluca’s history.” Excavations at the site began in 2006 and have since brought much of the ancient settlement to light.
Beste Tomay, an archaeology faculty member at Adıyaman University who advises the excavation project, said Rhodiapolis holds an important place among the ancient cities of Lycia, both historically and culturally.
Tomay said preparations are being carried out this year, including field surveys, assessments of previous excavation work and an inventory of artifacts held in storage. Full excavation activities are expected to resume next year under the coordination of the excavation leadership.
The site contains remains spanning the Lycian and Byzantine periods, including a theater, bathhouse, agora, temples, a church, cisterns and monumental tombs. Archaeologists believe further excavation could reveal additional elements of the ancient settlement and deepen understanding of the region’s cultural history.
Tomay said bringing the entire city to light would make a significant contribution to Kumluca’s historical and cultural profile, while strengthening the connection between the district and its ancient past.

Iran military shifting from defensive to offensive posture: army spokesperson
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:47:27 UTC
15:47:27 KST

The Iranian army has shifted its military doctrine from a “defensive to an offensive” posture, an army spokesperson said on Saturday, citing lessons from the country’s recent wars.
Brigadier General Mohammad Akraminia told state news agency IRNA that the shift had taken place gradually during what he described as the 12-day and 40-day wars.
“Our country’s military doctrine was defensive in the past, but gradually during these two wars, we witnessed the military doctrine moving from a defensive posture toward an offensive one,” Akraminia said.
He said the change was reflected in faster and broader responses to attacks as well as preemptive operations.
Bounty hunt for US troops
Akraminia said the army had also devised a plan offering rewards for killing or capturing US troops in the event of a ground incursion into Iranian territory.
Under the plan, members of the armed forces or civilians legally possessing hunting weapons would receive 5 billion tomans, about $26,000, for killing or capturing US troops entering Iran, he said.
The reward would be doubled to 10 billion tomans, about $53,000, if the action were carried out by a woman, Akraminia added.
He said the army would also purchase the weapon used for twice its value, preserve it in a military museum under the owner’s name and provide the individual with a similar replacement weapon.
Iran points to regional shift
Akraminia also claimed that US influence in the region had declined sharply, pointing to what he described as a defence and security mechanism established independently of Washington by Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and Pakistan.
He said that regardless of its future effectiveness, the mechanism demonstrated what he described as a decline in the US position in the region.
Akraminia described it as the first regional defence and security mechanism established without US participation.

Mayawati, Yogi Aditynath, Akhilesh Yadav and other to get bulletproof jackets ahead of Assembly polls 2027
NEW DELHI: Fifty-two leaders in Uttar Pradesh, including chief minister Yogi Adityanath, Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav and BSP chief Mayawati, have been provided bulletproof jackets as part of security arrangements ahead of the 2027 assembly elections, news agency ANI reported quoting sources on Saturday.Eleven state government ministers are also among those provided the jackets, including Sanjay Nishad, Nand Gopal Gupta "Nandi" and Om Prakash Rajbhar. BJP leader Aparna Yadav is also on the list, news agency ANI reported quoting sources.Sources said the bulletproof jackets cost around Rs 10 lakh each. Eight leaders received the jackets in the first phase, while 44 were provided them in the second phase.Security arrangements have also been extended to several other BJP leaders, including Swatantra Dev Singh, Jaiveer Singh and Mahendra Singh, news agency ANI reported quoting sources.In addition, 98 leaders and prominent individuals in Uttar Pradesh will be provided different categories of security, sources told ANI.The move comes ahead of the Uttar Pradesh assembly elections scheduled for 2027, with political parties stepping up preparations in the state.
The BJP has appointed general secretary Vinod Tawde as its Uttar Pradesh election in-charge, bringing an experienced organisational leader into the party's preparations for the crucial state polls.
Jagdish Ishwarbhai Patel has been appointed as the co-in-charge of Uttar Pradesh.Sources said the BJP is focusing on strengthening its social and caste equations in Uttar Pradesh, with leaders from Other Backward Classes and minority communities being given greater representation in organisational appointments.The party has also begun conducting surveys across Assembly constituencies to assess its organisational strength, potential candidates and local issues that could influence the 2027 election.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,475,270 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:41:13 UTC
15:41:13 KST

Russia has lost around 1,475,270 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 22.
The figure includes 1,240 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,292 tanks, 25,176 armored combat vehicles, 137,804 vehicles and fuel tanks, 48,382 artillery systems, 2,054 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,584 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 474,641 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,344 unmanned ground systems, 5,049 cruise missiles, 35 ships and boats, two submarines, and 4,565 pieces of special equipment.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs).
The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Nemrut’s ancient statues undergo nanolime treatment for preservation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:37 UTC
15:38:37 KST

Conservation work continues at Nemrut Mountain, a UNESCO World Heritage Site in southeastern Türkiye, where experts are using nanotechnology to protect its monumental ancient statues from further deterioration.
The restoration and conservation program, launched in 2022 to preserve the site’s colossal sculptures for future generations, focuses in part on sealing fine cracks in the stone with nanolime. The material is injected into cracks to prevent water from penetrating the sculptures and accelerating their deterioration.
Ayşe Ebru Çorbacı, director of the Gaziantep Regional Restoration and Conservation Laboratory, said teams are currently working on the head of Kommagene Tyche and the statue of Zeus Oromandes on the site’s western terrace.
The nanolime treatment is designed to fill microscopic cracks and strengthen vulnerable sections of the sculptures, she said, noting that earlier conservation work had produced positive results.
“2022 works produced results,” Çorbacı said, adding that the next phase began in 2025. During that campaign, conservation teams reinforced the head of King Antiochos and eagle heads on both the eastern and western terraces. This year, work has shifted to the heads of Kommagene Tyche and Zeus.
The monumental statues are part of the sanctuary built by the Kingdom of Commagene in the first century B.C. at the summit of Nemrut Mountain. The site, located at an altitude of about 2,150 meters, is known for its enormous stone figures representing deities and rulers, as well as its monumental eastern and western terraces.
Mehmet Alkan, director of the Adıyaman Museum, said the conservation project was essential to ensuring that the sculptures, which have survived for more than 2,000 years, remain intact for future generations.
“Restoration and conservation works at Nemrut Mountain resumed in 2026 with the support of the Culture and Tourism Ministry,” Alkan said, adding that the work is being carried out by specialists from the Gaziantep Regional Restoration and Conservation Laboratory.
The long-term effort reflects the challenges of preserving Nemrut’s sculptures in an exposed mountain environment, where water infiltration and weathering can gradually weaken the ancient stone. The conservation teams are therefore seeking to reinforce the statues while minimizing intervention and preserving their historic fabric.

In search of Longjing: The hands behind China’s most revered green tea
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-22
06:38:22 UTC
15:38:22 KST

I feel as though I am in a dream. I am standing in the very place where my favourite green tea in the world is grown. Yet Longjing goes far beyond my own personal passion; it is one of China’s most revered teas and among the world’s most prized green teas. For three days, I stayed in an ancient village tucked among Hangzhou’s tea-covered hills, where Buddhist monasteries and tea gardens have existed side by side for centuries. Each morning, when I opened my door, there was no hotel corridor waiting for me, but a stone village path, bamboo groves, tea gardens and people making their way towards the temples.
This is Amanfayun. Set along a pilgrimage route formed by seven ancient Buddhist temples, it is an extraordinary place where 46 old village buildings, some more than a century old, have been transformed into places to stay. It is not easy to tell where the hotel begins and the village ends. Rather than constructing a new and ostentatious world, Amanfayun seems to have quietly settled into the one that was already here. Walking along stone paths, through bamboo groves and shaded courtyards, you feel less like a guest in a large hotel operation and more like a temporary resident of the village. Perhaps Amanfayun’s greatest achievement is that, rather than drawing attention to itself, it makes you notice the place around it.
In China, tea is not simply a leaf steeped in hot water; it belongs to a vast culture in which agriculture, craftsmanship, history, philosophy and everyday life intersect. During the Qing Dynasty, Emperor Qianlong visited the place we know today as Longjing Village and granted imperial status to 18 tea bushes in front of Hu Gong Temple. Those 18 bushes remain among Longjing’s most powerful symbols today. The prestige that once carried this tea all the way to the imperial table continues, centuries later, to shape its value.
One of the most striking things here is that tea does not exist as an agricultural product separate from village life. Families sell tea outside their homes, meticulously ordered rows of tea bushes cover almost every hillside, and people carry glass cups of Longjing with them throughout the day. Even the waffle served at breakfast comes flavoured with Longjing.
So what makes Longjing so precious? To begin with, its production area is extremely limited. The leaves are picked by hand while still very young in spring, and it is after this that the craftsmanship defining the tea’s character truly begins. In traditional, high-quality Longjing production, the leaves are hand-roasted in heated, wok-like pans. The master presses, lifts, shakes and turns the leaves with the palm of the hand. This is far more than a drying process; it is a craft that gives Longjing its flat, slender and almost flawless form.
The most prized teas are made from the youngest leaves harvested early in spring. The picking season is brief and quantities are extremely limited. This scarcity partly explains reports over the years of exceptional batches of Longjing commanding prices per kilogram higher than gold. The precise day of harvest is critical. Pick a leaf a day too early and it may not be fully developed; a day too late and it may already have lost some of its delicacy. With Longjing, a window of just a few days can determine both the character and the value of a tea.
And then there are the Longjing masters. These are the people who determine the fate of the tea with their hands in a matter of minutes. They read the heat not through a thermometer, but through the memory of their palms. Over years, they learn exactly when the leaf has lost enough moisture, when it needs to be pressed and when it must leave the pan. Give the same fresh leaves to two different masters and you will not end up with precisely the same tea. That is the essence of their craft.
Because my journey fell in August, I should not, in fact, have had any chance of seeing Longjing being produced. The harvest and production take place in spring. Amanfayun, however, arranged something I will not forget. They invited the local tea master who produces tea from their own gardens especially for me and sourced fresh tea leaves so that he could give a small production demonstration. Within minutes, the entire room was filled with the scent of warm leaves, toasted nuts and that unmistakable Longjing aroma. After eight years of reading about, tasting and talking about this tea, I was finally watching it take shape right in front of me. Aman’s own approach to experiencing this landscape includes walking through bamboo forests and tea fields to Longjing Village and, during spring, witnessing local people harvesting and pan-roasting the leaves as a way of understanding this region.
In fact, this was far more than a small gesture; it was a revealing example of where Aman looks for luxury. For me, luxury that day was not the size of my room, the marble used in it or the number of people attending to me. It was making something I could not possibly have witnessed in August possible for a few hours, simply because they had genuinely listened to why I was there. That, to me, is personalized service: Before anticipating what a guest might want, understanding why that guest has come in the first place. This is also where Aman’s particular skill becomes apparent: Rather than using the culture of a destination as decoration, it attempts to become part of it. Perhaps this is why Aman properties in different corners of the world do not feel like replicas of one another, but rather like different geographical expressions of the same idea. Among the core values the brand says it continues to protect are privacy, service, architecture sensitive to its surroundings and pioneering locations.
The same approach can be felt in the kitchen. The summer menu at Steam House foregrounds produce from the lakes and waterways of the Jiangnan region, including Taihu prawns marinated in Shaoxing yellow wine. The continuation of age-old cooking methods in the semi-open kitchen feels like an extension of the same philosophy. Aman itself speaks of architecture that remains true to its destination and of experiences shaped by culture, community and nature. At Amanfayun, there is little need to read the theory; you need only look around.
Perhaps what truly distinguishes Amanfayun is the sense that it positions itself not as the owner of this village, but as one of its temporary custodians. The character of the old village houses has been preserved; the stone paths continue along their old course; the surrounding temples, tea gardens and village life are not a stage constructed behind the hotel, but life itself. This idea of seasonality extends all the way to the spa. Traditional Chinese Medicine holds that the body should be supported in accordance with nature’s rhythms; summer is believed to place greater demands on the heart, and treatments therefore focus on supporting circulation and restoring balance. You encounter a similar philosophy in the kitchen, in the tea and in the gardens: rather than resisting the season, you move with it. In the morning, you might pass a Buddhist monk, step into a tea garden a few minutes later and then have breakfast inside a centuries-old building. And gradually, you understand more clearly that Longjing is not simply a tea. Perhaps luxury can be exactly this: not making a place resemble you when you arrive, but allowing it, for a while, to bring you closer to itself.
